# TO GOD THE BEST
# AND GREATEST, THE INCOMPREHENSIBLE
# CREATOR OF MAN,
### FOR HIS IMMENSE BENEVOLENCE
### AND MERCY
### TOWARD HIM.

#### A PRAYER OF THANKSGIVING.

[Large decorative initial O] MNIPOTENT founder of all things, my incomparable creator, who out of your remarkable kindness toward man created him with such excellence and sublimity, *that* <margin>a Aristotle, Ethics, Book 2</margin> *you established him, in a certain way, as the end of all things:* <margin>b Theological Resolutions, Volume 2, part 2, page 3, question 1</margin> *indeed, by granting him reason, you made him meet with the Angels; by attributing sensitive powers, you made him equal to the beasts; by providing natural forces, you made him like the plants; and by bestowing a body, you made him agree with inanimate things:* <margin>c Aristotle, Politics, Book 3</margin> *nay, truly, you willed to create this provident, sagacious, acute, and mindful animal, full of reason and counsel, in an admirable condition,* <margin>d Hermes Trismegistus, Asclepius 4</margin> <note>Hermes Trismegistus is the legendary figure to whom the Hermetica, a body of Egyptian-Greek wisdom texts, are attributed.</note> *and you so tempered his lofty nature that you rendered it known to the heavenly inhabitants themselves and as close as possible to the Angels:* <margin>e Hermes Trismegistus, Asclepius 4</margin> *whose whole being you conformed from soul and body—that is, from an eternal and a mortal disposition—so that the animal thus affected by your creation might be able to satisfy both of its origins: to wonder at heavenly things and adore you (eternal God) <note>original: "Elohim"</note> and to inhabit and govern earthly things, so that he may love and care for those things which are below, and he himself may be loved and cared for by you and your superior ministers, namely the Angels:* <margin>f Hermes Trismegistus, Pymander 4 and Asclepius 3</margin> *likewise, so that he himself may cultivate the earth, be mixed with the elements by his swiftness, descend into the depths of the sea by the sharpness of his mind, and that all things may shine openly and clearly for him, insofar as no gloom of the air can confound the intention of his soul, nor the density of the earth hinder his works, nor the deep altitude of the water take away his view:* I, your man, your creature, glorified and exalted by the immense dignity and nobility of his creator, cry out through the fire, through the air, through the earth, through the heaven, through the universal spirit, through the abyss, and through the created things of the world:

6 ->PRAYER<-

You alone, You the Thrice-Greatest, O JEHOVAH, are God, whose unutterable name be blessed forever. <note>original: "nomen ineffabile" - referring to the Tetragrammaton, the four-letter name of God considered too sacred to pronounce in Jewish tradition.</note>

Therefore, your human—your creature, adorned by a ray of your unspeakable splendor—renders immortal and most righteous thanks to You (O Lord of highest, eternal, and infinite kindness), with sacrifices of the soul and heart preceding most humble adoration, on account of your immense mercy and goodness toward him: <margin>g Genesis 1 & 5</margin> because You, the Daedalian <note>A reference to Daedalus, the mythical Greek craftsman; here meaning "skillful" or "masterful."</note> founder of things, <margin>h Hermes Trismegistus</margin> prepared, disposed, and formed him according to the sacrosanct image of your very self, and according to the pattern and likeness of the most lively and noble world-machine <note>original: "mundique tuae machinae" - a common Renaissance metaphor for the universe as a perfectly ordered mechanism.</note> of yours, as much the visible as the intelligible; and You led him to the summit or happy conclusion: <margin>i Psalm 119:6; k Wisdom 9:2</margin> indeed, with your own hands <margin>l Job 7:10</margin> You fitted him as if from clay in his creation, and by your supersubstantial wisdom You so perfected him <margin>m Genesis 6:26</margin> that he might rule over the other creatures which You brought forth into the world: namely the fish of the sea, the birds of the heavens, the cattle of the whole earth, and all the creeping things of the same. <margin>n Genesis 9:2</margin> So it is that by your irrevocable ordinance, all the beasts of the earth and all the winged creatures of the air, and all the aquatic things of the sea, struck by fear of him, have been delivered into his hands; for You established him as a living being full of perfection, commanding all things, and even far excelling the other animals in virtue. <margin>o Job 33:4</margin> For your spirit, O mighty God, made him, and your almighty breath or inspiration gave him life, and in his creation You adorned him with a divine mind above all other animals: <margin>p Psalm 8:5</margin> Indeed, You were so mindful and solicitous of him that You made him a little lower than the Angels themselves, and crowned him with glory and honor, and subjected the works of your hands to his dominion, and placed all things under his feet; <margin>q Job 7:20</margin> and from the beginning You did not disdain to be his guardian, <margin>r Psalm 37:11</margin> firmly establishing his steps (delighting in his way) and bringing it about that when he falls he is not cast down, because You, JEHOVAH, uphold his hand; <margin>s Job 14:12</margin> likewise You number his steps, but mercifully spare him his sins; <margin>t Job 10:12</margin> You exercise kindness toward him with life, and your visitation preserves his spirit: <margin>u Hermes Trismegistus, Asclepius 6</margin>

Since, therefore, You, who are the highest and first Lord of eternity, out of your infinite favor toward your creatures, established the world or "Macrocosm" as the second Lord; and man or "Microcosm" as the third; <note>The "Macrocosm" is the great world (the universe), and the "Microcosm" is the little world (man), reflecting the whole.</note> inasmuch as You, O admirable Archetype, sitting above the highest peaks of the entire world in dignity and unexplainable brightness, fashioned them according to your own model and pattern: let the Macrocosm especially trumpet forth vast and due sounds in your praise, famous proclamations, and symphonic voices; and let it narrate your distinguished glory and the dignity of its creator through living actions; let its thunders re-echo your sacrosanct will with a mouth stupendous and terrible (full of divine Majesty), and let it proclaim your encomium and praise throughout the entire world like the exerted trumpets of your omnipotence...

<summary>A prayerful oration celebrating the creation of man (the Microcosm) in the image of God and the Universe (the Macrocosm), emphasizing man's dominion over nature and God's providential care.</summary>
<keywords>Jehovah, Macrocosm, Microcosm, Hermes Trismegistus, creation, divine image, providence, dignity of man</keywords>

Though you are exalted, yet you look upon the lowly; although you are high, you know from afar <margin>Psalm 139:1 <note>original: "Pf. 139 1."</note></margin>: For you have tested man, and you know his sitting down and his rising up, and you perceive his thoughts from afar; you observe his path and his lying down, and you are acquainted with all his ways. <margin>Wisdom 1:6 <note>original: "Sap 1. 6."</note></margin> For you are a witness of the reins <note>The "reins" or kidneys were historically considered the seat of deep emotion and sincerity.</note>, and a true observer of his heart and a hearer of his tongue; <margin>Psalm 134:3 <note>original: "Pf 134. 3."</note></margin> indeed, even when there was not yet a word on the tongue, you knew it all entirely. <margin>Psalm 139:7</margin> <margin>Job 28:11</margin> For nothing can be hidden from you, insofar as your eye sees whatever exists and brings hidden things to light; <margin>Joshua 2:11</margin> since you, in the heavens above and on the earth below, know the harlot, the innkeeper, and the peasant. Therefore, may you be adorned and elevated with perpetual praises, O most wise and most vigilant God, to whom all things are revealed, and from whom nothing can be hidden or covered. Similarly, <margin>Wisdom 9:13</margin> who can know or comprehend the secret of your most profound counsel, since the reasonings of mortals are timid and their thoughts unstable? <margin>Deuteronomy 29:29</margin> Therefore, although your manifest works are known to us and to our children, your hidden mysteries are revealed to no one; it is enough, therefore, for man to know this: namely, <margin>Proverbs 19:21</margin> that your counsel is stable and permanent. You are therefore to be feared and held in awe, O Jehovah, since mortals are not permitted to reach the sanctuary of your secret counsel. Can anyone, by any inquiry of reason, search out or know your beginning or origin, since you, insofar as you exist as the author of all things, existed before all things? <margin>Psalm 90:2 & 22:4</margin> Since you, existing from eternity, were before the beginning of the world: You undoubtedly had no beginning, insofar as you stood as the beginning of the beginning; <margin>Exodus 15:18</margin> and having no end, you shall reign forever and ever. From which we gather that you are the eternity of the world, of man, and of all things: which is also proved in this, that <margin>Ecclesiastes 3:14</margin> whatever you do, it shall remain forever; which indeed could not happen unless you were eternal. From this, therefore, we perceive that you lack beginning and end, and that consequently you sit upon the highest throne of eternity, above the peak and summit of the highest heaven of heavens, with triumphant victory, infinite joy, and perpetual justice and equity; may your name be blessed with most illustrious praises, and celebrated and sublimated with everlasting honor, you who alone with the Son and your Spirit are from eternity to eternity without beginning and end. Furthermore, it will be hard and difficult to depict the perfection of your glory in a worthy manner and measure, <margin>Exodus 33:20</margin> since you yourself would not make your internal glory visible to your servant Moses; for no one can see it while he lives. And yet we have received from your Holy Scriptures <margin>Exodus 33:22 & 23</margin> that your external glory appeared to some chosen ones; for although the glory of your face or essence was hidden from Moses from the front, yet he saw it with his eyes from the back

I implore you, let my soul be carried on golden wings in your crystalline spirit, and let me die in the fullness of balsamic grace in Christ and in your true word; so that at last, by the alacrity of your most holy Spirit, I may rise again to you—the first and only Unity of the created number <note>The author uses Pythagorean/Neoplatonic language here, viewing God as the "Monad" or "One" from which all numbers and things originate</note>, that is, the Principle from which my soul was first infused from simplicity into the multitude of matter—to the unspeakable unity and simplicity of your glory, once the resurrection is complete. Be to me, O GOD, I pray, a rock, a shield, and a fortress by your power and strength, so that my enemies may perceive that I am covered, preserved, and happily breathing under the shadow of your wings. Grant that I may be snatched up by the ray of your inexplicable majesty toward the true meditation of higher things, and that lower things may be held as most vile by my soul. Grant, I say, that the memory of your glory may be perpetually retained by my spirit in merited honor and just reverence and fear, and be engraved upon it in living characters. May your ineffable and most holy name be venerable and praiseworthy to me forever; be gracious and favorable to me in your justice. May your providence direct and govern me in my ways, while I adore your counsel with admiration, preach eternity to the world, extol the incomprehensible riches of your glory, and declare the perfection of truth to the entire orb of the earth. Make me capable of your science and doctrine <term>Scientia: here meaning divine knowledge or certain understanding</term>, so that I, illustrated by your most holy light and well-acquainted with myself, may be able to revere you in a manner accepted, pleasing, and decent to you; to admire your height; to most diligently search out the beauty of the nobility and sublimity of your place and seat with fitting meditation; to meditate on the mystery of infinity in ecstasy; to promulgate the inscrutable depth of wisdom to all people as if with the blast of a trumpet; to acknowledge the permanent will of your omnipotence; and finally, to sing your everlasting praise and honor—which shall be ended by no age—in a voice in unison with the whole world, to report it with the harmony of the lyre, to elevate it with triumphal glory, and to confidently entrust it to the monuments of immortal fame and perpetual letters that shall be erased by no century. Nor shall I, a son of man, ever cease to cry out with open mouth through the most holy rays of my mind, through the subtle and empyrean <note>The "empyrean" refers to the highest heaven, characterized by pure fire and light</note> spirits of intellect and reason, through the lucid substance of the vital soul and its ethereal liquid, and through the air which is the receptacle of every portion of my internal man, through fire, through water, and through earth—from which the composition of my muddy body is tempered—through my internal self, through my external self, and through my whole being, I cry, I say, and proclaim with a loud voice: YOU ALONE ARE THE GREATEST, O JEHOVAH, YOU ARE GOD, who made heaven and earth, the world and man, and benevolently fashioned him after your own image; may your name be blessed forever.

Your creature, most happy in the goodness of your light.

    In the latter section, the technical history of the Microcosm is treated, which consists of these seven sciences:

        Geomancy, which is the art of the soul's divination.

I beseech you, therefore, to be favorable and well-disposed toward this my Microcosmic work, so that in leading the rest to a peak and happy conclusion, I may—overflowing with no common joy—willingly and gladly consecrate these things to you. May you not cease to favor him who will always commend his obedience to your commands, while I commend you and my cause to the providence of almighty Jehovah, who is accustomed to abundantly clothe those worthy of him with the reward of his wisdom and to treat them mercifully and liberally. Farewell.

->### Concerning the Metaphysical and Physical ###<-

This section is divided into three columns.

<column-break/>

### CHAPTER I.
**Concerning the things preceding the Microcosm, and those assisting toward its creation.**

The things preceding the Microcosm are noted to be twofold:
1. **Internal**, namely <note>original: "videl." for "videlicet"</note> the Idea in the Divine Mind.
2. **External**, namely <note>original: "scil." for "scilicet"</note> the Material of the world, or the Macrocosm itself, out of which it is produced.

<column-break/>

### CHAPTER II.
**Concerning the very Act of the Microcosm's creation.**

In the creation of the Microcosm, two things are observed:
1. **The efficient cause**, which is God.
2. **The manner of creation**, which is described in Genesis, book 1 <note>The text likely refers to the first book of the Bible, though the OCR notes "lib 8.", this may be a shorthand or specific citation style for the volume of a larger commentary</note>.

<column-break/>

### CHAPTER III.
**Concerning the things following the Microcosm.**

The things following the Microcosm are:
1. **Its perfection**, by which it excels all other creatures.
2. **Its end**, which is the glory of God and the contemplation of the universe.

# FIRST TREATISE,
## SECTION I.
### BOOK I.
### On Divine Numbers.

#### CHAPTER ONE
#### *or a prelude to this subject.*

[Large decorative initial Q] Since we judge it impossible to engage with the most noble disposition of man—or the internal Microcosm <note>The "Microcosm" or "Little World" is a Renaissance concept viewing the human being as a miniature reflection of the entire universe (the Macrocosm).</note>—and the wondrous harmony of the human soul without an exact knowledge of worldly melody and symphony, we likewise cannot rightly judge or weigh number, weight, and measure (from which the world and its soul are forged by a miraculous ordering and chaining of concordances) without a due contemplation of divine, formal, and hidden numbers, and a mystical inspection of simple harmony. Indeed, all symphonic compositions, the essences of worldly things, life, and other effects of worldly and animate music are derived from these divine and original numbers, just as a number derives from unity, a point from a line, and a concord from a unison. Therefore, we deem it necessary first and above all—with infinite effort of soul and wit, and indeed with the indefatigable fervor of the divine mind itself, preceded by constant and faithful prayers—that we may happily arrive at a complete knowledge of these things through profound meditation on these divine numbers, and then through a sincere contemplation and investigation of the simple harmony that flows ineffably from them.

Because this is deemed impossible to perfect or to lead to a happy conclusion from the starting point—since no mortal has ever been able to describe or reveal God according to His essence (so hidden and recondite are the mysteries of Divine Majesty)—it will certainly be our task (we who, through the enjoyment of the mind and the Divine Word itself, are by no means lacking the faculty of attaining immortality) to redeem ourselves, who labor in want and are wrapped in the darkness of ignorance, as captives by the power of the mind dwelling within us. We must depart from the obscure light, claim immortality, and flee corruption. To do this nobly and beautifully, let us penetrate the fissures of bodily darkness with the sharpness of our mind, so that from the effect <note>original: "à posteriori" - a logical term meaning reasoning from observed effects back to their causes.</note> we may finally reach the goal of unity, rise to the yoke of light (adorned with supreme beauty), leap with a light bound into the super-substantial homeland of the mind, and climb the Jacob’s Ladder <note>A biblical reference to the ladder reaching to heaven seen by the patriarch Jacob; here used as a metaphor for the stages of spiritual and intellectual ascent.</note> eagerly but cautiously

<column-break/>

<summary>This page introduces the study of "Divine Numbers" as the essential foundation for understanding the harmony of the human soul and the universe, arguing that man must use his intellect to rise from material darkness toward divine unity.</summary>
<keywords>Microcosm, divine numbers, harmony, Jacob's Ladder, sacred geometry, musical theory, metaphysics</keywords>

--- Page 28 ---
20 TRACTATE I. SECTION I. BOOK I.

Let us ascend cautiously, relying on the spiritual wings of Saint Paul <note>original: "D. Pauli"</note> (leaning upon the power of the Holy Spirit) to rise toward the life of the third heaven and the immortal light. And if we cannot perceive the secrets of the supersubstantial numbers according to the essence of the Deity with our intellectual eyes, let us nevertheless behold in them at least an idea, an image, or an example of the glory of the Trinity. Let us compare the divine and formal numbers of that same Trinity with material numbers (preceded by the highest reverence and adoration of the most holy Divinity); let us mingle the divine with the worldly, and compare the worldly with the human. For in this way the world was made, and in this way man was propagated through creation. Therefore, let us ascend from the harmony of man to the symphony of the world, and finally (transcending that worldly symphony on the wings of reason) to the divine. And by this path, we can elicit from the "posterior" <note>knowledge gained from effects or experience</note> that knowledge which it would be impossible for the human grasp to comprehend through the "prior" <note>knowledge gained from first principles or causes</note> science. We, however, following the order of knowledge from the "prior"—as if from the beginning to that which begins (having first understood these things from the "posterior")—will start, for the sake of a superior method, from the divine and simple numbers and the most simple harmony woven from them. Thus, by their guidance, we may arrive step by step at the composite or material numbers, both worldly and human, along with the symphony derived from them, and so finally immerse ourselves more deeply into material things.

## CHAPTER II.

### Concerning the monad, or the supreme and mystical unity.

Let the Metaphysician, his eyes illuminated by the sharp edge of the divine mind, look around on all sides; let the Physicist, with the clearest telescope of nature, search the corners of the elements and the things composed of them through the deepest inspection of his intellect (occupied with concrete things); let the Mathematician, by the sharpness of his fantasy or imagination (leaning on the support of demonstration and braced as if by the shoulders of Atlas), look into Arithmetic, Music, Geometry, Optics, Astronomy, Astrology, and Geomancy with his prospective intuition (engaged with abstract things); let the Logician, with the most subtle point of reason, speculate upon the series and orders of the "predicables" <note>the five logical classifications: genus, species, difference, property, and accident</note> descending from the transcendent Being to the genera, and from the genera to their subordinate species, and from those to individuals—likewise the derivations, origins, predications, and relations of the "predicaments" <note>Aristotle's categories of being</note>, and especially the transition of the predicament of substance from the most general genus into a multitude of particulars; finally, let the Grammarian, by the trust of memory (not without the candid contemplation of the mind), remember the order and origin of the elementary letters, the propagation of the syllables derived from them, the birth of words from the union of syllables, and then the flowing forth of the sentence or speech emanating from the connection and concatenation of words to one another in a due manner. And all these men will finally perceive and discern with a manifest countenance and wide-open eyes that the origins and existences of all things spring forth kindly from that one and only mystical root, and are derived in an ineffable (but most certain) way. This root is called the Monad of monads, and the supreme and most divine Monad, which is that God alone, thrice-greatest <note>original: "ter maximus," likely referring to Hermes Trismegistus</note>, from whose fountain all things, both created and uncreated (and poured out into a multitude), are observed to flow and emanate by the sharp edge of the divine mind. For if we turn our contemplation to Metaphysical things, this unity is found to exist in them as the root of roots, since it is the GOD OF GODS, the summit of summits, the good of goods, the fountain of wisdom and the origin of all roots, the intelligence of intelligences, more powerful than omnipotence, unbegotten by any other, infinite in kindness, and the mystical mind; indeed, in the trinity of persons—

<summary>The author argues for ascending from human and worldly harmonies to divine unity, establishing the "Monad" (God) as the singular source of all sciences, from logic to music. He describes how every discipline, when traced to its root, reveals the same divine origin.</summary>

->ON DIVINE NUMBERS. 21<-

of the supersubstantial essence <note>original: "essentiae supersubstantialis"; referring to a reality that exists beyond the physical or material substance</note> holds the first place, since it is that sacrosanct unity from which the divine number proceeds, and into which it returns. Finally, looking out beyond its own essence into material and created things in a manner exceeding the imagination, it produced from its shining root the choir of Angels, the throng of Demons, and the assembly of souls in immense multitude; and by its ineffable wisdom, it disposed their cohort and company, each one, into the glowing and fire-flashing orbs. Similarly, by considering the physical creatures of the world and regarding them in the proper manner, we shall find that this mystical monad <note>The Monad represents the number One, symbolizing God or the singular source of all existence.</note> holds the first place among them, since the same unity is the root of the number ten no differently than it is of the hundred and the thousand; from which numbers we shall declare below that the fabric of the world was constituted in the beginning and now remains. Hence, among the physicists, it is called the divine principle, infinite nature, and "naturing nature" <note>original: "natura naturans"; a philosophical term for God as the creative force behind the natural world</note>, the principle of principles, the star of stars, the light of lights (or the light of creatures shining everywhere), the spirit of spirits and the maker and effector of spirits, the world of worlds, the leader, governor, and director of all, the exalter and the depressor.

Even the Philosopher <note>Likely referring to Aristotle, often called "The Philosopher" in medieval and Renaissance texts.</note> will not deny that Time had its origin from this root, insofar as this monad exists in its eternal nature—begotten by no other—as the beginning and end of all created things, or the Alpha and Omega <note>original: "$\alpha$ & $\omega$"; the first and last letters of the Greek alphabet, symbolizing the beginning and the end.</note>. Wherefore also from the said mystical root, Time received its beginning, the "Now" <note>original: "Nunc"; the concept of the present moment as the fundamental unit of time.</note>, without which no time would ever exist; since the "Now" is its boundary, from which it is drawn and moved, no differently than a line is drawn from a point. Without this root there would also be no logical relation, since by no reason do we call one a "Son" unless it be in respect to a "Father"—neither in supersubstantial things, where the Father is called the principle of himself (or the principle arising from himself), nor in lower things, since there this root is the hidden seed of beings, the parent of ages, producing all life, filling and satiating all things with the good and the goodness of itself.

Furthermore, when this root is considered in Geometry according to Mathematics, it is the point of the primordial line and the center of the circle, from whose multiplication all lines, all surfaces, and all bodies—both mathematical and physical—proceed; and again, with resolution leading the way, they finally return into it as into the principle from which they came. In Music, it is the origin of concord and harmony, namely that primordial unison, from whose supersubstantial tone the empyrean melody arises—whether it be spiritual, mundane, human, or even instrumental—insofar as the composite consonances of the Fourth, the Fifth, the Octave, the Octave-plus-Fifth, and the Double Octave <note>original: "Diapente, Diapason, etc."; these are the classical Greek musical intervals.</note> are derived from the boundary of its radical voice or sound (producing the Word). In Arithmetic also, this monad exists as the root from which digits, articles, numbers, hundreds, thousands, and so on unto infinity are observed to arise and emanate. Whence it is manifest that this root or monad and unity is one and all things: one of all, one before all, and one in itself; the root and center of things present, past, and future; prior to material unity because it is most simple; the number of numbers, unity and number, and the unity which penetrates every number by its simplicity. For in the Trinity, the Father is ineffable, looking back into the empyrean heaven; he is the mind of mind and the soul of souls; and looking further down into the material world, he is the nature of natures. O, how admirable then is the disposition of the monad or unity! Though it is the cause and origin of the existence of things, yet what it is cannot be discerned by the sharpness of genius—no, not even by the mind (which flows immediately from it)—nor expressed by any reason. And yet, the wonderful nature of this essence is clearly explained to our reason in the contemplation of arithmetical unity: for arithmetical unity is the common measure, fount, and origin of all numbers, containing in itself every number however great, and yet innocent of all multitude, always the same, immutable, indivisible...

visible and without equal: And hence it is, that this unity, when multiplied by itself, produces nothing except itself. For 1 multiplied by itself produces only 1, and that internally; from that multiplication, nothing but the sole unity will arise. From this it is clear that unity is its own root, square, cube, etc., and yet it is always this same thing. For however much it is multiplied into unities, none of the produced unities is greater or smaller than the radical unity, nor is a part smaller than its whole, since it is not multiplied into parts but into itself. Finally, it is the beginning and end of all things, while yet it has neither beginning nor end by which it might exist, since nothing is prior to the one, and nothing is posterior to the one. Therefore, the One is the principle of all things, and all things exist up to the one, and beyond it nothing exists. Furthermore, all things that are desire the One itself as their root, since they first proceeded from it, and they necessarily participate in that one. Hence it is that all things strive to return to that one, insofar as they flowed radically from it; which regression and return to the first principle would never be perfected unless plurality and multitude were stripped away from them step by step and little by little. Such, therefore, is that mystical monad of monads <note>original: "monadum monas"</note>, the unity of unities, the prior summit of simplicity, the seed and center of all things, devoid of all substance <note>In this context, "substance" refers to material or composite matter; the One is pure spirit above physical substance.</note>, the principle, root, and origin of all; a principle, I say, containing all number but contained by none, begetting every number but begotten by no number, the father of all, the father of himself, the father of the only-begotten son. Indeed, such and beyond what the human mind can imagine is that unity, that one and monad, the holy of holies, the summit of excellence, and the God of gods, who sits constantly—joyful and fulfilled—above the peaks of heaven and outside all existence of matter upon his throne flashing with immortal glory, thundering that whole sacrosanct, mystical, ineffable, and original tone to the world. By its pulsation, act, and breath—unison and uniform—the world and its creatures are imbued with various harmonies of forms by which they exist and live; and the most elegant and prominent harmonies of things (soothing the thirsty ears of the mind) are heard and are conceived and stored away in the inner recesses of human reason. By its ineffable melody and its effective voice and word (with the divine Spirit breathing everywhere), the framework of the macrocosm <note>The "Great World" or the universe at large.</note> is observed to dance with a certain joy, to leap in proportion, and to live as if by springing forth; and the stars, both fixed and wandering <note>The "wandering stars" are the planets.</note>, are noticed to lead eternal dances as if they were drenched in supernatural gladness. The proportions and consonances of the microcosm <note>The "Little World," referring to the human being as a reflection of the universe.</note>—in mind, intellect, reason, soul, motion, life, and the elementary construction of the body (by performing beautiful and admirable functions)—are perceived to be established by a support that is, as it were, divine. This unity, I say, is the player of the Monochord <note>A single-stringed instrument used here as a metaphor for the underlying vibration of all creation.</note> and the very form and soul of the entire macrocosmic and microcosmic harmony, whose string or instrumental matter is that universal spirit, which it liberated from the bowels of chaos by its ineffable act, and made out of nothing, so that something might exist in actuality and serve its stupendous actions in the place of a passive subject. To Him, as the King of Kings, all things of all nature must be offered, and as if a tribute due to Him, must be attributed and conferred (namely the lives, essences, souls, and bodies of things, insofar as they depend on Him); this, above all, every person of sound mind and adorned with even a small gift of reason ought to acknowledge and confess with the highest effort and final endeavor of the soul.

*Several examples by which the Unity of the most holy Trinity (by comparing it to*
*lower things) is demonstrated according to*

The beyond-substantial unity of essence is explained in Arithmetic by the number 1. For from this unity in Arithmetic, all numbers proceed toward infinity, drawn forth as if from their source and fundamental origin, such as 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, etc. In Mathematics and the Geometric art, it is demonstrated by the point, from which the line is derived, through which it is continued, and in which it is terminated (wherefore a line is most correctly defined as a flow of points bound together). But because every surface is composed of lines and a body from surfaces, it follows from necessity that lines, as well as surfaces and consequently the body itself, arise from a single point. In a similar way, from unity and its flow, the number ten is made, in which unity joins itself to composition—namely, the super-excellently substantial nature joining with the matter to be created—as 1 with 0. Without this cipher <note>The zero</note>, there will be nothing more than the matter of *hyle* <note>original: "hylæ"; the Greek term for primordial, unformed matter</note> deprived of essential and shining form. Hence, simple unity relates to the number ten as a point to a line; and the number ten to a hundred as a line to a surface (in which God, the Unity or Point, always precedes); and the number one hundred to one thousand as a surface to a solid body, as we shall indicate more extensively below. From these things it is clearly evident that unless God is placed before all things, things will no more exist in actuality than Arithmetical ciphers, which, no matter how great a multitude they are expressed by themselves, will signify absolutely nothing without unity or one of the digits flowing from it; just as 0, 00, 000, 0000, 00000 denote nothing, but 10, 100, etc., denote something. Through the point, God is also wonderfully explained in physical reality, since the point is the principle of motion in generation and corruption, and like this *now* <insert>now</insert> from which, as if from the foundation of its paternal origin or the "limit from which," time proceeded, and into which it again returns.

CHAPTER III.
Concerning the Dyad, or the mystical and beyond-substantial duality.

The first Monad of monads <note>Monad: from the Greek *monas*, meaning a single unit or the "One."</note>, and the holy Unity of unities, poured out in an ineffable manner by a beyond-substantial birth the simplicities of the heights, and gave birth to and produced them; for she, leaping forth through the first-born form, attained a threefold power. For where the depth of the Father is, there shines the brightness of the illustrious Son and the reconciling splendor of the Holy Spirit; and so that beyond-substantial fountain is crowned with the beauty of the offspring, which flowed out from its own center and revolves around that center. And the Son was begotten, who is the renowned Wisdom of the Father and the craftsman of all things. For through the pouring out of the One into the Son, an ineffable middle nature was born, which exists before all natures—a sacred birth indeed and the unspeakable fetus of the ineffable Father. No time has known his hidden and mystical rising, since he appeared together with the Father, always born, he who was to be born, and remains in him, although begotten from him, so that he might govern all things with a wise spirit. Leaping forth, I say, the Son from the Father remains in the Father forever, and again, outside, he rules those things which belong to the Father. He is the shouting Word of the Father and the most prominent speech, the first begotten from the first root. He is the root of all; for all things were established through his renowned birth, since he is the seed of all things.

Unity, therefore, is the fountain of the duality of that same essence: and duality, or the Son, is the form and image of the unity, or the Father. Unity, or the Father, is the power of the duality, or the Son; but duality, or the Son, is the beauty of the Father. And although the duality of matter is an ill-omened number—because it is the fountain and origin of strife, discord, impurity, and confusion, for this number, by taking matter to itself, is separated from unity, because it enters into the boundaries of contention, and by multiplying itself downward into a multitude, fleeing from the presence of unity, and tending toward the center and depth of dark matter, it flows forth—therefore this number in matter is called the most imperfect of all, because it can never be resolved except through dissolution, and reduced to the peak of essential and beyond-substantial unity. 

Nevertheless, this divine binary number of form, not receding beyond the limits of the essence of unity, is the most formal and most blessed number; because in the same essence, by the virtue of unity (with the Holy Spirit mediating and binding them together, proceeding from the center of the unity or Father, and the duality or Son), it is reflected back to unity, and is reunited with unity, according to that saying of Hermes Trismegistus: *The Monad generated a monad, and reflected its own heat back into itself.* <note>original: "Monas generat monadem, & in seipsam reflexit ardorem suum." Hermes Trismegistus is the legendary Hellenistic figure to whom the Hermetic corpus of mystical philosophy is attributed.</note> And this God-formed essence is uniform and triform, since although there is here a threefold nature of persons and numbers, with respect to—

Despite the difference of distinct offices and virtues attributed to each, there is nevertheless always a unity of essence and identity of the Deity; which unity, by the power of a spiritual glue, shall be inviolably preserved forever. Therefore, the duality of numbers is unity because it is trinity, and it is trinity because it is unity; namely, a trinity of persons and a unity of God-like essence.

### CHAPTER IV.
### On the origin of the Triad, or the supersubstantial number three.

Since God is Mind, most full of the fecundity of both sexes (I speak now with the mouth of Hermes Trismegistus <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure associated with alchemy and wisdom</note>), life and light, He brought forth with His word another creator mind; which God is indeed called fire and the power of the spirit, whom Synesius <note>A 4th-century Neoplatonist philosopher and bishop</note> called the Holy Spirit, the mediating principle proceeding from the center of the Father and from the center of the Son, whose shining light is called the Reconciler, because its number three is the truest and most sincere love, which joins the Father with the Son in an inviolable bond. For indeed, duality (which is the multitude proceeding from unity) is reduced into a harmonious unity by the bond of the number three. Such, therefore, was the origin of the world—a progression, I say, from unity into multitude—and such is its cycle: namely, the reduction of multitude back to unity. According to the progression of these divine numbers always contained within unity, the order, harmony, proportion, measure, or intervals of material, spiritual, watery, or moist nature are disposed. For from here comes the division of the entire world into three regions, of which the second received its essences from the first and third, and from both. From here come the three harmonies of every symphony: the Octave, the Fifth, and the Fourth <note>original: "Diapason, Diapente, & Diatessaron"</note>, of which the Fifth is from the Octave as if from unity, and the Fourth from both. From here come the double, one-and-a-half, and one-and-a-third proportions <note>The mathematical ratios 2:1, 3:2, and 4:3</note> of all things and of the world itself, derived from the various dispositions of divine light in the universal spirit within matter <note>original: "hyla"</note>. From here come the intervals of things, namely the line, the surface, and the body—or length, breadth, and depth; the line from the point, the surface from the line, and the body from both. From here come the three kinds of souls: intellectual, sensitive, and vegetative. From here the disposition of the world by three: namely number, measure, and weight. From here, finally, three Princes of the world are proclaimed by the Philosophers: GOD, Mind, and Spirit. And this was the reason why the Pythagoreans called unity "Apollo," the duality "matter," but the triad "form and justice," which is the highest perfection. Therefore the Poet says that God rejoices in an odd number, because the first and simplest odd number in the super-celestial essence is that love which joins the father with the son, whence (says Synesius): *Hail, O purest Spirit, center of the son and father.* And elsewhere: He called Him the companion of the son and the medium between the root and the bud. And elsewhere: *The reconciling light*, because derived from the two first persons and united with them, it composed the Trinity. Therefore this number three is called the sacred number, the number of perfection, and the most powerful number, because it is incomposite and the first odd number, by whose bond Duality becomes Trinity and Trinity is made Unity. And it is from this that the One has attained a threefold power, by which it is brought about that GOD is one and all things, one in Himself and through all things, and that He is Unity when He is Trinity, and Trinity when He is Unity; according to Synesius's second hymn: *I sing to thee, Unity; I sing to thee, Trinity. You are One, though you be Trinity; you are Trinity, though you be Unity.*

For Unity is the sole act in itself, while Trinity exists in its own perfection, flowing from that Unity, by which all created things are called perfect and good. We conclude, therefore, that Unity is the starting point <note>Latin: terminus à quo</note> and Duality is the first-born of Unity, acting as a middle number between Unity and the Triad. By the perfection of this Triad, Duality—or the middle—is joined to the two extremes in the divine essence by an indissoluble bond, which again cohere to themselves in a wondrous manner through a circular progression. From this it follows that all three persons, though distinct in their properties, are nothing but one in essence—namely, a single, supreme, and sole essence, which exists as nothing other than the three persons. These are three properties, of which one is not the other, nor are any two the third, nor is any third the two; for the two are that which the third is, and the third is that which the two are. What is this? One Deity, one essence, one thing finally. How can this be, if they are three? How are they three, if they are this one? It is incomprehensible and therefore miraculous: Faith alone knows it, yet the whole is received from the Divine Spirit, who established the formula for baptism under this number three and its relationship: *Baptize,* He says, *in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.* These three relatives receive further clarification, as we shall show more extensively below.

Or we can best adapt this concept to a pair of compasses, the top of which is like a point, or the unity of essence, which is divided into diverse properties. For one of its feet, fixed and standing immutably in the center, is always the same, nor indeed is it moved from its place. The other foot, however, is mobile and describes a regular circle at an equal distance from the center. And so that the mobile foot may be firmer and more obedient to the regular arrangements of the foot adhering immovably and invariably to the center, there is a certain bond of friendship and a link of love, as it were, passing regularly through the center of the mobile limb, which is fixedly attached to the fixed limb or foot; it governs the action of the mobile foot or limb so that it always agrees in number, measure, and proportion, and maintains a relationship to the fixed foot or limb, acting according to the laws and justice of the fixed limb. Such is the example.

Thus, one and the same compass is divided into various functions, one of which is to stand firm and to govern the double actions of other properties according to justice, and to arrange them according to its own disposition, without which it is impossible to describe a circular figure. ### CHAPTER V.

*That each person of the holy and individual Trinity has a distinct property in the fabric of the world and the production of its creatures; and concerning the universal property of unity, and its agreement with the number ten.*

The admirable reasoning of the mystical creation of the world lies hidden in the secret disposition of the Trinity and the bosom of the Deity, so that there exists no "finger" <note>A metaphor for a component or manifestation</note> in the Trinity—whether it be one, two, or three—which does not possess its own proper and peculiar mystery within itself, and does not produce a varied effect in the world (according to the vast and admirable efficacy of its office). For in unity (insofar as it cannot be multiplied in itself, or by its nature be reduced to a multitude or divided), as if in a single universal ideal and purely formal world, the image of the material world is delineated in a hidden manner. For one was, without doubt, the principal pattern in the mind of the Founder for the things to be founded. Therefore, just as the Monad <term>Monad: the philosophical concept of "The One" or the primary unit from which all numbers and things originate</term> was first in the production of the Trinity (which is the first root of things both uncreated and created), so also secondly, after the birth of that simple square, unity occupied the first place in the number ten <note>The "denary" number</note> for the composition of the world, since it is bound to the number ten by a strong connection. For unity is the father of the supersubstantial birth, and the number ten is the father of the substantial birth; these two parents do not differ from each other, since both are one God, but they differ in the property of their action. Because the former unity was simple and is engaged in an inexplicable way in the supersubstantial world, while the latter in the ten (that is, joined with a cipher <note>The zero, which turns 1 into 10</note>) acts upon the material world. Hence Hermes Trismegistus <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure associated with hermetic philosophy and alchemy</note> says: GOD is called the father of the cosmos, and the cosmos is called the son of God, etc. Therefore, GOD is unity in the formal world and holds the place of the number ten in the material world. For as the number ten is the end of simple numbers, so it is also the beginning of compound ones, and the middle or center between unity and the number one hundred. Therefore, unity begins the number ten among the simple numbers, and again that same unity is observed to terminate any tens of numbers.

And *Hermes Trismegistus* <note>original: "Mercurius Trismegistus," the legendary Hellenistic figure associated with the Hermetic corpus of mystical philosophy.</note> seems to support this opinion of ours, whose words are these: *The number ten is the progenitor of the soul; for life and light are united there, where the numbers of unity itself are born from the spirit; thus unity, according to reason, encompasses the number ten, and in turn, the number ten encompasses unity.* Indeed, with what great joy I was filled upon hearing these words of the wise man, so precisely and aptly agreeing with this discovery of mine, I can scarcely express with my tongue or the sharpness of my pen. For what else would this divine Priest <note>A reference to Hermes as the "thrice-great" priest and philosopher.</note> have intended, than that in the creation of the world the number ten (which he later calls unity) is the progenitor of the world-soul, and consequently of the human soul? Because, he says, *there life and light—that is, the spirit and the divine splendor or form—are united.* And he says that the numbers of unity are born from the spirit—that is, from spiritual matter—being clearly articulated and composed. From these things, therefore, he concludes thus, on account of the composition of the Spirit with light: Therefore unity, according to reason, encompasses the number ten; that is, the unity which was the progenitor in the supersubstantial and simple birth, encompasses the number ten in the composite birth according to reason; and he says there is a reciprocal embrace between unity and the number ten. From which he seems to argue that unity in the trinity is the same as the number ten in composition. And in another place he says, *that by the presence of the number ten, the intellectual generation is composed; that is, the intellectual heaven with its choir of Angels is divided into nine spheres or places of the first composition of the denary <term>denary: relating to the number ten</term> articulations,* etc. Finally, we say that unity has a twofold relation to the world: namely, insofar as it is everything that exists; and thus now the entire world is compared to unity (which is complete and universal in itself). Whence the world, on account of the integrity of its parts, is called by *Trismegistus* a **material and incorruptible GOD.** And elsewhere he says: **GOD is the one father of the one world; the one world is the progenitor of the one sun; and the unique sun is the origin of the one man,** etc. Or insofar as, on account of the property of its unity (encompassing the number ten), it claimed for itself the first workmanship of creation, and in its first disposition (insofar as it attributes to itself the reason of the first person of the machine of the upper world: since its fiery spirit in that region was first carried over the waters). From these things, therefore, it is established that the property and action of the first person of the Trinity in the structure of the world is concerned with universality, constituting one whole world. For since everything that exists is established under its inestimable command and is comprehended in its power, it necessarily follows that it regards the entire nature of things and the universal spirit of the world, reducing it from potentiality into act, sustaining it by its fiery breath of life, and finally supporting the entire machine by its immense strength.

### CHAPTER VII.
### Concerning material numbers, namely the Binary, Quaternary, and Octonary, and the properties of the Deiform Dyad.
<note>The Dyad refers to the number two; "Deiform" means having the form or nature of God.</note>

Formal Duality is a most auspicious number, because it is consubstantial with the formal Unity from which it arose. It is also a most perfect number, insofar as it is the middle, or the center of the trinity, and has its beginning from the supersubstantial Father of its own nature; it has its end in the number three <note>the ternary</note>, which is the infinite and incomprehensible spirit, and finally, it is itself its own middle, and the center of the number three proceeding from the center of the Father. Hence it is that this number is the center of concord, retaining in itself the image of the Father or Unity, and the radiance of the Holy Spirit’s number three. Therefore, this formal root is most auspicious, life-giving, and preservative, producing a most happy formal square, and a cube not unlike it. For this essential Binary (the germ of vital unity) does not proceed toward multitude like the material binary does; since this one, flowing out from unity, returns again through the ternary and is connected to the unity from which it was previously derived. 

For this reason, it is called the peculiar number of justice, and its proper act is justice itself, because it rejoices in two things equally weighted. It is also called the number of wisdom, science, memory, light, and indeed of man himself, and the knot of charity and mutual love. For just as two are reduced into one flesh by matrimonial bonds, so in the mystical binary, two are united in the same essence through the third spirit. Similarly, this occurs in its square, which is 4. For the formal square is ascribed to God the Father, and indeed it embraces the mystery of the entire trinity. For by its simple proportion—namely, the first of one to one—the unity of the paternal substance is signified; from which now proceeds the Son equal to Him. Moreover, by another procession, also simple—namely, of two to two—the Holy Spirit is noted by a second procession from both, so that the Son becomes equal to the Father by the first procession, and the Holy Spirit equal to both by the second procession. 

From this, therefore, the most high name of God and the divine Trinity, the *Tetragrammaton*, arose: namely, *Jod, He, Vau, He* <note>The four-letter Hebrew name of God, יהוה</note>, where the aspiration *He* denotes the procession of the Spirit from both; for the *He* itself, being doubled, terminates both syllables and the whole name. It is pronounced *Jova* and *Jehovah*, as some will have it. This number is therefore the origin of all divinity; whence the Pythagoreans called it the fountain of nature. It is also the number filling all knowledge. For the Son is called the knowledge and wisdom of the Father. Furthermore, by the addition of this number with 1, 2, 3, and 4, there is again a return to unity, namely to the number ten <note>1+2+3+4=10</note>, from which the structure of the material world began. Finally, the cube exulting from the number two, which is 8, the Pythagoreans called—

They called this the number of justice, because it is divided into "even-even" numbers <note>original: "pariter pares" — a Pythagorean term for numbers that can be repeatedly divided by two down to unity</note>, namely into four, which is its square, and again four into twice two, and finally the two is divided into two units. Because of this equality of division all the way down to unity, it claimed for itself the name of justice. It is also called the number of blessedness, because it pertains to eternity and the consummation of the world; for it follows the number seven, which is the symbol of time. Christ also teaches just as many degrees of blessedness <note>The eight Beatitudes</note> in the Gospel of Matthew. Finally, it is called the number of salvation and preservation.

Therefore, while the harmony of the Octave <note>term: Diapason — the musical interval of an eighth, representing cosmic harmony</note> of this radical and sacrosanct number resounded through the world, the Word descended into the formless world to give it shape, to cast off its horrid impurities, and to strike its foulest shadows back to the center. Once the downward penetration was made, this wisdom of the Father—this Demogorgon <note>A mysterious primordial deity often associated with the origin of the universe in Renaissance occultism</note>, one and three, or this middle of the Trinity—perceived and noticed that the chaos, or rather the *hyle* <note>term: hylam — the Greek word for "matter" or "raw substance"</note>, or prime and formless matter, was impregnated by power alone and was pregnant, ready to give birth to this "something-nothing" by the help of the Demogorgon and to be brought into actuality. For its belly, veiled in darkness, trembled; the limbs of the *hyle* were agitated by the disturbance of its contentious birth. Indeed, unity in potentiality strove to see the act and to look upon it face to face.

The only-begotten offspring of the Demogorgon took pity on the chaos of pain, and kindly stretched out a right hand to its laborious effort of birthing. Thus, with Act concurring with Potentiality, the firstborn of the *hyle*—the son of chaos, potential unity, and the seed of discord—was brought forth into actuality. As soon as he had drawn the rays of life to himself from the Word or Demogorgon, this author of sedition and prince of darkness (forgetting the benefits of his creator) immediately rose up, elated by pride and ambition. He did not hesitate to usurp the place and dignity of the supersubstantial unity; he refused to admit a superior over himself, wished no one to be preferred to him in eternity or empire, and dared to claim the first place in the world for himself. 

And so this fertile companion, full of malice, ambition, and sedition—having gathered his moist companions who clung to him and sprang forth with him from the abyss of the *hyle*—flew upward with "borrowed wings" <note>An allusion to Icarus or the prideful fall</note> toward the formal world, hostilely using the rays of the bright fountain expanded everywhere through the moist nature in the empyrean region due to the presence of the Word and the Holy Spirit. But being ignorant of the incomprehensible power of the supersubstantial essence before contact and effect, this rebellious traitor was cast down from the formal world by a single stroke of lightning and by the mere utterance of His word. He was submerged again into the abyss of darkness with his associates and cohorts, and finally driven to the center of the material world. 

Immediately after his casting down, the universal moist nature—the second offspring of the *hyle*—was brought forth. The Poets have imagined this to be Pan, by whose long beard they understood the rays of light and the sun; by his eye-spotted head, the firmament filled with fixed stars; and by his pipe composed of seven reeds, they signified the powers and harmony of the seven planets. From these things, therefore, it is clear that Discord <note>original: "Litigium"</note>, before the presence of the Word and the appearance of the spiritual splendor, was nothing at all except unity in potentiality. This unity could not be in act, because that actual and formal unity preceded it in the sacrosanct Trinity, which was its principle; and consequently, it was something secondary, insofar as it proceeded from the pre-existing unity. 

The same reasoning applies to the production of universal spiritual matter, which succeeded Discord in the material birth, since it is of the same genus and nature, except that its filth, impurity, and darkness are stripped off and set aside. By the virtue of the divine rays and splendor, this universal matter is made conformable to clear water, balanced in number, weight, and measure, and rendered more obedient to its creator. Whence it is established (to use the words of Hermes Trismegistus) that *since the mind, the word, and the moist nature, which shone forth from the shadow, are younger, they therefore occupy the place of the material binary number...*

This duality is not of the same nature as that formal duality which we demonstrated above to be most complete and perfect in its essence, and the preserver of all things. On the contrary, material spirit no more exists by itself in the nature of things without the divine rays and assistance than a cipher <note>original: "cyphra"; referring to the number zero, which has no value without a leading digit</note> exists without a digit among mathematicians, as was shown before. Furthermore, this material number is in itself the **origin of sedition and discord**, and consequently most imperfect, insofar as it possesses no actual principle consubstantial <note>of the same substance or essence</note> with itself. Indeed, its consubstantial principle was a certain "one" in potentiality, but after its production into act, it abandoned that title and put on the form of plurality, losing its unity and rightly attributing that unity to the formal Unity. And hence it is that it possesses the unity suitable to its nature in the least degree; wherefore it has neither beginning, middle, nor end. Thus it happens that matter itself is the worst of things without the presence of the divine number and the assistance of the Fountain—namely, of all goodness. For unless the supersubstantial Trinity rained down some of its perfection and goodness into this worldly matter, it would be nothing but a heap of evils, a gathering of envy, an accumulation of discord, an abyss of deformity, and an inclination toward the [disordered] multitude. Nor would any of these things even exist, except in potentiality alone, insofar as every act (as has been said) and all goodness comes from the luminous Fountain.

Hence, therefore, this material binary number has been called the **number of discord, confusion, misfortune, and impurity**. And hence also it was **that St. Jerome, writing against Jovinian, said that for this reason, on the second day of the world's creation, it was not said: "And God saw that it was good," because the binary number of the world is evil.** <note>Jerome's commentary on Genesis suggests the second day lacked the divine blessing because the number two represents a departure from the unity of the first day.</note> **Furthermore, it was for this reason that God commanded the unclean animals to enter the ark in pairs [by the binary number], because the binary number is the number of impurity and most unhappy in its omens.** This, finally, was the reason why the **Pythagoreans** (as **Plutarch** relates) called unity "Apollo" or "God," but applied to the dyad [the number two] "strife" and "audacity," while applying the triad [the number three] to "justice," which is the highest perfection.

By the progression, therefore, from this ill-fated material number—which tends downward—the divine soul is more and more imprisoned, and is wrapped in the thickest snares of darkness, and is rendered most unhappy, vexed by passions and deceived by the prestiges and illusions of the world. Whence it happens that the further the light descends from the sight of the luminous Fountain toward the base of the material pyramid, the more it is endangered and submerged in darkness. Thus this duality, multiplied into itself, produces the four elements, which first fortify the soul within their spirit by their viscosity; and again, plunging itself even deeper into its depth, the soul is reduced to a cube, captured by the snares of the spirit, and is introduced into the opaque body—or the triple dimension, or the "elementated" elements, or the composition of the four elements constituting the cube of the square—by the flatteries of the spirit which belongs to the side of matter.

And this is the reason why men are more affected by the world, the flesh, the devil, and inferior, deceptive, and vain delights than by supercelestial and divine things imbued with truth; namely, because the spirit existing on the side of matter neglects the mind and the [higher] soul, and clings to the animal or elementary soul. But truly, take heed and wait, O earth-born men! Listen, I say, creatures imbued with divine reason; rejoice, O men, or be filled with no small joy! For all that which matter has plotted by treachery against your souls—by sowing its discord or beginning from its duality, and progressing to the universality and depth of its mass toward the center of the base of its pyramid—all that, I say, the supersubstantial duality (which is Unity and Trinity) shall dissolve by its harmony through those same degrees of discord. Conversely, by ascending and rising from the peak of its formal pyramid toward its base, which is fixed to the formal world, it will liberate the captured souls from darkness, and finally exalt them to their connatural seat. For the root at the peak of the formal pyramid (situated near the earth or the base of the material pyramid) will untie the chains of dark—

### CHAPTER VIII.
### *On the property of the number three in the Trinity, or the third person in the fabric of the world.*

This odd number is supersubstantial and most holy, in which GOD is said to rejoice, insofar as it is an uncompounded number, sacred, most powerful, and most perfect. To that extent, it comprehends many mysteries of the Deity and has produced many secrets in the composition of the world. For first, since God is referred to by the number three <term>ternary: the number three</term>, it is therefore argued and indicated that this number is most perfect, since it is the beauty perfecting the beginning, the middle, and the end, and possessing these as absolute equals. Other numbers, however, which have those three degrees of perfection, do not have them absolutely and simply, but relatively and compositely. Therefore, this ternary brings forth God as the beginning, the cause, and the form from the principal form; it brings forth the most perfect from the beginning, middle, and end—as the one through whom all things are, and the end as that in which all things are. From these things, it is clear that this number is the most abstruse and admirable communion and indissoluble bond of the third person in the Trinity, clearly explaining the connection with the first and second, and connecting all three together in an ineffable knot of unity and an inviolable bond of the same. For the **Seraphim** (who are the superior order of this hierarchy) consist of a multitude of angels whose nature is to understand the highest things and to be kindled by the essential fire of God, insofar as they are closest to the formal world and near to the simplest dwelling place of God. The **Cherubim** are filled with wisdom and knowledge. And the **Thrones** are most full of divine judgment: For (as Isidore <note>Isidore of Seville, an influential 7th-century scholar</note> testifies) **GOD** sits upon them in his judgment, and through them disposes all things. Whence this hierarchy is rightly attributed to God the Father.

The second and middle hierarchy is called **Epiphonomia** <note>original: "Epiphonomia," likely meaning "manifestation of the name" or "shining forth"</note>, which signifies divine splendor and clarity with reverence, divided into **Principalities**, **Powers**, and **Dominions**: Thus the second person, who is the Word, is called the light of the world and the life of things, whom we ought especially to revere as the act of all things.

The third and lowest is called **Ephionia** <note>original: "Ephionia," likely referring to the manifestation of power or voice</note>, as if pertaining to virtues, because the spirits of that hierarchy—whether they be **Virtues**, **Archangels**, or **Angels**—have the power of performing miracles, of curing ailments of both soul and body (and this beyond the reason of nature), and of demonstrating mysteries; to this the third person is referred, since all virtues are attributed to the world by the Spirit from the mouth of the Lord.

From the first hierarchy, therefore, as if from a source or a lucid center, the second proceeds like splendor and light from a fiery body; and as color arises from light, so the virtues arise from the splendor of light. The first hierarchy is therefore like a fiery heat, the second a divine clarity (as if from that fiery heat), and the third a secret virtue, like warmth from both—namely, from the fire and the light. How most manifest, therefore, do we see here the agreement of the first heaven and its parts with the Trinity.

But in leaping forward from this heaven into the second, we shall also find there the Trinity under the same relation most evidently: For in its first and supreme triplicity, embracing the **Primum Mobile** <note>The "First Moved" sphere in Ptolemaic astronomy</note>, the **Starry Heaven**, and the **Sphere of Saturn**, we shall perceive the property of Unity and the Father. For as Unity is the first number from which the other numbers arise, so all lower things are moved by the power of the *Primum Mobile*. Similarly, as the firmament is called the heaven composed of fixed stars, so the Father is fixed in his nature, immobile and in no way to be altered, as is observed in the nature of Unity. Finally, as **Saturn** was called the father of the other gods among the Poets, so from the supersubstantial Unity or Father, the two other persons of the Trinity, the Son and the Holy Spirit, are propagated.

Again, the second and middle triplicity of this heaven is compared in its disposition to the second person of the Trinity. For as **Jupiter** was the son of Saturn, so the second person is the Son of the first; as he is called the father of lightnings (carrying lightning-bolts with him), so also is this the voice of the Father going forth with lightning and thunder, and thronged from the mouth of the Father with vast forces and ineffable power, striking where it wills. Jupiter is also esteemed for justice, benevolence, religion, piety, as a preserver and friend of the human race, and the distributor of the radical moisture and innate heat which most easily separates things unto life. Moreover, infinite passages of the Holy Scriptures have brilliantly explained the Son's incomparable power, justice, kindness, religion, piety, affability toward the human race, and his operation toward its life and preservation.

**Mars**, also found in the same triplicity, proves the power and victory of the Son against the prince of impiety and his followers—namely, the crowd of iniquity—whose role it is to overcome the beast, the false prophet, hell, and death itself. Finally, this second most holy person is appropriated to the **Sun** in many ways: For as mundane harmony is said to flow from Apollo, so in truth from the Son (or the Duality with his Spirit) is derived the universal symphony of matter—in the Fourth, the Fifth, and consequently in the Octave <note>original: "Diatessaron, Diapente... Diapason," the fundamental musical intervals</note>, which is composed of those two—as was declared above. The Sun is also, according to Hermes Trismegistus, the son of the material world, and according to Plato, of the immortal God...

ON DIVINE NUMBERS. 39.

CHAPTER X.

*On the reasoning according to Mathematics: first, why the Deity is designated by number, and then specifically by the number three; likewise, why according to the Logicians "relation" is attributed to the Deity.*

Now indeed, we have proposed to bring forth into the public view the reasons why Theology has dedicated God to number; next, we shall produce geometric reasons why she chose the number three <note>the ternary</note> above all others to express God—the first form and maker of all things—and dedicated the Deity to such a number. First, therefore, it must be known that "Theography" <note>literally 'God-writing' or divine description</note> wished to declare and explain the Deity to us through number because of a threefold consideration. The first of these is to reveal His infinity, since nothing is more infinite than number, seeing as there is no end to its magnitude. The second is to declare God as foreknowing; for number was (as the wise man says) *undoubtedly the principal model in the mind of the Creator for the things to be built.* The last is to indicate that God is immutable <note>unchanging</note>, for nothing is more immutable than the One and its properties, as was said above: for the things that were, are the same; the things that are, were the same, and always shall be. Number, therefore, suggests that God is simple while being immutable; it suggests He is wise while being foreknowing; it suggests He is incomprehensible while being infinite; and finally, it suggests He is wonderful and singular through these three attributes.

Theologians chose the number three <note>the ternary</note> above all others because they wished to show that God is the primary form of all things. That this number is the principle of forms and the first and highest root of bodies is taught to us by a most evident geometric demonstration: for if we consider that triangular figure with diligent insight, we perceive indeed that it cannot be resolved into others, nor is it subject to any prior principles, insofar as it is itself the principle of other figures for their composition, and the end-point for their resolution. For the square, the pentagon, and the remaining figures proceed from it and return into it, insofar as from this surface—which is the principle of linear shapes—all other surfaces as well as bodies forged from surfaces are derived; in their dissolution, it will again be necessary for them to return to that triangular surface. Such, therefore, is God, from whom all things come, and in whom all things are folded together in resolving simplicity. Finally, whatever exists receives its being what it is from form, and not from matter; matter itself also receives its being from form, while form furthermore is incapable of receiving "accidents" <note>non-essential or changing qualities</note>. From this fact, therefore—that the number three is the principle of forms—it suggests with wonderful and most secret truth the cause and principle of universality, incapable of difference, which is solely and truly One. Again, it is declared that this number three is most properly adapted to God alone because it is the most perfect number, completing all things. For it is beauty, perfecting the beginning, the middle, and the end, and possessing these as equal and absolute; whereas by contrast the number two <note>the binary</note> walks stripped of these three, having no beginning or end (because no middle point stands between) and consequently is destitute of this sacrosanct gift of perfection. As for the rest of the numbers, however many possess a beginning, middle, and end, they do not have that perfection absolutely and simply, but only in a composite way. The number three, therefore, brings forth God as the principle, cause, and form from the chief form; it brings Him forth as most perfect from the beginning, the middle, and the end: from the beginning, as He from whom all things come; from the middle, as He through whom all things are; and from the end, as He in whom all things reside. Furthermore, for this same reason, by number...

by such a number, which is similar in such a way to such a relation, or is spoken of in the Triad <note>The "Triad" refers to the Neoplatonic or Pythagorean concept of the number three as a divine structure.</note> as a monad <note>A "monad" is a single, indivisible unit; here referring to the unity of God.</note> found as if by itself, and a dyad <note>A "dyad" refers to the number two or a pair.</note> as if by itself; so also in the Trinity, there is a Dyad as if by itself, such as the Father and the Son, and again, because there is a monad by itself, such as the Holy Spirit. The Father and the Son, therefore, correspond to each other by relation, and not to the Spirit. The Spirit, as if by itself, is not to be referred to the Father by name, nor to the Son. By meaning, therefore, he is referred to, as the Spirit of the Breather is the Spirit, and the Breather of the Spirit is the Breather: the Breather is the Father and the Son, yet they are not two breathers, but one, and one spirit. <note>original: "Spirator" - a technical theological term for the action of "breathing out" the Holy Spirit.</note>

Finally, Divine Writing <note>original: "Theographia" - Holy Scripture.</note> uses relative predication, wishing to demonstrate God as being in harmony with Himself—or rather, to indicate that He is harmony itself and a full and singular connection: *For whatever the Father does, these things the Son also does likewise, and one and the same Spirit works these same things, dividing to each one as he wills.* <note>A paraphrase of John 5:19 and 1 Corinthians 12:11.</note> This is an incomprehensible harmony and a singular connection, so that many are one in the identity of person more than the first unity of a single Spirit or Angelic being; finally, it surpasses all sense. This is what gives life to distinct things, and which forces opposing things into a union: which is to be discovered from relatives, which rejoice together in mutual responsibility, and which use relative predication in their knowledge rather than in their separation, wishing God to be understood as invariable, to whom it is impossible for any change to succeed or approach; one majesty, one will, one operation of the three who are one, among whom "one" is not a transformation (so that it ceases to be what it was), nor a shadow of change (so that it stops now, and now returns to what it was). Finally, Theology accepts relative statement, accepting God as unsuspected, uncircumscribed, neither signifiable by a name nor comprehensible by the intellect. For relative demonstrations do not at all define the thing, they do not compose a definition, and they do not declare the substance: just as "servant" and "master," or "left" and "right," do not signify *what* a thing is, but rather only *toward what* it is related. Thus, there is no inference from relation to substance; it is not because the Father is God, and the Son is God, and the Holy Spirit is God, that there are therefore three Gods. The Father and the Son, therefore, are predicated not in what they are, but in their relation to what they are, as is known: as the Father is the Father of the Son, and the Son as the Son of the Father, and concerning the Spirit, as has been defined concerning him. Certainly, if they placed a related distinction of different substance, it would seem to follow that if the Father is God, and the Son is God, and the Holy Spirit is God, then there are three Gods, not one. But they do not place a relative distinction away from God, so that many things may agreeably come together into one thing, nor do they make it differently, even if one of them is taken away from the other. Therefore, the name of Father is separated from the Son, and Master from servant, and conversely the whole; and yet someone is a Father, and a Son, and a Master, and a servant, etc.
