Thus unity joined with a cipher multiplies itself ten times in addition with it; joined with two ciphers it multiplies itself a hundred times; if with three, a thousand times. O, how great a mystery of nature lies here, explaining our pyramidal descriptions of matter and form so often cited! For from this it becomes known that nothing can exist without the presence of the most holy unity, for she herself is the cause of the multiplication of matter in the composite world, and without her there is no increase of things at all, and nothing in the world can remain. For unity in her conformable palace does not use the cipher, because there is no matter there seeking multiplication, there is no composition; but she unites herself only to the cipher in the world of composition, where she finds unformed matter, and in a symphonic manner (like a thing imprisoned in darkness, and existing only in potentiality toward something) she leads it into act by ineffable virtue. ### CHAPTER XIII.
### *Concerning the number seven, and which mysteries are contained beneath it.*

The number seven results from unity, the number two, and the number four, from which is born the *Diapason* <note>original: "Diapason"; the musical interval of an octave</note>, which is the most perfect harmony; by its power and proportion, God descends from his immortal and purely formal throne into the universal sphere of the material world, informing and composing all things. Therefore, this number was powerful and effective in the mystery of creation and was concerned with holy things; it is called the *number of rest*. For *the seventh day was the Sabbath day*. It is also called the *number of perfection*, because beyond the harmony of the Octave (which consists of seven intervals) there is no passage for simple sounds in harmony. Likewise, it is the *number of blessing and bliss*; hence the Poet says: *O thrice and four times blessed, etc.* <note>original: "O terque quaterque beatus"; a quote from Virgil's Aeneid, where 3+4 equals the perfect 7.</note> Furthermore, even the unformed matter of the world is blessed by the perfection of this harmony. The Pythagoreans also called this the *number of virginity*, because it is the first <insert>prime</insert> number that is neither generated <note>by multiplication of other numbers</note> nor generates <note>any number within the first ten</note>, nor can it be divided into two equal parts. Moreover, it is called the *number of the oath*; thus Abraham, when he struck a covenant with Abimelech, set out seven lambs as a witness. It is also the *number of health and cleansing from unclean diseases*. Thus the Prophet Elisha said to Naaman the leper: *Go, and wash seven times in the Jordan*. Indeed, it is also called the *number of holiness and praise*, whence the Prophet said: *Seven times a day I have spoken praise to you*. It is also called the *number of vengeance and punishment*, whence it is written: *Vengeance shall be given sevenfold for Cain*, and elsewhere: *Cain shall be punished sevenfold*. And elsewhere: *He who kills Cain shall pay seven vengeances*. Furthermore, it is the *number of the salvation of the worlds*; for seven of every clean animal were introduced into Noah’s ark. It is the *number of servitude*, as Jacob served seven years for Leah. It is the *number of destruction and ruin*, as on the seventh day, all the fountains of the abyss being broken, the water flooded over the lands. It is the *number of mourning*, as for seven days the people mourned for Israel, etc. It is the *critical number* observed by all Physicians, such as: *And at the seventh hour the fever left the nobleman's son*. And infinite other observations can be devised in this hidden and mystical number, all of which it would be as laborious for me to express in this place as it would perhaps be tedious for the reader; so that I shall leave aside the number of the planets, the climacteric years, the seven ages, the seven metals, and innumerable other things. And the reason (unless I am mistaken) for all these properties of the number seven—why, namely, they turn as much toward good as toward evil—is because this number participates both with the nature of light, form, perfection, and purity (insofar as the first part of its composition is the number three) and partly from the nature of the matter of darkness (since its latter number, namely 4, is the number of imperfection and uncleanness). Therefore, this number is both the author of life and composition, and the author of death and dissolution; insofar as it is composed of the first odd number, namely the number three (the number of life), and the first even number, namely four. For the number two is not called a "number" by the Pythagoreans, but a confusion of unities. From the odd, therefore, as the active—that is, form—and from the even as the passive—that is, matter,

matter, all things are generated, and by that same path they are dissolved; but generation and life are a supernatural light and a harmonizing force, while corruption belongs to the lower regions and to the night and the tearing darkness. Hence it is that, according to the doctrine of *Orpheus, Hesiod, Euripides,* and others, the divine Sun exists in the archetype, from which all beauty, all ornament, all harmony, and the spring of life flow; in whose right hand is piety, kindness, and beneficence; in the left, severe punishment. This they call *Phoebus, Apollo, and the Sun,* whom they say carries the *Graces and Charities* in his right hand and a bow and arrows in his left; whom by night they named *Dionysus* <note>The Greek god of wine and ecstasy, often associated with ritual "tearing apart" or sparagmos</note> tearing and ripping apart, and breaking himself into seven parts; and in the daytime they named him *Apollo*, putting back together those things which he had torn apart by night, and dividing them into seven parts. In the night, therefore, he breaks apart and tears, and in the day he unites things, as if driving away evils. For this reason, therefore, he is called by the Athenians *Alexicacos* <note>original: "Alexicacos", meaning "averter of evil"</note>, that is, the driver-away of evils, and by Number *Hygieia* <note>original: "ὑγίειαν", meaning health or wholeness</note>, that is, the author of health. With these things also seems to agree that opinion of the Pythagoreans, who *enclosed the world and the soul within seven limits.* In the first place, they set forward unity, as the extreme step of the soul and mind, through which it contains the supreme unity in the Creator, and is made one and the same with him; for all things pre-existing in the Word were one with that Word according to the Theologians. *The second place* (containing a double proportion compared to the first) denotes the progress of the soul or mind with God. *The third* demonstrates the entrance into itself, and thus is described the proceeding of the persons of the Trinity, namely of one into another and the return of the third again into unity. But now one arrives at the sending forth of the Spirit of the Lord into the imperfect mass, and thus one proceeds to the number four. *The fourth* signifies the exit which it makes from itself, so that it may be occupied with things to be created, and those still unformed. And thus in the *fifth, sixth, and seventh* (which two last limits or places consist of solid numbers) it denotes the transformation of bodies to which the soul is joined—I say of bodies: for the world consists of a double body, namely of the incorruptible and celestial, and of the corruptible and elementary. So also man, to retain a perfect image of the world, according to the Platonists, was made of a double body, one elementary, the other celestial. The elementary is noted by the cube or solid of the number two, which designates matter, and the celestial by the cube of the number three, which cube we said above was rather a surface or square number, for the reasons we brought forward there. For although the spiritual elements are in themselves fluid bodies, yet if ether and air and fire are compared to solid bodies, they relate to them as a surface to a body, or as a square to a cube.

### CHAPTER XIV.
### On the wonderful property of the number seven and the changes in its square: On the number filling its square: and on the base derived from it.

It is certainly not to be doubted that great secrets lie hidden in this number seven, since it is frequently used in the Holy Bible both in the performance of divine mysteries and in other matters of nature and human necessity or custom. Nor should men, treading in the footsteps of the foolish and ignorant, say that there is no greater secret in this number than in the others, and consequently, that the frequent repetition of this number in the sacred writings signifies nothing more hidden than any other number. For as by demonstration—

For in 175 (which is the base of the septenary number), we find the number seven exactly 25 times. Similarly, seven multiplied by seven will produce 49. From the parts of this number, considered in arithmetic progression and arranged in a square fashion, the base of the septenary—namely 175—leaps forth in a certain miraculous way by proceeding from any point of the square to its opposite. Here, therefore, in the prescribed square, we see a progression has been made (though seemingly disordered) from 1 up to 49, so that seven multiplied by itself brings forth the number filling the square by its progression. If, therefore, we proceed in a straight line from one corner or point of any side to the side or corner opposite to it, the base of the septenary square will be produced, containing exactly twenty-five times seven. 

Thus, by crossing from **a** to **b**, we will find these numbers: 22, 5, 30, 13, 38, 21, and 46, which added together will produce 175. So also by collecting the numbers between **c** and **d**, which are 47, 23, 6, 31, 14, 39, and 15, the same base will arise. Similarly, by adding together the numbers found between **e** and **f**, namely 16, 48, 24, 7, 32, 8, and 40, this same base will result. So also by looking at the sides, the numbers between p & q and those also between r & s, likewise t & u, and between w & x and between y & z, and between Venus <note>original: V</note> & Taurus <note>original: ♉</note> and between Gemini <note>original: ♊</note> & Cancer <note>original: ♋</note>, we shall find that they produce the same unique base by their proper position and joining together into one; which indeed can be considered a miracle. From this, therefore, the admirable mutability and variety of the number seven <term>septenary: the number seven or a group of seven</term> is made manifest to the eyes, and it seems to reveal to the wise man, in a certain way, the wonderful effects and virtues of that number which undoubtedly lie hidden in secret (of which we spoke briefly in the previous chapter). Indeed, how great is the perfection in the base of this septenary number, and how much the completion of this number brings happiness to human life, seems to be clearly proved to us by that blessed age of Abraham, consisting of 175 years, of which the Holy Scriptures speak thus in Genesis 25:7: *And these were the days of the life of Abraham's age which he lived, a hundred and seventy-five years, and failing, he died in a good old age, and at an advanced age and full of days etc.* <note>The author links Abraham's lifespan (25 x 7) to the perfection of the number seven.</note> From this it is clear that this number of solar revolutions produces an advanced age, a happy old age, and a fullness of days; and from that it is evident that there is an infinite mystery in the consideration of this septenary number: Indeed, I myself have known a most learned man who, by the power of this number seven, with the assistance of a certain kind of oracle, did not hesitate to resolve doubtful and perilous questions, and even promised to divine in a certain way concerning hidden things, both present and future.

### CHAPTER XV.
### On the mystery of divine numbers in creation.

We mentioned above that simple numbers or digits refer to the supernatural essence and belong to the super-celestial region, which is indeed infinite; here, however, we have proposed to treat the divine reason of the number five <term>quinary: the number five</term>, and then finally of the number ten <term>denary: the number ten</term>. Indeed, as we demonstrated above that the monad or unity is the source and origin of all numbers—from which the Dyad <note>the number two</note> is derived, not as a number, but as a confusion of unities, insofar as it contains "one" twice within itself, and which we therefore called the principle of the imperfect number, because it has a beginning and a middle but lacks an end—not otherwise than we called the number three the beginning of the perfect number, insofar as it has within itself a beginning, a middle, and an end, and is therefore held among the numbers of perfection: so we have said that in respect to these three terms, namely 1, 2, and 3, there is a relation through all other numbers proceeding into infinity. Therefore, just as unity is the root of the first perfect number, namely three, which signifies universal form. (For what does it matter if GOD exists as unity, and the universal spirit in potentiality as duality, if that spirit is not informed and actuated by that GOD, so that the duality is finally perfected into a Trinity?) So also duality is the root of the imperfect number four <term>quaternary: the number four</term>, and of those which arise from it. And hence it is that, as 3 relates to 1, so in the same proportion 5 relates to 3, and 7 to 5, and 9 to 7. Similarly, as one relates to 2, so 4 relates to 2, and 6 to 4, and 8 to 6, according to which simple progressions all other compound ones are drawn out, but their perfection is unity: Wherefore, as in the middle movement from unity imperfection arises, so by its addition at the end the third term is brought forth, from which the first of the perfect numbers arises, namely three. From this it is clear that both imperfection and perfection—that is, both evil as far as we are concerned, and good—flow from the hands of God or unity, in whose power is that which is evil,

We see, therefore, that the imperfection of matter produced by God is present in duality <note>The number two, often associated in Pythagorean and Hermetic thought with division, opposition, and the material world</note>, which nevertheless becomes perfect through the presence of unity. Yet you should not believe that I have said or understood the second person in the Trinity to be imperfect, insofar as in the super-essential world the Spirit of the Father is always present with the Son, and consequently there is trinity in unity and duality in trinity: Which indeed that wondrous word, the Tetragrammaton <note>The four-letter Hebrew name of God, YHWH</note>, consisting of Jod, He, and Vau, He, explains most excellently; where the aspiration of the *He* denotes the spirit in each procession, and seems to join the *Vau* with the *Jod* from the right, and again the *Jod* with the *Vau* toward the right. Thus the Son, in the number of perfection, is said to sit at the right hand of the Father: thus also he is said to go out from the center of the Father, insofar as he is the medium of the boundaries of perfection. Wherefore it is to be understood that the middle of any number refers to the son and the center, because the middle of a number is always understood to be in odd and perfect numbers: Thus in the number three there is duality <note>as the two units flanking the center</note>, in five there is trinity, in seven there is quaternity, in nine there is quinary, which is also the exact middle (insofar as a middle is considered in even numbers) of the number ten, through which God, descending from his super-formal kingdom, immerses himself into confused matter, creating that thing out of nothing, and informing the shapeless by his act and light.

But here I would wish you to know, that where we speak of the middle of an even number, we do not mean its center, which is plainly empty and nothing, but its half part: As the center of the Dyad <note>the number two</note> is nothing, because it has only two boundaries, but its half part is 1. So the middle of the number four is two, but it lacks a center. And so in the others, as 6, 8, 10. From which it is clear that all perfection lies in odd numbers, where a center is found, as in 3, 1 is the center, and 1 is the boundary from which, and 1 is the boundary to which: And in the quinary <note>5</note> likewise 1 is the center, and 2 is one half part and 2 the other, and in 7, 1 is the center, 3 the boundaries, etc. Therefore, in perfect simples, unity is the boundary from which, trinity the boundary to which, and duality the medium, but in such a way that that duality is unity: So also trinity is the boundary from which, and trinity making six is the medium, and trinity completing nine is the period; but here the center is superficial; Or trinity is the beginning, five the middle, and seven the end; in the same way five is the beginning, seven the middle, and nine the exit: In all of which the trinity of persons considered in the super-substantial nature is found, that is, where form is totally regarded, and not matter. And by this harmony GOD acted for the ordering of his super-essential kingdom in eternity, before he had decreed anything in his most holy counsel concerning the creation of matter.

In this place, however, it must be observed that, as unity is of all forms, like a center, so also the number three is the first and nearest emanation of the divine majesty from its nature toward the thing to be created, and the number five the second, seven the third, and nine the last, so that there are five processes of the emanation of divine light, namely the emission of the luminous form from unity toward 3, and from three toward 5, and from five toward 7, and from seven toward 9, and from nine toward 1, which number by the apposition of a cipher constitutes 10. From which it is clear that if GOD does not enter the abyss of matter, then he reflects his rays into himself, or into his center and his unity, according to that saying of Hermes Trismegistus: *The Monad generates a monad and reflects its heat into itself.* <note>original: "Monas generat monadem & in seipsum reflectit ardorem suum."</note> Nor indeed does God, considered in his super-essential nature, depart from the odd number, insofar as he rejoices and delights in it: But, when he had proposed to himself to tread the path of the shapeless spirit, hiddenly immersed in the womb of *hyle* <note>The Greek term for primordial matter</note>, he immersed himself into the abyss of imperfect matter through his son proceeding immediately from him through the way and number of imperfection: for he alone...

<margin>†</margin> He alone, who has entered the field of the perfect binary number, was able to penetrate to the imperfect binary <note>The "binary" or number two often represents the first step away from the unity of God toward the multiplicity of the world.</note> which exists in potentiality toward something else. From this, the super-substantial duality, by doubling itself, rendered the middle as the number seven, and in this way joined perfection with imperfection in the first stage of procession from its super-celestial nature to the mundane. For the number four <term>quaternitas: the quaternary</term> is an even number, and consequently imperfect, whereas the number three <term>ternarius: the ternary</term> is a perfect number; thus, from their first meeting, it is likely that matter or imperfection (which is referred to by the number four) is to be joined with perfection, insofar as the number three (which is attributed to form) is connected with it to complete the number seven. Similarly, the number four is the superficial mean between two and six; denoting thereby that the Word <note>The *Logos* or Christ.</note> becomes, as it were, the center of the operations of the six days of creation. Hence, after the heavens were established by the Word of the Lord on the fourth day, this King, forming his tabernacle, placed it on 그날 in the Sun. This fourth day, by dividing six into three dualities, was the superficial middle of the six days, or the essential center of the seventh day. Whence also the sun, adorned with its own brilliance, was placed in the middle of the world or the heavens. Similarly, the number four is the half of the number eight, which signifies the "elementated" <note>The physical body or matter composed of the four elements.</note> or the cube, by taking the half, as is estimated among even numbers. For the number four is the square of the root 2. Whence the four represent the elements produced by the Second Person <note>The Son/Word in the Trinity.</note>, from which the world is forged, and eight is the cube, from which the composition forged from the elements is made. Therefore, the mundane duality—that is, the universal spirit—is truly imperfect, produced into light from potentiality by the power of the uncreated duality, in the trinity of complete unity, from which the quaternary (or element) and the number eight (or the elementated) arise. One proceeds further, therefore, from unity toward creation in this manner:

The number five <term>quinarius: the quinary</term> is the perfect mean between the number two and the number eight; it denotes, therefore, that the Second Person is in the middle between the universal Spirit and the elementated, and consequently, that the Word is in us and in all composite things as the center, life, and essence. The number five is also the center of all the digits, namely of the number nine, insofar as on one side are 1, 2, 3, 4, and on the other 6, 7, 8, 9 are found. Whence it is also the center among super-substantial things: Therefore the Son is the center between the Father and the Spirit, and is the center in super-substantial things, the center in things created and uncreated, the center of the uncreated Spirit and of the entire world dwelling in the Sun; he is the center of the elements, and the center of the elementated. He is therefore the life of uncreated things, the life of the darkness, the life of the spirit or the created waters, holding his palace in the heart of the firmament; he is the life of the elements in the middle sphere or the sphere of equality, sometimes appearing wonderfully in the center of the elements or the middle of the air; he is the life of the elementated, insofar as he is the essence and brilliance of wonders, the specific form of vegetables, the being of animals, by which the life, reason, intellect, and mind of men breathe, insofar as he dwells abundantly in him—since, according to the witness of Paul <note>Referring to 1 Corinthians 6:19, "your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit."</note>, his members are a temple and palace for his very divinity. Whence, by reason of the presence of this eternal Sun, he is called the Microcosm <note>The "Little World," i.e., Man as a reflection of the Universe.</note>. And this was that Word of whom Saint John makes mention, calling it the life and light of every thing of this world, which the darkness did not comprehend, nor the world know; that "LET THERE BE" <note>original: *FIAT*</note> cited at the beginning of the first book, by whose power every creature was made. And in this way, the super-substantial Dyad, overflowing with uncreated spirit, progressed to the threshold or vestibule of entering matter <note>original: *hylam* (from Greek *hyle*)</note>, namely up to the number ten; which was therefore divided by divine unity into the number two, so that it, existing as uncreated unity, might make man, who was nothing, into one double being: namely, God and man.

man, and consequently attributed a dual nature to his own exemplar of the human species—namely, a divine and a human nature. Thus, by the power of the first unity (which is formal, uncreated, and immortal), man might become immortal; yet, through the imperfection of the second nature (the material and created nature which produces confusion), he is rendered mortal due to the failure of his end. But truly, when the life-giving Spirit shall arrive, that imperfection of man will be corrected, and duality will migrate into a trinity by the arrival of the uncreated spirit. He shall be exalted from mortal imperfection to immortal perfection, so that there shall be a resurrection from death to eternal life. Was it not by the arrival, descent, and presence of this divine spirit that the dead were awakened to life at that time when the Creator of the world—with this, His most Holy Spirit, returning into His own dead body—triumphantly rose from death into life by putting on incorruption? And so man shall acquire a double spirit: namely, the first, which provides temporal life to the body, and finally the last, which is immortal and like unto the divine, making the other like a GOD <note>original: "quasi DEUM"</note>—namely, by the power and grace of the supreme Monad <note>The Monad refers to the ultimate divine Unity or the "One."</note> through the justice of the uncreated Dyad <note>The Dyad refers to the principle of duality or "twoness."</note>. He <note>The Hebrew letter He (ה), often associated with the breath of life or the divine name.</note> now possesses spirit in materiality or duality, and he shall possess a doubled *He* afterward, because he will approach the nature of the Tetragrammaton <note>The four-letter name of God, YHWH.</note> itself. Hence man, surrounded on all sides by the Holy Spirit, shall acquire and obtain divinity for himself through grace, and shall be made most similar to his own Creator. Wherefore GOD said after the sin of Adam: *Behold, Adam is become as one of us, etc. And now, lest he put forth his hand, and take also of the tree of life, and eat, and live for ever, Jehovah sent him forth from the paradise of pleasure, etc. Genesis 3:22.* Hence also Hermes Trismegistus says: *O Asclepius, man is a great miracle, a living creature to be honored and adored: for he passes into the nature of GOD, as if he himself were GOD.* The Doctors and Cabalists <note>Jewish mystics and scholars of the Kabbalah.</note> of the Hebrews also seem to give the reason for this matter according to natural intention in this definition of the human soul: *The soul of man is the light of God, and a created substance of God according to the image of the Word, the cause of causes, the first exemplar, and shaped by a seal, whose character is the eternal Word.*

### C H A P T E R XVI.
### *On the admirable mysteries of the numbers five and ten.*

From the aforesaid, therefore, it clearly appears that the number five <note>the "quinarius"</note> is the center of the number ten <note>the "denarius"</note>, in which unity doubles itself, or repeats itself beyond the limit of simplicity. And just as duality was the first midpoint of the number three—namely, the boundary between 1 and 2 (where both boundaries are odd, and consequently perfect)—so in the first number of composition, or the first article, where divine unity joins itself with the cipher or unformed matter (namely, in 10), the number five is found to be the center (speaking improperly) and the middle: namely, between 1 and 10. But from this a great mystery is revealed: namely, that just as in the prior terms 1, 2, 3, the "two" is perfected by the front and back parts because of the perfection of unity and trinity (for nothing except perfection exists in the super-celestial kingdom), so in the terms 1, 5, 10, in which unity proceeds through duality—or GOD through the Word—toward creation, 5 (which is the middle number) is found between its origin 1 and 10. Hence, because 10 is an even number, it denotes the imperfection of the matter to be created; wherefore its middle or center, which ought to be its life, is a perfect number, so that it may be perfected by its perfection. From this, it appears how the order of the parts of the created world was impressed upon the idea of the Archetype <note>The original divine blueprint of the universe</note> before creation. For between the first grade—namely, between 1 and 3—is found 2, to which is referred the universal spirit, which Unity produced into creation. Next, between 3 and 5 is the number 4, denoting in the divine idea that the universal spirit is to be divided into four natures in the second grade. Then, between 5 and 7 is placed 6, signifying the separation of the waters from the waters, and the pure creation of the higher living creatures. Afterward, between 7 and 9, the number eight <note>Latin: *octonarius*</note> denotes the composition of the celestial bodies derived from a simpler and purer cube; among these we can also count the human composition, insofar as we find that man was saved in the number eight from the flood <note>A reference to the eight people on Noah's Ark</note>; and from a coarser cube, all other elemental things are formed.

Here we see that the number five is the medium and center of all grades. And from this it has come to pass that among created things, the Quintessence <note>The "fifth essence" or ether, believed to be the pure substance of the heavens</note> holds the middle place, and the Sun, the palace of duality, is situated in the midst of the quintessence. Hence the order of unities, whose center is 3, disposes the super-celestial things; and the order of tens, whose center is 5, distributes the worldly things. Thus 1 and 3 constitute 4; and 2 and 3 make 5, which is the center of the number ten.

### CHAPTER I.
### On divine harmony and the simple consonances.

[Large decorative initial V] Just as material numbers in themselves produce nothing but discord and dissonance in the material world, so also the essential and simple numbers found in the formal world <note>The "formal world" refers to the realm of pure ideas and spiritual archetypes, as opposed to the physical world.</note> can, without doubt, propagate nothing except concord, union, and love, both in their own region and in the material sphere. But in its own immense kingdom, this divine harmony is heard with ineffable and incomprehensible joy and gladness, without any obstacle or impediment of discord (which entered into the material world from the beginning along with strife). In the world, however, this harmony acts, having been frequently multiplied, for the correction of litigious matter and dissonant darkness. This is indeed demonstrated by the number of the Holy Trinity in this manner: For the Monad <note>The number one, representing unity or God the Father.</note> joined with the Dyad <note>The number two.</note> produces the *diatessaron* <note>The musical interval of a perfect fourth.</note>, consisting of three intervals; yet four voices are found there, because the Spirit is present there in the union of unity with duality; thus the Son is said to be in the Father, and the Father with the Son, and the Spirit with both. Again, by the connection of the duality with the number three, the *diapente* <note>The musical interval of a perfect fifth.</note> will arise, since in such a number five voices are found constituting the *diapente* and four intervals (since it is merely the addition of one tone or "sounding person" to the *diatessaron*, which consists of three intervals). For under this consonance the two first persons meet, and a twofold spirit proceeds from both. Therefore, that most exalted name, the *Tetragrammaton* <note>The four-letter Hebrew name of God, YHWH.</note>, denotes these two consonances comprised within the Trinity: namely, *Jod He* and *Vau He*, where the aspiration (*He*) denotes the Spirit proceeding from both. For the letter (*He*) itself terminates both duplicated syllables and the entire name. It is pronounced, therefore, by these four letters as *Jova* <note>Jehovah</note>. And in this way, we have the two more simple consonances now open and manifest in the individual Trinity, from the union of which the *diapason* <note>The musical interval of an octave.</note> is made, which is integrated from the *diatessaron* and the *diapente*. In the <term>diatessaron</term> <note>original: "diatessaron"; the musical interval of a perfect fourth</note> with the <term>diapente</term> <note>original: "diapente"; the musical interval of a perfect fifth</note>, the last voice of the fourth is the first voice of the fifth; consequently, there are no more than eight voices found in the <term>diapason</term> <note>original: "diapason"; the musical interval of an octave</note>. Finally, since the octave draws the efficacy of its consonance from the unison, its symphony is therefore connected with unity, from which it is numbered and derived. Again, if we proceed by way of proportions, we find that unity and duality stand in a double proportion <note>2:1 ratio</note>, from which the octave is made. And 2 to 3 is in a <term>sesquialter</term> <note>3:2 ratio</note> proportion, from which the fifth consists. And 3 to the <term>Tetragrammaton</term> <note>The four-letter name of God in Hebrew</note>, or the conjunction of the Trinity with unity, denotes a <term>sesquitertial</term> <note>4:3 ratio</note> proportion, from which the fourth arises. Furthermore, if unity led into itself brings forth a unison, duality multiplied by itself will bring forth the four voices of the fourth. And again, 3 multiplied by 2, with unity added besides, will produce seven, denoting the intervals of that consonance which is called the octave; or by the addition of duality, its 8 voices will appear; or by the addition of 3, the number nine will leap forth, in which the voices of the fourth and fifth are encompassed.

Still proceeding by the backward way, 3 joined with unity denotes the four voices of the fourth, and 3 with duality denotes the five sounds of the fifth; to which if the Trinity is added, the eight voices of the octave will come forth. From this it clearly appears that, however the persons of the Trinity are taken, they are always found in concord and symphony, and are observed to be immune from all discord and contrariety. For if we look at twice three, there also we find the fifth with a tone, completing that concord which is called a <term>sixth</term> among musicians; finally, if the number three is led into itself, it will also produce a musical consonance, namely 9 voices fashioned and risen from the fifth and the fourth; since the fourth is fashioned from 4 voices and the fifth from five, which added together are observed to produce the most perfect consonance of the octave. The demonstration of this music follows here, insofar as it is found in the Trinity alone.

# CHAPTER II.
*How worldly harmony maintains itself in the same manner as divine harmony, and that worldly and material symphony proceeds from that which is divine and formal.*

As the number ten <note>The Decad, representing the completion of the universe in Pythagorean thought.</note> relates to unity, so also does the harmony of the material world relate to that of the formal and supersubstantial world. And as unity was the beginning of the Music and concord of the Trinity, so also the number three multiplied by itself <note>original: "ternarius in se ductus," referring to 3x3=9</note> is the starting point of symphonic composition, because 9 is the beginning of the number ten and the end of the simple numbers. Hence, for the formation and consonance of the material world, the Spirit of the Lord (who was the third person of the Trinity)—taking the place of unity as the Spirit of the Trinity within itself—was carried over the waters, imparting to them a fiery love and a melody proceeding from the most holy harmony. Therefore, the Spirit of Jehovah (with whom is the power of the Father, and consequently, supersubstantial unity; and the wisdom of the Son, and consequently, supersubstantial duality; and the grace proper to Him) is here, I say, found as three and one in the number ten. Because He was now occupied with material composition, He claimed for Himself the place of unity in the universal and material essence. From Him, the second person flowed forth: namely the Sun, whom Plato for this reason called the visible son of God; nor indeed did he wander far from the truth in this opinion, since, as the Royal Prophet <note>King David, in the Psalms.</note> testifies, GOD placed his tabernacle in it. The Sun is therefore like a second person in the material world, receiving its glowing and splendid virtue from the first, or the fiery Spirit of GOD, which is seen to illuminate the waters of the middle region of the world, as well as the lowest, in the likeness of its Father (from whom it held its power), and to pour lives into the lower things every year. However, we call the third person of the material world Man, proceeding from the first and second; hence, *Hermes Trismegistus* says, *God is the light and life of man*, and another Philosopher teaches us, *the sun and man generate man.* *Hermes Trismegistus* also says in another place: *The world is the son of God, the sun is the son of the world, and man is the son of the sun.* But we understand the "world" as the universal essence of matter, containing within itself three persons worthy of admiration (if it be permitted to compare substantial things with supersubstantial ones) in the same way as the divine essence contains its own. But God, the life of the world, and the fiery and loving Spirit, is esteemed as the first person of the world, from whom primarily the other two and all other things are derived. But GOD is present to his simple and formal world in unity, but to the material world in the number ten, so that He may mingle Himself with the formless waters to give them shape, and to drive away their dissonances and strifes by the symphony of His splendid countenance, and to bind the elements to one another in harmonious peace by an inviolable bond of concord. Since, therefore, the material world is only a type and image of the Archetype, or the supersubstantial world, we have deduced this our worldly Music and the consonances of its every region or heaven from the observation of that divine harmony. First, therefore, we perceive with diligent intuition that the unity of the Trinity joined with duality produces the consonance of the *diatessaron* <note>The interval of a perfect fourth.</note> born from three intervals. According to this model, we notice that the three hierarchies or regions of the empyrean heaven have produced a formula of melody not unlike it in their arrangement (by the breathing of the divine Spirit). Again, we perceive that, just as unity relates to duality in a double proportion, which constitutes the consonance of the *diapason* <note>The interval of an octave.</note>, so also in a similar way the upper proportion of the pyramid of universal matter, or the first region, beginning from its cone or the beginning of the first heaven, relates to the intersection made by the two pyramids in the heart of heaven.

of the second or ethereal heaven, since one portion of the pyramid found in the empyrean heaven is found to be in a double proportion <note>original: "dupla proportione"; the 2:1 ratio which creates an octave</note> to that of the middle heaven, as we have reviewed more fully in our account of worldly harmony. Next, because in the second place, 2 added to 3 produces 5, a number which denotes the *diapente* <note>The interval of a perfect fifth</note> consonance composed of five sounds or voices; similarly, because 2 stands to 3 in a sesquialterate proportion <note>The 3:2 ratio</note> (in which the *diapente* consonance is found), therefore this proportion is found twice between the second and third heaven; namely, once by counting upward from the Sun toward the highest heaven, and once by proceeding downward as far as the elementary heaven. Finally, since in the third place, proceeding circularly, the unity of the trinity stands to its own number in a sesquitertial proportion <note>The 4:3 ratio</note>, therefore the *diateſſarōn* <note>The interval of a perfect fourth</note> consonance is found in the third heaven, which is discovered in such a proportion just as it is between the first person of the Trinity and the last. But in this place (contemplating it in passing), a great mystery (as it seems to me) is to be drawn out: namely, that although bodies in the final and thicker proportion of the material pyramid resound in the most imperfect consonance, submerged in the abyss of imperfection and as if in darkness—namely, in the material *diateſſarōn*—they nevertheless have a relation to unity in the sesquitertial proportion. Thus, there is hope for the resolution of bodies after death, through which that form and mind veiled in human bodies, which rose from unity, may return again to unity by a circular path. From these things, therefore, it appears clearer than the sun to those looking diligently, that the *diateſſarōn* consonance of the empyrean heaven, joined with the upper *diapente* of the middle heaven, constitutes the supreme and spiritual *diapaſon* <note>The interval of an octave</note> consonance of the greater world, beginning from God and ending in the Sun; and consequently it is indicated that the *diateſſarōn* of the first heaven and the upper *diapente* of the second heaven are the simplest and most spiritual consonances of the entire mass of the material world. Similarly, by joining the lower *diapente* of the middle heaven with the *diateſſarōn* of the lowest heaven, these consonances joined together compose a material *diapaſon*, beginning from the Sun and ending on the earth. From this it is established that the lower *diapente* and *diateſſarōn* consonances tend more toward matter than toward form; hence they are called "material," whereas conversely the upper ones are so called insofar as they regard form and fully informed spirits. We see, therefore, that a triple harmony exists, composed of three consonances of symphony; of which the *former* is occupied in uncreated essence where there is no discord, in the middle world—namely the formal essence of the Trinity; the *two latter* are included in created matter, namely *one* in the material world, specifically in its subtler part, and the other in the denser part subject to opacity. But indeed, that uncreated symphony is united by an indissoluble bond to created harmony; namely, the supersubstantial form is united to the material and substantial by this path: by the triple number of the trinity (which contains the *diapaſon* within itself) added to the quaternary number of matter (for according to the Pythagoreans, two in matter is not a number but a confusion of unities, as has been said, wherefore they maintain that the quaternary number <note>The number 4</note> is the first even number), the septenary number <note>The number 7</note> is produced. This begets the consonance of all perfection, namely the *diapaſon*, which is that bond by which GOD has both bound the music of life and light to his creatures in the cosmos and liberally pours it into the sons of the cosmos.

### **C H A P T E R  III.**
*On the nature of worldly, elementary, and physical discord; and how*
**GOD** *bound the discordant daughters of chaos with harmonious*
*peace.*

**W**e have declared above the reason why the material "Two" <note>The "Dyad," representing the first departure from unity into division and matter.</note> is considered a most imperfect number; namely, because it is deprived of the members of perfection by which it might be completed. For even if matter had already been brought into action from the shapeless bowels of chaos or primeval matter, nevertheless it did not possess the active principle of its own essence through itself;

<summary>This page features a complex "Monochord" diagram illustrating the harmonic intervals (octaves, fifths, and fourths) that link God, the angelic realm, the stars, and the elements. The text begins Chapter III, explaining how God imposes mathematical order and "musical" peace upon the naturally discordant state of raw matter.</summary>

ON DIVINE HARMONY. 53

<meta>This page continues the philosophical discussion of the origins of musical and cosmic harmony, contrasting the divine source of order with the diabolical source of discord.</meta>

It acquired the principle of its perfection from an absolutely formal nature—namely, from the unity of the divinity, which was the author of its existence. For how is it possible for perfection to exist in a thing by itself (speaking in an absolute manner) when it cannot even exist without the help of another? Since, therefore, duality multiplied within itself and divided into intervals produces nothing but even numbers; and since every symphony is perfected from consonances <note>In Renaissance music theory, "consonance" refers to intervals that sound pleasing and stable to the ear.</note> which are composed solely of odd intervals, how is it possible for duality to propagate the consonances of melody, and consequently harmony, in any way (by producing only odd numbers through multiplication)? On the contrary, it will instead give birth to discords and dissonances most opposed to harmony.

From this it is established that GOD and the most holy Trinity are the sole and unique origin of concord; the Devil, conversely, is the parent of discord and antipathy, which is why he has also earned the name of Strife <note>original: "Litigii"</note>. GOD, therefore, uses formal light for the birth of proportional and most perfect symphony; the Devil, however, uses matter, darkness, and their veil for his dissensions and strifes. Hence arises the tireless repugnance between concord and discord, between light and darkness, between the mind and the spirit prone to downward paths, between the soul and the body.

And this is why the most powerful Father of concord uses the sublime peak of the universal organ <note>The "universal organ" refers to the "Musica Mundana" or the music of the spheres, where the universe is envisioned as a giant musical instrument.</note> as his throne; but the father of discord, cast down to the center of the machine <note>The "machine" refers to the physical structure of the cosmos.</note>, holds his dwelling there, and is forced to overshadow his envious face with a cover or veil of darkness, lest the author of concord utterly exterminate him with his rays. By this kind of concord and symphony of the Trinity, the power of Strife and antipathy is broken and scattered; the hierarchies of Angels are peacefully bounded and distinguished; the glowing fires are suspended in the equal scales of justice; the four quarreling elements are arranged and established in places of symphony through the bonds of concord, with peace and admirable harmony, by proportions proper and suitable to them.

The bodies of both simple and composite things are moved toward and harmonize with the music of their souls; and so, by the virtue of this super-celestial symphony, all material things would tend from imperfection toward perfection and would suddenly become perfect from being imperfect, were it not that discord—with its delusions, darkness, and world full of errors—interposed itself at every hour into the actions of concord. It blinds the wills of living creatures, and indeed the very eyes of men (both physical and intellectual), with its illusions, fantasies, and deceptions. By these, even good souls (dwelling in their temporary lodgings <note>A metaphor for the human body as a temporary home for the soul.</note>) are deceived by his errors and fallacies, and wrongly accept falsehoods or lies for truths, and iniquity for justice.

Hence comes the fear of death and dissolution; hence all the daughters of darkness, or the vices; hence the fall of Adam; hence evils are accepted in place of goods; hence the love of the world and its vanities; and consequently, the hatred of God the Creator and of truth itself. All these knots and bonds of the Devil, GOD—by the virtue of his symphony and through his mercy, when it shall please him—will most easily unknot and dissolve, finally revealing the rays of truth to the world.

# THE FIRST TREATISE,

## Concerning the internal microcosm. <note>The "microcosm" refers to the human being viewed as a "little world" that mirrors the vast universe or macrocosm.</note>

### PREFACE.
*In which the author endeavors to explain to the world, briefly and in very few words, the reason why he is engaged in an exact inquiry into his own soul.*

Since we are urged to know ourselves both by the admonition of the sacred scriptures and by the teaching of the ancient philosophers, we ought no longer delay in making ourselves—who have been unknown and hidden even to our own selves—finally known and manifest to the best of our ability. For it is a sign of the greatest negligence to be ignorant of that very thing by whose profound power we contemplate celestial, and indeed even divine matters; by which we investigate and finally track down natural things with such subtle inquiry; and by which we desire such sublime things from our Creator himself. The soul, by which we perceive these things, is not a foreign object, nor is it to be sought far from us in distant places; rather, it is always with us, present, acting, speaking, and born within. It has been granted the power to know the secrets of such vast things, and yet can it not know itself? It is permitted to few, indeed, to discern the soul by the soul itself; that is, for the soul to see itself. However, by a certain divine providence, it is impossible for the faculty of discovery to be lacking in religious souls who piously, purely, and diligently seek themselves and their God. For souls of this kind are capable of receiving the rays of the divine mind, and being removed from the mist of the darkness of errors, Truth itself will be ready at hand for them, day and night, to serve them. For us, therefore, to whom a portion of the mind has been granted, it is especially necessary to consider—

We believe that we are recognizing our own lineage and considering our immortal nature, beholding the temple of GOD and GOD himself fixed in the center of his temple with ineffable joy. And when we have gazed upon our internal, immortal self with spiritual eyes, and have thereby rightly known ourselves, we shall pass into God himself, the Founder of both worlds. Therefore, so that I might restore myself to myself—or rather to my God, to whom I owe myself most of all—I have dedicated myself to the inquiry of my own soul. Having now become a pilgrim to the world, and having consigned to oblivion the tracks of the body and the dense things of the visible world, I am carried by an aerial boat through the spiritual waves of the invisible world. Emerging from the dark waves of the world and of opaque bodies, and climbing the ether of the heavens by betaking myself to the palaces of reason and intellect, I shall begin to contemplate with an enlightened mind that Unity sitting upon the highest peak of the heavens and of blessedness in incomprehensible joy and gladness. Therefore, I shall first render myself invisible, and by leaving behind the sensible step of the ladder of the internal man <note>The "sensible step" refers to the level of the five senses and physical perception.</note> which has been trodden many times, I shall lift my foot to the second step, proper to the imagination; afterwards, I shall rise with a light leap into the tracks of reason, and from its dominion I shall elevate my internal self to the intellectual region. May the Founder of the heavens and the Worker of body and soul be eternally favorable and propitious to me; may he clarify my eyes with the benign spirit of his wisdom, illuminate my mind with the rays of his divinity, and make my middle soul <note>The "middle soul" or *anima media* usually refers to the rational soul that mediates between the lower animal instincts and the higher divine intellect.</note> obedient to him, so that by treading the right path directly, I may clearly discern in the revealed mirror of divine Majesty what I truly am.

### CHAPTER I.
### That GOD made man equal in perfection to the whole world: Whence he is called the Microcosm.

The great Archetype <note>original: "Archetypus"; referring to God as the original model of all things.</note>, whose immense virtue we sang of in the first treatise of the first volume, wishing to complete his universal work (namely, of creation) with no less admiration than he began it, decorated the machine of the sixth day in its creation with his Spirit, just as he did on the first day of his workmanship with that machine of all things containing the empyrean spirit. And as we see in the composition of a circle, the starting point is so joined with the end point that there is no difference in the perfection of either end; so also in the circuit of creation, the Worker operated at the end with the same motion of divine action as he did in its beginning. For he sent forth his life-giving breath <note>original: "spiraculum"; a reference to the "breath of life" in Genesis.</note> over the dark and muddy face of the body, by which he might illuminate that dark and immobile body, make it beautiful and mobile, and render this last work more divine. Thus, from nothing he might produce something noble in action on this sixth and last day of creation, no less than he had done on its first day; for on that day he willed his divine Spirit to be carried over

...over the waters, to create the entire world out of nothing, and to illuminate his material spirit—which was overwhelmed by darkness—and to bestow upon it inexplicable virtues. By these, it would not only become more noble, but would also be regarded as a universal living being, as the Platonists maintained. And this, therefore, denotes to us above all else that the same virtues and operations exist in man, according to the proportion and quantity of his body, as are contained in the entire world, both visible and invisible. This is also what *Hermes Trismegistus* <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure associated with the "Hermetica," texts on philosophy and magic.</note> seems to affirm, saying that GOD fixed two images according to his own pattern, *namely the world and man*. And indeed, what can be found in the world that is not likewise found proportionally in man? For if we consider the ideal or invisible world, we shall find a portion of every region of it within the internal man. For that mind—a divine ray of uncreated light—is communicated to the internal man by the pleasure and will of the divine Architect, along with a composite portion of created light established in the spiritual heaven. And similarly, just as in the visible world there are two parts, namely heaven and earth—the former of which rains down forms onto the earth, while the latter receives and preserves them—so also in man, that celestial ray with its ethereal vehicle confers life and form upon that muddy body, which is called the "earth" of man. Furthermore, in both worlds there are certain parts not subject to corruption, namely the super-celestial and celestial; but a certain portion of the visible world is corruptible, namely the elementary. In the same way, therefore, the portions of the internal man are incorruptible, while the body and its visible parts are subject to corruption. The world is revolved and governed by the divine Spirit, and by this same essential power, the human body is also driven and revolved. Finally, He who is One created one world in His own likeness; and the same One also founded one living creature, namely man, in His own image, in which He was greatly delighted. Thus, not inaptly, man has been called another world and another image of God; for he has within himself everything that is contained in the greater universal world, to such an extent that nothing exists anywhere in it that is not truly and realistically found in man, performing the very same functions for him as it does in the greater world. For in him is the divine mind, angelic reason, celestial spirit, elementary harmony, the vegetation of the planets, and the senses of irrational animals. In all things, finally, he possesses the symbol of the world, and has operation and conversation with all things. Why then should this ultimate creature not be called by his proper name, *Microcosm* <term>Microcosm: "Little World," the idea that man is a miniature map of the entire universe.</term>, since he is in all things most similar to the Macrocosm? Moreover, since God the Architect is infinite, He created the world round and perfectly proportional in its members; are not the measurements of all human members likewise proportionate and consonant with those of the world, and matching them in roundness? The center of the circular world is the earth; but the central point of human roundness is, according to some, in the navel; but we think it should rather be placed near the genitals, since just as the seeds of things are hidden in the center of the world, so also the seminal power of man lies hidden near the testicles. From this boundary, then, if compasses are drawn, we shall perceive the external man to be exactly round, following the example of the external world, as is clearly explained in the following example.

## CHAPTER II.
*Concerning the interior or invisible Microcosm, and that it contains within itself all the ideal parts of the world.*

We call the interior Microcosm the hidden, invisible, and immortal portion of man, forged from the invisible parts of the invisible heavens of the macrocosm. By these parts, he not only performs his natural functions but is also accustomed to engage in divine contemplations by the power of his super-celestial portions. It is for this reason that both Theologians and Philosophers have called the inner man a "living soul," enfolding within itself the powers of intellect, sensation, and growth. Each of these is derived from a specific heaven of the greater world: namely, the **intellect** from the empyrean heaven <note>The highest, most spiritual realm of fire and light</note>, the **vital power** from the ethereal heaven, and the **operations of the senses** from the more formal qualities of the elements. We say, therefore, that the inner man is forged from invisible matter and a most pure and spiritual form. He possesses his material part from the substance of the ethereal heaven, just as the visible body possesses its own from the elements; however, his spiritual part maintains itself within its ethereal body just as that ethereal spirit dwells within the composite elementary body. For the rays of the superior region are like life and soul to the inferior heaven closest to them. From this it is clear that the intellectual part of man is like a soul to his own ethereal spirit, which, because of its preeminence over the lower parts of the internal man, gives man his name and his very being. And this is what Trismegistus intended in *Pymander, Book 1*, by asserting: *that the internal man consists of life and light, which are*

### CHAPTER III.
### On the infinite and ineffable property of light, and how man possesses within himself a portion of every luminous species.

IN the first volume, Treatise 1, we proved by both reasons and authorities that every thing is more noble the more essential light it contains within itself, and that greater or lesser imperfection proceeds from a greater or lesser abundance of body and matter; whereas greater or lesser perfection proceeds from the exuberance or diminution of the luminous form. For we said that God is pure and most simple uncreated light without any addition of matter; that is, purely formal and simply fiery: whence he is called the true, proper, and first light by Saint John in chapter 1. We also said that the substance of the Empyrean heaven itself is the fiery domicile of the light created on the first day, which is called Empyrean because fire has dominion in it: and this is in no way to be compared to the uncreated intellectual light and splendor, neither in time (since it is created) nor in perfection (since the composition of this place consists of one fourth part spiritual matter and three fourths of the simplest light). Furthermore, we proved that the substance of the middle heaven derived its form from that Empyrean origin; but, because it is the middle of the interval between the material heaven and the formal heaven, it therefore seems to participate equally in both extremes. Whence it is certain that the substance of this heaven is more imperfect and less formal than that supreme one; since it has more matter, but less form, than that; for it consists of two parts of coarser spirit and as many of light infused into it on the second day of creation from its source through the diaphragm of the Empyrean heaven: and hence it is called ether, as if *aith-aer* <note>original: "athäer"</note>, that is, fiery spirit, or fused equally from spirit and fire. Similarly, in the last place, we declared that light is weakest in the lowest heaven, but the substance of matter or the waters is most rebellious; for it consists of three fourths [matter] and one fourth of light; and thus it stands in this extreme in the quantity of matter, as in the other, namely the Empyrean, in the abundance of form. We also demonstrated that light is the simplest act of all, insofar as it is the simple act of intelligence and of the uncreated intellect, and first diffused from the divine mind into all things, yet in a different manner, according to the more rebellious or more obedient nature of the bodies. We say, therefore, that uncreated light is totally and originally in God the Father himself: for he is the Father of lights, indeed he is the first and true light itself, whose rays exist as the first acts, as Trismegistus <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure associated with hermetic philosophy</note> testifies: whence that saying: *I am the light of the world*, etc. We also affirm with Trismegistus and the Holy Scriptures, that in the Son there is the illustrating and exuberant splendor, in whom is the light and life of men, as Saint John testifies.

*John chapter 1.* In the Holy Spirit, finally, there is a brightness surpassing all understanding, as *Dionysius* <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, a Christian theologian and philosopher.</note> says. After the creation of light, its most simple portion concurred with the composition of the Angels, along with the splendor of the uncreated intellect or divine mind. After this, a portion of this composite light descended to the formation of the celestial bodies, giving them an abundance of life and effective propagation: and this light is visible splendor. Finally, in man, there is a due portion of all these species of light, both uncreated and created. For by the "breath of life" is not meant the vital soul (for this is granted even to brutes and plants, by which they live) but the divine mind and uncreated light, which is infused into him immediately by God, whereby he first puts on the image of God. Next, he is adorned with angelic and rational splendor, and he possesses this portion from the empyrean heaven <note>The highest heaven, believed in ancient cosmology to be the realm of pure fire and light.</note>, by which he is called rational; and by these two endowments he is seen to excel the other animals and all other creatures of the world. Afterward, he receives the life-giving, vegetative, and multiplicative light from the Sun and the splendor of the ethereal creatures, by which he is led physically here and there, is increased, and possesses the growth of his species through propagation. From the light of the elements, he possesses the symbolic correspondence of the parts of his body and the nature and harmonious proportion of the elementary humors, according to that saying of *Trismegistus in the Pimander:* <note>Referring to the *Hermetica*, attributed to Hermes Trismegistus.</note> *The female, air and water, being capable of joining, took maturity from fire and spirit from the ether, and nature joined them together to fashion the appearance of man.* Who, then, will doubt that all these species of light are in man, since *Saint John in chapter 1* testifies that the origin of all these—namely the divine mind and the portion of uncreated light—is in men, from whose uncreated source all other species of created light are derived. For according to that saying of the *Royal Psalmist: By the word of the Lord the heavens were made firm, and all their powers by the Spirit from his mouth.* We conclude, therefore, that there are three species of rays, which are called "acts": namely, the supercelestial rays or acts of God, from which the nobler portion of the human soul is derived; next, the rays of the world or celestial rays, which are acts of nature and of the soul proceeding from it, from which the sensitive and vegetative life of man is derived; and in the last place are the elementary rays, which do not prepare life, but the dwelling-place of life, and are the qualities properly hidden within the elements. Concerning these rays of the Microcosm <note>The "little world," i.e., the human being as a reflection of the universe.</note>, we shall discourse more widely below.

### CHAPTER IV.
### *Concerning the supercelestial rays, which are the acts of GOD.*

**R**egarding supernatural rays, since we have indicated that some are in God himself, as the sacred Scriptures also testify, and others are as it were the substance of the empyrean heaven itself and its creatures, we say those existing in God are uncreated, while these of the empyrean heaven are created. With *Scotus* <note>Duns Scotus, a major medieval scholastic theologian.</note>, we call the divine ray the uncreated intellect; but that other ray, proceeding immediately from the divine, we call the created intellect. Moreover, the secondary super-celestial rays are those which were created immediately by God on the first day, for the purpose of leading the matter of darkness from potentiality into act and for forging the actual and visible world; by whose actions the darkness was driven down to the center of the worldly globe, and all power was given to the heavens and to all parts and creatures of the heaven: Whence also they can truly be called secondary acts of God, insofar as they flow immediately from the Spirit of the Lord. ### CHAPTER V.
### Why is man called the image of God? And concerning the nobility which he receives from the supernatural rays, both uncreated and created, which are within him.

**W**hen that uncreated Craftsman breathed the breath of life into the muddy body of man, that body, although thick and opaque, received the divine mind; and that mind, through its inexplicable and most lucid beauty, gave the highly polished splendor of a refined mirror to the muddy and coarse bulk of man, so that first the form and image of the Archetype <note>The "Archetype" refers to the original divine pattern or the mind of God.</note> might be spiritually beheld within it. Wherefore Trismegistus, in a certain passage, says that man, made in the image of God, represents the Trinity; and likewise the Holy Scriptures in many places say that man was made in the likeness of God himself. Trismegistus also, in the 1st book of the *Pymander*, called man’s own mind the "form of God." And elsewhere, he calls the mind of human reason "God," which is intellect, life, and brightness. And according to Saint John, chapter 1: In the Word of God is the life of men, which is the light shining in the darkness—that is, in the dark human body—and this is the true light or divine form. Moreover, that polished matter, receiving these rays of uncreated light, is the spiritual and intellectual substance of the first heaven, created in the image of the Word (the first exemplar and cause of causes), which according to the Platonists is derived immediately from God. This is the true rational substance of the soul according to *Proclus* <note>Proclus (412–485 AD) was a Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote extensively on the soul's descent from the divine.</note>, which he says the first Maker of the world procreated, and consequently concludes it to be the most noble of all creatures; *since, as he says, the essence of the soul's perfection proceeds from the superior Gods; indeed, this is that intellectual substance which Iamblichus* <note>Iamblichus (c. 245–325 AD) was a Syrian Neoplatonist who emphasized theurgy and the soul's connection to the divine through ritual and intellect.</note> *in "On the Mysteries" says is illuminated by the beneficent divine will, that is, by the presence of the divine mind;* and likewise it is that which is defined by Theologians as *an intellectual spirit ordained within itself toward blessedness,* as is held in the *Theological Resolutions*. This substance, I say, is twofold: namely, of essential light and of the simplest spirit, like a certain sharp edge and most clear medium, implanted in the muddy body, in which a portion of that divine and uncreated idea is perceived. In such an empyrean mirror, then, illuminating that muddy body, GOD the Maker himself—as *Trismegistus* <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure to whom the Hermetic corpus is attributed.</note> testifies in the *1st book of the Pymander*—beholding himself as if in a reflection, congratulated man as his own son, and being greatly delighted by his own form, granted all his works to human use. 

Man, therefore, perceiving that he had power over all things, began to observe the works of the seven governors (for according to *Trismegistus's Pymander, discourse 4, man was made a contemplator of the divine work*) and those governors, whom they call intelligences <note>The "intelligences" or "governors" refer to the planetary spirits that rule the celestial spheres.</note>, rejoicing in the meditation of the human mind, each made man a participant in his own proper order. After man learned their essence, becoming most skilled in Astrology, he began to ascend higher and busied himself seeking out the source and origin of his own brightness and life. From there, he penetrated and cut through the circuit of the seven circles with the sharpness of his mind, and attempted to comprehend the power of the Governor presiding over fire: For just as the rays of fire tend upward toward their natural seat, so it is the office of that divine brightness to ascend as many degrees higher than other rays as it is known to be more subtle, noble, and excellent than they are. Hence it was, as *Trismegistus* records in *Pymander 4, that man, by admiring and vigorously scrutinizing the divine works, finally found and knew the author of them and of himself.* 

And from this it also follows that the same *Trismegistus in Pymander 10 calls man a divine animal, not to be compared with the brutes, but with the celestial Gods; indeed, he wished him to be superior to the inhabitants of heaven, or at least to possess an equal lot with them.* Finally, man alone enjoys this honor: that he has a symbol <note>In this context, a "symbol" is a mystical correspondence or shared essence.</note> with everything in this world and has operation and conversation with all things by the virtue of that divine ray. For he symbolizes with matter in his own body; with the elements in his fourfold composition; with plants in vegetation; with animals in sense; with heaven by the medium of the ethereal spirit; with the Angels by intellect; and with God himself, as he contains all things in himself. He acts, therefore, in all things and upon all things; and he even has power over God himself, namely by understanding and loving Him: and just as God knows all things, so also man can know all knowable things, for there is nothing in him in which some part of divinity does not shine. And hence also *Trismegistus in the 10th discourse of the Pymander* dared to call *man an earthly and mortal God, and God truly his celestial and immortal Creator. And in the 3rd discourse of Asclepius, he says that man is a great miracle, an animal to be adored and honored: for he asserts that man passes into the nature of God, and is himself as if he were God:* and elsewhere, *he says the nature of man is kindred to the Gods, and joined to them by divinity.* 

And certainly this is the greatest glory of man, that he possesses a true ray and act of God, by reason of which he is a blood-relation to God himself, no differently than those who descend from great-grandfathers and grandfathers are called their blood-relations and kin. And all these perfections we have from the root of uncreated light, which we have called the mind and intellect infused into us by God himself; by which we say that man, because of that ray of divine form existing in him, is the image of God, and is compared with the Angels insofar as he is intelligent and rational, and finally even has a symbol with all the heavens and the creatures of the heavens, as we have declared before.

# On the Nature of the Soul and Spirit

In the treatise *On the Soul and the Spirit* <note>original: "de anim. & spirit."</note>, it is established that the distinction between these faculties is essential for understanding human nature.

Aristotle, in his *Book on the Spirit* <note>original: "lib. de spiritu"</note>, asserts that there are spirits <note>original: "esse spiritus"</note> which act as the primary instruments of the soul's power within the physical body.

In the *Theological Resolutions* <note>original: "Resolut. Theolog."</note>, it is further clarified that, insofar as the soul looks toward higher things, it is called the **intellect**; insofar as it looks toward lower things, it is called **reason**. <note>original: "quod, quatenus anima respicit altiora, dicitur intellectus, quatenus inferiora, ratio."</note>

The intellect of the foul <note>original: "fedi"; likely referring to the corrupted or base state of the mind</note> must be purified to perceive divine truths.

The physical seat of these movements often involves the **diaphragm** <term>diaphragma: the muscular partition between the chest and abdomen, historically believed to be a center of emotion or "spirit"</term>, which regulates the vital breath.

Through the wild bearing <note>original: "ferationem"; referring to a state of wildness or animalistic impulse</note> of the passions, the spirit can become clouded, losing its orientation toward the higher intellect.

<summary>This page explores the hierarchical definitions of the soul, distinguishing between the intellect (focused on the divine) and reason (focused on the mundane), while noting the physiological role of the diaphragm.</summary>
<keywords>soul, spirit, intellect, reason, Aristotle, theology, diaphragm, Scholasticism</keywords>
