just as plants are refreshed and rejoice in the presence and sight of the Sun, so too are [the lower faculties] refreshed by the presence of this intellectual splendor. But to prove the irrationality of this "heaven of the soul" <note>The author refers to the middle or vital soul, distinct from the higher intellect.</note> in a more familiar way: we see that when the light of the intellect guides the sense of sight, the further an object is from it, the weaker are the rays of the visible species <note>term: species - in medieval optics, these are the "images" or "forms" shed by objects that travel through the air to the eye</note> that perceive it. Indeed, truth itself sometimes does not shine clearly through them. This is exactly how things stand in our proposition regarding this soul, since its medium is different from that of the intellect and it is distant from the intellectual seat by the radius of the world. Hence, the rays of the intellectual heaven are, as it were, refracted in the middle heaven due to the diversity of the medium, and they do not operate rationally. Furthermore, if this soul were rational in itself, why would it not also be seen to impart reason to all things to which it gives life? For the substance of this heaven exists in metals as much as in plants and animals of every kind; for the "quintessence" <note>term: quintessence - the "fifth element" or ether, thought to be the pure substance of the heavens</note>, which is the sensible nature of all things, exists only as a sensible entity and not an intellectual one, as witnessed by Lull <note>Ramon Llull (c. 1232–1316), a major philosopher and alchemist.</note> in his *Book on the Quintessence*. We conclude, therefore, that the Empyrean heaven <note>The highest, fiery heaven of pure light</note> derives its soul from the uncreated rays of God, and its substance is entirely luminous; yet it is not the most simple light, for that belongs only to the Trinity, being uncreated. Nevertheless, the spiritual appetite of this heaven's substance is so fulfilled that it is entirely converted into a luminous and formal nature. Whence that composition is called "Empyrean," that is, fiery, by whose formal substance the dark spirit of the middle region is informed. Thus, the entire substance of the celestial region is made from a portion of this Empyrean substance, which is its form, and from its own spirit, which is its matter; this composition is called "ether," that is, fiery air. And just as the entire substance of the Empyrean heaven is the form or essential soul of the ethereal heaven, so again the entire substance of the latter (which they call the quintessence) is the soul and nature of all creatures of the lower world—except for man, who draws his greater perfection from a higher region. In this way, the previously mentioned words of Dionysius <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a Christian Neoplatonist.</note> in his book *On Divine Names* are verified: *Those things which are in the lower regions exist more perfectly in the higher ones* <note>original: "Illa, quæ ſunt in inferioribus, perfectius exiſtunt in ſuperioribus"</note>; that is, the higher one ascends, the greater the perfection found. For as the same author says in his book *On the Angelic Hierarchy*: *A higher Angel, by common law, illuminates a lower one* <note>original: "Angelum ſuperiorem de lege communi illuminare inferiorem"</note>; so also is the case with the regions of the world. For the internal or ideal world is the pattern of God himself, while the external and visible world is the image of that invisible one.

### CHAPTER VII.
### On the elemental rays and the sensitive soul.

*Timaeus* <note>Referring to Plato's dialogue, the Timaeus.</note> *says that the essence of our soul is not constituted from the first kinds of all things, as the higher souls are, but is composed of the second or third kinds; where by "first kinds" he denotes the natures and substances of the Empyrean heaven; by the "second," those of the ethereal heaven (which we discussed above); and by the "third," those of the lowest and elemental heaven, which we shall discuss here. The Pythagoreans, as we explained above, wishing the soul to be composed of the single, double, triple, and quadruple proportions, understood by the "quadruple proportion" the sensitive power of the soul, which Plotinus and other Platonists called the "idol" <note>note: "idolum" here means a phantom, reflection, or lower image</note>, because it is like an image and idol of the quality that is sensed. From these points it is clear that the **sensitive soul** participates in the body, since without the organs of the body it can perform or perfect nothing at all; indeed, unless it exists in some animated body, this function or power of the soul is nothing. It is established, therefore, that it consists of the elements and their virtues and mixtures, rather than being derived from the virtues of the higher heavens. Hence **Porphyry** <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 234–305 AD) who sought to reconcile Aristotle and Plato.</note>, in his *Book on Occasions* <note>original: "in lib. de occasionibus"; likely referring to Porphyry's "Sententiae ad intelligibilia ducentes."</note>, seems to distinguish it from the higher powers of the soul in these words: *The soul is indeed a medium between the indivisible essence, which is the intellect, and the essence divisible into true bodies; for qualities and material forms are divisible according to bodies.* Where by "soul" he understands that life-giving force of the ethereal heaven; by "indivisible essence," the intellectual substance and reason of the empyrean heaven; and by "essence divisible into bodies," the **sensitive power**. He denotes that this power is occupied with elementary qualities and material forms, which are divisible according to bodies, and that it arises and is derived from their actions.

Hence among the Philosophers it is defined that *this kind of sensitive soul is the act of a natural organic substantial body, by which it lives, feels, desires, breathes, and moves from place to place, whose apprehensive power grasps and perceives the species of visible things, both present and absent.* For the sense is as fit to receive the abstracted impressions of natural things as wax receives the image or character of a seal abstracted from a ring, without the gold or silver adhering to it. And this power is prepared both in the **exterior sense**, to which five species are subject—namely **sight, hearing, touch, taste, and smell**—and in the **interior sense**, of which there are three distinctions: namely **common sense, phantasy, and memory**. By its **motive power**, the animated body is moved, either externally in place, or internally by spirit and pulse; which indeed, if it be temperate, is the **concupiscible virtue** <note>The faculty of desiring or longing for something perceived as good.</note>, containing hope and joy within itself, or the **irascible force**, under which fury, rage, madness, fear, sadness, pain, and other such things are comprehended.

This sensible faculty is, therefore, the daughter of the earth and of darkness, the mother of all evils, the instigator of the flesh toward all wickedness, assidueously exciting the appetite for sinning within it and repeatedly offering objects of sin to man. For by the sense of the apprehensive power, present species inciting one to evil are perceived. Hence **Eve** was first enticed to sin by hearing the persuasions of the serpent; then by seeing that the fruit was beautiful and delightful to the eyes and sight, she touched that fruit, and finally she tasted and ate it; so that, for the completion of this sin, all those five species concurred, especially since smell is also a familiar companion to taste. But the species of the motive power also concurred in this action; for she immediately lusted after and desired the fruit, and to fulfill the appetite, she went to the tree and took of the fruit, and afterward, struck by fear and sadness, she fled from the face of God.

From these things it appears that there were three incitements for Eve to commit that sin of disobedience against her Creator: namely, the **Devil**, the **flesh**, and the **world** itself. The Devil tempted the flesh with some object. The flesh, through the operation of the apprehensive sense, apprehended and saw the worldly object, and being conquered by diabolical persuasions, it desired that sensible species; the motive power then led it to fulfill its appetite, and it delighted wonderfully in that worldly subject seen, which at last is subjected to her as a reward—or rather a punishment—for her disobedience toward her Creator. Hence, therefore, is the origin of all the evils of the entire human race, which, swelling up immediately from its birth, straightway defiled the universal human condition. For the woman herself also gave of the fruit to the man, who ate, and through that sin of his, he was reduced from an immortal state to mortality with all his posterity; so that **Trismegistus** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure to whom the Hermetic corpus is attributed.</note> now rightly described him as *an earthly God, but mortal*; for he lost his privilege of immortality through his disobedience; and the form

### CHAPTER VIII.
### *By what vehicles, or through what media, the lights of each heaven, which constitute the human soul, are joined to the body.*

Among the Philosophers who observed that divine virtues are diffused into all things, Democritus and Orpheus the Pythagoreans called them Gods, with whom they said all things are full. Zoroaster, however, called them "divine allurements" <note>original: "illices divinas"</note>. Synesius called them "symbolic attractions." Trismegistus and others called them "lives"; and all generally called them "souls" and "essences," attributing name and being to things. The Platonists, diligently investigating the descent of these souls into bodies and the manner of their union with bodies (for they perceived that the soul is primarily and spontaneously mobile, while the body is of itself ineffective for motion, and consequently these two extremes are entirely contrary by nature, and for that reason not easily joined), noticed that it happens by some spiritual medium. Thus, by its intervention, those two extremes and strangers might have some commerce between themselves, and be bound to each other by its ties; this very thing they further called the *ethereal vehicle of life* and the *chariot of the soul*. And they affirmed that this is that ethereal spirit which has familiarity with both extremes; not otherwise than the substance of air has with its opposites, fire and water. Whence also that ethereal spirit, enveloping the soul in the middle region of the world—that is, situated between the spiritual and corporal extremes—is defined as being neither soul nor body, but as if already soul, insofar as it is contiguous to the upper region, and as if not soul, but as if already body, insofar as it is joined to the elementary region. This spirit, I say, the Platonists noticed to be that vehicle in which and through which those wondrous gifts of forms are conferred upon lower things, and every occult faculty in herbs, stones, minerals, and animals is propagated by the power of the sun, moon, planets, and fixed stars. But truly Trismegistus, looking somewhat more deeply into human nature than those Platonists, discovered that the ethereal spirit is the vehicle of the divine Mind. And although Proclus, in his book *On the Soul*, mentions the garments of the human soul in these words: *The soul, in descending, is variously clothed and finally purified*, yet he speaks of them more confusedly. For in the first book of the *Pymander* <note>The "Pymander" or "Poimandres" is the first and most famous book of the Corpus Hermeticum.</note>, it is held that the garment of the Mind is the soul, but the garment of the soul is the spirit itself. Whereby the Author understands by "soul" the rational substance of the empyrean heaven, and by "spirit," the informed substance of the ether. Whence in the tenth sermon of the *Pymander*, he seems to open this same passage of the first sermon with these words:

through which he most effectively declares the true motion of the mind from its uncreated starting point <note>original: "a termino suo increato a quo"</note> to the created destination <note>original: "ad terminum creatum, ad quem"</note>: *The soul of man is carried in this manner; Mind in reason, reason in soul, soul in spirit, spirit in body.* By these words he clearly hints that the divine and uncreated mind—a ray of uncreated light—puts on the substance of the empyrean heaven <note>The highest, most spiritual heaven composed of pure light or fire.</note> as a garment. By this vehicle, it descends further down into the formal substance of the middle heaven; for the form of the middle heaven is of the true nature of the empyrean substance, and naturally "like rejoices in its like." Furthermore, that ethereal form, embracing a twofold super-celestial nature, is wrapped in the coverings of the ethereal spirit, in which, as if in its own proper vehicle, it is transported into the muddy body. The source of the Mind, therefore, is that uncreated Unity <note>original: "Monas"</note>, which *Trismegistus* <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure to whom various philosophical and magical texts are attributed.</note> in the *1st book of the Pymander* calls *God's own form, similar to Himself,* and which Holy Scripture calls the *Deiform breath.* And this, *Trismegistus* proves in *discourse 10 of the Pymander, cannot exist in an earthy mass, nor can an earthy dreg receive a mind so divine, or sustain such a great divinity.* It is for this reason (he says) *that the mind assumes the soul as a garment, because the soul, being divine, uses the spirit as a vehicle.* Certainly, this divine mind cannot be carried into the middle region without its empyrean vehicle any more than the nature of the middle soul can be carried into the lowest region except by the mediation of the middle spirit. For the same relationship exists between the heaven of the Trinity and the empyrean as exists between the empyrean and the middle heaven; and the same between that middle and the lowest as between the empyrean and the middle. Indeed, the soul of any higher heaven is more noble than the one immediately below it, according to that saying of *Proclus* <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote extensively on the soul's descent.</note> *concerning the soul: The rational soul is more noble than the irrational, because the first Creator of the world procreated the former, while the younger or ethereal Gods created the latter.* That is to say, the fiery spirit of the intellectual heaven, which they also call "rational," proceeding immediately from God the first Creator of the world, is more noble than the spirit of the ethereal heaven, inasmuch as the latter is only granted the faculty of pouring life and growth into lower things, but by no means of infusing complete reason. And this is why *Proclus* asserts in the same place that *some souls descend from the Solar sphere, others from the Mercurial, and some from the Lunar.* From these things it clearly appears that the first garment of the mind is far more noble than that ethereal one, since it is, as it were, the "form" to that middle spirit by which it is received in its descent. The Mind, therefore, is first enclosed in the rational spirit; then the rational spirit, with its most divine content, is received by the spirit that is vital in itself. This spirit, which is otherwise irrational, then becomes rational and intellectual through the presence of the Mind and its vehicle, according to that saying of *Iamblichus* in his *book on the Mysteries: The soul is illuminated by the beneficent divine will.* And *Aristotle* now correctly defined it in his *book on the spirit: as being an intellectual spirit, rational, and always moving,* specifically insofar as those super-celestial endowments are joined with its nature. Finally, this ethereal spirit, exalted by both super-celestial and mundane rays, is infused into bodies—which were aptly disposed and proportioned by God at creation to receive it—because of its constant communication and familiarity with lower things. Running through the entire human body, it first introduces into them a sensitive power from its own nature (which it is also accustomed to bestow upon other animals, namely the irrational ones, equally with men), and then afterwards also the rational and intellectual power, which it is accustomed to confer on man alone by virtue of the super-celestial lights. And in this way is fashioned that interior man, folding together the intellectual, vegetative, and sensitive faculties all at once.

CHAPTER IX.
*On the opinion of Theologians regarding the creation of the soul.*

In the preceding chapter, we clearly explained what the more divine Philosophers established concerning the creation of the human soul and its descent into the muddy <note>original: *lutosum*; referring to the physical, earthly body</note> body. Here, however, we shall deal briefly with the differing opinions of the Theologians themselves. The greater chorus of Theologians concludes that *the soul is infused into the body and created by being infused*, alleging for this that passage from *Genesis 2: He breathed into him the breath of life*, that is, He created the soul within the body. But Origen, along with several of the Greek Theologians who follow the opinion of the Platonists in this matter, openly contradicts this assertion; they all move toward this sentiment: *that all souls were created equally with the Angels in the beginning*. This is also what certain others maintain, as is found in the *Clangor Buccinae* <note>The "Clang of the Trumpet," an influential alchemical and mystical text</note>, where it is expressly written in these words: *The souls, which today and every day hereafter are infused anew into the mother's womb, are not created anew, but were created from fire alone in the primordial beginning of all things, and are cherished in the mind and power of the Creator until the preordained time when they must be infused into the body; and they do not depart from the body unless the spirit has first withdrawn and vanished, by which withdrawal the soul also vanishes.* And Augustine also seems to wish to agree with these, as is held in Book 7 of his commentary *On Genesis*, unless he should find the Holy Scriptures saying otherwise; hence he speaks thus doubtfully concerning the soul of Adam: *If no Scripture is found which contradicts it, it seems it should be said that the soul of Adam was created from the beginning with the Angels, and afterwards came voluntarily to the body to administer it.* But this doubt of Augustine’s will be most easily removed, in my judgment at least, if we consider that the eternal Spirit of God, carried upon fiery wings over the waters, assiduously infuses all virtues into the parts of the Macrocosm <note>The universe as a whole</note>, according to that never-sufficiently-repeated sentence of the Royal Psalmist: *By the Word of the Lord the heavens were made firm, and by the Spirit from His mouth all their power.* Since these things are so, why should not that same spirit, which the Maker once breathed into the face of the Microcosm <note>Man, as a miniature reflection of the universe</note>, suffice for all propagation of men, since it is seen to be reserved in the mind and power of the Creator until the preordained time when it must be infused into the body? This is surely so that, saving that passage in *Genesis*, that intellectual soul—which, insofar as it is the image of God himself, can be called infinite for the forming of men—extends itself infinitely, not otherwise than that spirit which God gave to the Macrocosm in the beginning of creation, by whose presence the Macrocosm itself is adorned daily with infinite gifts without a repeated creation of that spirit. Is it not also said according to *Saint John 1*: *that in the Word of the Lord is the life of man, and that life is the light*

Origen <note>Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–253 AD), an early Christian theologian who famously proposed the pre-existence of souls.</note> did not believe that new creations occur daily, but rather that all substances of souls—which we previously called "rays"—flow forth from this single source. This happens in different ways: either primarily, such as the soul of man proceeding immediately from God himself; or secondarily, as from that multitude of rays with which the ethereal region was filled at the time of creation. By these rays, the vegetable world was produced before the creation of the Sun, and the sensible but irrational creatures were produced after the Sun’s rising. It is manifest, therefore, from what has been said, that the human soul is composed of a purely formal ray, which we call the **Mind** <note>original: "mentem"</note>, and its receptacle, which is that rational spirit of the empyrean heaven; and from the vehicle of this spirit, which is the ethereal form or soul, which is finally enclosed in its "chariot"—namely, the ethereal spirit. Then, once this is done, that entire composition—by which the **inner man** is rendered similar both to God and to the world itself—descends into the **outer man**. Whence it is probable that, just as the aforementioned substances of the heavens are not created anew, so also the soul (which is a composition of those parts) is not created daily by infusion. But where am I being carried, or by what divine fury am I led? I pray for pardon from you, O most sacred choir of Theologians, if perhaps I have progressed beyond my limits, for I most willingly submit myself to your authorities. However, I thought it a good intention to reconcile the holy Theologians with these Philosophers, who are profound with a wondrous divinity, by a bond of peace, and to recall their differing opinions into harmony.

### CHAPTER I.
### *On the principle of the numbers and harmony of the Microcosm <note>The "Microcosm" refers to the human being as a "little world" that mirrors the vast universe.</note> and on the relationship which the numbers and consonances of the greater and lesser worlds have toward one another.*

[Large decorative initial 'C' containing a figure and foliage] Since the whole world is governed—as some wise men maintain—by the command and ordination of the three super-excellent superiors, who are one and the same in essence, and by the execution of seven others, which are called the lower numbers or the measures of the fabric, it follows from this that not only the entire world, but also its creatures, have received their origin from the number three <note>original: "ternario"</note> as the principle *from which*, and through the number seven <note>original: "septenarium"</note> as the medium *through which* they arise. For Unity is held in the same degree of proportion with the number seven as the unison is to the Octave <note>original: "Diapason"; the interval of an eighth.</note>. It must therefore be observed that the ordering of things exists in the number three, and that the action of the number three upon matter occurs by the power of the number seven. This seven participates both in the number three (which is purely formal) and in the number four (which is purely material), as we have reviewed above regarding the divine numbers. From these things, therefore, it happens that the single world represents the icon or idea of formal Unity; and according to the number two <note>original: "binarium"</note>, the multitude and diversity of matter is demonstrated in the world. Furthermore, through the division of even and odd numbers, males and females are produced throughout the entire machine of the universe. Indeed, the very part of the World Soul is masculine in its nature, insofar as it is a ray of Unity or the Divine Mind; but its vehicle—namely the universal spirit, which is of a moist nature—is as it were female. The masculine part of the soul, or pure light, acts upon its feminine part, or moist nature, no differently than a man acts upon a woman. And to this matter Hermes Trismegistus <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure associated with the "Hermetic" tradition of alchemy and philosophy.</note> seems to give his support, saying: *The Word, proceeding from the voice of light and standing by the moist nature, cherished it, etc.* For matter vehemently desires form, as a woman desires a man. Hence it is that the Platonists have said that the parts of the soul are unity and multitude, gathered together by a wonderful harmony; namely through uni-

By unity they understood the light gushing forth from the fountain of oneness; but by multitude, they understood matter or the spirit leaping forth from the dark chaos of duality, or the filth of *hyle* <note>original: "hylæ"; a Greek term for raw, unformed matter.</note>. From the sacred Scriptures we also gather that *all things were fashioned by number, weight, and measure.* <note>A reference to Wisdom of Solomon 11:20.</note> And the Platonists seem to acknowledge this same thing in almost the same words, asserting that all things are fused together by number, figure, and solid body. By *numbers* they understand the specific forms of things, insofar as a single form, having arisen from the fountain of unity, is dispersed into a multitude and is distributed and expanded through the vast immensity of matter; thus Aristotle also compares forms to numbers. By *measure* they denote the properties distributed to each thing: And hence the Evangelist says: *He, that is, Christ, gave to each according to his own proper measure;* <note>referencing Ephesians 4:7</note> that is, according to that which is measured, the Archetype <note>The original divine blueprint or Creator.</note> attributes to each, he who measures all things with the most just scales. Finally, by solid bodies they wished to signify the weights of things and the gravity of the elements, by which we are always drawn more and more downward. Similarly, by *number*, Arithmetic is understood; by *dimensions and measures*, Geometric moderation; by *weights*, Musical mediation, which balances in proportion; or in likeness it comprehends the lightness or slowness, or the sharpness or gravity of the voice and the inclination of things.

Therefore, through the threefold number <note>The ternary or number three.</note> GOD descends into worldly matter, for the construction of the world and of man, where he puts on the power of the sevenfold number, insofar as he participates in the nature of matter, so that he might complete composite worldly things by his most holy power according to his own image; according to the opinion of *Hermes Trismegistus.* <note>The legendary Hellenistic figure associated with the Hermetic corpus.</note> Wherefore we gather that this ternary number is that through which all things are made; and the ternary number within the quaternary <note>The number four.</note> is the figure from which all things are made; which relate to one another as a square to its root, or as a surface to a line according to the opinion of Plato, or rather by following the doctrine of the sacred Scriptures, where it is said that all things are made by number, weight, and measure. *By number* we understand the ternary root, through which, as the simplest and most perfect purely formal number, GOD descends to the construction of the world and man; *by weight* he divided matter, and the nature of matter, into the light and the heavy. Hence *Hermes Trismegistus* says: *The holy splendor flourished, which led the elements beneath the sand and the moist nature; and when they had been indistinct, the light parts presently flew forth into the high region, while the heavy ones settled beneath the moist sand, etc.* Finally, *by measure* is understood the triple dimension, constituting bodies or elements.

From these things, therefore, it is manifest that not only the world, but also man himself, both internal and external, is fused together by numbers and harmony. For the heaven is full of the consensus and the suitability of motions arising and derived from the ternary number. Hereafter, the rightly ordered life of men receives from there the suitability of morals and actions: Indeed, the gift of the higher beings descends even unto the brutes and plants. *For these,* to use the words of Iamblichus, <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher.</note> *are naturally participants in respect to harmony. For the higher beings contain and perfect all worldly things by a symphonic reason, and adapt them to one another, and to the world; they indeed harmonize the body to the intellect by means of the soul through a harmonic reason, etc.* Finally, they join the earth to fire through middle bonds. Furthermore, they cultivate any soul whatever by harmonic reasons, and couple every single body everywhere with similar measures. Therefore, the habit in man is Musical; it is indeed the task of the Muses. ->ON THE INTERNAL NUMBERS AND HARMONY OF MAN. 87<-

Geometry, in considering these parts of the world, finds that the superior numbers correspond to lines, the middle to surfaces, and the inferior to bodies. In terms of Music, the simple numbers or "divine digits" correspond to the super-excellent voices of the empyrean heaven <note>The highest, most spiritual heaven of pure fire/light</note>, the excellent voices of the ethereal or middle heaven to the high pitches, and the elementary heaven to the deep pitches. Furthermore, in terms of Arithmetic, the super-substantial realms correspond to units, the empyrean to roots, the ethereal to squares, and the elementary to cubes. Therefore, we are not considering "natural number" <note>ordinary counting numbers</note> in this place, but rather the **formal ratio** which exists within number. For the form of the world, flowing down from the essence of Unity into the nature of Duality or the Quaternary <note>the number four, representing the material world</note>, produces proportional numbers, weights, and measures in this world by its greater or lesser presence.

From this it follows that the portion of matter or "moist nature" that is deprived of this formal presence is more heavy, coarse, raw, and opaque, tending more downward; conversely, that portion of it which is rich and full of formal presence exists as more subtle, thin, light, beautiful, lively, noble, mature, and elevated more upward. This occurs according to many proportions: thus the spheres of the substances of the four elements are suspended higher or lower according to the merits of their form, weighed in the scales of Justice. Thus the stars and every sphere of the ethereal heaven, decorated with glowing fires, are sustained and suspended by an admirable craftsmanship and order of nature, according to the nobility of their form. And in their center, the beauty of the **Sun** is placed so that, like the eye of the world, it may look upon all things, or like a heart, it may disperse and dispense the life of its circularly flashing light everywhere. Even the empyrean heaven is distinguished into its hierarchies by the virtue of this form (of which one is more sublime and excellent than another in power), and so it is with the rest. These divisions of the material world are again subdivided into other infinite degrees, not defined by us.

And these portions of the world, differing in their portions of matter or form, we call our **physical numbers**; from their union and various mixing, diverse things—distinct in nature, species, appearance, and quality—are produced in the world. From these, therefore, the world and the parts of the world are constituted. From these, its Soul acts in different ways here or there in its spirit or its watery and moist matter; from these, the single Soul, expanded into the multitude of matter, enters into the name of "multitude" according to the species of creatures, and indeed the individuals of those species; so that any ray of the universal world, entering into the matter or body of a creature, is called its "soul."

Yet man, a **divine animal**, enjoys this honor above all other creatures of the world: that he received a special "breath of life" from God beyond that general gift of world-life. Whence, besides the gift of the world, he enjoys the Divine Mind, by a divine act and ray of God, by which he alone among all other animals is called intellectual and rational. These things having been duly considered, let us approach the **numbers of the human soul**; which indeed retains within itself a portion of every region or heaven of the world: whence man is called the **image of the world**, as the world is the image of God.

From the supreme heaven, therefore, he has his intellect and reason; from the middle, his vital soul and ethereal spirit (the vehicle of that same soul); from the lowest, he receives the more formal part of the elements, serving as organs for the other more excellent portions of the human soul. Above all these portions travels the **Mind** <note>Latin: *Mens*</note>, an offspring of the eternal essence, a ray of God and an uncreated gift, breathed out from the super-substantial mouth. The Mind, therefore, easily joins itself with the seeds of its own nature, namely with the "active intellect" or the fiery portion of the empyrean heaven; similarly with the soul, which is the fiery or lucid nature of the middle heaven; and these three portions of light join with the formal portion of the element of fire; which indeed happens more easily since they have arisen from the same lucid source. So also there is a single and easy mixing among the material parts. For the rational spirit or "passive intellect" unites itself with the ethereal spirit, and that with the air; for they are of the same nature, since they are derived from the same abyss and *hyle* <note>Greek: *hyle*, meaning primordial matter</note>. But yet the portions of light...

The various levels of creation are exalted in dignity, one above the other, according to their greater or lesser immunity from the bonds of matter. The **Soul**, however, being in the middle, is even more enclosed within the center of the spirit; hence it is not as free as that light of the composition of the Empyrean heaven, and is therefore also inferior in nobility, since it possesses an equal portion of the spirit in which it is included and by which it is surrounded. # ON THE INTERNAL NUMBER AND HARMONY OF MAN 89

All things draw their motion from [the first mover]. *Plato* also called the Sun the visible son of *God*: the ancient philosophers also called the Ether the *Spirit of Life*, because it is the vehicle of life by which lower things live. Therefore, the solar light is moved by the prime mover, and it draws the essence of the spirit, proceeding from the motion and light of the prime mover and the Sun. In the lower region, where unity is placed with three zeros <note>This likely refers to the number 1000, symbolizing a higher order of magnitude or completion in mystical numerology</note>; the Father is rightly compared to fire; the Son to air, insofar as he is a gentle governor and a kind mediator; and the Holy Spirit to water, for the reasons mentioned above. The Earth, however, lies as the foundation of the whole, in whose center unity is also found with three zeros. From this it is clear that GOD multiplies Himself as many times as there are persons reckoned in the Holy Trinity, so that the entire matter of the world may be transformed into His divine essence. Nor, certainly, was the earth, or the foundation of the whole, left empty; but the Savior himself entered into it, because, as it is said, the earth shall bring forth the Savior, etc. Therefore, everything that exists is GOD Himself. Outside the world, He is present to Himself in supersubstantial essence and is called *Adonai*. In the higher region of the world, He is present to the spiritual world and is called *Mind*. In the middle region of the created world, He is called *Life*. In the lowest, He is called *Body*. And the whole in the whole and every created thing are nothing but God; insofar as all things are called good, and truly nothing should be called good except God alone, from whom alone goodness comes. For by His goodness all things exist, and without it nothing could be brought into action; since only the goodness, light, and benevolence of God is the act of all things, in which, from which, and through which all things that are, exist, and without which there is nothing. Therefore, whatever is an act is GOD, because GOD alone is act: and consequently, the act and life of creatures is GOD, since in the Word was life, etc.

*A most lucid demonstration of formal numbers, both in the procession of the persons of the* DEITY *from the supersubstantial unity before the creation of the world, as well as in the emanation of the cosmos and its creatures at the time of creation, where it is explained by what rationale first the formal digits from the supersubstantial unity, then the articles, then afterwards the hundreds, and finally the thousands are produced for the diverse consistency of the world.*

# CHAPTER III.
## By what virtue of worldly harmony the Mind is enticed toward its opaque body.

It is a very difficult matter and scarcely accessible to human reason, how the divine and immortal Mind is introduced from its highest tabernacle and sacrosanct seat into the lowest, dark, unclean, and mortal mansion of man, so opposite to its own nature. Yet we see this happen by divine will, and that downward movement of the soul is undoubtedly induced by the charms and flatteries of the worldly spirit <note>The "spiritus mundi" or world-spirit, acting as a bridge between the divine and the physical</note>, inasmuch as it holds no small love toward the mass of darkness as if toward its own progenitor. This, however, is only perfected by the motion and will of the Creator, so that indeed even on earth and in the lowest heaven a certain noble creature might be found in the image of the Creator, who, imbued with reason, may know its Creator, contemplate and admire His works, and extol, praise, and honor God its Creator with divine worship. And this is indeed proven by the fact that it would be impossible for that mind to descend into this place, so contrary to its nature, without that excellent and admirable symphony of the Creator, from which all worldly concord and harmony arises.

Therefore, the mind first descends with the intellect into the sphere of the middle soul, carried on the wings of the rational spirit. But truly, since 1 (or the cone of the material pyramid) stands in relation to 2 (where the intersection of the pyramids occurs in the place of the sphere of equality) in a double proportion <note>original: "proportione dupla," referring to the 2:1 ratio of the octave</note>, it follows from this that the mind is carried downward from its connatural seat to that station by the virtue of the *Diapason* <term>Diapason: The musical interval of an octave</term> harmony. It is then transferred further downward through the *Diatessaron* <term>Diatessaron: The interval of a perfect fourth</term>, leaping forward to the base of the empyrean heaven or firmament, from which it is carried again through the *Diapente* <term>Diapente: The interval of a perfect fifth</term> to the circle of the Sun or the sphere of the world-soul, always penetrating downward.

The *Diatessaron* joined with the *Diapente* thus produces the *Diapason*: and this is its worldly harmony forged from the spiritual Octave. This is the middle station of the mind in its worldly journey, in which the soul of the world, with its spirit, receives the mind and the active intellect along with its rational vehicle. From this station, the mind glides down even further in its double lodging through the material or corporeal *Diapente* consonance; by whose harmony it is carried down to the convex surface of the element of fire; where the elementary region receives it, along with its double vehicle and its governors, into its airy embraces—not without adoration and respect for the divine. And so the mind, with its three satraps <note>The three "governors" or powers: intellectual, vital, and sensitive light</note>—namely intellectual, vital, and sensitive or elementary light—tends downward in its triple chariot, reaches the earth, and is enclosed in its dark prison by the virtue of the elementary or corporal *Diatessaron*.

In this manner, therefore, by the virtue of the material *Diapason* consonance, the mind descends with its subjects and puts on its corporeal veil. The consonance of the Fourth <note>original: "Diatessaron"</note> is found at both extremes, as is shown by the fact that such a proportion is found there between matter and form, namely from 3 to 4—that is, the sesquitertial ratio <note>A ratio of 4:3, which creates the musical interval of a fourth</note>, from which the consonance of the Fourth is composed. Similarly, the consonance of the Fifth <note>original: "Diapente"</note> is found by counting both upward and downward from the sphere of equality, since in those places the sesquialter ratio <note>A ratio of 3:2, creating the musical interval of a fifth</note> is found between the proportions of matter and form, namely 2 to 3. But since the mystery of this harmony has been more clearly explained in the harmony of our macrocosmic history <note>Referring to the author's previous work on the Great World or Universe</note>, I would wish you to be referred there, while in this place we shall say a few words (albeit concisely) concerning the harmony of the soul derived from the number seven; for this number seems to pertain more properly to the composition of the human soul because of its immense property and its secret disposition. It will escape no wise man that the soul is composed of light and the most subtle spirit—that is, of an active and a passive element. Since, however, the active portion of the soul bears the image of the Trinity—insofar as the Word is said to be in the Mind, and the Mind in the active Intellect—it therefore claims for itself the formal number or property of divinity, which is the divine Three <note>original: "ternarium"</note>; which, when added to the number of its passive portion, namely the Four <note>original: "quaternario"</note>, produces the number seven, from which the human soul is composed. Through the triple harmony of this number, the soul is carried downward into its incorporeal lodging. But since we shall speak more abundantly in our treatise on Death concerning both the admirable effect and mystery of this number in the composition of the soul and its harmony (which is introduced from on high into the body), as well as its secret disposition in the liberation of the soul from the body and the loosening of the elementary bonds, we shall omit the efficacy of this number regarding the existence of the human soul in this place, and we shall depict only a visual demonstration of the soul's harmony in relation to that of the world in the following manner.

CHAPTER IV.
*How the mind and intellect, penetrating from the higher realm through the universal world to its lower parts, even unto the center, may observe the mysteries of any heaven, and participate in the nature and disposition of any heaven, and introduce their virtues within itself into the mundane man.*

Just as the human soul migrated into its dark dwelling-place <note>The physical body</note> through the harmony of the world, so also, inhabiting the mundane man, it not only retains within itself the act of the world's symphony, but also seizes for itself the idea of divine concord. From this it happens that the soul is moved in a wondrous way by the sounds of common Music. Hence it is that Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 245–325 AD) who wrote on the mysteries and the soul's ascent.</note> put forth discourses of this kind: *The soul,* he says, *heard divine harmony in the intelligible world, which it remembers here when it hears a trace of divine melody; remembering it, the soul is vehemently moved toward it, if it is among the number of those souls which chiefly contemplated the very idea of harmony in their fatherland <note>original: "patria" — referring to the celestial realm of origin</note>. Indeed, having been made familiar with God by such an affection, it is now moved by a certain singular presence of God, from which it performs wonders.* Therefore, the cause of this inspiration and miracle is not a passion brought in from sounds, nor the nature of the soul being composed of harmony, but its likeness to God, and the presence of God. There are, therefore, primarily traces of Music and divine melody in the mind, by whose sweet pulsation we are enticed toward the highest good and the contemplation of divine things.

On the part of the intellectual soul, man (endowed with blessedness) tastes of the properties of the intelligences of the nine orders; namely:
*   Of the fiery intellect of the **Seraphim**, and the gift of their charity;
*   Of the most excellent gift of the **Cherubim**, consisting in the multitude of wisdom and knowledge;
*   Of the sincerity of the **Thrones** in judgment and justice;
*   Of the excellence of the **Dominions** in virtue;
*   Of the character and reverence of the **Principalities**;
*   Of the fortitude of the **Powers** for defeating malignant Demons in spiritual battle;
*   Of the illumination and miracles of the **Virtues**, whom the power of God illustrates;
*   Of the secrets of the **Archangels** and **Angels** in their offices, announcements, and obedience.

Man participates, I say, in all these endowments by reason of the excellence of his intellect, which bestows such thoughts upon men. By its virtue, the soul (with the mind surely going before to its aid) could undoubtedly perform as much as the intelligences themselves, if it were not confined by its thick and dark prison, and were not seduced by the deceptive errors of the same. 

Furthermore, the virtues contained in the ethereal heaven are not lacking to man, on account of the portions of the soul's middle nature <note>The "spirit" or "medial soul" connecting the high intellect to the low body</note> with its spirit. For from the **First Mover** <note>original: "primo mobili" — the outermost sphere of the physical universe</note>, which is contiguous with the intellectual heaven, man possesses such virtue that he has his will derived from it joined with the intellect, always tending toward the good of the mind. This intellect delineates the ways and paths for the will no differently than light does for the eye; yet it does not move the will against its own appetite, but the will remains the mistress of its own operation. Hence, this will is called **Free Will**; which, although it tends toward the good as its adequate object, is sometimes blinded by error and the deceptions of its dark veil, and by the impulse of the animal force, it chooses evil, believing it to be good. Hence it is that Free Will is defined as a faculty of the intellect and the will, by which good is chosen when grace assists, and evil when grace departs. Therefore, grace itself, which Theologians also call charity or love, is in the will like a prime mover; when it is absent, the entire consensus falls into dissonance. In these things, therefore, the ethereal part of the soul participates in the nature of the First Mover. The properties...

The soul also seized three properties from the starry sky, corresponding to each of the three <term>Zodiacal triplicities</term> <note>Groups of three zodiac signs belonging to the same element: Fire, Earth, Air, or Water</note>, which properties it joined to itself for the perfection of its office in the human body. For it drew its **attractive faculty** from Aries, Leo, and Sagittarius, which compose the fiery triplicity; it claimed the **retentive faculty** from Taurus, Virgo, and Capricorn; the **concoctive <note>digestive or transformative</note> faculty** from Gemini, Libra, and Aquarius; and the **expulsive faculty** from Cancer, Scorpio, and Pisces. 

Then, passing through the **sphere of Saturn**, it received its receptive power from him, as well as gravity and constancy in its purpose, and prudence combined with depth. From the **orb of Jupiter**, it snatched for its portion justice, the love of virtues, honesty, gentleness, and the governance of the natural faculty. From the **region of Mars**, it obtained impulsive and irascible <note>quick-tempered</note> force, audacity, power, and fortitude. From the **Solar circuit**, it drew its vital faculty. From the **circuit of Venus**, it took the concupiscible <note>desiring</note> virtue, cheerfulness, and delight in Music. From the **orb of Mercury**, it acquired its imaginative power and sharpness of wit, the love of sciences, and the perfection of memory. And from the **sphere of the Moon**, it attracted its power of increasing and decreasing. 

Finally, its lower portion, which we call the **sensitive and animal soul**, introduces the complexions, humors, and remaining properties suitable for the sensory organs into its dark lodging <note>the physical body</note> for its portion, toward the perfection and completion of the elemental composition. From these things it appears most evidently that the soul, in its journey—wandering from unity toward multiplicity—allures to itself infinite properties of the macrocosm flowing from its divine harmony. 

And here it must be diligently observed that discords do not strike the human soul from the **Empyrean heaven** <note>the highest, most spiritual heaven</note>, because that realm, on account of its purity, divinity, and simplicity, is always occupied with the Good; but discordant sounds are very often perceived to come from the **starry heaven**. For example: Saturn sometimes discordantly and discrepantly pours envious seeds into the soul; likewise hatred, baseness of life, melancholy, and other such things. Mars also sometimes sends anger, sedition, strife, derision, adultery, incest, inconstancy, and other such things into the lower realms because of its incongruous "beatings" <note>astrological aspects or vibrations</note> with certain lower natures. Hence these are called **unfortunate Planets**; the reason for which we have reviewed in our *Worldly Music*. 

The regions of the elements, however, are found to be most full of discords because of the vast amount of matter existing in them; for their number is **two** <note>the dyad</note>, which is the origin of discord and strife. And from this it happens that there are so many altercations in this region, so many corruptions of things, and their mutations from one form into another. Indeed, the elements themselves would struggle among themselves and wage perpetual war with one another, were it not for that honorable **medium** <note>a balancing middle force</note>, by whose virtue the struggling things are bound and connected by the bonds of peace and concord. 

But truly, the **Mind** <note>the highest intellect</note> is free from every passion and malevolent disposition of matter, and is always found constant and immovable in its state; for it is not bent by the influences of the stars or the impulse of the intelligences, but exists immune from every operation and action of things which are subjected to its connatural seat. Whence it is manifest that the stars cannot impose necessity upon bodies over which the Mind predominates. For the wise man, sprinkled with and imbued by the blessed rays of the Divine Mind, **will rule the stars** <note>original: "astris dominabitur"</note>. Certainly, the influences of the stars and planets have no power over that intellectual part of the soul, insofar as the rational spirit is the immediate vehicle of the Mind and is naturally exalted above the power of the constellations. 

But such men who, refusing the gifts of the intellect and the benefits of the Mind, are content with only the vital soul after the manner of beasts—preferring irrationality to rationality, and in no way beholding divine things with spiritual eyes—look only toward earthly things with a downward gaze, [becoming] animal...

# On the Nature of Light and Perception

The movement of the spirit is directed toward the internal senses, so that the soul might more clearly perceive the images of things. <margin>The soul acts through the senses</margin> For it is necessary that the medium be purged of all dregs <note>original: "fæcum"; referring to impurities or "sediment" that obstructs clarity</note> and obstructions, so that the light of the intellect may shine through without hindrance.

As it is written, we must ensure that the visual power is not clouded by the vapors of the body. It follows, namely, that those things which are perceived by the eye are not the things themselves, but their species <note>In medieval philosophy, "species" are the sensible forms or "likenesses" of objects that travel through the air to the eye</note> which are carried through the air.

<column-break/>

Furthermore, it is evident that the rays of light, when they encounter a denser body, are either reflected or absorbed. This is because, namely, the rays cannot penetrate the thickness of the material. We see this clearly in the case of a mirror or a polished surface, where the light is sent back to the viewer.

In the same way, the mind must be cleansed of all impurity <note>original: "immunditiei"</note> if it wishes to contemplate the truth. For just as a stained glass window prevents the sun's rays from illuminating a room in their true color, so too do the passions of the flesh obscure the light of reason.

This light does not act immediately <note>original: "immediatè"</note> upon the soul, but through the mediation of the vital spirits. By this desired <note>original: "deſiderato"</note> path, the knowledge of external things is brought into the inner chamber of the mind.

Hence it is that this golden, vital, and incorruptible plant of the world is not hindered in its ascent by the elements: because its matter is not contiguous with them, but rather the substance of the middle region is interposed between fire and the empyrean—or intellectual—heaven <note>The "empyrean" was considered the highest, most spiritual part of the universe in Renaissance cosmology.</note>. For before its appearance in the heart of heaven, no animal was created in the expanse of the lowest region or upon the earth. But truly, after the fourth day, in which the Sun appeared in heaven, from the beginning of the fifth day until the end of the sixth, animate creatures were produced step by step. From this, it is right to consider that an animal requires a greater quantity of heat and light for its composition and existence than a mineral or a plant, and that the various kinds of animals are procreated according to the greater or lesser effect of heat and light. For at the first appearance of the Sun from heaven, the vapors of a moist nature—the mists and material spirits leaping forth from the rebellious mass of darkness—were still raw and less "cooked" <term>concocted: a term from alchemy and early medicine meaning matured or refined by heat</term>; these were thereafter subdued more and more every day by the solar rays and actions, and having been made more obedient, they subsequently brought forth more perfect and mature things. Hence, at the beginning of the fifth day, since the humors were still very raw and undigested, the rawer animals were brought into the light by the life-giving operation of the Sun. For so we read, that on the first day <note>The author refers here to the first day of animal creation, i.e., the fifth day of Genesis.</note> fish and aquatic creatures were created immediately after the revelation of the Sun; then, the misty spirit of darkness having been made more obedient, the more airy and winged animals received life and saw the light in the second place; finally, after the fifth day of creation had passed, the warmer and more fiery animals began to live and draw breath, namely the four-footed animals and reptiles. It is clearly evident, therefore, that the dominion of the Sun, increasingly assailing the moist nature and the terrestrial mass, was the cause (the divine and immortal nature so willing it) that various and diverse kinds of animals were found in the lower world; of which some were colder, others warmer, some terrestrial, others aquatic, some aerial, and others more ignited. Truly, the bodies of all these were selected from that portion of the earth which was more obedient to the solar and formal rays, and more corresponding to their actions; for this earth is the mother of all elements, because from her they proceed, and into her they return. Indeed, the earth is the mother and nurse of all things which she has conceived in her womb from fire—that is, from heaven, or celestial action—because heaven, of which the Sun is the commander, is the father of all composite things; but the earth is their mother. She carries them in her bowels just as a mother carries her offspring. For into the depths of the earth flow all celestial and especially solar influences, which are enclosed there like the seeds of things, as if in a common matrix; whence, because of the varieties of the proportions of those descending influences, diverse generations of different things occur in the earth, and various impressions arise, all of which take place in the muddy substance of the earth. Indeed, the earth itself is the palace of the solar rays carried in the ethereal spirit, in which they are enclosed like captives and are called "vital spirits"; inasmuch as by their benefit even these houses and tabernacles of theirs are able to live, feel, and [reason...]

### CHAPTER II.
*What is the human body? That it is pure and select earth, precipitated when the darkness of the highest worldly region was struck downward on the first day of creation: and how it differs from the matter of other mixtures, whether mineral, vegetable, or animal.*

THEREFORE, the external MAN, before the breath of the soul was communicated to him, was nothing other than a corporeal mass fashioned from the mud or slime of the earth. Its color, as some maintain, was reddish; such as the Philosophers imagine is found pure and unadulterated in the center of the earth. By this, they signify that God chose this most perfect particle of earth of all to prepare a dwelling place for the spirit of His life, as it was filled with the purer and more mature spirits of the darkness, and thus most fit and suitable for receiving that most noble and God-like human spirit—which *Paul*, along with *Sixtus the Pythagorean*, called the temple of God. For, by the authority of some of the ancients, during the foundation of the earth completed on the third day of creation, this portion of earth was prepared and destined for this work by divine providence. It held and possessed within itself the purest and most suitable potential seeds of light and ethereal spirit for receiving that God-like breath of uncreated brightness—namely, the primary act or ray. This portion of earth, I say, the Creator formed into the likeness and essence of the external man, so that his internal part might receive it as a dwelling; wherefore He breathed His divine spirit into his nostrils. And this, without doubt, differed from other types of earth used for the structure of other more ignoble creatures, no less than the earthy composition of gold differs from that of other impure minerals. For, as *Plato* testifies, the acts of forms require suitable impressions of matter worthy of their operations; that is, the soul desires such a dwelling place in which to act and live as is like unto itself. ->102 TRACTATE I. SECTION I. BOOK V.<-

[Is it not true that the influence] of the Sun [is found] in the animation of these animal bodies, which were made immediately after its exaltation and positioning in the heaven, as if in a subject more natural and convenient to itself? Did not these species of composite things also receive their sites and stations according to the position of the heavens themselves—namely, minerals toward the center of the earth, vegetables in its upper region, and animals upon its surface? What is more evident than this to the wise? But what is more absurd than this to the foolish? Are not the bodies of minerals, vegetables, and animals opaque? If, therefore, all are opaque and dark, from whence comes this disposition of theirs except from the darkness? But perhaps you will assert that this discrepancy of theirs arises from their form; to which reply of yours, if we give place, what then follows? Is not form accustomed to require a subject suitable for its actions? Hence, the more noble the form shall be, the more noble a passive body it requires for itself, into which it may act. And accordingly, the superior lights descending into the darkness of the lower world require darknesses more suitable to their own bodies in which they may dwell. What passive thing, therefore, or what darkness is more suitable for the actions of the mind and intellect than the human body? Certainly none; since experience teaches us that the intellect with the mind chooses only the human body for its habitation and no other. Whence it is clear that the human body, out of all species of darkness <note>The author uses "darkness" here to refer to physical matter, which lacks the inherent light of the spirit.</note>, is the most known and familiar to that divine intellectual spirit, just as if even then, once before the creation of the world, the darkness of this body had existed as the unformed matrix <note>womb or origin</note> of that spirit. Thus we also see that the celestial spirit with its soul is more suited to vegetables than to minerals, because it is found more abundantly in the former than in the latter; and so it is in the rest. From which things we may clearly see what kind of earth, or dust, or mud, and that corporeal mass it is, out of which GOD formed man, and how it differs from the external matter of the other mixed species.

### CHAPTER III.
### *On the Geometric proportions of the external man, and how through them we may most aptly delineate the world.*

Will it not seem wonderful and miraculous to men stained with the spot of ignorance, that in the nature, position, and Geometric proportions of even the external man, the idea, image, and proportion of the material world is most exactly found? Hence, not ineptly, man is called by Hermes Trismegistus <note>original: "Mercurio Trismegisto"</note> the image of the world and the Microcosm <term>Microcosm: "Little World," the idea that man is a miniature map of the entire universe.</term>; because in him, as if in a mirror, the parts of both the ideal and the material or visible world are beheld. For we find that, just as the earth is the center of the greater world <note>the Macrocosm</note>, from which lines or diameters are drawn to the circumference, and is as it were the matrix of all elements, from which the generations, increases, and multitudes of all things proceed; so also the center of the lesser world <note>the Microcosm/Man</note> is the point of the genitals or private parts, and the root of the penis: from which if we measure to the bone of the pointed cartilage <note>the xiphoid process at the base of the breastbone</note>, and then from that to the base of the throat, located near the collarbones, and further from that to the crown of the head, we shall find the Geometric proportions of the Microcosm corresponding by equal distance to those three regions or heavens of the Macrocosm. For by proceeding and ascending from the pubic bone, or from the center or point of generation, to the bone of the pointed cartilage, we shall find the lower heaven of the Macrocosm, or the elemental region, to agree in all things with the lowest portion of the Microcosm, namely in whose re- <note>The text cuts off mid-word, likely "region."</note>

For as the blood of the veins has the nature of air, so that of the arteries is filled with ethereal and vital spirits derived from the Sun. And as the arterial spirit or blood is not very perceptible because of its thinness, so the spirits serving the reason in the highest heaven of the Microcosm <note>The brain/head.</note> are entirely imperceptible and are to be conceived by the imagination alone. This same distinction also exists between the natures of the ethereal and empyrean heavens. Therefore, it is clear by evident reasons that from the delineation of the Microcosm and the metric description of its regions, one may know what the regions of the Macrocosm are and their dispositions; and similarly, conversely, once the parts of the Macrocosm and their natures are known, it becomes very easy to delineate and distinguish the regions of the Microcosm.

*On the upright position of the Microcosmic body according to the four*

Although finding the proper position of the Microcosm <note>The "Microcosm" refers to the human being as a "little world" reflecting the universe.</note> corresponding to the four regions of the Macrocosm <note>The "Macrocosm" refers to the great world or the universe at large.</note> is a very arduous and difficult task, we nevertheless elicit from the fountain of Holy Scripture that there is a certain fitting relationship between these two worlds. For in many places therein we read that in prayers and the manner of supplicating, the face of the petitioner should be turned toward the East. Similarly, in Matthew 24:27, we find that the lightning comes from the East and shines even unto the West. And in Numbers 35:5 it is read: *Measure on every side toward the East region, etc., and toward the South region, and toward the West region, and toward the North region, etc.* Furthermore, it is also written in Job 23:8 and 9 according to Pagninus's translation <note>Santes Pagninus (1470–1541) was a Dominican friar and leading philologist who produced a new Latin translation of the Bible from the original languages.</note>, where the search for the place and seat of Jehovah is discussed: *Behold, I shall go to the East and he will not be there, and to the West, nor shall I perceive him; or to the North while he works, and I shall not see him; he hides himself in the south, nor shall I see him, etc.* Indeed, Jerome <note>St. Jerome, the 4th-century translator of the Vulgate Bible.</note> interprets this passage of Job thus: *If I go to the East, he appears not; if to the West, I shall not understand; if to the left, what shall I do? I shall not apprehend him; if I turn myself to the right, I shall not see him.* Tremellius <note>Immanuel Tremellius (1510–1580), a Jewish convert and leading Hebraist whose Latin Bible was popular among scholars.</note> also translates that passage of Job into these words: *If I go forward, he will not be present; if backward, I shall not notice him; when he acts on the left, I shall still not see him; He will cover the right region, nor yet shall I behold him.* Most evidently, therefore, we can perceive from these the proper position of man in the world according to his nature. For from that passage in Numbers, we gather that man ought primarily to look toward the East in every operation, and then in a circular regard toward the South, West, and North. From the words of Job, however, we discover that the Eastern region, according to both Jerome's and Pagninus's translations, ought to be referred to the face of man—that is, as Tremellius interprets it, to the "forward" or his anterior part—and the Western part to his posterior. From which it necessarily follows that his left side turns toward the North, just as his opposite side, namely the right, looks toward the South. The Holy Bible thus teaches us that this disposition of the Microcosm to the regions of the Macrocosm is more congruent with the laws of nature. Now, however, looking diligently into the nature of the matter, let us inquire whether this position of the Microcosm relative to the site of the Macrocosm agrees with the nature of the world or Macrocosm according to its physical constitution, or not. By accurate intuition, therefore, we find that every region of the lesser world agrees in nature, temperament, and disposition with every quarter of the greater world. For we attribute the light of the eyes to the solar splendor, and the intellect and reason to the First Mover <note>The "Primum Mobile" or outermost sphere of the heavens which gives motion to all others.</note>, whirling its orbs from the East toward the West; and we rightly compare the human heart to the Sun, as if to its prince; inasmuch as it is written that Jehovah placed his tabernacle in it; and so all things of man, both internal and external, rejoice to salute the Sun as the bright tabernacle of the Creator, with devout prayers and thanksgivings to their Creator and Lord going before; since it is the driver-away of sadness and darkness, and the author of gladness, joy, and light. Conversely, the posterior parts of man are not undeservedly referred to the West. For as the East is accustomed to bring day, light, and gladness; so on the contrary the West brings in night, darkness, and sorrow. Thus also through the posterior parts of man is found only a single way and a lone passage, through which the dreggy and useless substance is compared to the void earth, insofar as the nutritive faculty and power...

Behold then, O men imbued with true Philosophy, how notable is the relation and how admirable the affinity between these regions of the greater world and those of the lesser, which are perceived to agree with one another most exactly in nature, condition, and position.

### CHAPTER V.
### *A brief anatomy of each Microcosmic region.*

The head of the human body, which we previously compared to the Empyrean Heaven <note>the highest heaven of pure light and fire</note>, has been called by some the "supreme venter" <note>upper cavity</note>; it is bounded by the neck and contains the spark of the mind in its rational vehicle. Physicians distinguish the exterior of this head into the forehead, the forepart of the skull, the back of the head, the crown, the temples, and the face. They further observe its hair and its manifold uses, and the skin—dense, hard, dry, and thick—to which the roots of the hair adhere. Its interior, however, they distinguish into the skull <note>original: *cranium*</note> and its attachments, and the brain with its parts. They divide the skull into five sutures <note>the joints where the bones of the skull meet</note>, of which one is at the back, called the *Lambdoid*; another is at the front, called the *coronal*; the third is called the *straight and sagittal*. The remaining two are called the *false, squamous, and temporal* sutures. A certain membrane surrounds the convex surface of the skull, arising from the thick meninx <note>membrane</note> through the sutures; for this reason, it is called the *pericranium* and *periosteum*. Beneath the skull, two other membranes also meet, covering the brain in a circle: the one which is thicker and harder, adhering to the concave surface of the skull, is called the *dura mater* <note>literally "hard mother"</note>; the other, which is closely joined to the brain, is thin and soft...

Similarly, this region contains the stomach, the mesentery, and the upper and thinner intestines, namely the **duodenum**, the **jejunum**, and the **ileum**, as well as the lower and thicker ones, namely the **cecum**, the **colon**, and the **rectum**. Finally, we could fill entire volumes with the observations of this anatomy, and thus affect the eyes of readers with weariness in matters common to the world, rather than soothe them with delight or the pleasant whisper of novelty; wherefore it has pleased us to pass over the anatomy of the human body at least lightly in this place, so that we may gird our mind for matters more new, and not so commonly known, and yet true and demonstrable.

### B O O K  VI.
#### On the harmony of the external Microcosm.

### C H A P T E R  I.
#### On the comparison of the harmonic constitution of the regions of the Microcosm with those of the heavens of the Macrocosm.

[Decorative initial C] The human body, which we have called the external man above, is forged from the same matter as the world. And although the spirit of the world—on account of that thinness which it received from the property and presence of light—is discerned to be diaphanous, bright, clear, and transparent; nevertheless, that clarity and transparency of its spirit often becomes black, gloomy, and dark through thickening and coarsening. This usually happens to a greater or lesser degree according to the greater or lesser absence of light, or the dominion of thickening cold, just as is seen in the change of air into a dense cloud. Furthermore, by the freezing of cold, that cloud or condensed aerial spirit is changed into the appearance of white earth, as in hail, ice, and snow; indeed, it even changes into the thickest earth itself, as is demonstrated by the consideration of a thunderstone <note>A "thunderstone" or *lapis fulminis* refers to prehistoric stone tools or fossils once believed to have fallen from the sky during lightning strikes.</note>. For it is certain that the types of earth are of diverse natures: that is, participating more in the purity of fire, the disposition of air, or the quality of water. And yet all these types of earth are for the most part opaque and by no means transparent. Thus, the brain is observed to participate in the fiery element, the heart and lungs in the aerial, the stomach, liver, and humors <note>The four bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—thought to determine health and temperament.</note> in the aqueous, and finally the spleen and intestines in the coarse earthy element. This is because these parts of the body became the receptacles of those elementary natures after the soul was placed into them, as we shall teach below. But truly, all these portions of "earth" <note>The author uses "earth" here to mean the physical, material substance of the organs.</note>, though differing in disposition, are observed to have almost the same dimension of length in the geometric symmetry of the body, nor is one part more opaque than another. This occurs because God fabricated this external dwelling-place of the soul—or the breath of life—before He breathed the soul into it. From this it happens that although the element of water is greater in dimension than earth, and air than water, and so on with the rest (which occurs because the same matter, when dilated, requires more space for its existence; and similarly...

Hermes Trismegistus <note>original: "Merc. Trismeg." referring to the legendary Hellenistic figure associated with the Hermetic corpus</note> seems to give the reason for this matter in these words: *When God noticed that the form of the divine likeness could not be mindful of all things unless He covered it with a worldly garment, He clothed it in a corporeal house, and perceived that all should be such; blending and mixing them into one from both natures, as much as was necessary. For since the nature of the free mind and even the disposition of the middle soul—indeed, even the property of the thicker fire itself—is to neglect lower things and look back toward higher things by natural instinct when they are free and released from dense bonds, it is necessary that they be enclosed in an opaque body and possess material organs. By the direction of these organs, they may be occupied with corporeal, dense, and lower things. For the nature of the soul, and much more so the mind, is so much occupied with spiritual and invisible things that it could not notice visible and corporeal things unless it were enclosed in an opaque body, so that it might look upon these terrestrial and lower things through material organs. This, therefore, is the reason why the rays of both the mind and nature work upon opaque things. For if they were liberated from the corporeal prison, leaving the earth empty and void, they would leap into the heavens with a light bound. Mind, therefore, is given only to man, to distinguish his vital soul from the souls of other living things and to exalt it in dignity above others. And although the vital soul was granted by itself in creation to plants as well as to other animals, the soul of a beast—immediately strengthened and increased by the power of the Sun—is superior to the soul of vegetables in both reason and motion, inasmuch as the latter was infused into them before the placement of the Sun in the heavens. From the aforesaid, therefore, we see that the regions of the Microcosmic body <note>The human body as a "little world" reflecting the universe</note> do not differ in thinness and thickness according to the example of the regions existing in the Macrocosmic body <note>The universe or "great world"</note>, because the former was prepared before the breathing-in of the soul, and consequently remains the same after the infusion of the soul as it was before; but the latter <insert>the Macrocosm</insert> received its preparation and disposition in thickness, thinness, location, expansion and constriction, transparency and opacity, immediately from that divine soul which was moved over the waters and sent into it. Finally, from this disposition of the simple earthly mass (distinguished and prepared by the Creator into nobler and less worthy regions according to the dignity of the parts of the heavens, which the Architect decided in His divine counsel to arrange and harmonize before the ages), a material harmony is observed, suited to the celestial bodies as well as to the elements themselves and the symmetrical proportion of the earthly parts, as will appear more clearly in the following.

### CHAPTER III.
### *On the harmonic agreement of the heavenly bodies with the human face and hand.*

We also detect a vast symphonic agreement between certain parts of the human body and the stars. From this, we are taught through the discipline of *Physiognomy* <note>The historical practice of judging character or predicting the future from physical appearance, especially the face.</note> to behold the celestial bodies, and the seats and signs or characters of the Planets, within the human face. By these, we are accustomed to understand and predict a person's inclinations, both from the celestial and the elemental side. Indeed, to such an extent have both the wiser philosophers and those more skilled in medicine foreseen and divined wonders—both in the disposition of a healthy person and in the wasting sickness of the ailing—by observations of this kind. Nay, truly, they have gazed upon those characters of nature in the human forehead as if in a most polished mirror; these characters have such a relation to the characters of the ether and the Zodiac which they represent, as the Octave <note>original: "Diapason"</note> has to the Unison. From this it also follows that they are compared to one another by a symphonic agreement; a fact which the philosophers also sagaciously noticed regarding their symphony of hearing...
