Yet the reason why the brain is neither thinner nor more transparent than the other members is drawn from the creation of man, in which it is clear that the body of man was created and prepared by the Creator before his soul was infused into it. The cause for this was so that the soul, obscured by darkness, might perceive, distinguish, and look upon bodies through material organs; which indeed it could not have accomplished unless veiled in dark flesh, since by itself it understands nothing except invisible things—that is, things such as it is itself—while yet with the aid of the body it sees visible things and gazes with corporeal eyes. In this way, GOD rendered the dark mass subject to Himself and subdued both earth and heaven to His will, and moved dark bodies toward a respect for their condition.

The middle region of the body, however, insofar as it relates to moisture and heat, can be compared to the air, which indeed stands to the brain as air stands to fire; wherefore we judge that the entire chest of the Microcosm is to be referred to the element of air. As for the opacity and thickness of the heart and lungs, the reason for it is the same as that alleged above. In this same way the divine mind—the light and highest harmony of the Microcosm <note>The "Microcosm" refers to the human being as a "little world" that mirrors the vast universe or Macrocosm.</note>, the origin of human creation and existence—produced the beautiful image of the Microcosm, leading its spheres around by a motion that is as much voluntary or natural as it is involuntary or driven by the spirit, and most skillfully completing its elemental composition. Hence, man is called a God, but a mortal one, just as the Creator himself is called the only GOD, but immortal. Similarly, the Devil is darkness and discord and the author of destruction or deprivation, and a dissonant strife, who was the firstborn son of chaos, the adversary of the Word of God and of light, rendering the sphere of the earth immobile by himself, and causing the elements to quarrel through his discordant nature. So also the body of man is dark, the author of discord and diseases, the obscure son of chaos, most opposed to the mind, soul, and light, and immobile by itself. And all this happens because there is a duality. And therefore, if the unity of the soul is joined to duality, or the trinity of form is joined to the quaternary <note>The "quaternary" refers to the four elements of matter: earth, water, air, and fire.</note> of matter, the body will be reduced from discord into an exquisite harmony; by that means the darkness will then be illuminated, discords driven away, life preserved, and death cast into exile. Peace between God and darkness—or between the body and the soul—will be achieved through illumination by the divine presence of the mind, and the body, though immobile by itself, will now receive action and motion from an internal moving principle. From these things it is clear that these two extremes, contrary to one another, produce various effects by themselves: namely light and darkness, soul and body; since the former gives birth to concord, under whose dominion small things grow; while the latter is accustomed to induce discord, in whose presence great things fall apart. The contrariety of these extremes is denoted by the opposite placement of their triangles in the worldly composition; for the peak of the formal pyramid <note>The "formal pyramid" represents the descent of spirit or light into matter.</note> is in the earth, while its base is in the first heaven. But the position of the material pyramid is the opposite, since its peak is touching the center of that formal base, while its base is established, as it were, in the center of the earth. In the middle, however, where life alone is found, they meet; namely, in the sphere of equality, or in the place of intersection of the two pyramids, where the portion of one is weighed against the portion of the other in the scales of justice. And just as these two pyramids differ in position, so also the natures springing from their bases are perceived to be opposite in their disposition. For we see that the soul, emerging from the center of the formal pyramid, the longer it is in the body, the more perfect and lively it becomes, and it is observed to grow younger in its faculty and wisdom or prudence; whereas conversely, the more age the body acquires, the more it is recognized to decrease and fall into ruin, as if through a kind of senility. Furthermore, the stronger the soul is, the weaker the body, and vice versa. We conclude, therefore, that the human body consists of four elements: but in the flesh and bones, because of their fixed and solid earthy substance, earth appears most clearly. Similarly, the element of water has its power and existence in the humors; while air, besides being found abundantly in the blood of the lowest region, is also perceived to dwell in the lungs as if in its most proper place. From this it has happened from the beginning that this member of the body is always in motion, and serves in the place of a fan for the cooling of the heart, lest the heart—insofar as it is the chief seat of the fiery power—be consumed and dissolved by excessive heat. The shape of the heart is therefore pyramidal, and in this shape it is adapted to the flame of fire; since in a flame of fire ascending upwards we see its base, similar to the base of a pyramid, while its summit is sharp in the manner of a pyramid's peak. But in the body, the situation with the heart is as it is in the world with the Sun. For the base of the solar pyramid is in the body of the sun, but its peak tends downwards, contrary to the nature of common fire, and this by a singular divine will. For otherwise, if the power of light always tended upwards, inferior things would be destitute of the efficacy of life-giving light.

C H A P T E R  I.
*On the creation of man.*

[A large decorative woodcut initial 'A' set within a square frame, depicting a landscape with trees and a building in the background.]
As the human soul—according to the mode and reasoning alleged in the first book of this work—glides down from the higher realms to the lowest heaven by musical proportion and spiritual vehicles, it is prepared for entry into its own dwelling. Finally, it is infused and breathed by the breath of the Craftsman into that dwelling (fashioned from earth, dust, and mud by the hands of the Creator himself to receive such a God-like breath <note>original: "spiraculum Deiforme"</note>, as was said above). By the life-giving power of its presence, the soul moves, quickens, and animates the external man. And in this way, man was created twofold within a single individual, and was made a living animal, endowed with reason and intellect; a wonderful animal (I say), an earthly God, created immortal in himself but made mortal on account of sin—in short, the ineffable image of his own Maker. 

But since we have dealt copiously elsewhere—in our *Theologico-Philosophical Treatise on Life, Death, and Resurrection*—with the breath of his life and the purity, cleanliness, transparency, clarity, and perfection of his body in the state of innocence, and likewise with his placement in Paradise together with the description and explanation of the pleasure of Paradise itself, we shall pass over those things lightly in this place. Instead, we shall occupy ourselves with debating the opinions of the ancient Philosophers regarding the actions of the internal man within his external part. In the first part of this book, therefore, we shall treat the operation, dominion, and virtue of the human soul, as much from the supernatural side as from the celestial and elementary side, insofar as the soul is considered with the body in creation or generation alone. We perceive, therefore, that creation differs from generation in many respects; yet we do not wish that word "creation" to be considered so strictly,

we wish, as those do who define it as the production of a thing and its arising from non-pre-existent matter—that is, out of nothing. For in this way, we do not correctly say that man was created, insofar as in his beginning, his external part was made from pre-existing matter and stood prepared for the work: namely, from mud and earth, which was the material suitable for his composition. Rather, we define creation more accurately as that by which the species of things, previously non-existent, now begin to be. For in this way, the first species of man took its beginning in the creation of Adam, the Lion in the first production of terrestrial animals, and so on. In this, therefore, creation and generation differ: the former is concerned with the arising and production of species that did not previously exist; the latter, however, is concerned with the propagation, multiplication, and conservation of things or creatures already pre-existing—a species created then by the first *FIAT* <note>Latin: "Let it be done," referring to God's command in Genesis.</note> and lasting until the final *PEREAT* <note>Latin: "Let it perish," referring to the end of the world.</note>. In the former, therefore, GOD the Creator works immediately; in the latter, the second image of the first mind works, which is created nature itself, or the daughter of God, having proceeded and derived from Him before the creation of all things.

### CHAPTER II.

*Concerning the free disposition of the middle spirit, by which it is accustomed to participate in one or the other extreme; and concerning the cause of the internal man's blessedness, and the reason for his dejection and misfortune.*

Saint Paul, agreeing with Xystus the Philosopher, constantly asserted that the human soul is the temple of God. Hermes Trismegistus <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure associated with the *Hermetica*, a body of mystical and philosophical writings.</note> also demonstrates the reason for this in *Pymander*, book 12, with these words: *The Good Spirit,* he says, *declared the soul to be in the body, the mind in the soul, the Word in the mind, and God to be their Father. Therefore, the Word is the image and mind of God; the purest portion of matter is air; of air, the soul; of the soul, the mind; and finally, of the mind, GOD. Indeed, GOD is concerned with all things, the mind with the soul, the soul with the air, and the air with matter.* Hence it is that others, by more narrowly constraining the nature of man, have joined it together from three parts: namely, from the soul, the intermediate spirit, and the body—signifying by "soul" both the mind and the soul. But these, as it seems to me, have not so exactly distinguished the internal part of man; that is, they have not distinctly described the portions of the internal man which he acquired from each of the three heavens, and consequently, they have left it imperfect, since all perfection consists of a beginning, a middle, and an end. We shall therefore listen here to the opinion of the Platonists, which does not disagree with Hermes Trismegistus, who ascribed three things to the internal man: namely, the *highest, the lowest, and the middle.* By the *highest*, they understood that divine thing which they call the mind, the illuminated intellect, a portion of the uncreated light, and the act or ray of God. This is the superior portion of man, in which portion of the soul *Hermes Trismegistus*, ascending higher by the counsel of the good and never-lying Spirit, asserted that the Word resides. Saint John also seems to agree with this, calling the Word *the life of men and the light of darkness*; and likewise *Hermes Trismegistus* calls it *the life and light from which man consists.* And elsewhere he says: *The Word in thee sees and hears (Pymander 1).* So *Moses* calls it the *breath of life*, immediately breathed by God Himself into the external man. And this superior portion of man, embracing the enlightened intellect, is that through which man, excelling the other animals, approaches the nature of the Deity itself. Whence he is called the *image of God and the son of God* not only by the Philosophers, but even by the Scriptures themselves. By the mind, therefore, the Platonists wished to understand the intellect and reason—

By the lowest part, however, they seemed to signify the airy and lowest portion of the internal man, or the act of the elements, which is—as *Hermes* *Trismegistus* <note>original: "Mercurius Trismegistus," the legendary Hellenistic figure associated with alchemy and hermetic philosophy</note> testifies in the passage cited above—the ruler of the entire elementary region. This part, gathering to itself the formal dispensations of the elements according to the degree to which the matter exists in a more subtle and thin state, acts upon the body according to the corrupt disposition of the flesh and darkness, with the superior portions of the soul acting as assisting and preceding leaders. This is because its nature and position are more familiar to those lower things. Hence, this portion of the soul is more prone to the affections of the body and inferior things than it is suited by its own nature to the mind and divine matters. And this lowest portion of the soul is called the sensitive soul, which the *Apostle Paul* called the "animal man" <note>original: "hominem animalem," often translated as the "natural man" in 1 Corinthians 2:14</note>, and an idol drawn out from the bosom of corporeal matter. When the body is dissolved, this part perishes along with it, or its shadow does not long survive in the vapors of its dissolved body, participating in nothing of immortality but returning into the deformity of *hyle* <term>hyle: the Greek term for primordial, unformed matter</term>, unless it is also united to a more sublime power, by whose virtue alone it can acquire immortality. This portion of the soul is the motive power, the vivifying force, the ruler of the body, and the material origin of the senses, through which the soul itself unfolds its powers of perceiving within the body. For it perceives corporeal things through the body, moves the body through space, rules it in its place, and nourishes the body with bodily substance. In this portion of the soul, therefore, there are two most powerful virtues: one of which is the Phantasy—either imagination or thought—and the other is the nature of sense. Finally, by the middle Spirit, they understood the medium or ethereal and vital act and ray of nature, connecting both extremes: namely, the mind with the animal soul. From this it happens that this middle nature participates in both extremes. Thus, from the virtue of the Sun—on account of the relation of its light to the empyrean heaven—it possesses a spark of reason, which is subsequently increased by the presence of the mind and the intellectual spirit; and from the lowest extreme and the subtlety of the elements, it possesses the sensitive faculty. Hence it follows that this middle nature—uniting the extremes as it were and joining the intellectual portion with the animal or sensitive soul (that is, carrying the mind with its rational spirit and vehicle toward the lower things)—is in its nature essentially free. Thus, it is permitted to adhere more to either this or that: namely, either to be more occupied with inferior and sensible things than with super-celestial and divine things, or vice versa. It is exactly as if GOD said to the intermediate spirit inhabiting it with free will: *Accept whichever of these you prefer*; or according to the words of the Leader Moses: *You have before your eyes life and death, choose which you want*; or according to the choice of the Apostle: *Either be children of the world, or of the heavenly kingdom.* And similarly, it is said in this way: that Adam tasted of the fruit of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, he who in the beginning contemplated nothing but the secrets of the mind, and consequently was a participant in goodness alone. But how the matter stands, listen, I pray. This intermediate spirit, full of vital spirit and moreover imbued with both solar reason and especially with the empyrean mind, gives to the body from these the power of living in general; that is, it bestows all functions of life upon the body through the mediation of the sensitive organs adapted to the faculties of life. But truly, since every action of life is occupied either with good or with evil (since there is nothing in this world besides these two extremes), the first of which is the gift of light and the last the gift of darkness, it is necessary that this motion of the spirit in life tends either toward goodness—that is, toward the nature of God and the Father of light—or toward the malice of the Devil, the prince of darkness. For it is impossible for it to incline toward both extremes at once with an equal balance. Hence Christ says: *You cannot serve God and man <note>original: "homini," though usually "mammon" in scripture</note> at the same time.* And Saint John in his first epistle: *The children of God cannot be children of the world, nor vice versa.* From these things, therefore, it is clear that this spirit, like a Prince Elector, tends either more toward the higher things or toward the nature of the lower things or the animal soul; that is, it follows either the world, depravity, and dark-

And therefore, also, by the power of the mind, such a Spirit is eventually transferred to God because of its obedience, according to that saying of *Proclus*: *The soul, through acquired knowledge, becomes similar to the mind or intellect itself.* But on the contrary, if that spirit joins itself to the animal soul, or clings to the lower part, it is depraved, defiled, and submerged and detained in darkness, until from a good Spirit <note>original: "Dæmone," here used in the classical sense of a guiding spirit or genius, not necessarily an evil demon.</note> it becomes an evil one; because that lower portion, namely the animal soul, is always submerged in evil, sin, and concupiscence, and as *Saint Paul* <note>original: "Divo Paulo"</note> bears witness, it drags one toward the worst things. These are his words: *I see another law in my members, taking me captive in the law of sin.* <note>Romans 7:23</note> From this also arose this divine discourse of *Bernard*: *O soul, decorated and made beautiful through the image and likeness of God, betrothed to the spirit through faith, helped by angels, companion of blessedness, heir of salvation, partaker of reason, what have you to do with the flesh?* Indeed, *Bernard* did not see everything: For very often, in a treacherous manner, the spirit drags the middle soul toward lower things by flattering it, and shuts it up in the opaque body, where for the most part it leaves it alone and idle; and it effects this by the charms of the sensitive soul, to which it is more inclined to adhere than to the mind because of its moist and material disposition, which rejoices more in its own likeness. But nevertheless, where the proportion of the middle soul's nature is ample (which is always found in the spirit), there it makes its spirit more obedient to the mind; because the middle soul, or the "act of the world" and "ray of nature," is of the remote nature of the mind itself, or the "act of God"; whence it participates in its property. Therefore, matter naturally tends toward the works of darkness, but form toward the disposition of light, as we see in the flame of a burning fire.

Is this, O readers, a new and unheard-of doctrine? Is this opinion of the Platonists, I ask, in any way disagreeing with the truth? Examine yourselves, I beseech you, and you will find that this matter cannot possibly be otherwise. For example: perhaps some deed to be perpetrated is proposed to one of you—that is, he decides within himself to commit either debauchery, or adultery, or theft, or murder, or treason against the Prince, or some similar crime. But yet reason, which is always the companion of the mind, will resist this purpose of his to the best of its power; nevertheless, it very often happens that at the end of this contention, the spiritual sense and the appetite of the flesh are fulfilled, and the admonitions of the mind and reason are rejected, and thus that intended crime is perfected. Here, then, we see that this intermediary spirit neglected the counsel of the mind, and by adhering to the sensitive soul, immersed itself in darkness. But vice versa, if the spirit, struck by the fear of the Creator and following the footsteps of reason, strongly adheres to the mind and leaves the conceived deed undone, and—kindled by repentance and a sort of hatred for that evil counsel and purpose—turns itself to a better life, it is an evident sign there that this intermediary spirit has constantly embraced the mind, and has held the animal soul, or the idol <note>original: "idolum," referring to the lower, reflected image of the soul that governs bodily functions.</note>, in contempt. But what need is there for more talk? Is it not clear to us that there are two extremes in the world, namely light and darkness, virtue and vice, good and evil? It follows, therefore, as if granted, that there is likewise a certain and determined medium between them, which is apt to participate in this or that extreme, according as the object of one or the other shall seem more pleasant and delightful to it. And without a doubt the human soul, or the internal man, is fashioned from these parts, insofar as he is perfect and complete, and consequently is judged to consist of a perfect number, namely of a beginning, a middle, and an end: that is, of the mind, the spirit, and the idol (or animal soul), or what is the same thing,

### CHAPTER III.
***Concerning Reason; and why the Mind is enclosed in an opaque body, and concerning its dominion in the human body.***

It is a matter of wonder to one who reflects upon it, by what harmony those two things—so contrary both in the nature of their essence and in their local position, namely the Mind and the body—can be joined together into one. And yet we perceive with our intellectual eyes that this is achieved through the mediation of the intervening spirit. Similarly, it will seem marvelous that this most excellent image of God, or rather the very ray of God itself, should be removed so far from its connatural seat and become so debased in its condition that, although it is the most brilliant, effective, divine, immortal, and purest light, it is nevertheless cast into and enclosed within a prison so dark, gloomy, earthly, subject to corruption, and even so foul and filthy. <note>The "prison of the body" is a classic Platonic and Hermetic concept where the physical form restricts the divine soul.</note> But we acknowledge that this was done by the divine providence of the Creator, so that the Mind might both cherish the nature of particular things and be occupied with the multitude, while also looking back toward the arrangement and unity of universal things. Hence Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 245–325 AD) who wrote on the soul's descent.</note> says: *Souls and heroes are more concerned with the multitude; Gods and Demons with unity.* For the deeper the light descends into the material pyramid from its peak toward its base, the more it inclines toward the multitude, as was said above. Indeed, by this path the Creator willed that a certain "earthly God," though a mortal one, should observe the multitude of particular things on earth, just as He Himself, as the immortal God, regards unity and universal things in heaven. In such a way, God the Creator Himself is said to dwell both on earth and in heaven, and to be present everywhere.

Hermes Trismegistus <note>The legendary Hellenistic figure to whom the Hermetic corpus is attributed.</note> seems to support our opinion with these words in *Asclepius 4*: <note>original: "ἔγνω δὴ" (egno de) - "Indeed he knew"</note> *When God noticed that the form of the divine likeness could not be diligent over all things unless He covered it with a worldly garment, He covered it with a body as a home; He perceived that all such beings were created by blending and mixing the two natures into one in sufficient measure. Therefore, He fashioned man out of soul and body—that is, out of eternal and mortal nature—so that a living being thus fashioned could satisfy both of its origins: to marvel at and pray to celestial and eternal things, and to inhabit and govern earthly things, etc.* Therefore, the power of the mind in the human body is infinite, since, according to the testimony of Hermes Trismegistus in *Pimander 12*, it is born from the essence of God (if He has an essence) and is by no means divided from His essence, but is rather connected to it in the same way that light is connected to the body of the Sun. And hence it is that the mind dominates all things, and nothing that pertains to fate is impossible for the mind. Thus it happens that the human soul is superior to fate. And yet, it does not neglect those things subject to fate; and for this reason the wise man—that is, one endowed with the action of the mind—is said to "rule the stars." <note>A reference to the famous astrological maxim "Sapiens dominabitur astris" (The wise man will rule the stars).</note> From this also, the same Philosopher seems to acknowledge that every bodily motion in the body is produced by the mind. For the external man was not made a living creature until the God-like breath was breathed into him. Hermes Trismegistus in *Pimander 10* says *that the soul, destitute of the presence of the mind, is able neither to do nor to say anything.* From the sacred writings of the holy Philosophers, therefore, we gather that "mind" is understood in two ways: namely, either as the primary and superior mind, which is the act and ray emanating immediately from God; or as the inferior mind, which is the image or vestige of the primary and superior mind.

The image of this first mind also shone forth on the second day of creation in the midst of the abyss, and produced the ethereal heaven and the life-giving soul of the material or visible world: which image of the prior mind and secondary mind is not undeservedly called Nature itself or the worldly ray. And this is granted to individual animals and the other visible creatures of the world. Wherefore *Hermes Trismegistus in Pimander, book 12* <note>original: "Mercur. Trismegist. Pimand. 12." Hermes Trismegistus was the legendary Hellenistic figure to whom the Hermetic corpus, a series of mystical and philosophical texts, was attributed.</note> called this secondary mind the *nature of brutes and vegetables.* This opinion is supported by *Synesius* <note>A 4th-century Greek bishop and philosopher who blended Neoplatonism with Christianity.</note> in these words from *Hymn 3: The mind having glided down into matter (hyle), the immortal mind, the offspring of divine parents, small indeed but the whole of them, that one mind everywhere, the whole infused into the whole, turns the vast cavity of the heavens, preserving this universe; distributed into diverse forms, it is present; part of it is the course of the stars, part the assembly of angels, part also by a heavy bond has obtained an earthly form, and being disjoined from its parents, has drunk of dark oblivion, etc.* Similarly elsewhere, the same *Hermes Trismegistus* seems to confirm that very thing in these words: *Mind, he says, is GOD in men, and therefore some from the number of men are Gods, and their humanity is closest to divinity: For the good Spirit (Daemon) proclaims Gods as immortal, but men as mortal Gods. In irrational animals, however, that mind is nature. For wherever there is a soul, there is mind; just as wherever there is life, there also is a soul in living things without the discourse of reason.* But indeed, the middle soul in its nature is void of the first mind, although it is itself as it were a secondary mind, which suffices for the life of any creature. Hence, says *Hermes Trismegistus in Pimander, book 10: The soul, destitute of the presence of the mind, is able neither to do anything nor to say anything: but often the mind goes out from the soul, at which time the soul neither hears nor sees, but is like an animal lacking reason:* So great, I say, is the power of the supreme mind, which deserts a soul of this kind when it is entangled in the body and dragged by the same as if to the lower regions. For this eternal essence, to speak with *Hermes Trismegistus*, is very far removed from the ignorant, the wicked, the lazy, the envious, the unjust, murderers and those of like kind, or at least it is vacant in its lodging, permitting them to the judgment of the avenging Spirit <note>original: "Daemonis ultoris"</note>, who, striking with the sharpness of fire, afflicts the senses, and arms the man more and more to commit crimes, so that as one guilty of a more shameful fault, he may be subject to sharper punishment; it inflames him without any intermission to insatiable lusts, fights with him in the darkness, examines the sin, and in a wonderful manner excites and exaggerates the force of the fire for his torment. But indeed, to souls whose spirit adheres to it, the mind will be present most kindly and very fortunately; for it is accustomed to flow into the holy soul and to extol it to the light of wisdom; for it will be benevolent to good, pious, pure, religious, and holy men; by its presence it brings them aid, so much so that they immediately know all things, and it inclines them to give thanks and to bless piously; it makes them truly yield the body to its death, and to loathe the allurements of the senses, as those who clearly judge how lethal the enticements of the senses are; furthermore, the mind itself, performing the duty of a gatekeeper, by no means permits those falling into the snares of the body to achieve their end; for it constantly blocks the entrances through which foul flatteries are accustomed to flow, and extinguishes all the fuel of lusts. Hence *Hermes Trismegistus in Pimander, book 12: Over whatever souls the mind presides, it illuminates them with its own splendor, resisting their evil habits, just as a learned Physician afflicts the body of a sick person with pains, by burning and cutting it for the sake of recovering health: in the same way the mind afflicts the voluptuous soul, that it may pluck out the roots of pleasure, and purging the body of evil, procures the good of the soul no differently than a Physician procures the health of the body.* Indeed, of this divine mind there is yet a more wonderful...

The divine efficacy within bodies was declared by Hermes in his fourth discourse of the *Poimandres* <note>original: "Pimand." referring to the *Poimandres*, a foundational text of Hermeticism</note>, where he speaks in these words: *Whoever is supported by this creature of God, according to the comparison of their works, is held to be immortal instead of mortal; they embrace all things in their intelligence—those on the earth, those in the sea, and if there is anything beyond them above the heavens. They raise themselves toward God so that they may behold the Good itself; and truly, when they perceive it, they consider this life we feed upon here to be a kind of misery.* Conversely (as is clearly evident from what has been said above), as many human souls as are by no means strongly governed by the Mind suffer the same things as the souls of brute animals. For the Mind leaves them to the rule of their desires, toward the fulfillment of which they are carried with a certain burning impulse; in the manner of wild beasts, they are immoderately angry and lustful, and, what is worse, they set no end to their lewdness, nor do they find a limit to their evil passions. To these people, says Hermes Trismegistus in *Poimandres* 12, *God has proposed the Law as a sort of officer and avenger; according also to that saying of Saint Paul in Galatians 3:19: The Law was added because of transgressions.* But truly, in those men whose intermediate spirit adheres to the Mind, it restrains the impulse of lust and restricts the heat of anger, etc. But since the blessed actions of the Mind are not granted to everyone—for its essence, although it is in the body with the vital soul, will nevertheless be absent and void of divine actions unless the soul, with its spirit, seeks and loves it while neglecting the sensory soul—therefore, the method of reconciling this divine form so that it may operate in the soul and not remain idle must first be investigated. Hermes Trismegistus says in *Poimandres* 4: *The lover of the body cannot be washed in the liquid of the Mind’s mixing-bowl; for unless one hates his own body, he cannot love the Mind. But as soon as he loves not himself but God, he will immediately attain the Mind; and having finally obtained this knowledge, he will attain it in his very footsteps.* The discourses of Hermes Trismegistus seem to agree with the Holy Scriptures in many places. Hence Saint John in his 1st Epistle, chapter 2: *He who loves the world does not have the love of the Father in him;* and in the same place, chapter 3: *The world does not know the sons of God, because the sons of God have not known the world; because the whole world is placed in wickedness, as in chapter 5.* Similarly, in the 1st Epistle of Saint John, chapter 2: *Those affected by the lust of the flesh do not have the love of the Father in them.* And elsewhere: *Lust is everything that is in the world, which is not from the Father, but from the world.* From these things it is clear that the Mind is not present in those who are captured by the love of the body or worldly lust, since GOD does not know such people, but only the world knows them, insofar as their actions are occupied with worldly things.

***

### CHAPTER IV.
### That the mind and reason of man are not subject to fate, and that the stars cannot impose necessity upon them.

By "fate," the ancient philosophers understood the operation of the seven Planets within the fixed stars. For whatever is ordained by divine providence from the Archetype <note>The "Archetype" refers to the original divine blueprint or the world of ideas in God's mind.</note> in the intellectual world is committed to execution by the fixed stars and the seven Planets in the visible world. This is also confirmed by Hermes Trismegistus in *Poimandres* 1, calling fate the "disposition of the seven governors"; to which he asserts all animals <margin>* also</margin> are subject, except for man. When the mind uses the rewards granted by God for that which is fitting, it differs in no way from the immortals; indeed, once released from the shackles of the body, it is led by both <note>likely referring to the mind and reason</note> to the choir of the blessed and to God himself. The Platonists also put forward a discourse of this kind: *The Mind is above fate and exists within providence;* <note>original: "Mens supra fatum est in providentia"</note> therefore, it is affected neither by the influxes of the heavenly bodies nor by the qualities of natural things; thus, religion alone governs it. But why should we recite or cite the authorities of others further in this place, when the most evident reasons—drawn from the very marrow of sincere philosophy—are at hand? These reasons clearly demonstrate that the mind and reason of man dominate the stars and their influxes, and that the mind is not subject to the actions of the visible heavens. Would it seem equitable for a most eminent king to be governed by his subjects, or to be subjected to their punishments and passions? It would certainly be unjust to be led by such an imagination: that the Creator should be compelled to anything beyond His own will by His creatures, or that the act and ray proceeding immediately from Him—which is in no way separated from His divine essence but perpetually connected to it—should be subjected to creatures established and fixed by that very Mind and Word. What power, then, do the stars or the creatures of the middle heaven <note>the visible planetary spheres</note> have to act upon the creatures of the higher heaven <note>the Empyrean or spiritual realm</note>, and especially upon their author and creator? Without a doubt, gifts are poured downward from the Empyrean heaven through the divine benevolence of the Creator and are received in the desired manner; however, they are not thrown back upward by the creatures receiving them. For that would be to ungratefully return what is freely accepted for oneself and those below, and, in the manner of the Prince of Darkness, to forget the benefit of the Creator, to be carried on high by the wings of pride, and to foolishly seek the loftier kingdoms. Elsewhere, therefore, we have explained quite copiously that this matter stands differently; where, in our *Worldly Music*, <note>referring to the author's work "Musica Mundana"</note> we declared that the Sun, the commander of the middle heaven, received his gifts from the sublimity of the Empyrean heaven (God the Creator so willing) through the power of the *Diapason* consonance <note><term>Diapason</term>: the musical interval of an octave, used here as a metaphor for harmonic proportion between spiritual and physical realms</note>, so that from his abundance he might pour a portion of life, every day, hour, and minute, into the lower things, likewise by the power of the material *Diapason* consonance, into the earth. From these things it is clear that the lower region of the world receives its measure of life from the middle region in the same way that the middle receives it from the higher. Now, truly, it would be considered an absurdity if anyone were to say that the Sun and the middle heaven receive their life and formal nourishment from the lower region, or the highest from the middle—just as if one were to infer that a cause proceeds from its effect, or a beginning from that which it began. For the Holy Scriptures acknowledge the distinction of the works of the first three days of creation. The matter, then, to speak briefly, stands thus: The human soul, which we have declared above to be the internal man, is composed of three portions derived from the triple heaven, as we have said. It acquired the nobler portion of its composition from the Empyrean heaven—indeed, directly from God Himself—carried in the Empyrean spirit; namely, the ray of the mind sitting in the rational chariot. Its middle portion, which gives life to the body, acquired its power from the ethereal heaven; this portion, with its own spirit, receives the spirit of reason along with its lord. We have already explained clearly enough that the lowest portion of the soul, composed of the subtle part of the elements, is the disposition of the animal and sensitive soul. Now, it is manifest from what has been said that the nature of the middle heaven is governed by the nature of the supreme heaven, and that in turn by the essence of God: not otherwise than the lowest and elemental nature is governed by the higher ones joined together. From this, therefore, it follows that if the middle portion of the soul clings to its lower member, the divine mind itself will refuse to have communication with it; whence it will follow that the influences and operations of the stars will have the fullest predominance over such a soul and its entire body; for that portion of the soul superior to the essences of the stars will be vacant, nor will the mind be found present in its operations. The *Sun* makes him bilious and proud. *Venus* makes him luxurious and submerged in worldly lusts and desires. *Mercury* makes him inconstant and of light or easy belief. The *Moon* makes him a drunkard, sluggish, and negligent. Whence it happens that it forgets its Lord, and thus notices neither worldly vexations nor the torments of the Demon, until, totally abandoned by the mind, it pays the penalties and cries out in despair or too-late repentance: *I have sinned;* and thus it adheres eternally to its own mud, nor is it able to ascend higher, because, abandoned by its divine Lord through whom it ought to have risen, it lies prostrate and submerged in darkness. Therefore, let the scrupulous no longer say that the stars act by no necessity upon men destitute of mind, since we have most clearly proved by the reasons already alleged that they are in every way subject to the stars and the visible heaven. And in this way we see that it is not outside the nature of things to judge by Astrological virtue concerning theft, murder, debauchery, or other such vices of men. ### CHAPTER V.
### *That the mind and the soul adhering to the mind are not subject to passion.*
<note>original: "passioni" - in this context, "passion" refers to being acted upon or suffering external influence, rather than just emotion.</note>

Since the mind is a true act of God, arising from the very essence of God (to use the words of Hermes Trismegistus) and is by no means divided from the divine nature, as was declared above; likewise, since it is the prince of all things and, as it were, the center, and (if it is permitted to say so) speaking according to the opinion of Hermes Trismegistus in *Pymander* 12 and Synesius in *Hymn* 3, it is the very soul of the Creator himself, so that it can accomplish whatever it wills; for it rules over all things, and indeed even over law itself: it follows from this that it alone acts upon all things, and that all things suffer its actions (while the mind itself remains inviolable according to the nature of God). It is immobile and yet the first mover of things, and subject to the actions of nothing. For since it alone is the "act" of things, other things cannot act unless they receive the power of acting from it: Wherefore it is necessary that it acts upon itself and consequently tolerates its own proper actions, or that it suffers in no other way. But truly, since every action exists in a subject or a "patient" <note>The "patient" is the entity that receives an action.</note> fit to receive the acts of impression, and is in some way contrary to the agent; therefore the mind cannot act upon itself as if upon a passive subject; first, because its entire entity is identity and formal, and it has nothing of matter in itself, nothing subject to passion, nothing resisting its own nature, but its parts are homogeneous, and it is unity itself; wherefore no contrariety is observed to be in it. Hence it is that the Philosophers maintained that no pure element acts within its own sphere; but they said its actions are impressed upon a sphere contrary to it by nature. Much more, therefore, do we affirm that the mind neither acts upon itself nor suffers; insofar as it is the purest and God-like form, without any admixture of material spirit, proceeding immediately from God, which effects all things in this world and never suffers anything. Of this portion of the soul, Iamblichus speaks thus: *The soul in bodies is pure, and is not touched by disturbances, since it is an unbegotten supernatural life, nor by any dissolving pain, since it is outside every body.* And in another place: *Since the soul is an indivisible and uniform essence remaining incorporeal according to itself, communicating nothing with the body, it certainly does not admit the passions of division or alteration or any change.* Proclus also seems to affirm that the middle soul itself does not suffer, but that all passions proceed from the body, and are in no way present in the soul: *The passions of the body,* he says, *do not pass over into the soul, whence even if death is of the body, it is nevertheless not an evil of the soul:* Whose opinion, full of divinity, I can never sufficiently praise or admire, since it draws an argument from the greater passion, thereby proving that lesser things hurt the soul much less, as if he had said: not the lesser, because not the greater. For if the passion of death, which is the greatest of all, dissolving the bonds of the body itself, effects nothing toward the disturbance of the soul, but rather leads to its liberation from prison, much less will it be disturbed by the lighter affections of the body. But so that we may respond to his argument, worked out with a wonderful sharpness of wit, by proving that the matter does not stand absolutely as he thought; we say, that this liberty of the middle soul is not from itself, but because of its connection with the divine mind: Whence if its spirit adheres to the mind and embraces the rays of divine light, it feels the evils of the body in no way; but rather delights in its disturbances, so that, the body being finally dissolved, it may be more quickly freed from its bonds. Hence Porphyry says, that *the soul, though always wakeful by itself, nevertheless sleeps as if in the body.* And Proclus relates, that *the soul in bodies may be sick, and as if delirious.* But, if indeed that intermediate spirit, the middle soul—

For it is impossible for the soul to be liberated from the captivity of matter unless it be done through the mediation of the mind and the life-giving Spirit of the divine Word. Only upon their wings, and no others, can it be elevated and sublimated from the earth to the summits of heaven. For it is very easy for matter to descend, but most difficult for it to ascend and return without fiery wings, by whose aid a heavy spirit is carried and raised to heaven much more swiftly than a globe from a cannon is shot upward into the air by the force of fire. Finally, we say that the ray of the mind in the first creation, the further it descended from the source of unity, the more deeply it immersed itself in the multitude of matter, as was said in the "Harmony of the Soul." Whence it happens that although the ray or act proceeding immediately from God is simple and most pure, the ray produced from it (which is called the "second mind" and Nature itself) is more involved in the chains and wrappings of matter (which we called "spirit" above), just as was said in our *Macrocosm*. And therefore, it requires the help of the first Mind for its redemption. In this way, therefore, the world shall be renewed and exalted in virtue, as the Prophet Isaiah testifies in these words: *The sun shall be ten times purer and more excellent in its beauty*, for all things shall be perfected by the presence of the Word residing in the mind, which for that reason most rightly claimed for itself the name Alpha and Omega <note>original: "a & ω"</note>.

### CHAPTER VI.
->Why the human mind and reason inhabit the superior region of the Microcosm, the Empyrean heaven?<-

In our small book concerning the external man, it was shown that he is divided into three regions, according to the disposition of the macrocosm <note>The "Macrocosm" refers to the great world or universe; the "Microcosm" refers to man as a miniature reflection of that universe.</note>, the superior of which we have compared—not unsuitably or without most evident reason—to the empyrean heaven. For just as in the empyrean heaven of the macrocosm there exists the connatural place and seat of the divine mind and rational spirit, according to the opinions of the most learned Philosophers and Theologians alike, so also it is observed by learned Philosophers and Physicians that the place and lodging of reason and intellect is situated in the head, or the superior microcosmic region. 

And indeed, even if we look at common experiments: a sphere fashioned of empty glass, however much someone might attempt to submerge it in water by force, will always be found to rise back to its natural place, because the nature of its content (namely, airy) is to float upon the water. We perceive this same thing in wood, on account of its airy and fiery disposition. This, therefore, is also the reason why the mind, since it is the highest of all things, possesses the superior part of the place in which it exists. 

For although the rational or empyrean spirit is its vehicle, and the mundane soul <note>original: "anima mundana"; the soul of the world that connects spirit to matter.</note> with its ethereal spirit is in turn the chariot of the intellectual spirit, and for all these the air is like a wagon in which the mind is introduced into the body with the rest; nevertheless, the human mind possesses the summit of the entire animate semi-diameter. Like a most divine king or emperor, it always occupies the superior seat, both in the part of the internal man and the external. It seems to claim for itself the office of a sailor, as it were, cutting the corporeal ship through the fluctuating disturbances of the world and the tempestuous and stormy waves of this life, directing it safely to the land and harbor of happiness—provided that its other ministers (namely, reason, life, the natural spirit, and the senses) are rendered obedient to it. 

But if they should be rebellious and do not listen to the governor's commands, they will without doubt produce an inevitable shipwreck, fatal to themselves, in which they will be swallowed up into the abyss of the world's sea along with the bodily ship or skiff, and be gulped down alive by the gaping maw of darkness. Meanwhile, however, the sailor or governor, seeking the heights with immortal wings, will return to his blessed fatherland with his rational spirit; for the spirit, insofar as it is not subject to fate, is always accustomed to be obedient to the mind. 

Hence it is that, just as the governor of a ship sits in the superior part of the stern and directs the inferior sailors in their duties so that they may make their journey prosperously and favorably—and the sailors themselves are occupied partly in the lower part of the stern and partly in the upper, as occasion moves them—so also the mind inhabits the superior region of the human body. To its nod, the other ministers (namely the vital soul and the natural and sensitive souls) are present and ready to carry out and dispatch all its commands with diligence. 

But also, what more evident argument, I ask, can be sought for the fact that the mind inhabits this superior region of man, than that we see him standing more erect and orthogonally <note>Standing at a right angle to the ground.</note> than all other animals? From this it is most manifest that in his peak and summit there exists a most eminent power and act, raising and lifting the senses themselves toward heaven, not otherwise than the heaviest bodies are perceived to be elevated on high by the power of artificial fire. Indeed, so efficacious is this divine fire (which Hermes Trismegistus <note>original: "Merc. Trismeg."; refers to the legendary Hellenistic figure Hermes Trismegistus, the purported author of the Hermetic Corpus.</note> asserts is accustomed to put on a fiery garment as soon as it has been separated from the body) that it not only [lifts] the bodies of men...

### CHAPTER VII.
### That light throughout the entire worldly orb is the same, and likewise the Spirit is the same; and how light tends toward the purification and elevation of Spirits on high.

**I**n very many places previously cited in our macrocosmic book, we have abundantly and lucidly revealed the succinct and most intimate relationship of the light of each heaven. For we explained that the Light of the highest region of the world, created on the first day, is the icon or image of the divine mind; and that the secondary light, which informed the middle heaven on the second day, is as it were a ray or likeness of the former and higher one; and finally, that the third is the idol <note>original: *idolum*, here meaning a reflected image or representation</note> and effigy of the second. Similarly, we explained that by the power of the higher light, the rational or empyrean Spirit was created and called the "ray of the mind" (which is the ray of God); and that likewise the middle spirit, by the power of the middle light, was made vital or ethereal, or the "fifth essence" <term>Quintessence: the purest, fifth element that fills the celestial regions</term>, and is called the "ray of the world," the "soul of the world," and active nature itself. Furthermore, we showed that by the act of the lowest light in the lowest spirit, the four elements were produced and distinguished on the third day, and this is called the "ray of the elements," and acts as the element of fire, or a portion of thin light leaping downward into those parts. 

Therefore, all these alterations proceed from the actions of the divine light, whose entire effort is to purify the unclean and to subtilize <note>to make thin or refine</note> the coarse. And by this action, the Spirit of the universal world—which, according to the testimony of Saint Peter, is nothing other than Water <note>A reference to 2 Peter 3:5 regarding the earth being formed out of water</note>—is distinguished into regions differing in purity and impurity, thinness and thickness, and into the arrangement of the four elements. From these things it is clear that the universal light of the world is unique, derived from the eternal fountain with the same action and nature, and that the differences in its operations exist not in the light itself, but in the diversity of the resisting matter. 

For that which resists more strongly requires a stronger act, and that which is weaker in its repugnance needs a smaller impression; and yet the principle of the action is always the same. Similarly, the principle of "passion" <note>the state of being acted upon</note> proceeds from the diversity of matter, differing in thickness and thinness. For that which is dense and compact grants a place to the impressions of the agent with greater difficulty. Whence it happens that celestial light, because of the very minimal resistance of its Spirit, seems to us to heat imperceptibly, even though it nonetheless excels in its luminous office. So also we see that the same light, because of the narrowing of its rays in a thick spirit, becomes and turns into a destructive fire intolerable to the sense of touch; indeed, we are taught that the more it penetrates toward the center of the earth, the more vehement its burning and destroying faculty exists; since its rays, by tending further downward, find increasingly coarser matter, and are thus finally compressed in an ineffable manner. Whence it happens that it burns not without the greatest torment, and produces common fire. So also, nothing makes the flame of a fire visible other than the contraction of the thinner inflamed parts of the air, or the gathering into one of the rays of light that were hidden and dilated in the air. In which same way we also see that moist air, invisible in its thin nature, is condensed by contraction into a visible and palpable cloud, which...

From these facts, therefore, it is clear that the parts of the universal light do not differ from one another, but are of the same nature; consequently, the cause of the difference in how it appears to us is the diversity of its operation. Similarly, the entire matter of the world is the same, namely water; yet it is known to differ according to the greater or lesser proportion of light found with it and within it. Hence, we teach that the lower light acts upon its aerial spirit in the same proportion as the middle light acts upon its own; and again, that the middle light acts upon its ethereal spirit no differently than the light of the higher heaven acts upon its own. 

Therefore, the entire difference consists in this: the lower light is resisted more because of its small proportion and the multitude of matter <note>The "lower light" refers to elemental fire on Earth, which struggles against dense, heavy matter.</note>; however, the middle light is resisted less because of its equality with the ethereal spirit (the nature of which we showed above through the harmonious adaptation of the formal and material pyramids <note>A reference to Fludd's "Pyramidal Diagrams" where the pyramid of light/form and the pyramid of matter/shadow intersect.</note>), inasmuch as it finds a Spirit obedient to it in the same proportion. And so, further still, the superior light—being excellently abundant—acts upon the empyrean spirit with even less or the very least struggle; for that spirit is the most refined, and is therefore called incorporeal and plainly metaphysical, which is to say, placed beyond the boundaries of nature. 

And this is that most evident reason by which men—those illuminated by the divine mystery, and to whom God is consequently not demonstrated *a priori* <note>original: "à priori" — reasoning from cause to effect; here meaning knowing God directly from His essence.</note>—ascend as if by a ladder *a posteriori* <note>original: "à posteriore" — reasoning from effects back to the cause; here meaning knowing God by observing His creation.</note> so that they may arrive at the knowledge of God. For through the hidden operations of water with fire which we observe here on earth, we can divine the effects of the middle light in its own spirit; and thus also from the manifest actions of the Sun in the air, it will not be impossible to judge the power of the primary light in the secondary spirit. Finally, having discovered the rationale of the action of the middle light with its spirit, the diligent inquirer will not be entirely denied the ability to effectively behold, to some extent, the actions of the higher heaven and their effects. 

Thus, at last, it will be perceived that the light which has gone forth from the divine source tends toward the purification, cleansing, and thinning of matter, and consequently toward its elevation and exaltation from the gross to the subtle, and from a place subject to corruption to a seat filled with formal light, which satisfies its every desire. For the disposition of the divine essence is benign and inclined to always work toward the preservation, salvation, redemption, and promotion of things from darkness into the regions of light. Thus, it is always engaged in the reformation of deformed things, longing to lead the dispositions of the base back into beauty, to reveal the delusions of darkness and strife to the world, to confer and distribute the gifts of its kindness to everyone, and finally to seal all things with the characters of its divine love. 

Do we not observe in this elementary region that the flame of fire, by natural instinct, neglecting things superior and sublime, seeks the lower things with every effort? <note>Fludd refers to the way fire reaches down to consume fuel or how heat penetrates downward into matter.</note> Nor indeed can we turn it away from this inclination of its own without its sensible extinction. So in the nature of an artificial fuse <note>original: "fusi artificialis" — likely referring to a rocket or a pyrotechnic device.</note> we observe that, as soon as its fiery disposition is brought into action, its heavy body is lifted on high against its own [natural] disposition. From these things we can see how greedily the lucid nature desires its connatural seat, and endeavors to leave its corporeal mass and extricate itself from its bonds.

## CHAPTER VIII.

*Concerning the unequal proportion of the body and the luminous soul, and how light labors here on earth solely for the elevation of the body toward heaven and the purging of its impurity.*

The matter of the body stands in proportion to its luminous soul just as the spirit of the lowest region of the world <note>The "lowest region" refers to the sublunary or terrestrial realm in Renaissance cosmology.</note> stands to its light; which we have stated above is found in a sesquialterate proportion <note>A ratio of 3:2, often associated with musical harmony (the perfect fifth).</note>; insofar as one part of light and three parts of material Spirit are found there. From this, therefore, it happens that the body is said to weigh down the soul and impede it in its actions; so much so, indeed, that it does not allow the soul to accomplish what it desires, and it strives with all its might against the soul's actions, which tend toward elevating the body on high. 

That the soul is many degrees weaker in the body than matter is, is declared by experience. For if anyone should descend from a mountain, this motion will be very agreeable to the body; since every heavy thing, by a certain natural instinct, tends downward; indeed, the man even rejoices <note>The text breaks off here, suggesting the physical ease of descent compared to the spiritual labor of ascent.</note>

But, to set aside those artificial things, we also see the same disposition in plants; for in them, portions of light rising out of the earth lift themselves upward toward their natural place with their entire physical mass, with the rays of the Sun going before them as an aid. 

And now to press on with the investigation of animals, *I heard from a certain maidservant that once, because of its remarkable greediness, she caught an older and larger cat unawares in the very act of gluttony. Lacking any other weapon, yet unwilling to let the opportunity of the moment slip from her hands, she attempted to crush it mercilessly with her feet, and so try to suffocate it by treading upon it. But when she stood upright with one foot placed on the cat's throat and the other pressed and fixed upon its heart—torturing and afflicting that wretched little animal without any pity in a deadly war on account of its voracious appetite—she perceived such great force in its body, and such vigor and efficacy in that tiny part and almost-spark of light or action enclosed within it, that she was struck with a certain wonder and continually feared lest at any moment, even notwithstanding such a great weight, she might be lifted high and thrown down; namely, while she felt the huge vigor of the enclosed Spirit carrying her up and lifting the mass of her body on high.* 

From these things, therefore, it is most evident that the vital Spirit, with its acting light, has the greatest power. This is true not only in things made by art—in which the place of the aerial spirit is held by saltpeter <note>original: "sal nitri"; potassium nitrate, often associated by alchemists with the "spirit of the world"</note> (inasmuch as it is nothing other than congealed air) and the role of light is supplied by that sulfurous nature, whose lucid nature, when brought into action, is moved by the power of that Spirit—but also in vegetable things...

Hence, as was said before, the fixity and immobility of minerals, whose soul was produced from the light of the lowest or "third-rank" heaven; for this reason, on account of the weakness of the light and the strength of the matter and its compact nature, they rest around the center <note>The center of the earth, the point of greatest gravity.</note>. So also the plant, although it is more lively than the mineral, such that it rises up above the earth, is nevertheless fixed to the ground by a foot <note>The root.</note>, nor can it move by itself. But truly the animal is free, and is seen to move its body locally here and there, and sometimes to lift the burden of its body from the earth by a leap. From this, the difference of creatures in the disposition of light and its corresponding spirit is most evident.

However, before we proceed to describe the excellence of human light, which surpasses all other species of light in the rest of creatures, we will here, by touching upon it only briefly and in passing, make mention of a certain experiment devised by us; from which indeed we have learned two notable things: namely, first, that human light is far worthier, more excellent, and more powerful for elevating the body on high than the light of other animals. For if the weight of any living animal is explored, and then again that same animal, having been strangled without any loss of blood or excrement, is weighed on a scale, you will perceive that the dead body is far heavier than it was when alive. And indeed everyone notices this difference between the living and their corpses. From this it is manifest that the animal had its lightness from the vital light and spirit, inasmuch as these acted constantly with an upward-tending action; but because the heavy body was a hindrance to them, they moved only to the sides, forward, and backward. And this is the cause why a living animal is lighter than after death.

So also we see that a human, having drawn the airy spirit into the lungs through inhalation, is not easily submerged in water, but is kept above the water by the lightness of the inhaled air. Likewise, a vial filled with water and placed in water will suddenly sink; similarly, if a vial is melted by the violence of fire, coagulated into a mass, and thrown into some pond, we will see it seek the bottom as suddenly as any heavy stone. But if the same vial is filled with air, its burden will be elevated by the power of the air, it will be sustained on the surface of the pond or water, and will not migrate to the bottom. Similarly, if you look at the weight of a living human body and compare it with the corpse of the dead, and carefully examine the difference, you will perceive the corpse to exceed the living body in weight by its gravity. Indeed, you will observe that the proportion of weight and gravity in the human body and corpse far excels in measure and number the bodies and corpses of other animals—if indeed men worthy of trust are to be believed. Therefore it is evident that the vital light in man (which is not only solar and mundane, as in other animals, but also divine and supreme, insofar as it was breathed into man by a God-like inspiration <note>original: "afflatu Deiformi"</note>) has a greater efficacy for the elevation of the human body on high than the light of other living beings has. Furthermore, we can also investigate by a certain experiment how much essential light was lacking in a living human body for it to have been able to be carried up on high. Since this virtue exists in every man from the root of his creation (though it varies in the strength and weakness of its operation in different men), the way is revealed by certain saints, prophets, and wise men, by which it may be attracted from the luminous source through a continuous ray of that divine virtue to lower things, and consequently into man himself. CHAPTER IX.
*On the communication of human souls.*

From the preceding points, it will seem difficult to some who look upon these things only with bodily eyes, to believe that the soul of one man, by the power of its spiritual splendor, can communicate and have intimacy with the soul of another—even one far distant—in the same way that one man is accustomed to converse with another, insofar as the soul is covered and obscured by the shadow of the flesh. Indeed, even the solar light itself, from which the middle soul of the creature is derived, can be hidden and obscured by an obstacle of opaque substance much thinner than the impenetrable human body, as appears in rainy weather; how much more so, then, the soul of man which has descended from heaven. Similarly, following these sayings of Hermes Trismegistus <note>original: "Merc. Trismeg." referring to the legendary Hellenistic figure Hermes Trismegistus, the purported author of the Hermetic Corpus</note>: *The soul, deprived of its natures and conscious of the good, yet deprived of eyes, entangles itself in bodily passions, etc.* it is clear that the soul, covered by the mass of the body, is as if destitute of eyes, so that it cannot perceive things that are outside and in darkness. To these doubts, however, we respond that the matter is indeed so if the soul is considered only insofar as it regards life, which is merely the middle portion in the composition of the human soul. But truly, insofar as it is united with its mistress, the Mind <term>Mind: here used as "Mens," the highest, divine part of the human intellect in Neoplatonic thought</term>, without which the human soul cannot exist, the walls of the body can no more compress and restrain its rays than the water of a crystal-clear torrent is able to prevent the solar rays from penetrating to the very bottom. For Hermes Trismegistus says that the Mind can be raised by its own sharpness to heavenly things. And elsewhere he assigns the reason, namely in *Pimander* 12: *Because the Mind is by no means divided from the essence of God, but is rather connected to it in the same way that light is to the body of the sun.* For this reason, he called the Mind "God in men," and says that the humanity of men is closest to divinity; whence he called men "good Daemons" <note>original: "Dæmonesq; bonos," referring to tutelary spirits or divine beings, not "demons" in the modern evil sense</note> and "mortal Gods." From these things it is manifest that the sharpness of the human mind and the rays of its light are so subtle and penetrating that the pores of the body or its dark mass can in no way hinder them from penetrating the throne of the Creator Himself and moving everywhere through the world. Hence it happens, as the said Philosopher testifies, *that by the presence of the Mind, which he calls the nature of God, man embraces with his intelligence all things that are on the earth, and those in the sea, and if there is anything beyond those which are above the heaven, and he even raises himself so that he may behold the Good itself.* Therefore, the middle soul is raised by the supreme and God-like gift, and with that gift providing the way and opening the opaque pores, it pours out its rays invisibly here and there to the exterior. Nor is this indeed a wonder, since that Mind is an act immediately proceeding from God, to whom—to speak with the Royal Psalmist <note>King David</note>—*darkness is not darkness, but the night is as clear to Him as the day itself.* And this ray of God is like a spark of His divine wisdom, without which it is not possible for the human soul to judge manifest things which are before the eyes, much less those which are in heaven. But the truth of this matter can be clearly seen from the following discourse of the Wise Man in Wisdom 9:15: *The body which is corrupted weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the sense that muses upon many things, and we guess with difficulty at the things that are upon earth, and with labor we find the things that are before us: but who shall seek out the things that are in the heavens? And who shall know your sense, unless you give wisdom, and send your Holy Spirit from the highest, etc.* It is necessary, therefore, that the spark of the divine ray included in man be refreshed from on high, by the abundance of which a regeneration and a perfect union may occur between the increased Mind and the intermediate Spirit. From this comes prophecy and the foreknowledge of things done in remote parts; hence the Prophets were accustomed to be called "Seers." From this also comes the truth of dreams and the correct explanation of things through visions; because by the power of that spiritual and invisible splendor, united with the rays of the two lower portions, the whole soul...

The power of the human soul is emitted from the human body in no other way than the light and visible rays of the Sun are emitted from the solar body. Thus, someone remaining in *England* is able to send a ray of their soul like a messenger to *Rome*, or to the *Indies*, or elsewhere—even in this very instant—without any hindrance. This occurs so that, with the will leading the way, they are able to see and meditate upon those things in distant parts through the eyes of contemplation (which are truly spiritual) just as we behold things in nearby and neighboring places with our bodily eyes. Indeed, what is more, the soul of one person, through radiations and aspects <note>original: "aspectus" - an astrological term referring to the angular relationship between celestial bodies, here applied to souls</note>, can and usually does address the soul of another with a spiritual mouth, no less than the light of one candle can be brought together and joined with the rays of light from another. But because of the dullness of our bodily composition, we are unable to discern or perceive these mysteries. Hence it happens that, viewing these things with a blunt and dull sense, we pronounce them frivolous and impossible, calling them mere folly and vanity. And yet we perceive with open eyes the flame leaping out from opaque burning wood, illuminating everything in the black night with its light, and moving the middle spirit or the air by its presence; and we see how a lit candle, in due proportion, carries around images drawn on paper, and undoubtedly possesses a certain whispering within the moist medium or vehicle of its light—just as we can gather from the noise the flame makes as it mixes with the air. But since it is denied to our coarse ears to hear such things, or at least to understand what is heard, we foolishly reject them entirely; since, as *Solomon* the wisest of all testifies in the place cited above, the soul cannot perceive the secrets of the mind unless illumination is present from on high. Yet we cannot persuade ourselves that any things truly exist unless we see them, and like *Thomas* <note>A reference to "Doubting Thomas" from the Gospel of John, who refused to believe in the Resurrection until he touched Christ's wounds.</note> we do not believe those things which we have not touched. <margin>dot in margin</margin>
Are we not taught by daily experience that wonderful effects are poured into these lower regions from the applications of the rays of the Planets and stars—namely from the sextile, square, or trine aspect, and similarly from opposition and conjunction—as if there were a certain consultation of light with light concerning things that have been done on earth, or are presently being done? But fools are most loudly accustomed to cry out in derision of these things: "What have we to do with the heaven and the stars?" Ungrateful men, who reject the knowledge and recognition of their own parents <note>The author likely views the heavens/stars as the "parents" or macrocosmic origins of the human "microcosm."</note>, and impudently cast them aside, rebelling against God their Creator, believing the most excellent ornament of His machine to be of no use and utterly empty. Finally, what is your bodily speech, if not a proportional discourse of the mind, expressed through a bodily instrument by means of sensible sound and tone, so that the bodies of others (by the mediation of their souls) may understand the intention of the speaker's mind? For the body receiving such sounds cannot distinguish them without its rational soul. Do you wish, therefore, for the intention of this speech to be from the soul as the mover, or from the instrument?
He must therefore be judged most unworthy of reason who denies the communication of souls, since these lights are far more subtle, excellent, and rational than the lights or fires which are observed to act vividly upon these lower things. Indeed, the acts of the lights and stellar rays (making admirable and pregnant aspects) surpass the lights of the soul by many degrees, insofar as they have the power to produce the mind. Truly, the human soul is to be equated in this with the Angels, whose communication and intuitive discourse with one another will be denied by no Philosopher or Theologian, since this very thing is found in the prophecy of Daniel and elsewhere. When these things are exactly considered, it will clearly appear that human souls have among themselves—one with another—a communication and irradiation or similar aspect by virtue of the divine ray, such as even some lights of the celestial stars do not have with the lights of other stars; and that they are discerned to mingle a spiritual whisper or intuitive discourse with one another, no less than the Angels themselves, who speak to one another in their own manner. ...and concerning a declaration of the death or life of someone far distant.
