With the power of my soul calm and undisturbed, but entirely intent upon this business, I saw my hand governed in such a way that, having performed a projection of points and constructed a Geomantic figure <note>Geomancy is a method of divination that interprets markings on the ground or patterns formed by tossed handfuls of soil/rocks.</note>, I indicated through the information of my soul that his brother had been killed in battle, and pierced by a wound from behind; which indeed, as I predicted, the event proved true. For he had been wounded by a weapon thrust through his back, and finally died from it. But since we shall treat the wonderful operation of this science in its proper place elsewhere, where we shall declare it to be a most true science of the soul, we will omit those things in this place.

Furthermore, it also happens sometimes—when this vision of souls is somewhat hindered, either by too great a distance from one another, or even by a defect and weakness of divine illumination—that the souls themselves leave their bodies for a little while as if dead and fly out, until they encounter the radiation of the soul of the absent person whose safety or business is at stake. This is frequently accustomed to happen to those in Biarmia <note>An area in northern Russia/Scandinavia, often associated in early modern texts with shamanism and magic.</note>, of whom Olaus Magnus <note>A 16th-century Swedish ecclesiastic and writer famous for his history of the Northern peoples.</note> makes mention in his *History*. Namely, that when someone approaches them to consult them about the state of a friend far absent, two men of this condition and sort are accustomed to enter a certain chamber. There, with the doors closed, one of them, handling a bronze serpent in one hand and holding a small hammer in the other, strikes that serpent with his hammer, intermingling magical mutterings. When this is done, suddenly the other man falls to the ground as if deprived of his soul; and then, after a good interval of time, the soul returning into his body, he rises, returning to the former health and integrity of his life, and truly relates the state and health of the person living in the most remote places.

In the French Chronicles we also find that a certain King, named Gontran <note>A 6th-century Merovingian king of Burgundy.</note>, having by chance wandered away from his company of hunters during a hunt and accompanied by only a single friend, lay down exhausted under a great tree. Finally, with his head reclined in the lap of that companion of his, he peacefully fell asleep. In the meantime, while the king was sleeping, this companion perceived a certain very thin little creature <note>original: "animalculum"</note> emerging from the King's mouth, composed of air and scarcely visible. Carefully observing its motion and path, he discovered it hurrying toward a certain small stream and anxiously seeking a passage there through some safe fording place. He himself therefore rising, unsheathing his sword, placed it across both banks, and thus laid out a sort of bridge. By this means, the creature immediately hurried to the further side of the water, and entering a hole at the foot of a mountain, stayed there not long, returned by the same way, and entered the body of the King again. It happened, moreover, that Gontran, having woken up of his own accord, related to this companion of his that all those things had occurred to him in a dream which the royal companion had seen in the little creature or the "idea" of the animal. Namely, he indicated that in his dream he had been greatly troubled in crossing a river, and finally, having found an iron bridge, had safely crossed the ford, and then entering a certain cave under an immense mountain, had found there an incomparable treasure. Whereupon, having heard the companion's account of the little creature, he entered the mountain through the cave and found a huge treasure there.

But truly, as the Supreme Spirit strongly pours His divine impressions into the human soul, greater things than these are performed there; and indeed even without the powers of the soul departing from the body, but remaining entirely within. Thus Saint Paul confesses that he was caught up into the third heaven; thus the holy Prophets were accustomed to perceive the secrets of others even in far distant places, and to see with the eyes, as it were, of the mind, or by the rays of the divine soul, as if by a certain holy splendor and charity, as is most abundantly demonstrated in many places of the Holy Scriptures.

### CHAPTER X.
### That the illumination of the mind, arising from the influx and inspiration of the divine Spirit, is the cause of prophecy.

-><-

Prophecy or Prediction, according to the opinions of the ancient Philosophers, is that by which men—stirred by a holier order and way of life—both draw out the causes of present things and foresee the outcomes of future events. These Sages maintained that this oracular power descends into men either from the Gods or from Daemons <note>In the classical sense, "daemons" refers to intermediary spirits or guiding geniuses, not necessarily evil entities.</note>, for they taught that this divine spirit was breathed into and infused by them. Indeed, their opinion seems not to differ much from the words of the Holy Scriptures. For in Deuteronomy 13:1, these things are written: *If there arises among you a prophet, or one who says he has seen a dream, and predicts a sign or a wonder, etc., you shall not listen to the words of that prophet or dreamer, because the Lord your God is testing you.* Similarly: *He who, corrupted by arrogance, wishes to speak in my name what I have not commanded him to say, or in the name of other gods, shall be put to death.* (Deuteronomy 18:22). From this it is clear that what the Ethnic <note>Pagan or non-Christian</note> Philosophers understood by "Gods," the Holy Bible understands as Jehovah—either the persons of the Trinity or the one, only, and true God—and by "Daemons," they understood the same as the Holy Scriptures mean by "foreign gods." And yet we also see that those intelligences cannot produce such wonders except by divine permission, since every divine spirit flows from God as from the highest source, and from nowhere else. Hence Jehovah said: *You shall not listen to the words of the dreamer or prophet, for your God is testing you;* as if he had said: He has stirred up his ministers to test you. For Satan himself can do nothing against the permission of God, as is declared in the history of Job, and through these words of the prophet Micaiah in 1 Kings 22: *I saw the Lord sitting upon his throne, and all the host of heaven standing by him on his right hand and on his left, and Jehovah said: Who will deceive Ahab King of Israel, so that he may go up and fall at Ramoth Gilead? And one said one thing, and another another. Then a spirit came forward and stood before the Lord and said: I will deceive him, etc. I will go out and be a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets. And Jehovah said: Go out, for you shall deceive him and prevail, etc.* From this it is rendered manifest that no prophecies can occur without God's permission, and that the spirit of Prophecy proceeds either immediately from God himself, or mediately through one of his intelligences or spirits; these likewise act either by a lying spirit for the punishment of sins, or by a spirit sometimes producing true wonders and signs for the sake of testing. But all prophecies proceeding immediately from God are always true and infallible, since none of the words of God can fall to the earth in vain. Hence in 1 Samuel 10:5 <note>original: "1. Samuel 10. 5." likely referring to 1 Samuel 3:19 regarding Samuel's words not falling to the ground</note>, a faithful prophet is signaled when none of his speeches fall to the ground. And Deuteronomy 18:22: *If a prophet predicts in the name of Jehovah and it does not happen, the Lord has not spoken this.*

But leaving these things, let us return to the purpose. This prediction occurs, according to the Platonists, because of the descent or influence of higher souls into ours, which they call "illapses" <note>A flowing in or divine entry into the soul</note>. And Hermes Trismegistus <note>The legendary Hellenistic figure associated with the Hermetic corpus of wisdom</note> calls it the "sense of Daemons" and the "minds of Daemons," whom the ancients called *Eurideas* and *Pythons*, accustomed to entering the bodies of men and using their voices and tongues for the prediction of future things. Of this kind were those Pythoness women who, stirred by the divine Spirit and as if snatched outside of themselves, standing above the tripod of the oracle located near the cave, brought forth the oracles of Apollo in a prophetic manner with a bold voice, just as one reads in Diodorus Siculus and others. Authors testify that those ten Sibyls were possessed by a spirit of this kind, who are said to have left behind many writings in verse concerning God the Christ. And that Merlin, the eternal glory of England, whose like—

As for what the *Platonists* <note>Followers of Plato who believed in the soul's divine origin and its ability to receive celestial influences.</note> said—that prophecy occurs by the gliding in and descent of spirits or souls into our own minds—the Holy Scriptures also seem to confirm this in many places. For it was said of *Balaam*: *The spirit of Jehovah was present with him, namely the man with open eyes, who saw the vision of the Almighty, falling down, but with eyes uncovered* <note>original: "retectis oculis"</note>, that is, gifted with the light of the divine spirit. It must be known, therefore, that according to the Philosophers, there are three kinds of prophecy, distinguished by a threefold diverse action of the divine Spirit in man: namely *Fury* <note>term: Furor — a state of divine inspiration or "holy madness" where the human reason is bypassed.</note>, *Rapture or Ecstasy*, under which vision and dreams are included. For it is read in *1 Samuel 19:24* concerning *Saul: Stripping off his clothes, he acted in the prophetic manner; thus he fell down naked before Samuel all that day and all that night.* Similarly, for a fuller proof of the gliding in of the Spirit of God, *Samuel said to Saul in 1 Samuel 10:5: And the Spirit of Jehovah will rush upon you, so that you will prophesy with them, and you will be changed into another man.* We could demonstrate many other passages from the sacred letters here concerning the descent and infusion of the Holy Spirit into men of pious life, but since these are hidden from no one well-versed in the scriptures, we judge they should be passed over in this place, so that we may hasten to our main purpose.

Therefore, we have placed those things which have already been said as the foundation of our discourse, so that we might better explain, according to our intention, the power of the divine mind in men and its immense familiarity with the Spirit of Jehovah, and thus finally produce the rationale for prophecy and the true prediction of future events. But we are taught in *Numbers 11:25* that true prophecy occurs and proceeds solely by the benefit of the divine Spirit. We also gather from *Numbers 12:7* that God explained prophecies to us through riddles and likenesses. By these examples, he seems to argue that the Prophets, at the time they are inspired, live neither a human life nor an animal life using senses and impulse, but a divine one; and that their soul is at rest, because he says God is there in place of the soul and moves them as a more excellent soul. no contrary thoughts are perceived to be moved within us. Therefore the Mind or internal divine Spirit, being joined with the external and divinely infused divine spirit, moves the intellectual sphere of man against the motion of the animal sphere, which is led by the middle soul <note>The "middle soul" refers to the *anima*, the seat of emotions and life force, situated between the physical body and the higher intellect.</note>; and thus, although the soul may seem to be at rest, it is nevertheless moved by its own proper motion. But the Spirit, holding Dominion with the mind over both the soul and the body, snatches the whole living man away toward the contemplation of divine vision. It unites the soul itself to it, causes it to leave the human state for a time, and connects it to divinity, according to that speech of Samuel previously cited: *And you shall be changed into another man than you were before, etc.* <note>original: "Et mutaberis in alium virum, quàm fuisti antea." A reference to 1 Samuel 10:6.</note> We see also that a lit candle, when exposed to the rays of the sun, seems to lose its power entirely because of the glorious splendor of the Sun; so much so that its light, as if submerged in the glory and brightness of the Sun, does not appear to human eyes. Yet in truth, such light remains as it was before, and is not diminished in its action or power, but rather its heat and action are exalted by the power of the Sun. So also is the case with the inspired soul. For if, according to the opinion of Iamblichus <note>Iamblichus (c. 245–325 AD) was a Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote extensively on theurgy and the soul's connection to the divine.</note>, the human soul with the mind were entirely vacant of action, or even rested completely within the body, the necessary consequence would be that when that divinely infused spirit departed again, the body would remain inanimate or totally deprived of the power of action; for it is the property of light and first action either to act always, or, where it does not act, to cease to exist. Indeed, it follows rather that it acts with the presence and illumination of a greater action and splendor, and even more promptly, since a united force is usually stronger. Therefore, against these arguments of Iamblichus, it is necessary that the action of the inspired Prophet proceeds not only from God or the divine Spirit extraordinarily infused into him, but also that the soul itself with the mind—as if snatched up by the presence of the divine Spirit—is stirred by a motion unknown to nature and foreign and unusual to the body. Hence, no reason for this motion is perceived by the soul and sense; the powers of the soul, carried upward, forget lower things and, snatched by the intellectual sense, contemplate the higher mysteries of God. Therefore, the pious soul draws the mind to itself, and the mind, embracing its pious vehicle and nourishing it with divine splendor, attracts divine rays full of the divine Spirit to itself by the magnetic power of its divinity. It does this so that it may reward that soul according to its merit with their beauty and gifts, and lead it from the earthly to the heavenly path, according to that saying of *Hermes Trismegistus in the Pimander, chapter 10: A good soul, when it has kept all the commands of virtue and piety, certainly becomes either a God or a mind.* <note>original: "Anima bona, cùm omnia habuerit virtutis pietatisq; mandata, certè aut Deus aut mens efficitur."</note> Here, therefore, we must diligently observe that the miraculous works of the Prophets are not done by any power of the stars or of that portion of the human soul derived from them, nor by the body itself, but by the pure and free power of God. *But, if anyone should perhaps say that the middle soul could be the immediate cause of this power or divine gift, we shall demonstrate by an inviolable argument that the matter is otherwise.* For, since this portion of the middle soul is contained within a single man and overshadowed by a decaying body, it is impossible for it to have a power or virtue effective enough for a divine work. From this it is clear that if anyone is divinely inspired, it follows that he possesses a divine benefit through a holy illumination flowing from above, through which he is seen to be a participant in the action of God. For if divine works were from the soul, it would follow that the soul, by its own nature and power, was master of wisdom and divinity; and consequently, every other soul would also have the same property of divinity. Yet every soul is known to be far from such power. For that which seems to be a perfect soul is still imperfect in respect to divine things. *Wherefore not the soul (let me now use the mouth of Iamblichus) as the first mover, but divinity is the cause promoting divine works.* If this were not so, religion would be in vain, since without the worship of God we would be masters of divine things.

For we see in common experience that if we turn our mind's eye toward Rome, immediately—even though we remain in England as far as the external man is concerned—there presents itself to us the person, the place, or the event previously enacted there before us, so that suddenly, and as if in the blink of an eye, we behold it, etc. And it is the same even in the most remote places, namely in Judea, etc. Indeed, we may even raise the simple ray of the human mind toward God himself through serious contemplation. What, then, will this admirable essence <note>The human soul or mind</note> accomplish if it be illuminated by the divine Spirit, from which, as from a ray of God, it first flowed forth? But truly the human body is so lethal and full of illusions to the soul without the influx of this divine grace, that the things which appear to the soul are not real, and the things which truly exist are not seen by it. Whence it happens that the whole man, if not illuminated by such a Spirit, is carried away by fallacies. Indeed, every external sense is deceived regarding its own objects; how much more, therefore, the internal sense, which is covered on all sides by the shadow of the flesh. And Proclus seems to confirm this with these words: *Matter,* he says, *seems to have all things, when in truth it possesses nothing.* <note>original: "Materia... omnia habere videtur, cùm nihil reverà possideat."</note> From this it follows that carnal men are so distrustful and incredulous, and utterly deny those things which are not subject to the senses, mocking the truth of philosophy when it describes the internal nature of man, and mocking the searchers of mystical and spiritual nature themselves. For they are unwilling to admit by any reasoning what they have not seen, or, like Saint Thomas, touched. For just as men illuminated by the presence of the divine Spirit look only upon spiritual things, while despising all corporeal things by holding them to be false and trifling, so also, conversely, worldly men occupied only with the senses are accustomed to hold spiritual things for chimeras and illusions, but corporeal and sensible things for infallible truths, and thus they are deceived. Solomon clearly declares the reason for this matter to us in *Wisdom 9* <note>Wisdom of Solomon 9:14-17</note> with these words: *The thoughts of mortals are timid and our foresight uncertain. For the corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that muses upon many things; and we guess with difficulty at the things that are upon earth, and with labor we find the things that are before us. But the things that are in heaven, who shall search out? And who shall know your counsel, unless you give wisdom and send your Holy Spirit from the highest, etc.* From which it is clear that the external man cannot become internal unless he be illustrated by divine illumination. Whence, from what is said in the *1st Epistle of John*, we perceive that one is a son of the world and another a son of God, and that the son of God ought not to perceive the world or its dark acts, because the world does not know the sons of God or his acts. But now we shall bring forward the reason why those inspired by the power and presence of the divine Spirit, and by its conjunction and union with the mind of the internal man, are able to draw out and perceive the voices and secret whisperings of men who are not present. The Holy Spirit of discipline, although it expands itself everywhere throughout the entire world and grants power, motion, action, sound, and the voice itself to all things; nevertheless, it is not powerfully present to all by its help, but only to those to whom God, out of his mercy, grants it abundantly. For in some it is present simply for the functions of life, in others in a double proportion, and in some triple, etc. Whence arise the various gifts of that Spirit recited by *Saint Paul*. This, I say, most holy Spirit, inspired abundantly by God into some, makes the man into whom it is poured hear and understand any voices of animals at will, because it is itself the cause of the production of vocal sounds. Whence, when it fell upon the Apostles in the form of fire, it rendered them skilled in every tongue; and Philostratus relates that *Apollonius of Tyana* <note>A 1st-century Greek philosopher and reputed miracle-worker</note> understood the chirping and speech of birds, or the meaning of those voices, by a certain divine power. Indeed, this divine Spirit, governing the universal spirit and expanded through its universal members, tells the man in whom it dwells—and as it were echoes to him—those same voices and tones which are heard in more remote places. Nor indeed will this seem impossible to the wise man, since the *Apostle* himself,

Therefore he that speaketh unjust things cannot be hid, etc.* <note>Wisdom 1:6-8</note>. Therefore, considering these things, it is evident that to whomever the presence of the divine Spirit is copiously granted, to him is given the knowledge of both voice and vision, according to that passage: <margin>Numbers 24:15</margin> *Balaam the hearer of the words of the strong God, who knows the knowledge of the Most High, who sees the vision of the Almighty, falling down, but having his eyes opened, etc.* Regarding other miracles flowing from the illumination of this Spirit, one may read and perceive much throughout the Holy Scriptures; to recite all of these here for the reader would perhaps be tedious and seem superfluous.

### CHAPTER I.
*Concerning the properties of the vital soul and its ethereal spirit*
*within the human body.*

[Decorative woodcut initial 'Q'] What this worldly portion is, which constitutes the middle part of the human soul, we have openly and clearly explained in the first book of this work; namely, that considered in itself, it is like a spark of light from the Soul of the World descending from the sphere of equality. This Soul of the World we have called the "worldly ray," the "nature of things," the "second act," the "fifth essence" <note>original: "quintam essentiam"; the quintessence or ether, the purest element beyond the four earthly ones</note>, and the origin of the life of all living things; and this is so insofar as it is considered by itself in its own nature, without the admixture of the Mind <note>the higher intellect</note> or the sensitive soul <note>the lower soul responsible for senses and movement</note>. But truly, insofar as it is the middle portion by itself, both in the composition of the universal world and in that of the human soul, it is rightly defined by Hermes Trismegistus in the *Pymander*, chapter 12, as "life void of mind." According to its being, it is divided into matter—which is pure spirit—and form—which is the light carried in that Spirit as if in a vehicle, acting incessantly upon it as if upon its own proper passive subject. Hence, that form or light is properly called by the Philosophers the "innate heat" of the living being, and this ethereal Spirit is called the "radical moisture" <note>term: "humidum radicale"; the fundamental fluid or "fuel" believed to sustain life's heat</note>. These two, essentially joined, constitute life, and therefore, according to Porphyry, they do not die. By their virtue and presence alone, the four elements in a composition are balanced with such justice, and are bound together by the chains of this fiery Spirit in such harmonious peace, and are ordered toward vital and symphonic motions, that the life of the animal, the plant, and even the most compact mineral is procreated from them. Therefore, the total violation of the bonds of that soul brings about death and dissolution; but a partial violation brings about disease and sickness, which is nothing other than the loosening of the bonds of celestial harmony, and the unbridled and rebellious discord of one element against its fellows, a nature unsuitable to it; concerning which things, hereafter...

The Sages have demonstrated that there is a twofold reason why this soul is infused into the human body by divine will. The first concerns the mind <note>Latin: *mens*, referring to the highest, divine intellect</note>, which is the superior portion of the soul. Hence *Hermes Trismegistus* in *Pymander, Book 10* says: *Since the earthy dregs cannot receive so divine a mind, nor sustain so great a deity confined in a divisible body, the mind took on the soul as a garment; furthermore the soul, being divine, uses the Spirit as a vehicle, and the Spirit runs through the whole living being, etc.* And for this reason, this soul is not inaptly called the "temple of God" by Paul and the philosopher Xystus <note>Likely referring to Sextus Pythagoreus</note>, as was said before. Conversely, the mind rewards the soul in infinite ways for its blessed labor and duty, insofar as the soul finds its highest good within the mind. For this soul was full of the Mind and of God in man from the beginning, as *Hermes Trismegistus* testifies, agreeing in this with the Holy Scriptures. From this it follows that, just as the soul in itself is the cause of life, so also the mind joined with it—and firmly adhering to it—is the cause of a pious, holy, honest, and blessed life, which is the beginning of eternal life. And thus *Hermes Trismegistus* in *Pymander, Book 10* uses these words: *The human soul, not every soul, but the pious and blessed one, is divine.* And elsewhere: *The good soul, when it has undergone all the commands of virtue and piety, certainly becomes God or Mind.* Furthermore, the soul acquires knowledge through the presence of the mind; through acquired knowledge, it becomes similar to the mind or intellect itself, as *Proclus* testifies *On the Soul.* Hence it is, according to *Hermes Trismegistus*, that the soul united to the mind is said to be *standing and not falling.* And *Iamblichus* also excellently explains the impotence of the soul enclosed in the body with these words, where at the same time he seems to indicate and show that infinite utility which obeys the act of the soul from the presence of the mind: *The human soul is confined in one species, and too much overshadowed by the decaying body; therefore it has no effective power for divine work. If ever we seem to be able to do such a thing in some way, we only do it by divine illumination flowing in from above; through which we also seem to be participants in divine action.* And elsewhere he mentions this matter again in these words: *Since, he says, the soul, which seems perfect, is still imperfect regarding divine things.* For it is not the soul, but divinity itself that is the cause of divine works; otherwise religion would not be necessary for these things, but we would be masters of divine works without the worship of God, if these things were done by the power of the soul itself. By which, as it seems to me, he most evidently demonstrated that the mind is required first of all for the composition of the human soul, and then that the middle soul acquires its highest good from it: for otherwise prayer to God for grace and illumination would be superfluous if the vital soul possessed that property of itself, and thus there would also be no difference between a human and a brute animal. Finally, the greatest reward the soul receives from the mind is that the power of its resurrection after death consists in the virtue of the mind. For as the soul with its spirit was the cause for the mind descending into the body, because of the Spirit's inclination toward material things; so also the mind is that power by whose life-giving wings the soul is exalted to its natural seat. Hence most miserable is that soul which, neglecting the mind, clings to the corporeal soul; for when the dissolution of such a soul and body occurs, the mind flies upward on its own wings, and leaves the soul obscured in the earthy mud or the abyss of matter <term>hyle: the Greek term for primordial matter, often viewed as a dark or chaotic substance</term>. It is clear, therefore, what kind of wages or reward the middle soul receives from the divine mind for its labor, by which its nature covered the mind like a garment or a defense, by means of the Spirit, and preserved it untouched by the base body. It remains now to be investigated what benefit or what grace the inferior portion of the soul—the daughter of the elements or the sensitive soul—is accustomed to repay to this middle soul for its benevolence toward it, by which it not only descended with its Spirit and brought life and motion to it and its body, but also brought down that most excellent super-celestial gem

Thus, although by its arrangement it is most suited to it, its presence is nevertheless exalted all the more, the more it is able to entice the middle portion of the soul to itself; and consequently, it is inflated with all the more pride, the more eminent a victory its prince (namely, the Prince of Darkness) obtains against the portion of divine light present there, which bears the image of the Prince of Light. From this it happens that the lowest portion of the human soul <note>The "animal" or sensitive soul, associated with bodily desires.</note> first tempts the intermediate spirit with worldly delights and pleasures, so that it may then better and more easily deceive the soul itself, while this Spirit solicits it. Did not the serpent tempt Eve—the female or passive principle—in this way, so that he might afterwards circumvent Adam—the male or active principle—to such an extent that they were both then bereaved and deprived of God's presence? Truly, by this reasoning, the moist nature of the Spirit (or Eve) and the active light of heaven (or Adam), by consenting to the counsel of the animal or sensitive soul and adhering to it, lost the presence of the Divine Mind. Hence their misfortune and loss, which could never have been repaired or made whole again, were it not for that abundant presence of the fleeing Mind which we have received from the Savior of the world and the infusion of the fertile Mind, in which the Word of God resides.

      Hence our enigmatic explanation of the described pleasure of Paradise is made clear, which we set forth in our *Theological-Philosophical Treatise on Life, Death, and Resurrection*. For Adam's soul, through the abundant presence of the Mind, was inclined toward the contemplation of higher things alone; but when it chose instead to adhere to the allurements of the sensitive soul and the false and malignant instigations of the Devil, then the portion of the Mind flew away, and death succeeded, as if in its place. And so likewise, through a repeated and abundant infusion of the Mind into these lower regions—in which the Word is—the regeneration of the internal man follows, as well as the resurrection of both the internal and external man.

      But now we shall produce the authority of the Philosophers, speaking of the allurements and enticements of the sensitive soul (or the "idol" <note>original: *idoli*; referring to the "image" or lower reflection of the soul that clings to matter.</note>), and making mention also of its lethal inconvenience and ineffable unhappiness. *Hermes Trismegistus says that the soul, though conscious of the nature of things and of the good, being deprived of its eyes, entangles itself in bodily passions, and that it is necessary for it to look about with the eyes of the mind, lest it perish utterly.* And elsewhere he says *that the impious soul, loving the body, remains in its own nature and torments itself excessively.* And elsewhere: *he calls the soul, on account of its disjunction from the mind, not "standing" but "falling";* Thus also in his *Pimander, book 10, he asserts that the soul, destitute of the presence of the mind, is able neither to do nor say anything, and he says that this soul differs in no way from the soul of brutes.*

      Such, therefore, is the hope of the carnal and worldly soul; such is the wages of the animal soul, which it pays to the vital or middle soul for its descent from the heavens; such is its reception; this is the end of carnal hospitality; these are its riches—the effects of which are nothing other than frauds, lies, deceits, illusions, and no certainty; since all truth flows solely from the rays and virtue of the Mind, and proceeds from nowhere else.

      And certainly, most unhappy was this lot of the soul, by which, in descending into such a dark abyss of matter <note>original: *hylæ*; from the Greek *hyle*, meaning matter or substance.</note>, it migrated as if into a lodging-house and dark prison, utterly foreign to its dignity, and indeed against its own will. This is also confessed by *Iamblichus* in these words: *The soul, which glides downward, meets [its fate], dragging with it the signs of chains and punishments, and shows itself weighed down by the composition of material spirits, and occupied by the discordant disturbances of matter.* The Wise Man seems to confirm this opinion of Iamblichus in *Wisdom, chapter 9, in the place cited above: The body, he says, which is corrupted, weighs down the soul, and the earthly habitation presses down the sense (or the mind) as it thinks on many things, and we can hardly discern those things that are before us.*

      To this also, in my judgment, the opinion of *Plato and Proclus* is consonant, which holds that it is not natural for souls to spend their lives with bodies and to be occupied in generation, but on the contrary to be separated, and that an immaterial and incorporeal life is rather more agreeable to souls; and they say that when

when they are engaged in the process of generation <note>The act of being born into physical matter</note>, they are like people living in a plague-ridden region; but when they live outside of generation, they are like those who dwell in green meadows. This, therefore, is the reason why Proclus, in his book *On the Soul*, affirmed that all forms <note>The spiritual essences or "ideas" of things</note> become sickly when in the body. And for the same reason, Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonic philosopher and student of Plotinus</note> said that the soul, which in itself is always most vigilant, sleeps while in the body. Hence Synesius also said that a part of the worldly soul, having obtained its form through a heavy bond, and being separated from its parents <note>Its divine origins</note>, has drunk of dark oblivion, admiring the unpleasant earth with blind anxieties. Since the enclosed soul is afflicted by all these disturbances of the body, there is no doubt that its descent into the corporeal tabernacle of man is contrary to its nature; not unlike the disposition of fire, which by its own property always seeks the higher realms, yet is sometimes forced by violence to move downward.

Whence, then, comes this unnatural union between these two extremes? Certainly from the divine will, so that He might enrich both the lower and the higher things with His living blessings; and especially so that man, made in the image of God, might look upon both the lower and the higher. For the Universal Creator sent the "middle soul" <note>The mediating force between pure spirit and gross matter</note> into man for a twofold reason: First, to use the words of Hermes Trismegistus <note>original: "Merc. Trismeg." - the legendary Hellenistic figure associated with the Hermetic corpus</note>, *neither could the earthly dregs receive so divine a mind, nor could such a great divinity endure being confined in a fragmented body.* Therefore, the Mind took up the soul as a garment; because even the soul, being divine, uses the spirit as a vehicle, and the Spirit runs through the entire living being. 

Furthermore, Hermes Trismegistus provides a second reason in the *Poimandres*, book 3: *The human soul,* he says, *is veiled by the shadow of the flesh, in order to undertake the discourse of the celestial Gods, to attend to the works of God and the progress of nature, to observe the signs of good things, and to gain knowledge of divine power: a certain portion was granted for the judgment of good and evil, and for the discovery of the various arts of good men, etc.* From these things it is manifest that the soul in its own nature is good and most useful to the constitution of man. Indeed, it is that middle nature in the composition of the human soul without which its two extremes could not be joined together. 

But through the inclination of the flesh toward worldly pleasures and the deceptive allurements of the sensory part, the soul is deceived; and thus, through the excessive, dark overshadowing of the opaque body, separated from its parents, it drinks the oblivion of truth, and being robbed of its eyes, entangles itself in corporeal cares and passions. Hence Hermes Trismegistus in *Poimandres*, book 10: *When the compacted body disperses and distracts the soul into its own mass, then the soul is subjected to oblivion, and is deprived of the vision of the beautiful and the good. Moreover, oblivion itself is wickedness, etc.* 

Wherefore the assistance of divine illumination is necessarily required for its salvation, since without it, the soul can produce nothing good or holy in this life. Blessed, therefore, is he whose soul adheres firmly to the divine mind. Blessed is the soul which, avoiding the voracious barking of *hyle* <note>Greek: "matter" - often personified as a beast in Neoplatonic thought</note> and emerging from the earth with a light leap, carried by the wings of the mind, directs its steps toward God. Blessed is the Spirit which, after the fate and dissolution of the body, after hard labors and bitter earthly cares, having entered the paths of the mind, sees the summit and height of happiness shining with divine light. Blessed, therefore, is the Spirit with the soul, and thrice blessed is he who remains most faithful and constant to the mind until the end, for such a one shall have a foretaste of the cup of happiness and shall taste of the eternal fruit of immortality. 

Do not look back, therefore, O my soul, at the deceptive flatteries of the flesh and the world; raise yourself joyfully to the higher things according to your own proper disposition; be nobler than common fire, whose nature is always to tend toward the heights, and to despise and naturally recoil from lower things. For since you are decorated and made beautiful in the image and likeness of God, betrothed to the Spirit through faith, bought and redeemed by the blood of Christ, aided by Angels, a companion of blessedness, an heir of salvation, and a sharer in reason, what have you to do with the flesh, with the senses, and with the world? 

But now we shall deal briefly with the manner in which this soul, along with the mind and Spirit, enters into the body fashioned from clay.

CHAPTER II.

*How the middle soul, with its Mistress the Mind, is infused into the body by means of the ethereal Spirit; and concerning the nature of its fortunate, unfortunate, and mixed actions.*

**H**ermes Trismegistus <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure associated with the "Hermetica," a body of texts on philosophy, alchemy, and magic.</note> asserted that *the Word is carried into the mind, the mind into the reason, the reason into the soul, and the soul into the spirit, and this into the air; and then all things, gliding downward through the aerial sea, are transferred into the body with that spirit and in it, as if in a final vehicle.* We would also prove this same thing in a certain way, were we not to consider the mind itself to be a ray of the Word of God. For as Saint John testifies in chapter 1: *In the Word itself was life, and that life was the light of men, etc.* <note>original: "in ipso Verbo vita erat, & illa vita erat lux hominum"</note> Hence, when Jehovah uttered that word: *Let man be made, etc.*, the mud prepared by the hands of God passed into a living animal; and by the power of the breath of life, which went forth from His mouth with the Word, all human virtues were produced. And thus Adam was made a rational animal, using discourse at the same time as he was living. For we must not believe the fictions of those skilled in the art of painting, who, depicting God in the form of an external man—and thus not blushing to circumscribe Him in a physical place—falsely imagine that He immediately applied His own mouth to the muddy face of Adam. Indeed, the "mouth" and "limbs" of God are found everywhere according to His divine pleasure; rather, they are present everywhere and yet are nowhere circumscribed. For God Himself is seen by intellectual eyes to be expanded everywhere through the universe, filling all things with His presence, so that according to the doctrine of the Holy Scriptures, *the earth is His footstool, and the heaven is to Him like a seat and a throne.* <note>A reference to Isaiah 66:1.</note> Hence, whatever He speaks in the heavens is fulfilled immediately on earth in the twinkling of an eye. Therefore, sitting in heaven He said: *Let the earth be made,* and by the power of the Word the earth was established, and that indeed instantly. He also said: *Let man be made,* speaking thus from the holy heavens: and suddenly and in an instant, what He commanded was done; for the impression of the Word infused the breath of life through his nostrils, etc. Moreover, just as the world is said to be the image of God, and the threefold distinction of its regions is referred to the threefold property of the persons of the Trinity (wherefore they held the first place in creation, as was said in our *Treatise on the Microcosm*); so also man, who is the image of the world, and consequently the image of God, received this by a divine and god-like breathing. Man therefore obtained, immediately for his existence, the power of the Word and of the Spirit of the Creator; and consequently he is a partaker of the divine essence, no less than the world itself is a partaker of the Spirit of the Lord, which was moved over the waters. He also received a portion from the visible seat or throne of Jehovah the Creator, namely from heaven: for from it he obtained his life-giving soul. From the elements also, in whose region the footstool of Jehovah is placed, he received formal purity, from which his "idol" or sensitive part is made; and finally from the earth, or the center of the whole machine, he claimed for himself the muddy or external and opaque subject of his internal dwelling-place. Thus, therefore, Jehovah breathed the breath of life into the Microcosm on the sixth day of creation, on which he himself was founded, no differently than He did into the Macrocosm on the first day. It is certain, therefore, that the Word, emitted from God speaking at the creation of the divine animal man, like a true supersubstantial ray and attended by the Holy Spirit, and tending downward through the intellectual Spirit...

For thus it finally notices that through its own disobedience it has neglected the mind. Hence grief, hence tears; hence there is constant suspicion and fear within it, lest its bulwark be shortly invaded and destroyed; hence its frequent contractions, and its constant passions and perturbations which lack all reason. But some, destitute of reason, will cry out: how is it possible for this to happen? And since all these things are in nature, they will say: show us the natural reason for this matter, so that we may better understand how these things are so, and lest we utterly reject these reasons of yours. To these skeptics we respond that, just as the Sun of the world, placed in the center of heaven, shoots its rays both upward and downward by means of the Spirit—and indeed its rays leaping forth from above are most full of divine grace, by which it infuses life into the lower parts—and truly this would not happen unless there were a certain magnetic force in the sun, granted to it from creation to perform such things; so also the matter stands in that portion of the middle soul of the world (which is from the sun) situated in the human thorax or middle belly: For if it eagerly expects benefits from the superior mind, and attracts good to itself from it by the magnet of piety, its gifts will flow down most easily and without trouble to the lower parts of the bottom belly; and while its arterial branches tending upward will overflow with the Spirit of light—since the nature of the soul looks upward toward the supreme region with the nature of fire, and by its own motion catches at higher things through a certain divine appetite—then its lower branches will either be filled with the dreggy or thicker liquid of the vital Spirit, or will remain more empty, since the more excellent part of them, rejoicing in the vision of the mind, now aspires upward.

## CHAPTER IV.

*That the breath of life was given not only to men, but also to beasts, and concerning the difference between the two breaths, likewise concerning the creation of souls.*

Since we gather from the Holy Scriptures that the breath of life was given not only to men, but also to other animals (for in *Genesis 7* it is read: *All men and all things in which is the breath of life on the earth, are dead.* And likewise in chapter 6: *I will destroy all flesh in which is the Spirit of life*), therefore a no small doubt may arise as to what the difference is between the breath of life of men and of beasts. For the solution of this doubt, it must be understood that the breath of life in creation is twofold: *First*, namely, that conferred upon the world to complete the constitution of its fabric, and breathed by Jehovah on the first day into the *hyle* <term>hyle: a Greek term for primordial matter or "stuff" before it takes form</term>, so that from nothing, or rather from that which did not yet exist in act, He might produce something, indeed all things, into act. Hence *Hermes Trismegistus* <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure associated with a syncretism of the Greek god Hermes and the Egyptian Thoth, credited with sacred writings</note> called the world the Son of God, and all the Platonists called it the image of God. From this divine breath, therefore, the world was immediately created and the waters were informed, from which according to the teaching of *Genesis* the world was made; *And the Spirit of the Lord moved over the waters, etc.* And by the power of this vivifying and fiery Spirit, informing the world, all the creatures of the world received the breath of life mediately <note>meaning "indirectly" or through an intermediary</note>, as if by a certain inspiration of the world flowing from God as its root; so that the Platonists, agreeing with *Hermes Trismegistus*, said not inaptly that God is the Father of the world, but the world is the parent of all creatures. That is, God first with the Word breathed His Spirit of life into the world, by whose presence the world and all its creatures received their powers, both vivifying and otherwise, according to that of the *Royal Psalmist*: *By the Word of the Lord the heavens were made firm, and all their powers by the Spirit from His mouth.* From which it is established that beasts and vegetables and minerals received their lives immediately from the *Soul of the World* <term>Anima Mundi: the concept of an intrinsic spirit that animates all nature</term>, but the world drew its life and its spirit from the breath of God. Consequently, it is manifested that the Spirit of elementary life proceeded mediately, and not immediately, from God, and that that single breath of life, once breathed into the *hyle* at the beginning for the existence of the world, suffices to continue the virtue of all creatures until the final PERISH. But truly man, the prince of all animals, and thereafter called no less than the world itself the image and likeness of God—whence he also obtained the name of *Microcosm* <term>Microcosm: "Little World," the idea that man reflects the structure of the entire universe</term>—attained this same grace from the Creator on the last day of creation which the world attained on the first day. For in the same way that God breathed into the formless and dark *hyle* for the existence of the world on the first day of creation, in the same way, I say, Jehovah breathed the same breath into the obscure

the external mass of man; and this was not done indirectly—namely, as the other creatures of the world received it from the world—but was made directly by the Creator himself. Hence, man is as complete in his essence as the world itself: indeed, there is no nature in the world that is not likewise found in this most noble creature, man, just as we have clearly explained above. From this, therefore, as it seems to me at least, no doubt or scruple can remain regarding that opinion which asserts that the soul proceeds through transmission <note>original: "ex traduce"; referring to Traducianism, the theological theory that the soul is transmitted from parents to children through the act of procreation, rather than being newly created by God for each individual.</note>. For if the first breath of life is sufficient for the perpetuity of the world and the continuation of its creatures—since, as the Psalmist says, *by the Spirit of his mouth all the powers of the world and its creatures proceed* <note>A paraphrase of Psalm 33:6.</note>—why should his second breath not likewise be sufficient to perform the same without repetition and renewal in the succession of men, as it did first in the continuation and preservation of species in other creatures? Therefore, the contrary opinion seems rather to detract from the power of God than to add any honor to him; insofar as it seems to argue that God was not as strong and powerful at the end of his creation as he was in the beginning. For otherwise, his Spirit would be believed to be as strong at the end as in the beginning, and consequently to perform the same in the Microcosmic preservation of the species as it performs in the Macrocosm and its creatures. But truly, if a single breath of God can continue and preserve the succession of mortal men until the final "PERISH" <note>original: "PEREAT"; referring to the end of the world or the final destruction of all things.</note>, what need will there be for more? Since, as the Philosopher <note>Aristotle, often referred to simply as "The Philosopher" in Renaissance texts.</note> testifies, it is in vain to do through many things what can be done through fewer.

Having considered these things, we see, first of all, how great a difference there is between the breath of life in brutes and that which is in man: namely, that the former is indirectly from the world, whence it is also devoid of manifest reason; but the latter is directly from God, whence it adorns the internal man with intellect and clear reason, joining him by its nobility with his Creator. Next, we see that the divine breath in man differs in no way from that which was communicated to the world. And yet, the one and the same breath of the world suffices to forever perpetuate the species and the power of the world and its creatures. Therefore, the breath of man will likewise be sufficient to continue the human species, and consequently, there will be no need for the constant creation of souls. Regarding this argument, however, we shall say no more, because we have discussed the reasoning of this doubt quite openly above.

## CHAPTER V.
*On the nature and different grades of the soul in the body, and on the reason for the vigor and strength of the body, and on the reason for the differences in created species, and how the middle spirit of man differs from the middle spirit of other animals?*

It follows from those things which preceded, that there are many grades of lower souls, and that the dignity of the human soul is to be placed before all others. But since we perceive that one man surpasses another in the excellence of his genius and in the abundance and readiness of soul and reason, while in another we detect more excellent effects of the middle soul <note>The "middle spirit" or "middle soul" usually refers to the vital spirit or "anima belluina" that connects the rational mind to the physical body.</note>, insofar as he is more lively and agile than others; and again, we see another more robust in the vigor of his body and more powerful and strong in his forces, we think it necessary to diligently seek the reason for this matter. It must be known first, therefore, that the effects of reason and genius flow from the act of the mind and the rational spirit. Although this body may contribute something by way of help or hindrance, the power of the Mind <note>term: Mind (Mens) — in this context, the highest, most divine part of the human soul.</note> presiding over the rational spirit is so great in man that, if it is only effective and full in its action, the darkness and opacity of the body can in no way resist its influences; for the divine splendor illuminates the darkness within them; indeed, the darkness is not darkness to it, but the night is as clear to it as the day. Furthermore, the Word—which, according to Hermes <note>original: "Mercurio" — referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of Hermeticism.</note>, is in the Mind—consists of life, and is the light shining in the darkness; and the Mind itself, which Hermes Trismegistus calls the soul and essence of God in *Pymander* 12, dominates all things. Therefore, by the copious breath and fullness of this Spirit, the truest and most divine prophets are made from simple men; the most courageous from the faint-hearted; and the most skilled from those ignorant of art or science—if only we give any faith to the Holy Scriptures. And it follows, therefore, that the body is not an impediment to the actions of the Mind, but rather that the Mind itself, being unwilling to act in a malignant body, is said to be "at leisure" <note>original: "vacare" — meaning the Mind is present but inactive or disengaged.</note>, or else its Spirit has not been increased and multiplied by the Most High. Hence Hermes says: *the Mind is not given to all;* and elsewhere he says *that it is given to all, but in some—namely in the malignant and impious—it does not act at all, or remains idle.* For in others it acts indeed, but sparingly; but in the good, the pious, and the reborn, it works abundantly, and is multiplied by its inward flowings. From this, therefore, we see the reason for the variety in the actions of the Mind, and that the diversity of its operations is the cause of exaltation and dejection in man; since its more intense benevolence or full presence renders one wise, while its neglect and absence leave men ignorant and not much different from beasts.

However, the reason why one man is more agile and lively than another consists in the good disposition of the "middle soul" <note>term: middle soul (anima media) — the vital or sensitive soul that links the divine Mind to the physical body.</note>, which, because it exists in irrational animals as well as rational ones, produces the same effects in any animal. Hence comes an animal's lightness in leaping, speed in running, and ease in movement and life. And this disposition is also very often accustomed to occur in those animals whose bodily members are not strong, but weak. From this it is clear that this animal faculty arises from the source of the middle region—namely, from the heart, in which the middle soul (or the vital and ethereal soul) is cherished. Therefore, the cause for the greater or lesser action of the middle soul is provided by the multitude or scarcity of the "worldly ray" or secondary light, or the soul of the middle heaven, which is also called the Soul of the World. And here we recognize with Proclus that the body can do much to hinder the operations of *this* soul; because this is that portion of the human soul which is said to be weighed down by earthly dregs and burdened by the shadow of the flesh. The vastness of matter, however, longing to be given form, divides that universal soul—which revolves around unity—into infinite parts, giving these to each member of the multitude. From this arises the multitude of species and individuals; from this comes the ignorance, self-forgetfulness, and errors of the uniform soul when divided into parts; and from this arises its sorrow from such captivity. For according to Proclus, *souls grow sick and rave as if in a human body; or as Porphyry maintains, they sleep perpetually in the body as if in a dream.* <note>Proclus and Porphyry were influential Neoplatonist philosophers who viewed the physical body as a "prison" or "tomb" for the divine soul.</note> For this reason, Iamblichus says *that the characteristic of souls is a leaning toward the multitude and the motion of generation <note>The process of being born into the physical world</note>, even though by themselves and in their own nature they look toward the unity of the Deity, which is permanent in itself and yet the immovable cause of all motions.* For since the nature of the soul is always to move, insofar as it is a simple act, it produces a multitude through its own accidental motion by means of generation. Indeed, the bodies enclosing the souls, blinding their eyes, are accustomed to turn the motions of the souls toward their own appetites, which revolve around the multitude. And thus it happens that the motion of the soul in bodies produces the generations and the growth of individuals of every species.

This same thing also occurs in human bodies, which enclose the most noble form; it is theirs alone, by virtue of the divine splendor, to possess a soul more exalted than other creatures. Whence it happens that the soul, although bound in its prison by spiritual chains, sometimes nevertheless remembers its fatherland, and its edge <note>original: "acies" - referring to the keenness of mental sight</note> is sometimes raised on high by the wings of divine rays, according to that saying of Iamblichus: *The soul in the intelligible world <note>The realm of pure thought and divine reality</note> heard divine harmony, which it remembers here when it hears melodies that possess a trace of the divine; remembering it, the soul is vehemently moved toward it.* Similarly, according to Synesius: *there is also in those who have fallen down here a certain power calling them back to heaven, etc.* Indeed, to holy men, even in this life, the way is revealed by which the human soul, by leaving the multitude, can return to unity, which Hermes <note>original: "Mercurius" - referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of Hermeticism</note> calls the way of regeneration; namely, the breathing-in and flowing-in of the divine spirit.

And Proclus also seems to depict for us a certain way by which we can return from the multitude to unity; namely, the acquisition of knowledge <term>science: from the Latin 'scientia', meaning structured knowledge or certain understanding</term>. Whence he says, *that the soul through acquired knowledge becomes like the Mind; that is, the soul, by leaving the multitude through the power and illumination of knowledge, approaches unity.* For every multitude is so diverse in itself that some things seem contrary to others in every respect. Whence it will be necessary, if we wish to ascend to unity where there is no contrariety, to betake ourselves to true knowledge, in which the multitude has no contrariety. For although emotions may be contrary to emotions, senses to senses, thoughts to thoughts, and opinions to opinions, yet no knowledge is found contrary to another knowledge. For in knowledge we gather a multitude of propositions and notions into one; we also connect a number of sciences by a certain single bond; and so far are they from being contrary to one another, that even notion serves notion, and the lower sciences serve the higher, and thus the latter have their beginnings from the former.

Thus we see many notions of Geometry contribute to a single Theorem and its demonstration; thus we observe points, lines, angles, and surfaces with their notions being referred to the body or triple dimension. Thus we see numbering, addition, subtraction, and multiplication depend one upon the other, and are necessary for division and the extraction of roots. So also the rules or propositions concerning sounds, tones, semitones, the Fourth <note>original: "Diateſſaron"</note>, the Fifth <note>original: "Diapente"</note>, the Octave <note>original: "Diapaſon"</note>, and the notions of temporal signs designating proportions lead to the truth of a single symphony. And although such notions exist in a multitude, they nevertheless denote a single thing, namely melody. Thus we perceive that Arithmetic, Music, Geometry, and Optics lead to the cognition of Astrological truth. There is, therefore, no contrariety in the multitude of the sciences, since they lead to unity, but rather in the multitude of matter, which distracts and always wanders...

All sensible things <note>Objects perceived by the physical senses.</note> are to be avoided; since they are heaped together, divided, and utterly changeable. From these, therefore, let us transfer ourselves to the incorporeal essence. For every sensible thing has an accidental unity, and is by its own nature dispersed and full of weakness. For this reason, its good is also partible and accidental, distant and discordant from itself, and residing in a foreign seat. But when we have ascended there, and have been stationed within the body <note>Likely referring to the "celestial body" or the soul's proper station above the physical.</note>, we shall behold that animal order above bodies, moving from itself, acting through itself, and possessing its own substance in and from itself. Let us therefore leave behind the multitude foreign to souls, and by cutting through the ether and ascending still further upward, let us betake ourselves to the intellect and the intellectual realms, so that we may possess the unity of things, and there become contemplators of that nature. We shall behold that nature remaining in eternity, a flourishing life, a vigilant intelligence, which lacks nothing of life. Thus, where we find this, we shall very easily observe how much more suitable and better it is for souls, and we shall see whether any multitude is found in it, and whether it is uniform or multiform. Here you will perceive, therefore, that highest good, which the human soul always desires to reach. Here is the source and origin of all created things. Here is the summit and peak of joy and gladness. Here is the true and only simplicity and that truth of which *Plato and Pythagoras treat, when they admonish us so greatly to flee the multitude, so that we may attain the simplest truth.* Indeed, so that we may do this, they prescribe for us a manner and a way not at all dissenting from the way of *Proclus*; namely, *that we ought to avoid the various multitude first of the affections, then of the senses, thirdly of imaginations, and fourthly of the opinions depending on them.* And indeed the judgments of these do not seem to differ in any way from our intention. For, when the soul is enclosed in darkness, it uses the sense as if it were its leader. Whence its sharp edge is thereafter turned in the third place toward so many subjects that they produce uncertainty and inconstancy in the soul; and so the rays of the soul, distracted by so many and such great objects of the senses and the contemplation of them, allow their sharp edge to be blunted, so that they cannot penetrate to the throne and seat of unity; and in that way the soul is doubtful and uncertain as to whether it ought to turn itself to find the truth, insofar as it is no less deceived in matter than it is deceived by the illusions of the matter itself revolving around it. Wherefore *Proclus* says not ineptly: *just as matter seems to have all things, when in truth it possesses nothing, so also the soul, laboring under a double ignorance, seems to itself to possess what it does not have.* And this happens because of the manifold effect of the sense. For which reason the multitude of the external sense is first of all to be cast away. Finally, we also ought not to conceive in our imagination feigned, vain, and false things, which are like phantasms conceived in the air; since these likewise distract from that unity, which is the only truth. And furthermore, we do not think that the opinions of men, contradicting themselves and the truth, should be believed in every way. Thus, then, at last, by returning toward unity through the steps of the thousand-fold scale, we shall ascend to the middle heaven, where we shall find greater certainty and perfection. ### CHAPTER VII.

*Why has this mediating soul given only vegetative life to vegetables and plants, while it grants sensation along with vegetation to all animals?*

CONCERNING the variety and difference between the soul of vegetables and animals, we have indeed spoken somewhat in the preceding sections. In this place, however, we shall debate more extensively regarding that difference and distinction of the soul in these kinds of creatures. We have declared elsewhere in the premises that the souls of vegetables are from the clearer spirit of the "middle darkness" <note>original: *mediarum tenebrarum*. This refers to the primordial state of matter before it was fully illuminated by divine light.</note> of the second day of creation, reverberated downward from the middle heaven of the world, with portions or sparks of fertile light enclosed within it. And we likewise demonstrated there that this same spirit is also the soul of all animals. But to some, perhaps, it will seem absurd or scarcely probable that the same light with such a spirit should be the origin of both types of living things (since they differ by such a great distance between them); for they will argue that the same things cannot differ so much from themselves. To these we respond that the soul of a plant does not differ from the soul of an animal except according to "more and less" <note>A philosophical concept suggesting a difference in degree or intensity rather than a difference in fundamental kind.</note>. We shall briefly declare here the reason why a plant has less of the mediating nature, while an animal has a more abundant portion of it. The sacred Scriptures teach us that plants and vegetables, rising out of the pores of the earth, were created with the earth itself on the third day of creation; at which time the celestial rays were not yet contracted into the Sun, but were diffused through the universal mundane spirit and especially dilated and dispersed around the celestial spirit. But as according to that old axiom of the Philosophers, *united force is stronger*, so is it weaker when dissipated. Hence it happened that the soul of a plant was not as strong, luminous, clear, and effective in performing its functions as is the soul of animals, inasmuch as the latter arose from celestial rays narrowed and collected together and united into the solar body. For on the third day of creation, before the creation of the Sun, light was equally dispersed around the earth and mixed and enveloped with the dense and thick vapors of *hyle* <term>hyle: a Greek term for "prime matter" or the raw, unformed substance of the universe</term>; whence it happened that it was obscure, and no more to be compared to the beauty of the Sun than the splendor of a shining cloud can be compared to the Sun, or illuminated air to fire. But after all the rays of heaven were gathered to the solar spirit leaping upward from the earth with the sparks of its light, the wonderful effects of the rays contracted together suddenly revealed themselves to the world, and first the fish, then the birds, and finally the animals were procreated; and thus according to the increase of the solar dominion—or the operation of its predominance over the rebellious vapors of matter rising and exhaling upward from the earth into the elementary region—thereafter, day by day, a soul was produced that was gradually stronger and more powerful and brought into the light through creation. From this, therefore, the admirable operation of the Sun in the production of more perfect creatures is clearly demonstrated, and consequently the defect of vegetables is explained, inasmuch as only dilated rays of light and coarser spirits concurred in their creation; so much so, that no help from the Sun—that most noble and lively creature produced from rays contracted together with spirit—was present in the vegetative work. These things, therefore, having been considered again and again, we shall perceive...

This, therefore, is the difference of lives in both those kinds of living beings; this is the reason for dignity in the one, and for depression and abjection in the other, since one is richer in celestial fire and Spirit, while the other is more cast down by poverty and humidity.

### CHAPTER VIII.
*That the vital soul is composed of innate heat and radical moisture, and that it participates in the nature of the Sun; likewise concerning the pyramidal shape of the heart, and that it is the palace of the vital soul; and how this soul, by means of the Spirit, is dispensed through the entire body.*

Since both the ancient Philosophers and the princes of Physicians are accustomed to make frequent mention of the **innate heat** <term>calidum innatum: the natural internal heat that sustains life</term> and the **radical moisture** <term>humidum radicale: the fundamental fluid or "fuel" that prevents the innate heat from consuming the body</term>, from the mixture of which they say life arises, it seems worthwhile that we briefly declare what this heat and likewise this moisture are. Those more skilled in the secrets of nature are accustomed to say that heat is derived from motion, and motion from an act or a moving principle. Nor certainly is heat anything other than the effect of motion, just as motion is nothing other than the action or act of visible or invisible light. 

From this it is manifest that where heat is, there motion is also present, and consequently with motion there is essential light, acting as the mover. Hence it happens that by some, heat is taken for the effect of motion, or as a mere quality, or sometimes for the mover itself. For in Hippocrates we find it written thus: *That immortal thing, which we call heat, when all things were in disorder, flew forth into the highest region, which the ancients called the ether.* <note>original: "Illud mortale... [sic, likely 'immortale' intended by context] ...æthera vocaverunt."</note> Here, therefore, Hippocrates did not take heat for a mere quality or accident, but for an essential thing endowed with immortality; namely, for the universal substantial light, from whose nature that portion of living beings is derived which is called innate heat, without whose motion and warm effect the lives of creatures could in no way have been brought forth, because its presence [governs] the rebellious dispositions of the composite elements...

It is also proven that this lower fire is very closely related to the celestial fire, even by the single fact that, through its own power in the correct proportion, it is accustomed to hatch eggs and produce chicks just as successfully as the natural heat of a hen derived from the higher realms. For this experiment has been discovered and made manifest not only in parts of Africa, but even in Europe itself, and confirmed in these our own days; namely, that chicks were drawn out from their own shells or husks and brought into the light by the benefit of a moderately warm furnace, yet they lived according to the custom of nature. Similarly, we perceive that in a heated stove-room <note>original: "hypocausto," a room heated from below, common in early modern Europe for winter gardening</note>, flowers and shrubs not yet budding suddenly blossom by the power of the fiery heat and thrust out their inner parts. 

But, to ascend now to the celestial fire, do we not say that **the Sun and man beget man**? <note>A common Aristotelian maxim: "Sol et homo generant hominem."</note> Whereby "the Sun" is understood as the entire fiery substance of heaven, from whose spark—combined with the specific form of man—a human is generated. Do we not also see that the worms of the earth receive their bodies from the earth, but receive the form or soul by which they live from the ethereal region? Whence the Philosophers maintain that these are generated through putrefaction. This was also the opinion of the Poet <note>Ovid, in his Metamorphoses</note> regarding the generation of the serpent Python from the rays of the Sun and the mud of the earth, mixed with a small amount of watery moisture after the flood. 

We ourselves have been taught by similar experience: the entire substance of a dead raven, hung in a place exposed to the Sun or in the open air, was converted into innumerable worms within the space of a few days by the quickening power of the Sun. We also read in several authors that bees have emerged in great abundance from the head of an ox through the operation of celestial heat; these certainly did not receive their souls from a dead thing, but from the celestial rays. Is that heat of horse manure much inferior to this fire? By its power, hairs are very often converted into worms and snakes; animals of this kind I have beheld with these my own eyes. 

What should we think of that monster which, bearing the form of a Dragon, was found in a certain cavern receiving putrid and foul waters mixed with the blood of animals flowing through a pipe from the kitchen of a certain English nobleman? Truly, it received its soul without doubt from the light-filled heat of the decay, but the substance of its body from the putrid and, as it were, menstrual matter, after the example of that Python. Diodorus Siculus also relates that after the flooding of the Nile, when the water had almost dried up and the earth—having become drier—had acquired the form of mud from the Sun, many beasts were created as if anew; among which he relates that some were found created only halfway, while others were found with a completed form. 

By all these examples it is manifest that vital souls, suited to living bodies, are nothing other than celestial rays and sparks, as it were, derived from the luminous fountain of the universe, which we have named above as the "heats of nature." Since, therefore, the matter stands thus in these two lower heavens, why should not reason and intellect also proceed from that universal fountain of super-celestial light, of which they are rays, since they are the acts of that Creator? These super-celestial and divine rays have been spoken of not only by the Philosophers, but also by those most skilled in Theology. 

But here a certain doubt comes to our memory, not unworthy of resolution, namely: **Whether the soul is nourished by any food or not?** It is certain that the soul requires its own proper food for its presence no less than other things in nature have need of their nourishment; this can indeed be demonstrated by many arguments. For we see that the action of any body proceeds from the soul: but truly its entire operation is occupied with nourishment, namely in the appetite for food, its preparation, its attraction to the stomach, its retention, the making of blood, and other similar things. Therefore, the vital soul seems to require nourishment as much for its own sustenance as for the sustenance of its machine <note>The "machine" refers to the physical body</note>. the light of the soul may be extinguished and die. We also observe that fire requires the presence of air, as if it were the food of its life. For if a burning fire is shut up in a place enclosed by walls, so that air cannot enter there, it will suddenly be extinguished and, as it were, killed. From this it is certain that the food of the lower fire is air, and that the nourishment of the ethereal fire is the ethereal Spirit. But what of this? Will the vital soul therefore die? Certainly, as far as we are concerned, it dies, and as far as we are concerned, it requires nourishment; yet, if we consider the nature of light with our intellectual eyes, it is established that it neither requires food nor dies. For although the soul, light, and fire seem to crave an aerial fuel <note>original: "fomitem"</note> for themselves, it does not do this out of a necessity for food, as if it could not live without it; but rather so that it may acquire a passive object in that manner, upon which it may act as a well-disposed subject. For it is impossible for light, which is pure act <note>A Scholastic term meaning something fully realized or in operation, as opposed to "potential."</note>, to subsist unless it acts upon some subject: for it always acts, and never ceases to act upon some subject to a greater or lesser degree. However, the effects of its action do not aim at nourishing itself, but rather at first heating the patient subject, and through its heat thinning and refining it, and finally exalting that refined thing and making a spiritual thing out of a corporeal one. Hence we see that when it cannot find other sufficient food to act upon, it consumes its own tabernacle <note>The physical body.</note>; as we see in those suffering from wasting diseases <note>original: "tabidis"</note>. From this it is certain that it does not work for its own sake, but for the sake of the matter—both spiritual and material—with which it dwells. But truly, that innate moisture, born within it, is suitable to it and endures with it forever; it is like Psyche joined with Cupid in complete love. And although fire, when the wood is burned or the air excluded, seems suddenly to be suffocated, it does not die; rather, due to the failing succession of thicker air, it is dissipated through the air (whether enclosed or open), and thus is rendered invisible again, just as it was before. For the entire atmosphere is filled with invisible fire; which is indeed invisible because it is dispersed and rarefied through the medium. It seems, therefore, that fire is extinguished and deprived of life when it returns to its own invisible nature: since those things which we see in body and matter behave in a different and contrary way in the soul. For the body, the more it ages, the more it is weakened, while conversely the soul, the longer it lives in the body, the more it grows young, and grows rich in knowledge, counsel, and prudence. So also the weight of the body lies in gravity, but that of the soul in lightness and subtlety; since its perfection consists in those degrees. And so it is in other matters. It is established, therefore, how the soul requires its food, and how it is thought both to die and be extinguished, when in truth it is being reborn and liberated from the narrow straits of the body.
