## Concerning the act of the sensitive soul within the body.

### CHAPTER I.

*Concerning the properties of the sensitive or animal soul, or the lower portion*

[Decorative initial Q] Although the middle soul <note>The "middle soul" refers to the human psyche or vital spirit, positioned between the divine intellect and the physical body.</note> is by its own nature of a most free condition, and of infinite dignity, knowledge, beauty, and perfection; nevertheless, insofar as it is comprised under one species with the mind—which it carries within itself—and is excessively overshadowed by the frail body, it is to that extent weighed down. Contrary to its nature, it is made prone to contemplating lower things, as if it were destitute of spiritual eyes. And hence it is that it is led by the senses against its nature, and, by looking downward against that nature of its own, it is rendered inclined to contemplate and admire vile and abject things; for its natural disposition, when it is free from the body, admonishes it to tend upward and gaze upon higher things, according to the nature of a fiery flame. Therefore, the middle soul enclosed in the body has two leaders; the higher and more worthy of which entices it toward the good, and exhorts it to engage in celestial meditations. The lower leader, however, solicits it toward evil and vile things and toward embracing the effects of darkness; so that this soul seems to be placed in the middle of two extremes, differing in condition and disposition, according to that saying of Porphyry <note>Porphyry (c. 234–305 AD) was a Neoplatonic philosopher; the work cited is "Sententiae" or "Launching-points to the Intelligibles."</note> in *Occasions*: *The soul is middle between the indivisible essence, which is the intellect, and the essence divisible into true bodies. Moreover, qualities and material forms are divisible according to bodies.* Proclus <note>A later Greek Neoplatonist who heavily influenced Western mysticism.</note> also describes the miserable conjunction of this lowest portion within the internal man with the middle soul thus: *The descent of the soul into the body indeed separated it from the divine souls, by whom it was filled with intelligence, power, and purity; but it joined it to generation and nature—to material things—by which it was imbued with error, forgetfulness, and ignorance. For to the soul descending from the world, multiform lives and various garments are attached, drawing it indeed into a frail composition, but obstructing the contemplation of separate things.* Iamblichus <note>A Syrian Neoplatonist philosopher who focused on theurgy and the soul's descent.</note> also in his *Mysteries* seems to assert this same thing: *The human soul,* he says, *from the*

->They are more clear and simple, and weighed in the just scales of Astraea <note>Astraea was the Greek goddess of justice, often depicted holding scales; her presence here signifies divine or cosmic balance.</note>, since in this place she is joined with the most chaste Psyche <note>The Soul</note> in a simple marriage, and is occupied with the chaste and pure life of the world. Thus also in the second region of man <note>The middle part of the human body/soul, often associated with the heart and emotions.</note> it generates joy, gladness, hope, mercy, and other such pious and chaste children. Indeed, when the faculty of desire in the soul is established with prudence, fortitude, and justice, it then receives the gift of illumination from the Spirit. By the effect of this, it rises into four most chaste daughters, born of the super-celestial fatherland, which are called the Cardinal Virtues: namely, **prudence, temperance, fortitude, and justice**; which are, as it were, the origins and hinges <note>The word "cardinal" comes from the Latin *cardo*, meaning hinge.</note> of all virtues.

Nor indeed does the faculty of desire in the soul perform this alone—that is, love by itself—but joined with the irascible faculty <note>The "irascible" faculty refers to the part of the soul dealing with anger, courage, and rejection.</note>, which is hatred. For through hatred of the world and of the self, one progresses in the love of God and neighbor; through contempt for temporal and lowest things, the desire for eternal and heavenly things grows. Therefore, in the object of lower desire, there is no path leading to higher things, but rather it acts as an obstacle. Truly, carnal children are nothing other than worldly and plainly adulterous in respect to those celestial children which men ought to produce so that they may pass toward God. Of these children—both the spurious or adulterous ones and those born of chaste generation—excellent mention was made in the 3rd chapter of Wisdom <note>The Book of Wisdom in the Apocrypha/Deuterocanon.</note>. Wherefore, even regarding carnal generation, it is said there: *Blessed is the barren woman who is undefiled, who has not known the bed in sin; she shall have fruit in the visitation of holy souls* <note>original: "quòd felix sit sterilis & non coinquinata..."</note>, that is, she shall enjoy spiritual children. *And the eunuch who has not wrought iniquity with his hands, etc. For unto him shall be given the chosen gift of faith, and a most acceptable portion in the temple of God.*

Similarly in *Wisdom chapter 4: O how beautiful is the chaste generation with charity; for the memory thereof is immortal, because it is known both with God and with men.* Hence, therefore, the holy men of past ages, so that they might live chastely and without carnal appetite, led an austere life, so that they might diminish the increase of the seminal object and predominate over worldly desire. For they observed that by the luxurious act and the impulse of intercourse, their chaste thoughts were defiled, and the operations of the soul occupied with God were called away from heaven to lower things by the sensible allurements of the flesh. Indeed, the Apostle Paul himself complained of the depraved effect of this appetite, saying: *I see another law in my members captivating me in the law of sin.* <note>Romans 7:23</note> Therefore, the faculty of desire in the lower region of the Microcosm <note>The human body viewed as a miniature map of the universe.</note> leads man to the worst things. Hence it is read in 1 John 2: *He who loves the world has not the charity of the Father in him, because all that is in the world is the desire of the flesh, and the desire of the eyes, and pride.* And in the same place, chapter 3: *Wherefore the world knows not the sons of God, because the sons of God have not known the world.*

And certainly, I believe it would come to pass that one would deserve the name of a saint, as it were, and be able to perform miraculous operations, if anyone, by constantly overcoming carnal temptations, kept his seed untouched in its own vessels. For every year his light would be multiplied; which indeed, without its own emission, would grow into such an abundance of light that it would illuminate the entire dark tabernacle of that man, and would lift up the mass of the body, as if transfiguring it, with fiery wings. But a double obstacle resists this virtue: one of which is the pollution or defilement of the seed, contracted by infinite mixtures, which the divine light does not love insofar as it is concerned with unity. And the other is that immense dominion which the flesh has with the senses in the human composition, soliciting the soul day and night to the fulfillment of its appetite; so that I think there is almost no one born of a mother who has so preserved his seed untouched for himself that he has not handed over a portion of it to others. But if such a person were found, he surely, as I judge, would be able to perform wonders both in prophecy and in the curing of diseases, and in the prolongation of his life, for many reasons which it would perhaps be tedious to recite all in this place. etc. CHAPTER.

### CHAPTER III.

*How the soul is clouded by carnal sense and forgets itself: And by what means it passes into the nature of the body through vices or sensual things; and also, conversely, how the flesh is accustomed to migrate into the nature of the spirit through virtue. Likewise concerning the powers of the soul in general and concerning the senses.*

[Large initial Q] Just as this middle soul, when clinging to the mind or illuminated by the rays of wisdom, looks back toward its beginning, contemplates the highest good, and knows itself; so too, when deprived of the rays of the mind and divine illumination, it is lulled to sleep by bodily passions and led away from itself through sensible forms. It seeks those things outside of itself which it could find within itself; indeed, it entirely forgets what it is or what it was. Remembering nothing else of what it has been, it believes itself to be nothing except what is seen. It is occupied solely by the senses regarding bodies, and by the imagination regarding the likenesses of bodies and places, and is exercised in them whether waking or sleeping. Therefore, the absence of the rays of the mind is the cause of such great friendship between the body and the soul; according to which friendship "no one holds his own flesh in hatred." <note>A reference to Ephesians 5:29.</note> For although it is weighed down by the company of the flesh or body, according to that saying of the *Wise Man: The corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the sense that muses upon many things, etc.* <note>original: "Corpus, quod corrumpitur, aggravat animam..." from Wisdom of Solomon 9:15.</note> nevertheless, in an ineffable way, the soul loves it and loves its own prison. Therefore it cannot be free, but is vehemently affected by the body's pains; it dreads destruction, though it cannot die; it fears failing, though by its nature it cannot fail. It feeds on the sight of the eyes, delights in sounding voices, rejoices in the sweetest odors, and is refreshed by lavish feasting. And, although the soul itself uses these things in no way, it is nonetheless afflicted with heavy sorrow if they are withdrawn. From this also, vices contrary to reason sometimes creep in, while the soul, by indulging too largely in the delights of the body, is known to provide a place for sin.

The manner, however, in which this happens is as follows: the soul proceeds through the senses to move and enliven the body. There are also nine openings in the human body through which, according to a natural tempering, flows in and out everything by which the same body is nourished and ruled. There are also certain similarities in both: namely, the highest part of the body and the lowest part of the spirit, in which—though without a personal confusion of their natures—they can nevertheless be easily joined in union. For "like rejoices in like"; thus the soul, which is spirit, and the flesh, which is truly body, are easily and conveniently united at their extremities. In the "phantastic" <note>The *phantasticum* or imaginative power of the soul.</note> part of the soul there is indeed no body, but something similar to a body (as will be said in the following harmony), nor is there body in the sensuality of the flesh, which is almost spirit and cannot exist without the soul. 

Just as the highest part of the soul—namely the intelligence or mind—carries the image of its superior, which is God (whence it was able to receive Him and, when He willed, took Him into a personal union without any lessening of nature); so in a similar way the highest part of the flesh—that is, the sensuality—carries the likeness of the soul and is able to receive its essence into a personal union. Nor is that surprising, since even in the sense and memory of a beast there is a certain shadow of rationality, and in its appetite a shadow of will, and in those things which it flees, a shadow of rejection. For the "corporeal spirit" <note>A term for the subtle physiological fluids or "animal spirits" thought to bridge mind and matter.</note>, which is truly body, discerns among many things by natural sense; it chooses by the power of desire and rejects by the power of anger. It is certain from these things, therefore, that these are the most fitting intermediaries of flesh and soul: namely, the sensuality of the flesh, which is fire, and the "phantastic" of the spirit, which is fiery

vigor.

<note>original: "vigor dicitur"</note> is called vigor. From this, I say, arises that wondrous fellowship which exists between the flesh and the soul, between the spirit of life and the threshold of the earth <note>A poetic reference to the physical body made of dust</note>. However, since the soul, possessing its own rational faculty even without the flesh, is rational, desiring, and spirited <note>The author uses the Platonic triad: rational (logistikon), concupiscible (epithymetikon), and irascible (thymoeides)</note>, it follows that through its rationality it is capable and fit to be illuminated to know the truth below itself, above itself, within itself, and beside itself. For in this way it knows God above itself, itself within itself, the Angel beside itself, and whatever is contained within the circuit of heaven below itself. Similarly, through its desiring and spirited powers, it is capable of the affections of seeking or fleeing something, of loving or of hating. And therefore, from the rationality of the soul every sense arises; just as from the other two all affections arise: namely, from the desiring power arise joy and hope, and from the spirited power arise pain and fear. These four affections of the soul are, as it were, certain principles and the common material of all vices as well as virtues. And it seems a wonder of no small size that the same affection of the soul can produce offspring and children so contrary in nature as are vices and virtues, since *virtue is defined as a habit of a well-composed mind; vice, on the contrary, as a habit of a soul ill-disposed and overwhelmed by darkness.* But, unless I am mistaken, there is the same difference between illuminated reason and obscure or dark reason as there is between virtue and vice. For reason lacking illumination is prone to dwell in darkness and error, and to produce vices of every kind; yet when that same reason is illuminated, it is governed by the intelligence and directed in the way of truth. And this is what we said above: namely, that the Spirit adhering to the mind produces virtues, but when the mind is destitute of these rays, it generates or draws to itself vices and errors. From this, I say, it happens that when the rational soul lacks illumination, its desiring power gives birth to carnal joy and worldly pleasures; insofar as it is accustomed to beget and produce as *effects* impudence, gluttony, the allurements of the belly, sluggishness, ambition, avarice, vain glory, and infinite other vices of this sort. So also its spirited power is observed to generate and bring forth rage, fury, beastly anger, quarrels, war, unjust hatred, injury, fear, shame, audacity and faint-heartedness, treachery, dissimulation, falsehood or lying, and innumerable other things of that nature. Yet, conversely, if the rational soul is illuminated by the mind, its powers (namely the desiring and the spirited) produce fruits of a contrary nature; namely virtues, which are the habits of a well-composed mind. For in the light of the mind we compose, establish, and order the affections of the soul toward that which they ought to regard, and in the manner they ought, so that they may perfect the virtues. Whence it happens that without such light, the aforementioned affections of the soul slide most easily into vices. Therefore, when the holy splendor is present in our souls, then our loves and hates will be established prudently, modestly, strongly, and justly, and they will rise into those four original or cardinal virtues: namely, prudence, fortitude, justice, and temperance. Similarly, through hatred of the world and of ourselves, we profit in the love of God and neighbor; through contempt for temporal and inferior things, we grow in the desire for eternal and superior things. From these things, therefore, we see that just as the soul by its presence gives life to the body or flesh, so also the soul itself is so bound to that body by this kind of life-giving power that it cannot segregate itself from there when it wishes, nor can it be restrained there when it hears the voice of the Creator. Indeed, in the life of the soul consists the life of the body, and from the death of the body descends the death of the soul <note>The author likely means the moral or spiritual death caused by bodily corruption</note>. For just as the soul makes the flesh living by its own life, and waters it from the fountain of its own nature by animating it, so the flesh through the corruption of its matter kills the soul if it binds it with illicit desires. And, since one leans upon the nature of the other, each passes into the nature of the victor; so that either the soul renders the flesh spiritual by its virtues, or the victorious flesh makes the soul carnal. By scorning the allurements of the flesh and the senses, the soul is said to be victorious. But truly, if she—by offering the least obedience to the mind—should drink the poison of the flatteries and deceptions of the flesh and the **animal soul** <note>original: "animae animalis" - referring to the lower, animating principle of the body shared with animals, distinct from the rational spirit</note>, and is thereafter driven and enticed by those flatteries of the flesh and lust downward toward the admiration and contemplation of vile and earthly things, then the flesh claims the trophy of victory for itself. Yet the soul can have nothing of death, except what comes to her through vices; nor indeed can the flesh possess anything of life, except what it has drawn from its fellowship with the soul; just as neither can pass into the nature of the other, unless it has first been either infected by vices or imbued and grafted with virtues. Therefore, the soul, illuminated by the mind, is exercised by her aforementioned affections and gives birth to virtues; for sorrow concerning sins, fear concerning punishments, desire concerning promises, and joy concerning rewards are certain exercises of the virtues. Furthermore, there are various virtues in which the soul, imbued with divine piety, is occupied while she is instructed and armed against vices by others; namely, by those four original ones, which are also called **cardinal**. For through *prudence* the soul knows what she ought to do; through *temperance* she rules and governs herself in prosperity; likewise through *fortitude* in adversity; and through *justice* she knows what is fitting to render to each. Moreover, it also advises and teaches her: *prudence* indeed to know what she can do, *fortitude* to do what she can, *temperance* not to presume what she cannot, and finally *justice*, not to wish for more than she can. Therefore, her *prudence* is in choosing, *temperance* in using, *fortitude* in enduring, and *justice* in distributing. *Prudence* is to seek nothing that must be repented of, nor to wish to do anything except what is just; *Temperance* is to fear nothing except what is shameful, and to direct whatever we do or think to the rule of reason; it is the part of *Fortitude* not merely to restrain earthly desires, but to forget them entirely; finally, it is the part of *Justice* to raise every thought of the soul to God, and, as if there were nothing else, to gaze upon Him with the sharp edge of the mind alone. The soul is initiated by other virtues: and such virtues are called *sacramental*; of which kind are *faith, hope, the sacrament, baptism, anointing, confirmation*, and *the rest*, by which she is consecrated to God. By others she profits and is joined to God, such as *humility, purity, and charity*. For *humility* subjects the soul to God, *purity* joins her, and *charity* unites her. There are also lesser virtues concerned with a viler matter, namely the body, by which the soul is joined to the body, the lowest of which is the *natural*, the middle the *vital*, and the highest the *animal* <note>These refer to the "three spirits" of medieval physiology: natural (liver), vital (heart), and animal (brain)</note>. And just as God, three and one, holds all things, fills all things, sustains all things, exceeds and embraces all things; so the soul is diffused through the whole body by these three powers; not indeed by a local descent, but by a vital extension. For the **natural power** works the blood and other humors in the liver, which it transmits through the veins to all members of the body, so that they may be increased and nourished therefrom. This force is fourfold, since it is divided into the *appetitive*, which attraction serves; the *retentive*, by which it retains what is attracted until a useful concoction <note>digestion or refinement</note> is completed; the *distributive*, pouring the chylous humors of good foods through all the members as is expedient for each; and the *expulsive*, expelling and evacuating harmful and superfluous things, or the dreggy and useless substance. But the middle power of the soul, namely the **vital**, which has its empire in the heart, is occupied in the tempering of the heat and fervor of the heart, and by breathing in and out air, it distributes life and health to the whole body; for by means of pure air it drives the purified blood through the whole body via the arteries or "pulsing veins"; from whose motion Physicians recognize health and illness. Finally, the **animal power** is found in the highest region of the body, namely in the brain, and from there it quickens the five senses of the body, and also commands the voice to be uttered and the limbs to move. This power of the soul chiefly uses three chambers or ventricles, of which one is the anterior <note>front</note>, from which comes all sensation; the other the posterior <note>back</note>, from which comes all motion; the third, middle between both, is the *rational*. ### CHAPTER IV.

*Concerning the origin of the external senses; Why they are expressed in the face; that they are the causes of errors in man; likewise concerning the origin of the imagination.*

In the anterior part of the brain, or the face, the senses are formed in this way. There is something in the body that is most subtle and active, and therefore most similar and close to the soul—indeed, it is as if it were the external effect of the operative power within the soul itself—which the Philosophers have called "light." This central light is first diffused through the eyes, and it shines forth in the rays of the eyes to behold visible things; then [it forms] the hearing,

refined and made subtle, so that it is immediately joined to the spirit itself; yet truly retaining the nature of the body, and its property or rather its likeness. This **imagination** <note>The author uses "imagination" here not as "fantasy," but as the faculty that forms mental images from sensory data.</note> in brute animals does not transcend the "phantastic cell" <note>A reference to medieval ventricular theory, where specific areas of the brain were thought to house different mental faculties.</note>. In rational beings, however, it becomes purer, and proceeds and is carried forward until it touches the rational and incorporeal substance of the soul. Imagination is, therefore, a likeness of the body, conceived externally through the bodily senses from contact with physical objects, and led inward through those same senses to the purer part of the corporeal spirit, and impressed upon it. It exists, as it were, at the highest point of the bodily spirit and at the lowest point of the rational spirit, informing the bodily and touching the rational; which I call air or rather fire, which cannot be seen due to its subtlety, and which gives life to bodies by nourishing them from within.

Now, this force nourishes some things but does not give them sensation, such as trees, herbs, and all things germinating in the earth; some things it both nourishes and gives sensation to at once, such as brute animals. Among these, some have sensation but lack imagination; others, however, have both sensation and imagination. Since it is a greater thing to be endowed with sensation than simply to be nourished, it is certainly clear that this force is more subtle; and where it is more subtle, there it is more "spirit." Consequently, it approaches closer to an incorporeal nature when it forms an imagination than when it provides a sense. For nothing in the body can be higher, or closer to a spiritual nature, than that place where the power of imagining is conceived after the sense. This is indeed so sublime that whatever is above it is nothing other than reason.

From this it is manifest that sense and imagination consist of corporeal spirit; but the former from a more dense and perceptible spirit, while the latter from a more subtle spirit, closest in its thinness to the rational spirit. Thus, the spirit of sense can be compared to **air**, and that of imagination to **ether** <note>The "quintessence" or purest element of the heavens.</note>, from which the visible world consists. But truly, if we wish to reach the ultimate boundaries, it will be necessary to purify our spirits yet one degree higher. Unless this is done, it will be impossible to pass from corporeal and sensible things to spiritual and intellectual ones, from the visible world to the invisible, from darkness to light, and from the deceptive power of the devil to the vision of God and the investigation of truth.

Therefore, from the sensible and intellectual spirit is forged the existence and power of the "animal" or "sensual" and "sensitive" soul (or the *idolum* <note>original: "idoli" - likely referring to the "astral body" or the image-reflecting part of the soul in Neoplatonic thought.</note>), whose violence makes the soul more prone to the flesh and worldly pleasures, as we declared above. Hence the struggle of the animal soul with the mind, because just as it rarely becomes a receiver of the mind's rays, so the rays of the flesh arise from animal sense and motion. This animal force was produced from the mind in no other way than **Lucifer** was from God: Lucifer, participating in matter and darkness, became rebellious against his Creator; the animal or sensitive soul, brought forth from nothing into a noble act by the operation of the mind, has become rebellious toward the author of its existence. It joins itself with the flesh and the body, and moves the soul against the laws of illuminated reason, unless it is hindered by divine rays and governed by the bridle of most holy justice, according to that word of the Wise Man in *Wisdom 9:*

->*We account the things that are upon earth with difficulty, and find with labor the things that are before our eyes; but the things that are in heaven, who shall search out? And who shall know your counsel, except you give wisdom and send your Holy Spirit from above? And so the ways of those who are on earth were corrected, and men learned the things that please you.*<-

For through wisdom all who have pleased you, O Lord, from the beginning were healed. From this it is manifest that the disobedience of the senses and the flesh is removed by the splendor and virtue of the spirit descending from on high, and that their malice is converted into goodness. Thus, the never-satisfied appetite of the body may now rest in the presence of divine wisdom, be lulled to sleep, and be rendered obedient to illuminated reason. But concerning these senses, we shall speak more extensively in the following chapters.

# CHAPTER V.

## Concerning the external senses; and first regarding sight and hearing, and why the senses are deceived concerning their own objects.

The external senses, therefore, which we have declared above to be five in number, receive their power and effect from a fiery force <note>original: "virtute ignea" — referring to the Vitalist belief that a subtle "fire" or heat drove biological processes</note> through the nerves and other organs, as if through dispersed instruments. Through these, and also by means of the life-giving color of the muscles, the sensory spirits are moved downward from the animal faculty. It is observed that they move the muscles and other parts by an involuntary motion, according to the instinct of reason. Of these senses, however, two are primary and simple, namely **Sight** and **Hearing**, as was demonstrated in the preceding chapter. The others are truly less primary, namely **Touch**, **Smell**, and **Taste**. We call those former ones "primary" because they correspond to the simple parts of the world's constitution, whereas these latter are less primary insofar as they embrace and are affected by the entire substance of the world, consisting of both matter and form. Furthermore, we call the "simple parts" of the world's composition that simple spiritual matter which, as we remembered above, is called and named "the waters" by the Scriptures <note>A reference to Genesis 1:2, implying a primordial, fluid spiritual substance from which all things were made</note>.

To the Spirit. Similarly, that sight is a simple sense, and more active, and existing through itself, insofar as it is completed by the power of the luminous act; whereas hearing is likewise a simple sense, but more passive and accidental, insofar as that medium through which hearing occurs is subjected to the actions of light, and brings sounds to the ears through various reverberations and multiplications. Therefore, the effect of sight is wonderful, since by its power the true craftsman, by following the optical discipline of mirrors <note>The study of catoptrics or reflective surfaces</note>, can gaze upon the icon and likeness of God in the multiform color of the rainbow, and even in a thousand other ways. This is done not without stupendous admiration, so that it seems the gaze of such a craftsman is called back to the memory of those divine colors of the Deity and His glory, which once, while the soul was still free in its super-celestial homeland, it beheld with spiritual eyes. How ineffable, therefore, the power of this sense may be on account of the nobility of its object, and how many wonderful, abstruse, and hidden things it is able to reveal to us, the human genius has scarcely ever been able to explain to the world, even if it were permitted. Similarly also the Spirit itself, which is the medium without which hearing cannot occur, contains within itself miraculous secrets through the presence of divine light; which indeed the wise have been unwilling to disclose, or to emit and promulgate into the public; indeed, they have not dared, lest they should incur the curse of the Lord. In these two <note>Sight and hearing</note>, therefore, consists every operation of magic, both natural and supernatural, every governance of animal life and the universal act of the world, the effects of the heavens, and the shaking of the stars. By these, the eye of the world sees all things that are carried out in the cavity of the world; by these, the angels behold these lower things and look back even to the throne of God; by these, animals are accustomed to distinguish good from evil; by these, the intention of one man is understood by another; by these, one thing is discerned to differ from another; and by these, the harmony of one soul, enclosed in a body, is perceived to harmonize or disagree with the harmony of another. Indeed, we could fill an entire volume with the praises and virtues of these two senses, were we not called away to other things by the necessity of this subject. But here, with a single word, I would wish the Reader to understand that the bodily eyes behold very few true and certain things, but infinite falsehoods and delusions; the reason for which is the dominion of darkness within us, which deceives us with fallacies and makes those things appear to us which are not as they seem. For whatever is discerned is seen in the body, which indeed in itself is nothing, since whatever it has, it receives from the luminous form. We follow matter, therefore; but we neglect form, and thus we are deceived, because matter is from darkness, and darkness is from nothing, and therefore also that which is corporeal is, through itself and in itself, nothing. But if it is anything, it receives its entire being from the form, which is from light, from whose fountain is the life of things; for the Word <note>original: "verbum"</note>, in which and from which is life, is the only truth, and whatever exists outside of this truth is delusional and from the prince of lies. But let us now hear the Ethnic <note>Pagan/Gentile</note> Philosophers. Proclus concludes all of this in almost a single word: *Matter,* he says, *seems to be all things, while in truth it possesses nothing.* We see also in a variety of mirrors that a different figure of the same thing and a discrepant dimension of that body appear, even though the truth of the thing is unique. Thus we notice the same face in a convex mirror contracted in length, but loosened and extended beyond measure in width; whereas in a concave mirror we see it horribly produced and extended according to length, but contracted in a marvelous way according to width. But in a flat and polished mirror, we behold this same image again in a just manner, and disposed according to the indication of the natural eye. We are all deceived, therefore; and it is impossible to discern what things are true, unless it be done in the splendor and holy truth, in which we gaze upon all things as they truly are. For how many delusions, illusions, and fascinations an impious mage is accustomed to induce by the help of the devil, both the accounts of histories and infinite oral narrations have indicated to us; the effects of which, however, are nothing—

I would also wish for you to observe this unique experiment regarding the sense of hearing: that its medium is both water and thick air, nor is air anything other than thin water. For when I was living in Nîmes <note>original: "Nemosii"</note> in Languedoc, France, in its famous "bottomless" spring (as they call it, because its depth is not known), I sometimes swam in the evening hours around sunset for the sake of my spirit and refreshment; and taking two stones separately in each hand, I immersed myself quite deeply for the sake of performing an experiment in the water among the bare rocks protruding everywhere, and so remaining under the water, I struck those stones against each other. From this it happened that a horrible and scarcely believable sound was heard. By which I was made more certain that hearing, on account of the density of the medium, becomes many degrees more evident and more vehement in water than in the air itself, inasmuch as in the air all things are more benevolent, mild, and better suited to human nature.

## CHAPTER VI.
## On Touch, Smell, and Taste.

JUST as God, in the creation of man, deposited and placed the mind and reason in his highest and most noble region, namely in the head; so also He joined to it five porters or ministers, by whose use and motion—or rather through whom, as corporeal and sensible organs—it might exert and exercise its powers regarding the perception of things. For the nature of the human soul is, by itself without the body or sense, to behold and contemplate spiritual and insensible things. But truly, insofar as it regards sensible things, it is necessary that it acts by means of the body and its exterior senses, as those without which it cannot judge concerning gross, visible, tangible, and other such things. Therefore, the five senses offer to the sight of reason whatever things are necessary to it for the knowledge of bodies, and they show to it those things by which it is aided in the knowledge of things concerning visible, audible, and tangible bodies, etc. These serve the human body no differently than sailors serve for the direction of a ship, whose pilot and principal leader, or ruler and conductor, is the mind within the reason, directing the journey by a certain magnetic virtue, and observing the ship's course at its summit by the property and direction of the mariner's needle <note>A compass needle.</note> looking toward the Arctic pole. Through these ministers of his, he is advised of the external accidents occurring to the ship, and of its prosperous journey, or of the reason of a rock threatening danger to the ship, so that, whatever evil to it—

To each of these carriers <note>original: "bajulorum"; literally "porters" or "carriers," referring to the senses as the vehicles of information for the soul</note>, a distinct property is assigned. For **sight**, by its very nature, is concerned with ten things: namely, light and darkness, color and body, figure and actions, distance and proximity, motion and rest. However, as was said above, all these are reduced to the single property of light. For darkness is known by its opposition to light, color is discerned through the operation of light on the surface of a body, and so it is with the rest. The property of **hearing** is to deal with two kinds of sounds: namely, animal voices and non-animal sounds. The former are either rational, pertaining to human speech, or irrational, such as the roaring of lions, the neighing of horses, the chirping of birds, and so on. The latter lack animal life, such as the sound of a drum or a pipe, the whistling of the winds, thunder, and so on. We shall not write much here regarding these two—the primary carriers of reason—since we have spoken of their internal arrangements above. But I would only wish for you to observe in passing that the invisible and spiritual light of the mind, sent out through the optical organ and meeting the external light, renders the sense of sight more noble than the others. Similarly, the spirit of reason and life, breathing out through the ears and joined in the same way with the resonating medium of the air, introduces sound into the palace of the mind. There, it is received by the common sense <note>the faculty that unifies sensory data</note> and the imaginative power, to be examined by the royal counselors and ministers—namely, by the rational spirit and the intellect—and recorded by their scribe, Memory, as if in the official records of remembrance. Therefore, because of this excellence, this sense of hearing is next to sight in dignity, both in location and in nature. For whatever the "sounding light" produces by its action, this spirit also represents to the intellect through the integrity of the organs of hearing.

We have called the three exterior senses "lesser" or "less principal" because they are subject to the first two in power and necessity; indeed, they are composed of more "mixed" matter. For just as the first two are concerned, one more with the properties of light and the other with the spirit in its motion and action, so also these three latter senses participate in both natures—namely, in light and spirit mixed together in greater or lesser proportions. For **Touch**, which is the palpable force contained between two skins—one on the surface of the body and the other covering the flesh—this power, I say, arises from the subtlest spirit, through the effect of heat or the power of imperceptible light, pushed and infused from the brain through the nerves into the entire body. By the mutual action and passion <note>in the philosophical sense of "being acted upon"</note> of these, the sense of touch operates in both the internal and external parts of the body. Its movement or sensible operation is found in heat or cold, or in roughness and smoothness. From these things it is clear that, just as the first two senses are concerned with the essence of light and the matter of spirit, so also **Touch** is more occupied with the active qualities of both: namely, with heat (which refers to light, proceeding immediately from the motion of light) and cold (which is more properly attributed to darkness and matter, since the resisting force of matter against the actions of form comes from cold).

Furthermore, **Taste** acquires its power from the aforementioned parts of the world's composition in a different way. For as the operation of **Touch** lies in judging between the intensity or lessening of the degrees of heat and cold, so the action of **Taste** or **Flavor** is concerned chiefly with the passive dispositions of light and spirit: namely, with the moisture proper to spirit and the dryness that accompanies light. From this it happens that we perceive flavors to be altered by the greater or lesser dominance of moisture or dryness. Hence sweetness, bitterness, saltiness, oiliness, sourness, insipidity, astringency <note>original: "ponticitas"; a harsh or punchy flavor</note>, sharpness, etc. That all these things contribute to the diversity of flavor, we are taught by notable experiment. For we perceive that "styptic" <note>astringent/contracting</note> qualities and harshness participate in earthly dryness—a dryness they received from congealing cold—and that acidity follows astringency in a progressing order...

...proceeding from the nature of the earth or of spirit condensed by cold toward the resolving region of fire and light. Then, ascending still higher from rawness <note>original: "cruditate"; referring to the state of undigested or unprocessed matter</note> toward a temperate balance, one reaches a certain weight or sweetness, or even an insipid flavor, where the <term>stiptic<gloss>astringent or mouth-puckering</gloss></term> power of cold is entirely dissolved by the rays of the approaching light. And so, at last, we reach sweetness, in which the beneficial disposition of the Air and of Jupiter is felt, along with the exact harmony of form with matter, or of light with spirit. And this is the middle path of progress between rawness and <term>adustion<gloss>the process of scorching or burning by heat</gloss></term>. 

Therefore, by proceeding further, we approach saltiness, which is the first degree of adustion; then we pass to acridity, and finally from acridity to bitterness, from which we arrive at the burning of bile and blackness. In the completion of this action, the fire is finally turned back into earth. We see, therefore, that vitriol <note>original: "vitriolum"; a sulfate mineral, often associated with acidity and green or blue colors</note> when congealed is full of astringency, and that its oil, to which a portion of violent fire adheres, converts its astringent disposition into acidity. We also see, conversely, that **Salt of Tartar** <note>original: "Sal Tartari"; potassium carbonate, often used as a base in early chemistry</note> tastes in some way of the bitterness of scorching, which, when converted into an oil by the admixture of air or external spirit, possesses acridity within itself. 

If, therefore, we mix that acid oil with that acrid one in an equal proportion of qualities (though not necessarily of physical bulk), we will produce a quite evident sweetness. But truly, if the portion of acid exceeds the portion of acrid, an insipid taste with a certain harshness will result; if the acrid exceeds, there will be saltiness and the beginning of sharpness. And in these diverse actions and passions of oils, salts of different natures will be produced: namely, we shall find the taste of **alum** at the beginning of the motion from the austere; **sugar** in the middle; and **saltpeter** at the end. 

I have also been taught by a most certain experiment that through the mixing of a liquor brewed from vinegar, vitriol, and antimony with "hepatic" <note>original: "aloë hepatica"; a common medicinal aloe, named for its liver-like color</note> aloes, and the application of these to a bread oven, that aloe loses all its bitterness and nonetheless purges the body to which it is applied sweetly and without any discomfort. 

Finally, we are taught that the power of **Smell** also consists in the operation of light mixed with Spirit. But the action of this sense differs from the actions of the two preceding ones for a twofold reason. For first, just as the force and power of **Touch** is absolutely enclosed within the membranes of the body and is concerned with cold and heat; and further, as **Taste** consists in the property of the tongue and operates around the distinction of the effects of moisture and dryness; so **Smell** does not necessarily act upon the hot and cold, nor upon the moist and dry, but regards the substance of Spirit mixed with light. 

For the vapor of fragrant things, springing from the action of the sweetest Spirit of fragrant light, swims in the common spirit—namely, in the air—and is accustomed to aromatize it by its invisible nature, just as saffron <note>original: "crocus"</note> immersed in clear water is seen to visibly occupy and tint the entire substance of the water with its tincture; or just as ink poured into clear water turns it to a black color. For in this way, the odors of things are expanded from their own proper subject in an invisible manner through the surrounding air, filling it with their sweet scent. And likewise, if the odor of a thing is bad or foul, it infects the common medium in a similar way. The sense of smell is the index of this kind of quality hiding in the air, showing whether it is pleasing or unpleasant to nature. 

Therefore, the disposition of the sense of Smell ought to be excellent, and its proportion equal to that temperate mixture of light and spiritual nature, so that it may best receive the medium infused with odors, and once received, may rightly judge the quality and temperament of its goodness or malice. Regarding the natures of different odors, it must be known that the more a fragrant thing is tempered in quality and proportion around the essence of light and the substance of the spirit or ether, the sweeter and more pleasant it is to human nature. Indeed, it is assimilated to human nature, which among all the natures of other animals is more temperate and effective in its innate heat and radical moisture; so much so that even the **Demons** themselves, according to the testimony of Psellus <note>Michael Psellus (c. 1017–1078), a Byzantine philosopher and politician known for his writings on demonology</note>, by contact with human nature...

But in truth, foul odors become such on the part of the element of fire, namely on account of the impurity of its spirit and the scorching nature of light. For I myself have been taught by experience that every stench comes from the element of fire mixed with impure spirit or air. Furthermore, air also produces some stench, though less than fire, because of its own impurity and uncleanness which it draws from the other elements. All sweetness, however, in which the soul delights, flows forth from heaven, where the ether stays in concordant peace with the light and maintains equal weights and proportions in the scales and balances of **Astraea** <note>The Greek goddess of justice and balance; here used to signify perfect celestial harmony</note>; just as I myself have frequently experienced with wonder in the **chemical anatomy** <term>chemical anatomy<gloss>the alchemical process of breaking down a substance into its fundamental elements</gloss></term> of bodies. It is manifest, therefore, that every stench, or every heavy, unpleasant, and disagreeable odor of human nature, comes from impure and corrupt airy or watery moisture, scorched by fiery heat, and is thus contrary to nature. 

But truly, a sweet, good, and pleasant odor to the sense arises from pure spirit with such heat. On the other hand, the earthly nature, insofar as it is the source and origin of constricting coldness, harms this sense more and hinders it more in its action than it can benefit it in any way. Indeed, coldness is contrary to the faculty of every sense, affecting the organs with a <term>stupor<gloss>a state of numbness or loss of sensation</gloss></term> rather than offering them any help. For it is in every way contrary to the faculty of the senses, whose perfection requires the presence of a temperate heat through which they may operate. Coldness, by its predominance, usually takes this heat away. Similarly, the dilation of the pores and organs is required for the complete function of the senses. Yet it is the nature of coldness to obstruct and close the passages. The senses also desire subtle spirits, by which they may carry out their functions quickly and effectively. However, it is the nature of coldness to condense and thicken what was subtle, and consequently, it is most opposite to the senses in its nature. 

It is for this reason that coldness usually induces the blockage of pores and the thickening of the membranes, leading to blindness of the eyes, as well as the thickening and condensation of the humors in the optic nerve. It likewise damages hearing by obstructing the organs and by thickening and drying out the glutinous matter, and by affecting the limbs with numbness and stupor; hence coldness is also adverse to **Touch**. It also blocks the nostrils and extinguishes the natural heat of the organs, by whose virtue the senses ought to correctly distinguish odors. It hinders **Taste** by numbing the parts of the tongue, through whose benefit this sense is accustomed to operate; and it is sometimes observed to induce mortification and gangrene in the throat and gums. 

When all these things are correctly understood, it is certain that earthly coldness is not the cause of an odor, whether foul or sweet; rather, smelling and the sense of smell always occur because of the presence of heat. And although some might perhaps object that ***opium, since it is cold, emits a most foul odor*** <note>original: "opium, cùm sit frigidum, odorem fœtidissimum emittat"</note>, it is nevertheless recognized that this does not happen because of the coldness of the medicine, but rather emanates from a hidden hot disposition. For in the same **simple** <term>simple<gloss>a medicinal plant or mineral used as a single ingredient</gloss></term>, contrary qualities and natures are often observed to exist. For example: ***Fumitory, or "Earth-smoke," although it is cold and dry in its operation, yet no one of sound mind would doubt that it drew its bitterness from fire.*** <note>original: "Fumaria seu fumus terræ"; a flowering plant traditionally used in herbal medicine</note> And so, having explained the dispositions and natures of the external senses clearly enough, as it seems to us, we shall briefly bring this part to an end.

CHAPTER VII.

*On the natural faculty, and how all growth occurs via the liver*
*or the airy mass of the Microcosm.* <note>The "Microcosm" or "Little World" is a traditional philosophical term for the human being, viewed as a miniature map of the entire universe (the Macrocosm).</note>

Concerning the natural faculty in the generation of blood, and in the composition, preservation, nutrition, and maintenance of the body's parts and elements in their proper state, we have spoken somewhat in the preceding sections. Here, however, we shall show that the primary method of the body’s **growth** <term>growth<gloss>original: "vegetatio"; in this context, it refers to the functions of the "vegetative soul," which governs nutrition and development</gloss></term> depends on this faculty of the internal man. It must first be known, therefore, that all growth and multiplication of the body, in animals as much as in plants, proceeds from an **airy disposition**. Yet this airy nature cannot accomplish this on its own, unless it is aided by the higher powers, both of the Macrocosm and the Microcosm. For the natural faculty, according to the opinion of the astrologers, is governed chiefly by the Moon and Venus, as they increase and foster the force and the natural, vegetative, and genital spirit; to these, Jupiter also joins himself wonderfully in such work, insofar as he is moist and warm in a most temperate degree.

We, however, instructed by notable experience, have found that the operation of the Sun possesses a place in this faculty above all others, regarding both growth and multiplication. For in the **chemical anatomy** <term>anatomy<gloss>the alchemical process of separating a substance into its fundamental components</gloss></term> of a certain wondrous plant nutrient, we saw a water that was superfluous in itself, which in that vegetable took the place of urine, or acted like the serum of the blood in man. Then we observed a most subtle air, which behaved quite differently from the water itself, and yet possessed a liquid form, verging more toward the nature of an oily salt; it was friendly both with the water because of its moisture, and with the fire because of its heat. Whence it joined itself very easily with both extremes; whereas the fiery part could never be joined with the water. And thus I became more certain that this is the internal air of the plant; which, when I made it volatile with the gentlest fire, I observed to be converted and congealed at the top of the glass into a most white salt, like hail; yet this most white salt, by the sudden application of heat or even the slightest warmth, was dissolved into a golden oil.

By these things I was incidentally instructed that the mundane air is a kind of "dry water," which, if it is congealed, is nothing other than salt. The proof of this matter is also declared in the observation of **saltpeter** <note>original: "salis petræ"; nitre or potassium nitrate, which early chemists believed contained the vital spirit of the air</note>; which, according to the opinion of all Philosophers and Chemists, is nothing other than congealed air. The remainder of that airy part, which did not congeal into salt, descended into the receiving vessel as a white liquor, very similar to crystal.

But I seem to hear you even now whispering these words: *What comes of this? Either $^a$ **principles**, which are: supreme heat, supreme cold, supreme moisture, and supreme dryness, considered in themselves without any consideration of matter. Hence, it is not found in intermediate places, but only at the extremes with the qualities of the active and the passive.

Or $^c$ **elements**, such as fire, air, water, and earth, which are also called by their excesses: hot, cold, moist, and dry. Of these we have likewise spoken copiously in the Treatise and book cited above.

This diversity consists in time—from which a pulse is called frequent, or fast and slow—or in three dimensions—from which it is called long, short, wide, narrow and thin, high and elevated, deep, hidden and submerged, great or small. It may also consist in the strength of the power or in the striking of the vein against the fingers; thus we call a pulse vehement and strong, or weak and languid. Or it may consist in the body of the artery itself; and so we say a pulse is hard or soft. It may be judged by the primary qualities; by considering the pulse in this way, we call it hot, cold, moist, or dry. It may also be judged by the fullness of the artery; and so a pulse is called full or empty. Or it may be judged by the time of rest; and so it is named frequent, dense and thick, or rare, loosened and slipping. It may be judged by the rhythm; and then such motion is called arrhythmic <note>original: "arhythmos"</note> or eurhythmic <note>original: "eurhythmos"; having a good or harmonious rhythm</note>. It may consist in equality or inequality, and this either in a single pulse—and then it is called equal, disparate and unequal, vibrating and dicrotic <note>dicrotic: a pulse with a double beat</note>, caprizant <note>original: "crapizans"; a "goat-leap" pulse where the beat seems to jump</note> or double-striking, nodding, circling-nodding, or intercurrent—or in several pulses, and then it is called collective. Such motion is either failing, intermittent and interrupted, ant-like <note>original: "formicinus"; a very small, fast pulse feeling like ants crawling</note>, mutilated and shortened, failing-shortened, and reciprocal-shortened. Finally, it may be judged by its composition; in this way a pulse is called wavy, worm-like, ant-like, hectic or trembling, convulsive, and serrated <note>serratus: saw-like</note>.

*Galen* treats these types extensively in Book 1 of *The Causes of Pulses*, chapters 5 and 6; and Book 1 of *Prognosis from Pulses*, chapter 3; and Book 2 of *The Diagnosis of Pulses*, chapter 2; and Book 3 of *The Differences of Pulses*, chapter 5. Indeed, you should read all these books of Galen: namely, *On the Differences of Pulses*, *On the Diagnosis of Pulses*, *On the Causes of Pulses*, *On Prognosis from Pulses*, *On the Pulse for Beginners*, *On the Synopsis of Pulses*, and so on. Or, the pulse may consist in the heart's *contraction* alone; the effects of which are sadness, despair, fear, hatred, envy, anger, fury, shame, and the like.

Or *involuntary action* is natural, and it is either secondary—namely, attraction, retention, alteration, and expulsion—or primary—namely, nutrition through apposition, union, and assimilation; growth in length, breadth, and depth; and generation through change and formation. In this way, we have briefly delivered these things by way of an epitome <note>epitome: a summary or condensed account of a larger work</note>, and we have succinctly set forth the opinions of the Physicians concerning the nine species of natural things concerning the twofold composition of man. In the following chapter, we shall explain our own principles regarding the human composition and its elements, humors, body, power, and actions according to our own intention.

#### Concerning our principles of the Microcosm, and how they agree both with the principles of the Holy Scriptures and with the intentions of all Philosophers and Chemists?

We have condensed these into three spheres, according to the distinction of the elements; specifically, just as the matter of the elements was water or spirit, so the matter of the humors was <term>chyle</term> <note>original: "chylus"; a milky fluid produced in the intestines during the first stage of digestion</note>. Furthermore, just as the fiery element was produced by the excessive heating of the elementary matter, so also <term>bile</term> <note>original: "bilis"; specifically yellow bile or the choleric humor, associated with fire</note> is generated by the excessive <term>concoction</term> <note>original: "concoctio"; the process of "cooking" or digesting substances within the body using its natural heat</note> of the chyle. Thus we see that men endowed with a hot liver are more prone to the procreation of bile. But truly, if it is scorched too much, it returns to earth no less than wood turns into coals and then into ashes. Hence, from the same sphere, we have both fire and earth. For in the elementary rotation and circulation, fire matches the dryness of the earth.

However, there is also a simple earth in its own nature, which produces natural <term>melancholy</term> <note>original: "melancholia"; also known as black bile, associated with the element of earth</note> and the dregs of the blood; that which is thicker, colder, and rawer is the portion of animal water. And so we have natural or yellow bile, and natural melancholy, as well as that which is numbered among the animal humors from scorched bile.

The middle sphere, however, participates more or less in both extremes. It is, nonetheless, of the true nature of the sphere of humidity. For <term>phlegm</term> <note>original: "pituita"; the cold, moist humor associated with the element of water</note> is referred to water, which because of its proximity to the earth is rawer and colder; but blood, compared to air, is more mature and more "cooked," insofar as it is compared to bile or the element of fire. Therefore, the entire mass of humors is assimilated to the universal Spirit of the elements, and the intermediate sphere is produced from the sensible action of each extreme humor, not unlike how the sphere of humidity is produced by the action of terrestrial cold and the heat of the element of fire.

For coldness leaping out from the earth to meet the actions of fire—being by its disposition cold, dry, and congealing—resists the actions of fire descending downward in the middle path between fire and earth. The dissolving heat of fire, by liquefying and relaxing the gathering power of the cold operating in the spirit or intermediate water, resolves it into a certain dampness, which is left with more or less thickness according to its greater or lesser proximity to either extreme. Furthermore, because this collision of the rays of heat and the cold of the condensed spirits happens in the very center, as it were, between fire and earth, it happens that we see clouds continually gathering toward the periphery of the lower aerial region.

This, therefore, is the cause of life: namely, the action of heat in the humor to impede the congealing assaults of coldness, which, if they should gain dominion, bring mortification with them, as is demonstrated in the evil of <term>gangrene</term> <note>the death of body tissue due to lack of blood flow or infection</note>. And from this it follows that the <term>innate heat</term> <note>original: "calidum innatum"; the vital warmth believed to be present in all living things from birth</note> always accompanies the <term>radical moisture</term> <note>original: "humidum radicale"; the fundamental fluid that sustains the innate heat, like oil in a lamp</note>. For without heat, the moisture will very easily be congealed by the presence of cold, which is the cause of death. For as heat is the cause of motion and life, so conversely cold is the cause of rest and death.

As the effects of light and darkness behave in the <term>Macrocosm</term> <note>the "great world" or the universe at large</note>, so also do the effects of the soul and body behave in the <term>Microcosm</term> <note>the "little world," referring to the human being as a reflection of the universe</note>. For by the presence and act of the soul's heat, the blood becomes fluid; but by its absence, it is congealed, and all motion is taken away. Similarly, just as water is derived from the darkness from which the elements were forged, so also the matter of all humors has arisen from the body, from which it has its corporeal and visible substance.

From this, therefore, the health and infirmity of the body, life and death, proceed from the humors; and by their succession, the members of the body arise and are nourished. From the faculty of heat, the good virtues and actions of the body arise—both voluntary and involuntary—which, conversely, are depraved by the dominion of cold.

# OF THE FIRST TREATISE,

### BOOK X.
## On the threefold vision of the soul in the body.

***

#### CHAPTER I.
*Concerning the first type of vision, by which the soul perceives physical things*
*through the sense; and how in this vision of its own*
*it may sometimes be deceived?*

[A large decorative initial 'T' set within a square frame of floral and vine motifs.] We observe from an infallible effect that there are three types of visions in the soul; the first of which is physical, by which, through the senses of the body, the colored bodies of things and their dimensions and other things encountered by the senses are perceived. For although the substance and condition of the soul is invisible, and consequently it remains invisibly in the body; nevertheless, looking out from the body and, as it were, emerging invisibly, it sees bodies through the body, namely the heaven and the earth and the creatures in them, visible to our eyes. And this vision of the soul is perfected by the mediation of the body’s external senses. The second type of vision in the soul is spiritual, by which the likenesses of bodies are discerned by the spirit alone, and not by reason or the mind. For whatever is material, and yet is not a body, is rightly and deservedly called <term>spirit</term> <note>original: "spiritus"; in this 17th-century context, this refers to a "subtle" vaporous substance that acts as a bridge between the physical body and the immaterial soul, rather than a ghost or holy spirit</note>. Therefore, by a certain hidden and spiritual power, the soul is so carried away that it sees, in place of the actual bodies, their clearly expressed likenesses, as if in a mirror. The third type of vision is intellectual, by which those things are seen which have neither bodies nor the forms of bodies; such as the mind itself, God, justice, wisdom, and every good affection of the soul. For by intellectual vision the soul is never deceived. For either the soul understands, and that which it understands is true; or if it is not true, it does not understand. In physical vision, however, the soul very often errs and is deceived, according to that old and true <term>axiom of the Philosophers</term> <note>A common Scholastic principle: while the senses accurately receive data, the "deception" occurs when the mind incorrectly judges the external reality based on that data</note>; *the sense is deceived concerning its own and true object* <note>original: "sensus fallitur circa proprium & verum objectum"</note>, when it thinks that what seems to appear in the <term>imagination</term> <note>original: "phantasia"; the mental faculty that processes and stores sensory images</note> is actually happening in the bodies themselves. For example: to those who are sailing, the earth, cities, trees, and similar things seem to be moving; likewise, to those standing firmly on the earth and looking up at the sky...

<summary>The author defines three modes of perception: physical vision (sensory), spiritual vision (mental images), and intellectual vision (direct understanding of abstract truths). He argues that while intellectual vision is infallible, physical vision is frequently subject to optical illusions and errors of judgment.</summary>

the stars seem to stand still; yet diligent observation has taught men that all these move from east to west, and vice versa. Furthermore, when the rays of the eyes are spread apart <note>original: "divaricatis oculorum radiis"; this refers to double vision or being cross-eyed</note>, one thing will seem to have a double form, and a staff in water will appear broken, and many other things of that kind. Indeed, among all other senses, *sight*, though it is the most excellent, is most greatly deceived. For we see in a mirror sometimes a larger <term>image</term> <note>original: "idolum"; in this optical context, it refers to the reflected form or "species" of an object</note>, sometimes a smaller, and sometimes equal; similarly, in another, the right will appear to be the left, and vice-versa; so also that which is above will appear to be below, and vice versa. Sometimes the image will appear outside the mirror, as is proven in concave mirrors; sometimes truly inside the mirror. And likewise in one mirror—namely in an oblong concave one—a thing will appear longer than is right, while in a convex one it appears shorter than is fair, but in a flat mirror it appears just as it exists in its natural form. Yet in flat mirrors the right will appear to be the left, and the left to be the right; and so in infinite other cases, which those skilled in the science of optics have explained clearly. Indeed, we ourselves, in our own optical science, in the little books on refracted and reflected rays, have outlined all these things succinctly and, as it were, in a single word.

The sense of *hearing* also sometimes deceives the soul, as when someone, hearing the caterwauling of a cat or a dog, thinks it is some cry or complaint of a woman, a man, or an infant. Similarly, the noise of <term>artillery</term> <note>original: "tormenti bellici"; literally "war engines," referring to cannons or early firearms</note> is not rarely mistaken for thunder, and the voice of one man is taken for the tone of another; so also in music, dissonance is sometimes approved as consonance, and vice versa.

Furthermore, the soul is deceived through *taste*, insofar as it is itself mistaken regarding its own object. Thus, skilled physicians are known to, and often do, convert water into the color and flavor of wine by adding aromatic mixtures, so that it is accepted by the sick as true wine; indeed, I do not deny that I myself have performed this with various artifice. Quite often taste is also deceived, taking one thing for another because of the similarity of their natures.

The soul also hallucinates in the sense of *Scent or Smell*; for we very often see that, based on odor, a thing is believed to be something other than what it truly is; and we perceive this to happen by reason of both good and bad odors.

Finally, *Touch* deceives the soul in infinite ways. Thus was Isaac's soul deceived by Rebecca <note>A reference to the Biblical story in Genesis 27, where Jacob, prompted by his mother Rebecca, used goat skins to mimic the hairy touch of his brother Esau, deceiving their blind father Isaac</note>. From these things it is evident that this physical vision of the soul, which uses the external senses as its organs, is mistaken regarding physical objects. And this is the first degree of vision in the soul, by which we perceive bodies, which function the soul is accustomed to carry out through the five senses of the body.

In the second type of vision of the soul—by which we gaze upon things that are not physical, but similar to physical bodies, and even see ourselves as nothing other than likenesses of bodies—things are seen in the <term>fantastic spirit</term> <note>original: "spiritu phantastico"; referring to the "spirit" or subtle medium of the imagination</note>, just like an image in a highly polished mirror. And just as the image of a body in a mirror relates to the body existing outside the mirror (which exhibits the figure of the image by its presence), so also the icons and likenesses of bodies seen by the external sense are imprinted upon the spirit of imagination.

In *bodily vision*, however, the soul is often deceived, as was said in the preceding chapter. But the soul is also deceived and mocked in *spiritual vision*, which we shall treat here; for the things it sees are sometimes true, sometimes false, and occasionally disturbed, yet at other times tranquil. These true things sometimes appear as likenesses of future events, or as things said apart or in secret; sometimes they are pronounced through obscure signs and, as it were, figurative speech, or by an oracle, a vision, a dream, a nightmare, or an ecstasy of the soul; about which we shall speak here in a proper and methodical order. From this, therefore, it appears that the soul is not bodily, but rather like a likeness of a body, which is not a body itself; just as a spirit is not a body, but participates in the nature of body and light. For to a person sleeping, the soul will appear as if bodily in a dream, yet that is not his body, but the soul—not a true body, but the likeness of his body. For while his body lies still, the soul will walk; the tongue of his body will be silent, yet the soul itself speaks; your eyes will be closed, yet the soul will see; and thus in the soul is discerned the total and complete likeness of his flesh. In this likeness, the soul runs through known and unknown places and feels joy or sorrow. Moreover, the soul of the dead, just like that of a sleeper, feels either good or evil in that same likeness of its body; these things are not bodily, but similar to bodies, like the image of *Narcissus* in the water of a fountain. Souls stripped of their bodies are affected by these things, whether for good or ill, since they appear to themselves as similar to their own bodies. These are, however, either true joys or troubles transferred from spiritual substance into spiritual substance, like a reflection from one mirror into another. It is certainly true that there is a certain spiritual nature in us, where the likenesses of bodily things are either formed or, once formed, are introduced. This happens either when we perceive things present through some bodily sense, so that their likeness is immediately formed and stored in the memory; or when we think of absent things already known, or even things we do not know, so that a spiritual understanding is formed from them. We also fashion innumerable things according to our will and opinion, which either do not exist or are not known to exist. Likewise, innumerable other forms of things are painted in our mind when we are doing something or are about to do it. Sometimes also, with the spirit seizing it, the soul is lifted up so that it may see things of this kind, whether good or evil. The soul is also deceived and suffers through the intensity of thought, or by some force of disease (as often happens in delirium arising from a fever), or by the mingling of some other spirit, whether good or evil. For the images of bodily things are expressed in the spirit and are presented to the senses of the body itself just like actual bodies; so that absent things seem to be present, and those things which are not before the eyes are believed to be there. However, I would like you to note, O Readers who read these works of ours with an even mind, that we are not now speaking of the mind <note>original: "mente". In this context, the "mind" refers to the highest, divine part of the human intellect.</note>; which we proved above to be subject to no passion or changeability. Rather, we speak of the "middle soul" <note>original: "anima media"</note> in the body, which is mixed with the senses and the bodily spirit attributed to the imagination. If this soul is joined to the body through the senses—that is, if it gazes upon visible corporeal things through bodily vision—it can be called "corporeal" based on its effect. If, through phantasy, it is occupied with the vision of spiritual things and the likenesses of bodies, it is called "spiritual." Likewise, if it is occupied through the intellect with vision in which neither bodies nor the likenesses of bodies are perceived, it is called "rational" and "intellectual." For if this soul adheres to the mind, then its vision is occupied more with the mind and the intellect. But if it is more subject to the sensitive soul, then it uses its lower visions. 

This soul is, therefore, a spiritual substance, forged from light and a middle spirit; consequently, it is simple and indissoluble, incorporeal, yet capable of feeling and change in respect to the abundance of its spirit, which is capable of feeling. Yet, regarding its luminous form, it is permanent, fixed, and immutable. Therefore, the more it inclines downward, the more it is submerged in spirit, and consequently subjected to passion. But the more it is elevated upward toward the mind, the less it is weighed down by the disturbances of matter. Hence, in the region of the mind, where it performs intellectual visions, it always gazes upon the truth because of its freedom from passions and the extraordinary operation of its most powerful light. 

However, in its lower visions, it very often looks upon false things as true because of the thickness of the medium in which it swims. Thus, an oar or a straight staff, when dipped into water, will seem to be broken and bent because of the density of the medium. <note>A classic philosophical example of how a physical medium (like water or the "spirit" of the lower soul) can distort perception.</note> Hence, such things will appear to be what they truly are not, and thus the soul is deceived. The soul also lacks weight, shape, and color, insofar as it is invisible and cannot be grasped by the senses. Nor indeed should it be understood as a "part," but as a creature of God; nor is it made from the substance of God, except insofar as it participates in His luminous good. It is not made from the matter of the four elements, but was created out of nothing with a "fifth essential spirit." <note>This refers to the "Quintessence," a celestial substance distinct from earth, air, fire, and water.</note> Indeed, if God had made it from Himself, it would by no means be subject to vice, passion, changeability, or misery. Furthermore, if it were made from the elements, it would be corporeal. It has a beginning, therefore, but it is certain that it lacks an end. 

And since it is spiritual and ethereal, it has nothing of the earthly mixed or solidified within it; nothing of airy or watery humidity, and nothing of the heat and dryness of the element of fire. Therefore, just as its nature is invisible, so it remains invisibly in the body and departs invisibly from the body. Through the body, it sees bodies, such as the heaven and the earth and those things which are conspicuous to our eyes in them. Through the spirit, however, it gazes upon the likenesses of bodies. For whatever is not a body, and yet is something else, is not foolishly called "Spirit." Through the intellect, it sees those things which are not

### CHAPTER IV.

*On the transformation of men into the likeness of beasts through the deceptive operation of sorceresses. How good or evil demons take up the spirit of a man; and by what way evil demons foretell future things and deceive with false apparitions?*

It happens sometimes, according to the opinions of some worthy of belief, that by a certain sorcerous art of women and the power of Demons, men are converted into wolves and beasts of burden. Like brutes, they carry whatever loads are necessary, and once this work is completed, they return to themselves and their original form. However, this occurs in such a way that their mind does not become that of a beast, but remains rational and human. *Saint Augustine* <note>The author refers to Augustine's famous work *The City of God*, where he discusses stories of Italian innkeepers using cheese to turn travelers into pack animals.</note> left recorded in his writings that this faithfully happened in Italy in his own time. But this, unless I am mistaken, is to be understood as follows: that Demons do not actually know how to create new natures, but they can nevertheless do something to make a thing appear to be what it truly is not. For neither by any art nor by magic or diabolical power can the mind—nor even the body—be truly converted into beastly limbs and features. However, it can be converted into a "phantastic" man. Indeed, even in thinking or dreaming, a person is varied through innumerable types of things; and, since a thought is not a physical body, it takes the forms of bodies with wondrous speed.
