*While I was living in Marseille, France, I observed a certain demon-possessed girl being driven by priests with the sign of the cross; although she was entirely ignorant of the sciences, she produced several Greek words by a kind of inspiration of her own, and revealed many things about both the past and the present to the crowd, not without great wonder from those standing by.* This truly could not have proceeded from her own spirit; but because of the mixture made with that evil spirit, she produced such things as if with a single breath. And here we think it worthy of note how an evil spirit is accustomed to join itself with the spirit of one who curses, to execute the impious purpose of the curser. For the mother of this girl, weak and worn down by sickness, because of her daughter's neglect—or because the girl had lost some money (as was rumored) or had spent it on trifles—attacked her with dire imprecations, and finally burst out with these words: *“I wish,” she said, “that the devil with his legions would suddenly enter your body.”* Once this was maliciously spoken, the effect followed the will immediately. For the girl was suddenly obsessed by evil demons, and indeed—as the Devil himself confessed through the girl’s mouth—by six Legions <note>In the New Testament (Mark 5:9), a "Legion" refers to a vast number of demons. In Roman military terms, a legion was about 6,000 soldiers.</note>, and was miserably tortured by them. Therefore, the demons immediately entered the spirit breathed out in a malevolent and wicked manner by the mother; and thus Satan, because of the proximity of nature between the spirit of the mother and the daughter, very easily penetrated into the daughter’s spirit, carrying a crowd of demons with him.

But truly it must be noticed that although demons are permitted to possess the spirit of men, it is nevertheless impossible for them to penetrate into the lucid region of the mind and reason; because that is solely the seat and tabernacle of the Trinity, not otherwise than the celestial Sun, as the Royal Psalmist <note>A reference to King David, the traditional author of the Psalms.</note> testifies. And yet Satan is said to "fill the mind" of someone and the "ruling part of the heart." But this is understood to happen not indeed by entry into it and into its sense, but by fraud, iniquity, and all malice, by which he attracts and seduces that rational soul to himself, deceiving it and making it seem through thought that those things are goods and virtues which, in truth, are full of falsehood, vices, and deceptions. For the Devil is a fallacious, wicked, and fraudulent deceiver of souls. Therefore, the Devil does not occupy the lucid soul of a man by a participation of nature or the substance of the rational soul, as some think, nor is he made an inhabitant of it; but being joined to the aerial spirit <note>In early modern psychology, the "aerial spirit" was a subtle vapor that acted as a bridge between the physical body and the immaterial soul.</note> of the man on the part of his own composition, he is said to possess the mind and soul through fraud, deception, and malice—that is, by darkening the splendor of reason through phantastic imaginations in the sensual spirit of the obsessed man, which he is accustomed to excite by his artifices, so that those things seem to be which are not. Nevertheless, the sense is rendered subject to the Devil. Whence the tongue of the obsessed speaks, and he sees those appearances of the phantasy as certain and infallible truths, as he indeed believes.

And yet, despite his cunning, the mind <note>original: "mens"</note>—which is the true and immediate ray of God—suffers the follies of the Devil no more than the Sun of heaven bears the obscurities of aerial clouds, or the crashes and noises of thunder. Though these may appear to the earth and to earthly beings as dark and thick clouds, or horrendous thunders, or terrifying flying Dragons, or prodigious Comets, and so on, the Sun of heaven is in no way disturbed by them. It is always constant in its motion, always the same in its beauty and splendor, because God is always present with it, as it is His own tabernacle.

In a similar way, I say, the matter stands between the Devil’s deceptions of darkening and the mind, or the rays of light, within a human being. For although the eyes may be made to tremble, and the senses may be deluded by the vain fictions of the Devil, and the imagination may be oppressed by clouds and false meteors <note>In the 17th century, "meteors" referred to any atmospheric phenomenon, including rain, wind, or strange lights in the sky.</note>—whence it happens that in the middle region of the air we see some clouds that seem to take the shape of Dragons, others of mountains, others of castles, or men warring among themselves and countless other images, when in truth they are nothing of the sort but are mere fictions, accidents, or vain phantoms (and indeed more vain than any painter's work, since they vanish quickly)—nevertheless, the illuminated reason and the royal mind stand like the mundane Sun itself: firm and immovable, existing in its own truth and faith. 

From this it follows that against those men in whom faith is present—that is, whose souls adhere to the mind—the Devil can achieve nothing with his illusions; for through the clarity of light, they understand his fallacies. But those whose souls are bound to the flesh and the senses believe all things to be exactly as the Devil makes them appear, due to their lack of faith and the rays of the mind. Thus, they are submerged in ignorance, overwhelmed by darkness, and they slide down into the foulest abyss of matter <note>original: "hylæ abyssum" — 'Hyle' is the Greek term for raw, unformed matter, often associated with spiritual darkness.</note>, where they are buried alive, as if dead.

Let us mortals, therefore, reflect on the excellence of the mind, which the Devil cannot enter, just as he cannot enter a soul that adheres to the mind, because it is the temple and tabernacle of God. Therefore, the Devil flees the sight of the mind as he would the very sight of God; for this reason, he is called the "Light-Shunner" <note>original: "Lucifugus"</note>. And yet, so great is the power of Demons, so sharp is their perception, and so swiftly do they excel in aerial movement, that it is no wonder they easily surpass the senses of earthly bodies in sharpness, speed, and the power of motion. It is for this reason that they foretell things never before thought of, which men—owing to the slowness of their own bodies—seem to marvel at. Furthermore, because of the great length of their lives, Demons have acquired a far greater experience of things than any human can attain in the brevity of our lifespan. Thus, they predict certain future events through an exact understanding of the signs of nature and their positions, and they perform other wonders by which they entice and seduce those men who are not illuminated by the rays of the mind to follow their will.

For to these women, on a certain clear night with the moon <note>original: "Diana"</note> shining, Satan had very often appeared in various figures, around whom they themselves, leading dances with great joy, had held him as their only God. Moreover, we believe this happens through angelic operations, by the disposition of God's providence—who wishes well for both the good and the bad according to the inscrutable depth of His judgments—whether the souls of mortals are being instructed, or deceived, or raised up by consolation, or terrified, as mercy is shown or justice is imposed upon each person. But since we will speak and discourse more broadly about these things in our Treatise on death or the dissolution of the soul from the body, we will omit them here.

### CHAPTER V.
**On the third kind of vision of the soul, namely the intellectual, which never fails.**

**T**he third kind of vision of the soul is the intellectual, as was said above, by which those things that have neither bodies nor the forms of bodies are perceived. And indeed, the soul is never deceived by this type of vision. Yet, in sensory and phantastic <note>imaginative or image-based</note> visions, the soul is often mocked and seduced for the reasons we have alleged above. Therefore, only through intellectual vision can the mind arrive at a true knowledge of itself, and in no way through those former visions of sense and imagination, which instead deceive the soul and make things appear to it as they truly are not. It is through a withdrawal from the senses and from bodily images <note>original: "simulachris"</note> that the "inner man" is accustomed to reach the knowledge of himself and of God; since this is the only way in which one who is unknown to himself learns to know himself. But this is the labor, this is the task <note>original: "sed hic labor, hoc opus"; an allusion to Virgil's Aeneid regarding the difficulty of the journey</note>, for there is need of diligent habit and great constancy in withdrawing from the senses, so that a person may draw his mind away from the "many" toward the "one"—that is, that he may call it back to itself and keep it within itself. Indeed, the soul is hindered by these senses from being able to discern itself and its Creator, whom it ought to look upon alone and simply, without eyes. Therefore, it is necessary that, having left behind the levels of the senses, the soul transcends toward the goal of reason, treading the path of justice. For the rational soul surpasses all things created by God; and therefore, when it is pure and close to God—and thus, as far as it clings to the charity of the mind, bathed and illuminated by that intellectual light—it sees God not through bodily eyes, but through its own principal part, that is, through the intelligence. In Him is the most perfect beauty and the most blessed vision, by which vision the soul itself becomes blessed. Therefore, the soul must remove from its consideration all knowledge received from the outside through the senses of the body: for bodily things, and their likenesses, and even...

The senses themselves and the imaginations revolving around them—and those things sticking in the memory when one remembers by recalling them—belong to the outer man <note>original: "exteriorem hominem"; a concept from the theology of St. Paul, referring to the physical, sensory, and mortal part of a person as opposed to the eternal "inner" spirit</note>, although the soul perceives external things through these as if through certain messengers. The soul is also simple and free; nothing is more present to it than itself, by a certain internal and true presence, not one that is merely simulated. It sees itself in itself; for it knows nothing so well as that which is at hand to it, and nothing is more at hand to it than its own self. For it knows itself to live, remembers that it is, wills, thinks, knows, and judges; all these things, I say, the soul knows in itself. It does not imagine them outside itself, as if it touched them with some bodily sense in the way that any physical things are touched. From the thoughts of physical things, nothing is added to the soul that would make it think it is such a thing; whatever remains of itself to itself, that alone is what it is.

For nothing in the soul is as illuminated as the soul itself, nor does anything know the soul like the soul itself. When the soul asks what the soul is, it surely knows that it seeks itself; and it knows that it is the soul which seeks itself, for it seeks nothing other from itself than itself. Therefore, while it knows itself seeking, it knows itself entirely. And if it knows, surely it knows everything it knows entirely. Even if, having found a part, it does not seek its whole self, nonetheless, because it seeks itself entirely, it is present to itself entirely, and nothing can be more present to it than its own self.

However, as for what it asks about itself—what it was before, what it will be in the future, or what it is now—it asks how similar or dissimilar it is to God, how humble and devoted, how beautiful and how holy. But because it is in these bodies, which it thinks of with love and with which it is accustomed to mix its love, it cannot see itself without their images. For these things which are outside—these animate things <note>original: "animalia"; here referring to physical, sensory objects or the animal nature of the body</note>—adhere to it with such a strong glue that even when they are absent, their images are present to the soul as it thinks. Therefore, it cannot separate them from itself so as to inspect and see itself alone.

Therefore, let the soul return to itself and stand in itself; let it not seek itself as if absent, but care to see and discern itself as present. Let it fix the intention of its will, which wanders through other things, upon itself, and think of itself so that it may know and love itself. Thus it will see that it has never not loved itself, never not known itself, but that by loving other things along with itself, it has confused itself with them. Thus, it cannot be separated without great labor from those things to which it has adhered with great love.

Wherefore, the soul is deformed by the phantasms <term>phantasms: mental images or "ghosts" of sensory objects that remain in the mind</term> of bodily imaginations, with these being deeply impressed upon it; and even when released from the body, it is not stripped of them. For if it is not cleansed here from the corruption of bodily affections, once stripped of the body, it is held by bodily passions. For, as has been said, there is a very great cohesion between the spirit of the soul and the body. Thus, if the spirit of the soul clings to the bodily spirit, neglecting the beauty and blessing of the mind, then that elementary and sensitive spirit, after the soul's departure from the body, clings to and connects itself to its aerial spirit; and so the soul, stripped of the body, will be held by such passions as those it was subject to while existing in the body.

For as we see in the growth of a plant, the ethereal spirit with its soul or spark of light, flying and striving toward its homeland, raises itself up above the earth. To this is connected a portion of the other element, fire, as it is contiguous to the ethereal heaven; then air is glued to fire because of the dignity of its place, and water to air, and finally water to earth. Thus, the active will of the light and ethereal spirit is weighed down by that thick and heavy, dregs-like spirit, so that against its will it is detained in the air and cannot be carried further upward or raised.

So too, if the ethereal soul of man does not adhere to the portion of the mind, but is neglected by the divine ray—which is from the empyrean heaven <note>the highest, most pure region of the heavens, often described as the dwelling place of God and the source of divine light</note> and has no connection or familiarity with the elements—it behaves in almost the same way as the soul of a plant or a beast. For it is bound with the body by the fiery force of the elements and with the aerial part of the sensitive spirit, and sometimes it is linked with an even thinner portion, so that it is weighed down from the place of joy and gladness. It is detained in a place liable to those passions by which it was disturbed in the human body; because all...

All the bad passions <note>In this context, "passions" refers to emotions or states of being acted upon by external forces, rather than just strong feelings.</note> of the soul were located in the **coarser spirit**—specifically that of the senses and the imagination—which is a spirit that still clings to the soul even after it has been stripped of the body. But truly, if the soul, while still in the body, rejects the pleasures of the flesh and clings instead to **illuminated reason**, to the intellect, and to the higher mind; then it will be within the power of the mind to carry that soul upward—along with its clinging coarse spirit, once it has been purified—outside and above the region of suffering. It can then lift the soul out of the place of disturbances and terrors and into a place of happiness and joy. 

For this is the way of the **true resurrection** from death to life—that is, from darkness into light—accompanied by its **glorified body**. This glorified body is nothing other than the spirit of the sensory body, which has been so rectified by the power of the rays of the illuminated mind that, by its own refined subtlety, it can penetrate all things and pass through closed doors and windows. This is certainly something denied to other spirits stripped of the body, if any credit is to be given to histories both ancient and more recent. 

Furthermore, so great is the perfection of the soul when joined with this glorified corporeal spirit, that God grants it the power to cut through the ethereal heaven—being immune to all bonds of the elements—and to penetrate through the "sieve" <note>original: "cribum"; a metaphorical boundary or filter between the physical/ethereal realms and the divine realm</note> of the highest region on the wings of a mind free from all passion, which carry and lift it upward. 

Therefore, let the soul strive in this life, while it is still joined to its opaque body, to cling to the mind. In this way, it may free and cleanse itself from the defilements of the body and the sensory spirit. Indeed, if it does this, its reward will be excellent and its prize distinguished: when it departs from here (that is, from its body), it will drag nothing corporeal or unclean along with it, but will be immune to every bodily passion. 

At this point, I would like you to note in passing that many names are bestowed upon this soul according to the diversity of its actions. Just as the entire World Soul <note>The "Anima Mundi," or the spirit that animates the entire universe in Neoplatonic philosophy.</note> is composed of a lowest or elementary part, an ethereal part, and a manifold empyrean <note>The highest, most heavenly part of the universe, associated with pure fire and light.</note> part, so too is its **middle spirit**. This is also called the "middle soul," and it is its nature to participate in either extreme at will. 

*   When it perceives and is occupied with fleshly and earthly operations, it is called **Sense**.
*   When it gives growth and quickens the body, it is called **Life**.
*   When it records, it is called **Memory**.
*   When it distinguishes between things, it is called **Reason**.
*   When it tastes [wisdom], it is called the **Mind** <note>original: "animus"; often referring to the rational soul or the seat of the will and emotions</note>.
*   When it understands, it is called the **Higher Mind** <note>original: "mens"; the highest part of the intellect that connects to the divine</note>.
*   When it contemplates, it is called **Spirit**.
*   And when it desires, it is called **Will**.

Yet these do not differ in substance, but only in name; for all of them are nothing but a single soul, diverse in its properties but one in its essence. We see this same continuity in the spirit that stretches from the circumference of the world to its center; and likewise, we understand the pyramid of light to be continuous from the earth (where its point begins) to the outer boundary of the world. 

And yet, we perceive that both this universal spirit and the light possess various properties within themselves, depending on a greater or lesser quantity of light, or according to a greater or lesser thinness of the spirit. Thus it happens that the **coarser portion** of the spirit is changeable, corruptible, and subject to infinite alterations. Its **middle part**, however, is tempered by the properties of many different planets and distinguishes the celestial spheres; it exists as a moderate degree between the weak and the intense. Finally, its **highest region** is the most formal, the most subtle, and the most intellectual, filled with divine intelligences distinct in their order and nature. 

All these differences within one and the same spirit occur because of the variety of the proportions of light, which performs all things. Therefore, just as this spirit is said to be one and the same, yet contains various operations—whence it is called earth, water, air, fire, ether, fiery spirit, and intellectual spirit—so also is the same soul usually called sense, imagination, life, reason, intellect, and mind. It is one and the same spirit created by God, adorned with many-sided rays, which has received various names through its different operations. Thus we see that in the lowest region of the world, the lack of light is the cause of so many and such great changes. But if God were to confer as much grace upon this region of spirit as He does upon the human spirit through the mind, it would suddenly be exalted into the excellence of the higher region of the world. For the lower portion of the spirit does not differ from the higher, except...

218          TREATISE I. SECTION I. BOOK X.

Here are demonstrated the three visions of the soul: namely, insofar as it is sensation, imagination, and reason, intellect, and mind. When it is sensation, it sees, hears, smells, tastes, and touches bodies and visible things as they are—that is, it perceives all these things in their physical composition immediately through the external senses. Therefore, the soul is deeply involved in the multitude of things when it claims the name of sensation, and consequently, it is more remote from the contemplation of divine and spiritual matters. From this, it happens that the senses behold only the outer chest or the husk of things, the covering and veil of truth; they cannot discern the truth itself hiding in the center, nor can they perceive it through the organs of the external senses. 

Thus, the corporeal and visible world is presented to the sensitive soul <note>The "sensitive soul" refers to the part of the soul responsible for physical perception.</note>, whose earthly portion corresponds to Touch, the watery to Taste, the thick and mixed air to Smell, the simple and thin air to Hearing, and fire with ether to Sight. 

Furthermore, the soul residing in the front part of the interior mountain—or the Microcosmic head—is called the imaginative soul, or phantasy and imagination itself; for it beholds not the true images of bodily and sensible things, but their likenesses and, as it were, shadows. Therefore, it contemplates the ideas and icons <note>original: "icones"</note> of the world and worldly things insofar as it is imagination and perceives things in the abstract, rather than real or concrete things as they are. 

In the center of the brain, however, the soul neither sees in a fantastical way nor considers bodies in a sensible respect; rather, by the spirit of reason and the light of the mind, it contemplates intellectual things. These were neither present in the senses nor are they grasped by imagination alone, but are held and esteemed as true things by reason itself. For the secrets of the intelligences never fell under the scope of the senses, nor did the ineffable mystery of the triple Essence <note>A reference to the Holy Trinity.</note>. Indeed, the imagination cannot even grasp their ideas, since reason itself and the sharpness of human wit can hardly ever reach such grace, and only through a great illumination of the mind. 

Thus, reason rises first to the intellect through divine speculation, and then, with a light leap, elevates itself from the intellect into the sphere of the mind, so that in its light it may see spiritual things from afar. Through such a vision, it is seized by a great joy, beholding Jehovah—according to the Prophet Isaiah—sitting in heaven, raised upon a most high throne, and placed above the worldly palace, where His seat is heaven and His palace is most full of glory, even light itself. Thus, the soul always looks upon super-heavenly things as if in an ecstasy, neglecting lower things; it clings, I say, to the contemplation of things so noble that they are abstracted from the base senses. 

Finally, in the back part of the brain, the soul is called the memory and the motive power: for in that part, it stores away, guards, and remembers the objects of its visions, both of the sensible world and of the imaginary and intellectual worlds. Similarly, it is called the motive power insofar as it grants and sends motion downward through the spinal marrow to every member of the "lesser world" <term>Lesser world: The "Microcosm," or the human body as a reflection of the universe.</term>.

Just as there are 22 Hebrew letters, introduced by God—the Founder of all things—for the use of humanity to express or denote the shapes and natures of created things (for those things which God created in the first week do not exceed the number 22), so too must the pious soul, when departing from the body, ascend through just as many steps. It rises from the earth—that is, from the center of the spiral line depicted above, or from the "many" toward the "One"—signifying that the Word, in which the life of all things resides, exists in every creature, beginning from Unity and proceeding to the foundation of the multitude. Thus, he <note>Referring to God or the Word</note> is most rightly called the Alpha and Omega <note>original: "α & ω"</note>; just as his various actions in matter are distinguished through those Hebrew letters, some trustworthy authorities conclude from this that each of these letters denotes a specific work of creation. Therefore, the beginning of this motion, or the journey of the soul, is a withdrawal from sensible and external things toward spiritual, insensible, and internal things: from the earth (the object of touch) to water; from water (the object of taste) to thick air; from thick air (the object of smell) to thin air; and from this (the object of hearing) to fire. Leaving behind the sensible world through fire (the object of sight), the soul ascends to the world of imagination and the likeness of bodies. From there, it passes through the object of the Moon, where it imagines it sees Endymion <note>A figure from Greek myth; here used to represent the "Man in the Moon" folk belief</note> in the Moon, burdened with a massive bundle of thorns, and imagines itself gazing upon infinite other chimeras in the abstract within the planetary region.

It seems to itself to traverse Aries, Taurus, Leo, Scorpio, and Capricorn, and likewise, outside the Zodiac, to wander past the Wolf, the Dog, the Bear, the Snake, and so on, through the meadows and celestial fields with a bold gaze, feeding and nourishing itself there day and night. Similarly, it believes that imaginary men live in this starry sphere—namely, Gemini, Virgo, Sagittarius, and Aquarius within the borders of the Zodiac; and likewise outside them, Orion, the Centaur, the Charioteer, Hercules, the Serpent-bearer, Perseus, Cepheus, the Herdsman, Antinous, Cassiopeia, Andromeda, and others. Here also, within the limits of the Zodiac, it dreams it discerns Cancer and Pisces, and outside them the Great Whale, as if swimming in a watery heaven; and it sees the ship Argo furrowing the ethereal waves in a fantastical manner, so much so that it believes these things are truly physical bodies.

From here, this human spirit rises higher, carried on the wings of divinity into the invisible world, which is also called "spiritual" because it is scarcely material at all. There, it finds total truth, and can behold nothing within it except truth alone. For it either sees, in which case it must necessarily see the truth, or it does not see, in which case it is impossible for it to see falsehood. Indeed, in this seat of blessedness, it always sees; and what it sees is true and good, because the eye of uncreated providence—seeing all things there and everywhere—ensures, through the rays of its eternal vision, that whatever exists in this heaven is seen by the eyes of reason, intellect, and wisdom, not without ineffable joy and gladness. Therefore, the soul's first journey in this illuminated region is through the kingdom of the Angels, the second through the kingdom of the Archangels, and thus by ascending upward in order and by degrees, traversing the regions of all the Intelligences, it continues until it reaches the supreme peak of the invisible world. 

In that peak resides that Unity from which all multitude is derived; the goal where motion goes from "something" to "nothing" <note>In the sense of moving beyond material "things"</note>; the sole principle from which the world was made; the fountain of essence from which forms were bestowed upon things; the Being of beings <note>original: "ens entium"</note> by whose being all things were made into beings; the first act <note>original: "actus primus"</note> by whose presence and action all things were led from potentiality into act; and the nature that natures <note>original: "natura naturans" — a term for God as the creative force behind the natural world</note>, by whose nature the natures of all things are nurtured. This Unity benevolently and abundantly pours down its incomprehensible glory, its ineffable light, and its kind gaze upon all its creatures forever. Here, therefore, the soul, overflowing with inexplicable joy, finds rest. Then, seized with wonder, it immediately descends back down, so that it may imprint the traces of its acquired wisdom upon its own body—which has remained all this time in a state of near-permanent ecstasy—and thus upon the entire Microcosm <note>The "small world" of the human being, reflecting the "Macrocosm" of the universe</note>.

# THE FIRST TREATISE,
## SECTION I.
### BOOK XI.
### Concerning Sperm and Generation.

#### CHAPTER I.
*On the nature of generation and multiplication.*

[A large historiated initial 'I' within a square frame, depicting a figure and decorative elements.] In the secret of generation <note>original: *generationis arcano*</note>, many mysteries—of the super-celestial as well as the celestial and sublunary realms—which are commonly still unknown and not yet proclaimed, must be explained and diligently observed. Regarding what first pertains to the super-celestial things, it should be noted that, according to the doctrine of Iamblichus <note>Iamblichus (c. 245–325 AD) was a Neoplatonist philosopher whose works on the divine hierarchy and theurgy deeply influenced Renaissance occult philosophy.</note>, living beings are divided into four orders: namely, Gods, Daemons <term>daemones: from the Greek *daimon*; in this context, these are intermediary spirits or divine messengers, not the "demons" of modern horror</term>, Heroes, and Souls. That is to say: God; the Angels who serve God like architects in the worldly workshop; the Olympic spirits or governors of the Planets and celestial bodies; and finally, Souls. 

Hence, in his opinion, there appear to be two radii <note>original: *semidiametri*</note> drawn from the center (that is, the Earth) to the furthest circumference—meaning the upper capacity of the Empyrean <note>The Empyrean was considered the highest, most spiritual part of heaven, associated with pure light and fire.</note> heaven and the elementary heaven. The former is considered the dwelling place of God, while the latter is thought to be the dwelling of souls. Daemons and heroes, however, are said to claim the intermediate places for themselves. 

From this it follows that Daemons, because of their proximity to the fiery tabernacle of God, are said to participate in His primary property, which is Unity. For their properties, as Iamblichus witnesses, consist in containing within themselves the gifts of the Gods—though in a lesser manner than the Gods themselves—and by their very nature and idea, they occupy a lower condition. Thus, they participate in unity and stability. But at the other extremity, tending further downward, is the property of the inhabiting and operating soul. Since the soul represents a turning away <note>original: *declinatio*</note> toward multitude, motion, and the filling of natural things with vital movement to complete the work of generation, it is observed to be most distant from the nature of unity (the property of God); for indeed, the soul tends toward number and plurality. Finally, Heroes...

It establishes that while higher beings share in divine stability, souls are responsible for the movement and "multiplicity" required for life on Earth.</summary>

Finally, since they lean more toward the placement of souls, they agree with their natures in almost all respects. For their own property is understood under the condition of multitude and motion, and by the disposition of mingling, status, and excellence; as was declared more broadly by us above, in the division of the mundane pyramid <note>Fludd uses a "Mundane Pyramid" as a visual and mathematical model to explain the transition from pure spirit (at the peak) to dense matter (at the base).</note> into the squares and cubes of the roots. Therefore, Daemons differ from Heroes in this: that Heroes lean somewhat more toward particular and moving things—to use the words of Iamblichus—than do Daemons. For those two types of intermediaries, namely Daemons and Heroes, are composed of the properties of the extremes, namely of God and of souls; these are indeed denoted by the simple fingers and joints of the first composition or roots in the aforementioned material pyramid; but in Daemons there is more of the divine, in Heroes more of the human. From these things, therefore, it is clear that the governors of the Planets with their legions dwelling in the elementary region, whom they call Heroes, pouring life into lower things from their orbs, and consequently agreeing with souls, promote multiplications in plants and generations in animals. And the place of these Heroes is described in the order of the squares of the material pyramid, just as souls are recognized as being submerged in the depth of its cubes. God indeed, since he is the purest and simplest form, and the most exact and primary light, made the purest and simplest generation of the monad <term>monad: from the Greek *monas*; a single unit or the number one, representing the divine origin of all things</term>, reflecting it into himself: so that unity might remain whole and untouched in its nature without any pollution of matter. For matter itself was the cause of multitude and the increase of number, as will be declared from this enigmatic history or the following fable.

*Demogorgon, who is the highest and first God, surrounded, accompanied, and adorned by eternity before the origin of the world, and reposing himself within it, gazed upon formless Chaos with the ineffable splendor of his eyes. Perceiving its belly to be shaken and disturbed in a wondrous way by struggle, wrestling, and tumult, he stretched out his hand to assist that pregnant birth of Chaos. From this, Strife* <note>original: *litigium*; here Fludd personifies the initial discord of the elements</note> *immediately took its origin at first sight; which, brought forth into the circuit of the world by the benevolent favor of Demogorgon, with a truly dishonest and impudent face, and accompanied by an unheard-of noise, strove to be carried on ambitious wings on high and upward to the peak and summit of heaven. Thus it happened that it was deservedly cast down and destroyed by Demogorgon into the deepest abyss. But Chaos, the mother of all things, after the birth of this rebellious first-born of hers, now remaining purer, burned with sweat and fiery sighs, and began to labor toward birth for yet another turn. Again, with the assisting hand of Demogorgon, she brought forth a second, male offspring, whose name was Pan—signifying nature, matter, or the universal spirit. His head was filled with eyes like the starry sky; his two ears the two poles of the world; his long beard the solar rays stretching downward; his pipe composed of seven reeds represented the seven Planets with their harmony; and his goat-like feet signified the nature of time. Again, after the birth of Pan, his three sisters—namely the Fates* <note>original: *Parcae*; the three goddesses who spin, measure, and cut the thread of life</note>—*were brought forth and born from the womb of Chaos, proving the changeability of things. Finally, the Pole, Titan, Earth, and Erebus* <note>Erebus: the personification of darkness</note> *followed in linear succession.* From this account, therefore, it is demonstrated that matter or Chaos—constituted from a heap of formless spirits or waters—was the origin and matrix of generation before creation; which, however, could have brought forth or produced nothing unless the act of Demogorgon had been present, since without his assistance the powers of Chaos could by no means have been led from potentiality into act. Hence it is manifest that God, by his unique essence and formal property, which is unity, produced fertile nature into act, which the Pythagoreans placed in the category of imperfect things—namely, in duality. From then on, with unity informing the formless spirit, the arrangement of the ternary and the Trinity was produced; so that by the virtue of unity, the imperfect duality was brought forth, which by the addition of unity was illustrated and brought back from an imperfect number into a most perfect number and nature: namely, into the Trinity. Thus God in the Word, the Word in the Spirit flowing from both...

...you, and God in all things. So the Word of God is in every nature or spirit filling the whole universe. So God with the Word and the Spirit is everywhere. And thus through the symphony of this divine harmony, peace shall be continued among the elements even until the final PERISHING <note>original: *PEREAT*</note>, for Strife <note>original: *litigio*; Fludd refers to the Empedoclean concept of Love and Strife as the forces of the universe.</note> has already been cast down from heaven to earth and thrust into its center. Thus perpetual happiness will belong to the first region of the world, durable friendship to the middle, and rest with little disturbance to the lowest. 

But in this lowest region, the tumult of opposing winds, the conflict of waves and waters, the generation of meteors <note>In the 17th century, "meteors" referred to any atmospheric phenomenon, including rain, wind, and lightning, not just falling stars.</note> forged from contrary qualities, and infinite other accidents happening to this inferior world are very often found, on account of its proximity to Strife. These things being understood, the reason is at hand why the lower parts are more suited for generation than the upper; since the denser and more effective part of the womb of Chaos is found in this region. 

Hence the earth is called the mother of all things, which fire has sent into her womb. Nor indeed should there be further doubt about this, since we observe that neither air, nor fire, nor ether in their own regions are fit for the generation of animals, vegetables, or minerals. There was, therefore, from the matter and substance of Chaos the capacity for generation, which received its form, soul, and act from God for its essence and existence. 

For generation cannot happen without action upon a well-disposed passive subject; and consequently, God, who is unity and the monad <term>monad: a single, indivisible unit representing the divine source</term>, does not generate a multitude by Himself, but through the abundance of the matter of Chaos, or the fecund spirit, or the moist nature, which—as Hermes Trismegistus <note>original: *Mercur. Trismegist.*</note> testifies—the Word and light and pure fire cherished; or the Spirit of the Lord, which moved over the waters. From this, souls arise, prone toward a multitude of particular things; and by the Heroes or Lords of the Planets, who pour prolific and vital matter downward, those souls are urged, enticed, and strengthened toward constant generation and procreation. 

Therefore, the dominion of the Heroes and souls is from the solar sphere down to the center or the earth; because from that point, proceeding downward, the cone of the formal pyramid tends from formal universality toward its particularity, namely ending at the point of the cone in the earth; while, conversely, the base of the material pyramid, resting upon the earth, supplies a multitude of matter to the scarcity of form found there in the cone of the formal pyramid. 

Hence arise so many generations on earth, and so many corruptions, mutations, or alterations. For much matter, never content with a scarcity of form, desires to change its habit daily, so that it may acquire for itself a nobler form, whose presence and act may fully satisfy its appetite. 

But indeed, ascending upward from the sphere of the Sun, nothing of generation can be found; there, the part of the material pyramid tending upward becomes increasingly refined <note>original: *subtiliatur*</note> as it gradually approaches the base of the formal pyramid. Thus such matter, because of its refinement from form and light, is altogether unfit and unfruitful for generation, since its womb is too tender and subtle, so that it cannot retain the seeds of light because of their intense strength. For this reason, souls are said by the Philosophers to possess the lowest part of the world and the final order of intelligences, and to claim for themselves a place near the earth, or in the lowest region; because there their appetite, occupied with particulars and the multitude of generation, is sufficiently fulfilled according to the opinion of Iamblichus <note>Iamblichus was a Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote on the soul's descent into the material world.</note> cited above.

### CHAPTER II.

*On generation, and what the difference is between it and creation?*
*That heaven is the origin of the generation of things.*


**P**eripatetic philosophers <note>The "Peripatetics" were the followers of Aristotle, known for walking while they taught.</note>, treating faithfully of the natural birth of things and diligently inquiring into the reason and arrangement of generation, finally perceived that **Genesis** <note>original: *Genesin*; meaning "becoming" or "origin."</note> or generation itself is nothing other than a change from one original **substantial form** <note>original: *forma substantiali*; a technical term for the essential nature that makes a thing what it is.</note> into another. That is, it is the progress of matter toward a substantial form which is not yet within it, but soon will be. For example: they maintain that the generation of an apple is the progress of the bud—acting as the matter—toward the apple—acting as the substantial form. This is because the apple is a substance, yet the form of the apple is not in the bud, but will be present soon, once generation is perfected. 

However, it seems to us—and may this be said with the kind permission of the Peripatetics—that the form of the thing to be generated is actually present within the **seed** <note>original: *spermati*; in this context, the term refers to the reproductive "germ" or essence of any living thing, whether plant or animal.</note> or bud from the very beginning, even if it is not immediately apparent to our senses. Instead, it works hiddenly more and more every day within the mass of the seed from that moment when it is cast into a **womb** <note>original: *matricem*</note> suitable for generation for the perfection of the thing to be produced, as we shall declare below. 

The difference between generation and creation was mentioned above, where we clearly explained that **creation** is the origin of a species that did not previously exist, and consequently of every individual of that same species proceeding immediately and primarily from it. But we say that **generation** is the method of preserving and continuing a species that already exists and was brought into the world through creation. From this it is clear that creation concerns a thing that does not pre-exist, while generation necessarily concerns a preceding thing that exists in the nature of things by the benefit of creation. 

Furthermore, we gather from this that just as God is the author of creation, or the father of created species, so also the creature itself is recognized as the father of the generated thing. For without the seed of the creature, it is impossible for any generation to occur, since without an occult **seminal virtue** <note>A "virtue" in this sense is an inherent power or life-force.</note>, matter cannot put on the form and species of living bodies.

This is also confirmed by the words of the same Hermes Trismegistus in *Pimander*, book 4, which are as follows: *Whatever is generated is certainly imperfect, divisible, increasing and decreasing; but to that which is perfect, none of these things happen.* <note>original: *Quicquid genitum, utique imperfectum...*</note> 

Therefore, the Father of the creature was the only good and the highest perfection—namely, the **Monad** <term>Monad (the number one, representing the indivisible Unity of God)</term>, the principle, root, and origin of all things, yet without a principle itself. It contains every number but is contained by none; it begets every number but is begotten by none. It communicated its goodness and perfection to the first creature. Thus, all created things were called good. Indeed, this perfection and goodness was disturbed by the sin of Adam. For he, who had received a portion of the form only for his own composition and perfection, wished to bestow a portion of it toward the generation of others, and thus to impart it to others in a prodigal fashion; so from a perfect creature, he was made an imperfect creature, stained by the pollution and filth of darkness. But may God, the Best and Greatest, reform all these things for the better according to His good will.

Afterward, by their power and with the cooperation of heat, the other parts are also gradually produced: namely, the lungs and the other parts of the chest, the stomach, the intestines, and the things that cover them; likewise the bladder, the kidneys, and in the last place, the remaining parts of the entire body. Then, on the thirtieth day, males usually appear, and on the thirty-seventh, females. Thus, when the limbs and organs of the body are completed, the fetus remains in the womb for its total maturation and "cooking" <note>Early medicine compared fetal development to a slow culinary ripening or "coction."</note> until the completion of nine months. *Why the animal soul does not act as quickly in the fetus,*

It is from this, therefore, that Mind and Reason appear only in the final place. And yet, life or the "living soul" does not yet appear then, although it is manifest that it works secretly through the production—or rather, the opening up—of the vessels, arteries, veins, and nerves. Therefore, once the organs of the body have increased and become perceptible, the movement of the soul and its effects also become more perceptible. From this it happens that life usually begins to appear in the middle of the growth process, so much so that the fetus is even perceived to move by the sense of touch; yet the mind and reason do not seem to act, except by a certain mystical movement in the soul, which the human sense is in no way able to perceive. For just as the spirit acts in the body, so the soul acts in the spirit; but as the actions of the soul cannot be perceived by the bodily sense without the spirit, so neither can those of the mind and reason be perceived without the effect of the life-giving soul. From this it is clear that the acts of the spirit are familiar to the bodily senses, because they are closer to them and, as it were, contiguous. But the acts of the soul are not so familiar to them, because the spirit is interposed between the body and the soul. Similarly, the acts of reason are even more difficult for the bodily senses to know than the acts of the soul, because the mediums of spirit and soul are interposed between the body and reason. Most difficult of all for the bodily senses to perceive, however, are the acts of the mind and the operations of God, because they are more distant and are, as it were, in the center of spiritual mysteries. But the operations of the senses are placed on the outermost surface. Indeed, it would be extremely difficult for a sense dwelling and acting on the surface of the earth to perceive the secret operations performed in the center of the earth and the mysteries of nature hidden there; thus, it will be much harder and more difficult still for gross and earthy matter to understand those mystical operations and intentions produced in the super-celestial heaven. It is for this reason, therefore, that the mind and reason seem to be at rest in the spermatic mass as far as the human sense is concerned, even though by a hidden and mystical...

# FIRST TREATISE,
# SECTION I.
# B O O K XII.
# On the harmony of the internal and external man.

## C A P. I.
## That human Music is fittingly related to world music: And on the proportions of the material Triangle with the formal in the internal man.

[Large decorative woodcut initial P] **T**he Pythagoreans <note>Followers of the ancient Greek philosopher Pythagoras, who believed that the universe was structured according to mathematical and musical ratios.</note> have handed down in their writings that in the construction of the world, the **Monad** or unity is referred to the Artisan or Creator; the **Dyad** or duality to spiritual matter with its dregs-filled base; and the **Triad** or Trinity to form or light, by which all things are shaped. Thus, they asserted with conviction that the entire world was fashioned from the number three. Similarly, from a composition of these aforementioned parts, they affirmed that man, the most worthy creature of the earth, was born—namely, from the **Hexad** <note>The number six.</note>. For 1, 2, and 3 added together constitute 6. For from a more worthy, more complex [source], a more worthy, less complex thing was made, namely man. For God first fashioned the world from the number three in its primary composition, for which reason the world was called the "Son of God" by the Philosophers; and from the composite parts of the world, as if from its own number three, man was born, whom for this reason the ancients called the "Son of the World." 

The same Pythagoreans also say (not disagreeing with the Platonists in this) that the human number is the **Heptad** <note>The number seven.</note>, and indeed not without reason; since the Heptad is formed from the formal number, which is three, joined with the material number, namely four. They said, however, that the being, life, and existence of the other creatures were made from the number ten or nine. From these things it is clear that the human number approaches more closely to the nature of unity than the number of other creatures, and that it responds to the unity of the world—namely, the seat of the mind—in the harmony of the **Diapason** <term>Diapason: The Greek term for an octave, the most fundamental and harmonious interval in music, representing a 2:1 ratio.</term>. ### CHAPTER II.
*Concerning the symphonic melody between the soul, spirit, and body.*

**[I]**n the common observation of Music, we see that its system or scale consists of a triple series of letters or notes, which the Artists call **keys**. All of these, except for three, are said to be "hidden." But those three are manifested clearly to distinguish the differences between the aforementioned invisible keys. Thus, the first series of keys is **Γ. A. B. C. D. E. F.** <note>The letter Γ (Gamma) represents the lowest G in the medieval musical gamut.</note> expressed through simple letters of a larger order, as you see; these are called the **grave** <term>Grave: the low-pitched or "heavy" notes that form the base of a composition.</term> keys, acting as the bases and foundations for the others that rise above them. The manifest key of these is **F**, which is expressed thus: 𝄢. The second order of letters is as follows: **g. a. b. c. d. e. f.** This series is called the **Middle**, and its letters are called excellent and acute <term>Acute: high-pitched or "sharp" notes.</term>; from these the middle parts of the melody arise, specifically the "middle song" <note>original: "medius cantus"; likely referring to the alto or tenor range.</note>, just as the **Bass** is drawn from the lowest. There is also yet another series, even more eminent, excellent, and acute in the elevation of its voice, from which the **High** song <note>original: "cantus Altus"</note> is composed; and it is of this sort: **gg. aa. bb. cc. dd. ee. ff.** These letters, superexcellent, very acute, and supreme, exist within the full power of man.

From this proportion of harmony, the machine of the world is composed in a triple seven-fold number. Its elementary portion, consisting of a more **grave** symphony, seems to support the other parts of the world's harmony. For the elements are heavier than the other regions of the heaven, and are like the bases and foundations. Similarly, the **middle heaven** is likened to the series of acute and excellent letters, insofar as it creates the first melody with the elements or the Bass. Its seven Planets are the seven keys. And just as in ascending from **g. a. b.** to **c.** we find that **c.** is the principal key, by whose manifestation the others (not expressed) are understood; so also in ascending from the **Moon ☾, Mercury ☿, Venus ♀,** to the **Sun ☉**, we find that the **Sun ☉** is as it were that open or manifest key of heaven. By its visible presence, the other Planets (which are hidden in themselves) are made manifest; they sound symphonically toward the lower grave regions, they are illuminated, and they operate livelily upon the elements and things made of elements. Finally, the **super-acute** and superexcellent letters are referred to the supreme region, where the cone of the material pyramid ends in a super-acute point, beyond which there is no passage for a created spirit. However, as we have demonstrated in the preceding pages, man is called by the wise the "son of the world," because his subtle, invisible, and internal part was made from the simpler parts of the world...

Just as the gross, visible, and external part of the world is fashioned from the thicker parts or elements of the universe, so we say that the human body—inasmuch as it is composed of the world's elements—is the basis and foundation of the whole music of the composite man. Furthermore, his ethereal spirit, which secretly retains the traces of the seven Planets and their natures, is compared to the sharp and high keys <note>original: "clavibus acutis," referring to high-pitched musical notes or the "treble" range</note> that look toward the celestial melody, while it gives life to its body by means of a secondary light or mediating agent. Finally, we say that the super-celestial light, or the **Mind** <note>original: "mens"</note> itself, striking the rational spirit, creates a most excellent melody alongside the lower steps of the letters <note>original: "literarum gradibus," likely referring to the notations on a musical scale</note>. By these means, three species of melody are perceived, differing most widely in sound and variety, yet sounding and moving most perfectly through the bonds of harmony or consonance linked within the **Microcosmic** <term>Microcosm: "The little world," a Renaissance concept that the human being is a miniature map of the entire universe.</term> composition. By that reasoning, through the harmony of the middle melody—namely the spirit—the mind and soul, with their intellectual symphony, are mixed among the sounds of the deeper voices, and thus introduced into the opaque body fashioned from the elements.

Therefore, the harmony of the soul is a spiritual and luminous (or formal) **fourth** <note>original: "Diatessaron"</note>, **fifth** <note>original: "Diapente"</note>, and **octave** <note>original: "Diapason"</note> composed of "superexcellent" voices. Likewise, the harmony of the spirit is made of middle voices or "excellent" steps; in its symphony, this spirit agrees both with the "superexcellent" (or super-celestial) and the "deep" (or elemental). Finally, the human body is, as it were, the *organon* or instrument of the entire human harmony. Its lowest melodic step or "grave accent" occurs in that subtle elemental part from which the sensitive soul and natural faculty arise. The string <note>original: "chorda"</note> of this instrument is the elemental spirit—either thicker or thinner air—which the fiery or more formal power of the elements is observed to strike. This striking of the spirit causes a certain harmony of the elements to sound in the "ears of reason."

The principal origin of this Music is in the lowest region of the Microcosm; nevertheless, the effect of its harmony is dispersed and sown throughout the entire human fabric. It is observed to move the natural harmony with the higher parts in no other way than how, in common music, the sound of the **Bass** part is heard to resonate indifferently with the sounds of the **Middle** <note>original: "Medii," or Tenor</note> and **High** <note>original: "Alti," or Alto/Soprano</note> parts, or how the melody of one part is usually mingled with another through a certain essential and natural mixture of life. Hence, the veins are perceived to be dispensed throughout the body alongside the arteries, and both alongside the nerves.

So also the middle spirit or ether is struck by the middle soul; by its vibration, an "excellent" melody is made in the middle of the instrument. This attributes life-giving tones or sounds to the whole body, no less than when a struck string of a lute <note>original: "barbiti"</note> makes the whole lute resonate. Furthermore, this string, by its vibration, creates the melody of the rational heaven from its high "magical" reason in an ineffable way, joining it with the deep music.

And thus, a complete music constituted of three different melodies is perceived to sound in the human body: namely, the **sensory**, the **vital**, and the **rational**. The sensory acts in the preservation of the flesh and the growing parts; the Vital in the quickening and movement of the mass or "machine" of the body; and the Rational in the government and direction of the entire fabric.

Therefore, the **Bass** song of the Microcosm is **cubic**, because it is elemental or corporeal. The **Middle** is **planar** or square, because it is spiritual. Finally, the **High** is **radical** or linear, because it is formal <note>Fludd is using geometric metaphors here: the "solid" body is a cube, the "surface" spirit is a square, and the "divine line" of the mind is a point or line.</note>. In that Great World, there is only one resonating spirit, one organ receiving sounds into its cavity, and one striking light; but because of the thicker or thinner disposition of that same spirit's substance, that which is one and the same in itself appears to be distinguished into a plurality. So also this same...

For the higher one ascends from the tip of the formal pyramid toward its base, the sharper or more slender the accents become, and the subtler the works that are perfected. But in the material pyramid, the further one progresses from the tip toward its base, the heavier and denser the sounds become, and the works become coarser, more opaque, and more visible. The reason for this is certainly at hand: namely, because the formal expression of light more strongly stirs the spirits, and consequently, through their subtlety, renders the voices clearer and more effective.

By its power or accent, the very shadows—dreadful and terrible—were driven out and beaten back downward; the waters or "moist nature" were purged of their deformity; all things were made from nothing; the elements were bound in harmonious peace; the heavens themselves were strengthened in a marvelous way; the earth was balanced on equal scales, established on firm columns, and suspended in the middle. Indeed, this ineffable Word of the Creator performed wonders even in the fabrication of man himself; for He made man's soul a palace and a tabernacle for Himself, or rather a temple, to speak with Saint Paul and Sixtus the Pythagorean. Whence Hermes Trismegistus says, speaking with the mouth of the divine mind: *I believe that the Word of God sees and hears within you, etc.*

### THE UPPER REGION AND THE TREBLE HARMONY

However, in the highest region of the human instrument—which corresponds to the head and the purest part of the mind—the **formal pyramid** <term>Formal pyramid: Fludd's visual metaphor for the power of God or Spirit, which is widest at its source and tapers as it descends into matter.</term> is at its broadest base, while the material pyramid has dwindled to a mere point or apex <note>original: "conus," the tip of the cone</note>.

For this reason, the music produced in this celestial part of man is:
*   **Acute** and high-pitched
*   **Swift** in its vibrations
*   **Pure** and clear in its tone

This happens because three parts of the divine light now hold dominion over a single part of gross matter. Just as the density of the earth produces a deep, slow bass, the subtlety of the spiritual ether produces a sharp treble. Thus, the soul moves the spirit with great agility, creating a harmony that is closer to the divine source.

->**Table of the Triple Harmony in Man**<-

| Region of Man | Dominant Element | Musical Character |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Upper (Mind)** | Light / Form | Treble / Swift |
| **Middle (Heart)** | Equality of Both | Mean / Moderate |
| **Lower (Belly)** | Darkness / Matter | Bass / Heavy |

<margin>The Internal Monochord</margin>
We must therefore conceive of the whole man as a single **monochord** <note>original: "monochordum internum," a one-stringed instrument used to demonstrate mathematical ratios</note>, where the length of the string stretches from the top of the head to the soles of the feet. The player of this instrument is the soul, which, through the medium of the **vital spirit** <term>Vital Spirit: In Renaissance medicine, a subtle, airy substance that acts as a bridge between the physical body and the immaterial soul.</term>, strikes the strings of the limbs and organs.

If the body is well-tempered <note>original: "temperatum," meaning balanced in its four humors: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile</note>, the music of health is produced. But if the string is slackened by too much moisture or tightened by the heat of fever, the result is discord and disease.

<insert>The physician, then, is like a tuner of the human string.</insert>

In this way, the **internal harmony** of the microcosm <note>The "small world" or man, reflecting the "macrocosm" or universe</note> reflects the **music of the spheres** <note>original: "musica mundana," the silent, mathematical harmony of the planets</note> found in the great world. Without the light of the soul, the body would be nothing but a <unclear>motionless</unclear> and heavy mass of clay.

<meta>This page continues Robert Fludd’s exploration of the "Internal Monochord." It moves from the physical description of the regions of the body to the mathematical and metaphysical principles of harmony that bind the soul (unity) to the body (multiplicity).</meta>

->ON THE INTERNAL AND EXTERNAL HARMONY OF MAN, 247<-

...it lacks both a beginning and an end, because duality <note>original: "dualitas." In Fludd's philosophy, the number 2 represents division and the fall into matter.</note> possesses no middle point; from this, all discords—the daughters of darkness—are produced. But in truth, concords, which are the offspring of light and truth, arise from the perfect and the odd numbers.

Hence it happens that if the unity of light, which is the soul, is joined with the duality of matter, it produces an odd number, which is full of harmony. Likewise, if the trinity of the soul (which is the same in essence as unity) is added to the quaternary <note>The number four, representing the four elements of the material body.</note> of matter, it produces the number seven <note>original: "septenarium."</note>. In this number, a most perfect consonance is heard, which contains within itself the **Perfect Fifth** <term>Diapente: A musical interval of a fifth.</term> and the **Perfect Fourth** <term>Diatessaron: A musical interval of a fourth.</term>.

Consequently, this union of the soul with the body now renders that which was previously dissonant into a wondrous consonance. It makes regular, I say, that which was previously and by its own nature rebellious, irregular, and entirely opposed to motion or action. From this we find that man is nothing other than a unity and a multitude gathered together in admirable harmony.

Thus we see that just as there is but one Sun of the world, there is but one soul; yet its rays are diverse—indeed, infinite—and these rays are shared by the soul. So also we observe that all rays of light are derived from the one **Jehovah**, as if from the **Father of Lights** <note>A reference to the Biblical Epistle of James 1:17: "Every good gift... cometh down from the Father of lights."</note>, which is to say, from a single source or supersubstantial essence. His rays, flowing from Him both mediately and immediately, are in no way divided, but are rather connected in the same way that light is connected to the body of the Sun—light which is nonetheless recognized to be present in the earth, the waters, the air, and all compound things.

For this reason, the soul is called "One" because of its indivisibility from its primary form; likewise, matter is called "Multitude" because of its duality or quaternarity, which consists of a multitude or number of units. Yet for matter, an imperfect number is the principle, rather than unity. This is the reason why Democritus, Orpheus, and many of the Pythagoreans <note>Ancient Greek philosophers who believed that the universe was built on mathematical ratios and that a divine spirit permeated all things.</note> were of the opinion that all things are full of Gods; they referred all of these back to the one Jove <note>Jupiter/God</note>, just as one refers a multitude back to unity.

But to return to this human music of ours: we have composed it from three strings and three instruments joined together, bringing forth three parts of melody. Each string and each instrument corresponds to a specific region of the world. However, because the two higher strings—namely the spiritual and the formal—coincide equally with the harmony of the string on the lowest instrument, we see it just as in the music of various melodies: the **Bass** part mingles with the **Mean** <note>The middle voice or tenor.</note>, the Mean with the **Alto**, and the Alto with the lowest parts in an equal arrangement of melodies. In this way, a multiform harmony is found within a single consensus.

Therefore, we have attributed seven keys to each triangle or pyramid, differing from one another in double or quadruple proportion. From their consonance and mutual relation to one another, we can very easily conceive and perceive the symphonic composition of the internal man with the external man.

...we have depicted according to their natures; one of which is the pyramid of form or of the **soul**, the other is the pyramid of **material spirit**, which is elemental, coarse, and opaque or bodily, and consequently shrouded in darkness, corresponding to the body. We see, therefore, that the upper part of the pyramid, or the portion of its base adorned with **mind** and **intellect**, corresponds to the upper part of the spiritual pyramid (which is full of the **animal** <note>In this context, "animal" refers to the *anima* or soul—the spirit responsible for sensation and movement—not brute creatures.</note> and **rational spirit**) in a harmony of the <term>Diapason [an octave]</term>, which consists of a double proportion, namely as 1 to 2. For the mind is a unity, and the purer portion of the spirit. It brings with it a Crown <note>original: "Diadem." Likely referring to the *Kether* or the highest spiritual point.</note>, as has been demonstrated quite often. Hence it happens that they have a correspondence to one another, just as the low $\Gamma$ <note>The Greek letter Gamma, used in medieval music to denote the lowest note of the scale.</note> corresponds to the G above it.

But truly, as far as the mind immerses itself into matter—that is, when it mixes itself with the spiritual pyramid—to that extent both constitute a **unison**, which sounds an octave with the midpoint of each pyramid. Thus, each summit is related to each mixed midpoint in a double proportion, namely as 1 to 2, or like $\Gamma$ to g. Therefore, there is a corresponding **rational heaven** sounding in a double proportion in the chest, descending from the rational harmony to the vital harmony through the spiritual <term>Diapason [octave]</term> consonant, which contains within itself the <term>Diatessaron [a fourth]</term> and <term>Diapente [a fifth]</term>.

And this is the reason why the **Sun of the world** is so complete and perfect in its vital disposition, and the **human heart** in its own region is such an effective dispenser of life. Again, if the higher mixture of the formal and spiritual pyramids looks toward the lowest region, it does so by the power of a quadruple proportion, constituting a <term>Disdiapason [a double octave]</term>. For such is the proportion between **intellect** and **reason**, and similarly, such is the concordance between the **animal spirit** and **natural spirit**, between which are placed the **spirit of life** and the **imaginative faculty** of the soul.

The intellect of the formal pyramid, therefore, embraces the rational and animal spirits in a consensus of unison; and both, since they are of a fiery nature, are stored in the head or the highest region of the dark pyramid, where they sound this same harmony. For the **mind** acts upon the highest spirit to produce a unison, and the spirit undergoes the operations of the mind just as a vibrated musical string bears the action of the player; and the **head**, as the organ of both, forged from the black and bodily pyramid, receives within itself the effects of that action and passion, no differently than the body of a **lute** receives the sounds of a melody.

Therefore, the intellectual light sounds the **accent of reason** into the spirit as a medium, rendering it rational; and the spirit, moved by the action of light, spreads itself as a medium through the ventricles or organs of the brain as a receptacle. Thus, the rays of reason flow downward to produce other harmonies with the vital and natural faculties. Then, through the harmony of the octave, the **rational harmony** is joined with the **imagination** and the **spirit of life**. The voice of reason therefore vibrates the **string of life** and the imaginative spirit; its life-giving harmony, mixed with reason, later pours itself out and disperses through the entire **natural spirit** or the **elemental string**, resonating in the subtle elements with deep sounds and mixing the bodily or material octave with sharp and very sharp tones.

The human body is the receptacle of these modulations, a general organ and, as it were, a **musical instrument of human music**, in which the harmony of the world is contained, and from whose organic parts the proportional effects of that same harmony are drawn out.

252 **TREATISE I. SECTION I. BOOK XII.**

In the figure outlining the spiritual cube, we have described the proportional relationship of matter in both the world and the Microcosm <note>term: Microcosm. From the Greek 'mikros kosmos' or 'little world'; the Renaissance belief that the human being is a miniature reflection of the entire universe.</note>. The **material cube** in the description of the world is associated with the elements; for, on account of its weight and density, it tends downward. However, since the **formal cube** <note>term: Form/Formal. In this philosophical context, 'Form' refers to the soul or the shaping spiritual essence, as opposed to physical 'Matter'.</note> is of a contrary nature—tending upward due to its lightness and rising to the heights of the heavens—the middle portion of both the formal and material descriptions is recognized to share nearly the same geometric logic, since the square surface of one corresponds to the square of the other figure.

But indeed, we see that the summit, or the line of the material demonstration, is entirely contrary in position and site to the line of the formal description, insofar as that formal line tends downward. By these things it is clearly declared that the greatest force of **matter** dominates downward in the world and in man; but truly the greatest virtue of **form** is found upward, and is contiguous with the **shining source** <note>original: "fonti lucido," referring to God or the primordial light.</note>. Therefore, if these two figures—as they are described here—are joined to one another, they will demonstrate the exact composition of the world and of man out of matter and form.

Furthermore, it must be considered here in passing that the world, in its composition, exists more simply than man. For the world was made from a simple composition; but man is said to be forged from a "composite"—that is, he is made from the mundane composition itself. For this reason, man is more "shadowed" <note>This implies that humans are further removed from pure divine light because our physical makeup is a complex mixture of already-mixed elements.</note> by various mixtures in his composition than the world is. And it is for this reason that, just as the Philosophers called the world the **visible son of God**, so they handed down that **man is the son of the world**, being made immediately from the world in the same way the world was made by God. From the beginning, the world was divided into elements, distinct and balanced in a marvelous way; from the mixture of these elements—confused with one another and bound by a natural bond in harmonious peace—man was made.

We see, therefore, that in the joining of the formal cube with the material line, the square of one is united with the square of the other; and consequently, the formal line tending downward is joined with the material cube. By these things it is clearly declared that the smallest part of **form**—namely, its line—is joined with the greater dimension of **matter**; just as, conversely, the smallest portion of the spiritual figure is united with the greater dimension of light. Moreover, since the two middle parts have the same shape, they agree easily and produce life. And in this way, we have also explained the logic of the **pyramids of mundane composition** <note>Fludd frequently used a diagram of two overlapping pyramids—one of light descending and one of darkness ascending—to show how spirit and matter interact.</note> that we have so often cited.
