ON THE INTERNAL AND EXTERNAL HARMONY OF MAN 255

In the preceding sections, we discussed the nature of the ternary number <note>The number three, often representing the Trinity or the three spiritual realms.</note>, as demonstrated in the three pyramids; we also spoke of the nature of the quaternary <note>The number four, representing the material world and the four elements.</note> in a geometric manner by way of a line (whose root was two), and by means of the square and the cube. Here, however, girding ourselves more specifically for the matter at hand, we shall speak of the seven steps <note>The "septenary" or the seven notes of a musical scale.</note> of each region—both of the world and of man in relation to the world—and of their relationship to the **Diapason** <term>Diapason: An octave. In this philosophy, it represents the perfect horizontal harmony that links the highest spirit to the lowest matter.</term> consonance, which encompasses the power and property of the **Diapente** <note>A musical fifth.</note> and **Diatessaron** <note>A musical fourth.</note>, and consequently the whole of music. By this reasoning, we are taught that the semi-diameter of the peripheral fabric—of both the world and also of man—is compared to a musical system. In this system, three orders of keys are placed alternately, by which the consonance of every melody is measured, and any musical proportion is drawn out.

Furthermore, regarding the fact that at the beginning and summit of the upper septenary <note>The highest group of seven levels in the cosmic hierarchy.</note> we represented **God the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit** within the material mass, it must be understood that we take the properties of the Deity in this place not as they are accepted in themselves and apart from all hidden matter, but insofar as they, looking down from the supersubstantial throne, have unanimously penetrated into the deformed hyle <note>original: "hylen". A term for the primordial, unformed matter of the universe.</note> with their sacrosanct gaze, so that by their presence in the dark abyss, all things were made from nothing. Thus, we say that God is found in the supreme region of the spirit, just as unity is said to return into itself in the number ten, as we shall declare more at length below.

Here, therefore, in the aforementioned demonstration, we have the three regions of the **Macrocosm** <note>The "Great World" or the entire universe.</note> corresponding to the three regions of the **Microcosm** <note>The "Little World" or the human being.</note>. Of these, the lowest region—since it is the coarsest, slowest, heaviest, and most base of all—requires seven notes for its music that are slower, weightier, and deeper: **Γ. A. B. C. D. E. F.**

*   **Γ** <note>Gamma, the lowest note in the medieval musical scale.</note> in the Macrocosm corresponds to the **Earth**, which is the base or foundation of all things; in the Microcosm, it corresponds to the stercoreal <note>Relating to dung or excrement.</note> **feces of the intestines** gathered above the center of the Microcosm.
*   **A.** refers in the Macrocosm to the **salt water** of the sea; in the Microcosm, however, it refers to the **salt water of urine**.
*   **B.** in the Macrocosm refers to the **fresh waters** of rivers and springs descending from the mountains of the earth and flowing into the sea; in the Microcosm, it alludes to the **chylous or pituitous** <note>Relating to chyle (digestive fluid) or phlegm.</note> **liquid of the stomach** flowing downward from that organ, as if from the more elevated and mountainous part of this region, toward the bladder.
*   **C.** in the Macrocosm refers to the **lowest region of the air**, where, because of the reflections and influences of the celestial bodies, the most temperate moisture of life is found, nourishing both plants and animals; in the Microcosm, it refers to the **mass of blood** springing from the lowest region of the liver, as if from its own source through its little streams.
*   **D.** in the Macrocosm is compared to the **middle region of the air**, subject to clouds and meteors; in the Microcosm, it refers to the **middle region of the liver**, through which (because the zone of the spleen passes through it) many alterations proceed, namely flatulent vapors, sticky obstructions, and infinite hindrances of this kind, or "coarse meteors," caused by the cold and dry winds arising from the splenic region of the Microcosmic north.
*   **E.** in the Macrocosm we have referred to the **highest region of the air**, which is nearest to fire; in the Microcosm, however, it refers to the **deep cavity of the liver** placed next to the gallbladder.
*   **F.** finally, in the Macrocosm we have likened to the **element of fire**; but in the Microcosm, to the **gallbladder**.

And so in the elementary region, both Macrocosmic and Microcosmic, we find those keys attributed in a consistent manner to each sphere, which pertain to the base or fundamental harmony of both worlds. Furthermore, with these, the acute <note>high-pitched</note> keys of the middle or ethereal region, and likewise those very high-pitched and excellent keys of the supreme heaven, agree perfectly in the symphony of the melody. Hence it is that:

*   **g.** in the Macrocosm looks to the **Moon**, and in the Microcosm to the **superfluous moisture of the lungs**, which the Moon governs.
*   **a.** refers to **Mercury** in the Macrocosm, and in the Microcosm to the **faculty of speech** originating from the lungs.
*   **b.** in the Macrocosm is compared to **Venus**, and in the Microcosm to the **moist air inspired and expired**, by which life is nourished.

And so that we may at last reach the supreme region of both worlds, in which the most excellent and loudest sounding keys are found, it must be known that **gg.** <margin>In man this corresponds to the sphere of the Will, which we compared above to the "First Mover" <note>The "Primum Mobile," the outermost moving sphere of the universe in traditional astronomy.</note> of the world.</margin> And since man speaks according to his will, this sphere is adapted to the tongue. All these spiritual keys are found in the human head: for God, by speaking the Word, breathed the Word, the Spirit of life, the mind, the intellect, and reason (not lacking free will) into the face or nostrils of the external man. Thus the man made of clay, by the power of this God-like breath, became a living animal, imbued with will, reason, intellect, mind, the divine Spirit, and the very character of the Word. From this, we think it is not foolishly said that man was created in the image of the Creator, insofar as he retains within himself these divine characters of the Craftsman, and these admirable and ineffable impressions of the most Holy Trinity. Hence, as has been said, the internal man is called the "Temple of God," both by the deeper Philosophers and by God Himself. 

But now that the steps of the tripartite system of both worlds have been well considered, we believe we must arrive at the proportions and consonances of harmony. We see in the worldly system depicted earlier that there are three orders of keys, one placed alternately above the other, and that any series of the said keys corresponds to the orders placed below them as they ascend upward. Thus we find that **Γ** <note>The Greek letter Gamma, used here as the lowest note of the scale.</note> of the lowest series corresponds to **g** of the middle order in a double proportion <note>A 2:1 ratio, which creates the musical interval of an octave.</note>; and again **g** to **gg** in a double proportion. So also **A** is referred to **a** in the same proportion, and **a** to **aa** of the highest region. Such is also the ratio between **B** and **b**, and similarly between **b** and **bb**; for a letter always corresponds to the next similar letter in a double proportion. Furthermore, the interior and less perfect proportions are drawn out by this path: namely, the <term>Sesquialtera</term> <note>A 3:2 ratio, forming a musical fifth.</note> between **Γ** and **D**, between **A** and **E**, between **B** and **E**, between **C** and **g**, and between **g** and **d**, and between **a** and **e**, and so on for the others ascending upward. So also they agree in the <term>Sesquitertia</term> <note>A 4:3 ratio, forming a musical fourth.</note> proportion: **Γ** with **B**, and **A** with **C**, and **B** with **D**, and **C** with **E**, and **D** with **F**, and **E** with **g**, and **F** with **a**, and **g** with **b**, and **a** with **c**, and **b** with **d**, and so on for the rest. Finally, the **Sun** regards the sphere of equality in the elementary region—namely, the region of moisture. For it is just that the sphere of equality of the middle heaven should correspond to its likeness in the elementary heaven. For just as the Sun’s sphere is positioned at the middle aspect between spirit and light, so also the middle part of the lowest region of air (which in the *Macrocosmic Treatise* we called the "spurious sphere of equality") is the place in which the rays of the element of fire and the vapors of the earth meet equally. The middle region of the air sounds an **Octave** <note>original: "Diapason"</note> with **Mars**, and does so unhappily and with a contrary quality. Whence it happens that, although this planet in the heavens and in its own nature is just as good as the rest, with respect to lower things it is called an ill-omened planet and a misfortune to the human race. And from this it follows that great disturbances are said by astrologers to be excited in this region—namely thunder, lightning, flashes, and other such things terrifying to men. To this planet, however, the element of water responds in a double proportion, simply by dividing the lowest region of the world into four elements, just as **Jupiter** responds to the air, as was said in our *Macrocosmic Harmony*. But these two explanations tend toward the same thing. For Jupiter, to whom **e.** is attributed, corresponds to the upper portion of the air, which is hot and moist, and favorable to life. Astrologers confirm that such is the nature of Jupiter; wherefore it is called a lucky star and most friendly to human nature, and for this reason is called the **Greater Fortune** <note>original: "Fortunium majus"</note>, just as **Venus** is called the **Lesser Fortune** <note>original: "Fortunium minus"</note>. Finally, **Saturn**, to whom **f.** is attributed, insofar as its Octave ends in fire, is considered an ill-omened star by those inhabiting the lowest spaces of the world, though in itself it is as good as the others. For although its dryness agrees with the earth—of which **Γ** <note>The Greek letter Gamma, referring here to the lowest note of the musical scale</note> is kin to **f.** and to which **g.** is contiguous—it does not, however, agree with the dryness of fire, insofar as it is joined with a lethal cold, which is entirely opposed to fiery heat. 

But now at last we have reached the highest series of keys, which measures the highest region of the world; where the sphere of the **will** **gg.** is found in an **Octave** <note>original: "Diapason"</note> with the nature of the **supersubstantial essence** <note>God or the Divine Source</note> marked **ggg.**, since God does all things according to His will in the heavens and on earth. Those things which lie beneath this sphere are moved by it, as if by a **Prime Mover** <note>original: "primo mobili"; the outermost sphere of the heavens that provides motion to all others</note>. For the lower bodies are said to be moved involuntarily by this sphere in no other way than the world is carried around by its power in a "rapt" <note>swift or seized</note> motion. For bodies naturally desire to be at rest; therefore the Sun and other planets are said to move according to the motion of the Prime Mover. 

We see, therefore, how miraculously the spheres of both worlds—namely the **Lesser** <note>Man</note> and the **Greater** <note>The Universe</note>—consonate with one another; so that the keys of the higher heaven with the keys of the middle, and the keys of the middle with the keys of the lowest, constitute symphonic melodies together. Thus water with earth denotes the act of the will and the subject moved by involuntary motion for the constitution of the **Moon**. The **Moon** and water denote the changeability of the will in humans; the **Earth**, which is the basis and foundation of everything, denotes the stability of the will of God. Water also, by its fluid nature, denotes the changeable nature of **Mercury**, and their relationship joins these together in an Octave with the sphere of reason. From this comes the variety of human reason, the multitude of opinions and sects; and hence Mercury is said to preside over wit, science, arts, and music. And so it also happens that, just as the senses are referred to the element of fire, so the **imagination**, the focus of reason, is referred to water. Also, fresh water and the lowest part of the air are related to **Venus**, and Venus to the **intellect**, which is fiery love. These three agree, therefore, in the act and passion of love. The Air, the Sun, and the **Mind** also denote the mind, soul, and spirit, which are joined together in the best harmony. We could present infinite other reasons for this harmony here, but since the secret of Music is not open to everyone, and it would perhaps be more tedious than pleasant for the reader to unravel or explain them in this place, I shall now pass over them in silence.

260 TREATISE I. SECTION I. BOOK XII.

In the preceding demonstration, we have explained the numerical ratio of the entire fabric of the world, which we declared above to be derived from the harmony of the divine essence. For from simple unity—the property of the <term>super-substantial</term> <note>original: "supersubstantialis"; referring to a divine essence that exists beyond the category of physical substance</note> first essence—the <term>dyad</term> <note>original: "dualitas"; the number two</note> flowed forth. This is nothing other than unity repeated twice, or a <term>monad</term> <note>original: "monas"; the number one as a metaphysical principle</note> from a monad or with a monad; that is, the most fitting connection of two unities of the same essence, producing the number two. By the movement of this back toward unity, three unities of the same super-substantial and uncreated nature are joined together, which produce the first number adorned with the fulfillment of perfection; in which unity is the beginning, unity the middle, and unity the end. Therefore, the whole is nothing other than unity alone in trinity, and trinity in unity. 

The quantity of this most complete number <note>The number 3</note>, when multiplied by itself, produces the final odd number among the simple and uncompounded numbers—the <term>digits</term>—namely 9. Through the multiplication of this number in its root, those compounded numbers are produced, according to whose order the three types of compositions in the three regions of the world are made. For the number 27 is the most complete number of worldly compositions <note>In Pythagorean thought, 27 is the first odd cube ($3 \times 3 \times 3$), representing the physical world</note>. Its first set of nine denotes the first nine "joints" of numbers: 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70, 80, 90. The second set of nine denotes the hundreds, and the third set denotes the thousands. From the first set, the first heaven was produced; from the second, the second heaven; and from the third, the third and lowest heaven. 

Therefore, the first "joints" of the tens correspond to the roots concurring in the creation of the world; the second set of hundreds corresponds to the squares; and the third set of thousands corresponds to the cubes. This is because such is the proportion between the thinness of the highest heaven and the middle, or between the density of the lowest heaven and the middle. Thus, the higher joints of the tens are to be compared to lines, the middle ones to surfaces, and the lowest—expressing the thousands—to bodies. Thus 10, or the number ten, is the root of the square 100, and of the cube 1000. So also 20 is the root of the square 200 <note>The author's math here follows a specific symbolic logic where 20 multiplied by the primary root of 10 creates the "cube" of 2000</note>, which when led into the first root (namely 10), produces 2000. Similarly, the root 30 will produce 300 for the square, and from the first root of 10, 3000 for the cube; and so it goes for the rest. 

Therefore, the Artificer Unity, joining itself with a <term>cipher</term> <note>original: "cyphra"; the number zero</note> or ciphers—that is, looking out beyond the margins of simple numbers and connecting itself with unformed matter so that it might exist—enters into the limits of compounded numbers. In this way, every distinct property of the one divine essence, joining itself with unformed matter, makes it exist out of nothing. It is from this that the cipher, signifying nothing in and of itself, is most aptly compared to unformed matter as if by its very essence. But if unity, duality, or trinity is placed before the cipher, then it makes that cipher significant out of nothing. For example, 0 signifies no more than 00, nor does 00 signify more than 000; all these joined together signify nothing. But truly, 1 before 0 signifies the number ten; 2 before 0 signifies twenty; 3 thirty; thus 10, 20, 30, etc. So also, if 1 is placed before 00, it will denote the number one hundred, and so on. 

This very same ratio is found in the creation of the world. For God the Father, as Unity, doubling Himself as it were and joining with matter—as if with nothingness, or <term>primordial matter</term> <note>original: "hyla"; from the Greek 'hyle'</note>, or a cipher—produced the first degree of simple composition. Then the Son, or Duality, presenting Himself to the second unformed sphere of the higher region, led the second degree of creatures into existence. And finally, the Holy Spirit, or the Triple property, by mixing Himself with matter, brought the third degree into the light. And thus the three circles of the first hierarchy of Angels—namely the Seraphim, Cherubim, and Thrones—were created and established. By that logic, through the multiplication of 3 by itself, the remaining triple-number proportions are produced in the radical and simpler region of composition. Similarly, the first person of the Deity, tripling Himself—that is, appearing the first time in His unique essence, a second time in the simple composition of things, and a third time in the middle constitution of the world—now precedes two ciphers, signifying by this very act that in the middle...

This is indeed that unique harmony by which God the Creator Himself immersed Himself into the multitude of matter.

### CHAPTER V.

### On the harmony of the soul through the entire system of both the minor and major worlds.

Since the intellectual soul, in descending from the throne of the Creator into man, penetrates through the entire <term>semidiameter</term> <note>The radius; the path from the center of the universe to its edge</note> of the world before it enters the human body, it follows that it participates in the harmony of every creature which it encounters on its downward journey. Hence, it is that the soul finds as many properties within itself as are found in the world (counting between the seat of God and the earth, which is "His footstool"). And yet all these properties exist as nothing other than the soul itself. In this respect, the soul is compared to the Deity: namely, just as the essence of the Deity is one, but the persons are many, in the same way, the properties of the soul are diverse, but its essence is one. Thus, sense is indeed one in the soul—and indeed is the soul itself—which, although it is not a body, is called "corporeal"; and although it is only one, it is varied and named differently because of its various exercises. It is called the soul, sense, imagination, intellect, intelligence, or mind; yet all these in the soul are nothing other than the soul itself. These are different properties among themselves because of various exercises, but there is one essence of reason and one soul; the properties are indeed diverse, but the essence is one. According to their exercises they are many, but according to their essence they are one in the soul, and indeed the soul itself is that essence. And just as this visible world is ordered by a certain fivefold distinction—namely, earth, water, air, ether (or the firmament), and the supreme heaven itself, which they call the <term>Empyrean</term> <note>The highest part of heaven, thought in ancient cosmology to be composed of pure fire or light</note>—so in the soul of the body traveling through the world, five progressions toward wisdom are counted: namely, sense, imagination, reason, intellect, and intelligence. By these five progressions, I say, rationality is exercised toward wisdom (about which we will speak more broadly below). And likewise, by four affections toward charity, the soul proceeds into itself as if by nine progressions; these progressions [we shall name] after the names and orders of the Angels, in the simpler...

From this, therefore, it is evident that the soul, made in the likeness of all wisdom, carries within itself the likeness of all things. For this reason, it is defined by the philosophers as the "likeness of every thing," since it possesses within itself the powers by which it apprehends and investigates all things and exists as a likeness to all, while remaining one. For since all things are made from the four elements, the soul itself is found to be like the earth through sense, like water through imagination, like air through reason, and like fire and the firmament through understanding, and like the <term>Heaven of Heavens</term> <note>original: "cœloque cœlorum"; the highest spiritual realm.</note> through intelligence. It is like stones through its essence, like trees through its life, like animals through its sense and imagination, like humans through its reason, like Angels through its understanding, and like God through its intelligence. And just as God is capable and a partaker of all things, so likewise is the soul.

But, to return to our number nine, under which we have declared the properties of the soul to be related to the nine spheres of the intelligences of the higher heaven, it should be noted with diligent observation that there are nine moderate properties or virtues of the soul which correspond to the nine spheres of the middle region of the world. For the <term>Primum Mobile</term> <note>The "First Mover," the outermost sphere of the classical universe.</note> is related to the **will**, for reasons stated in the explanation of the third demonstration. To the **Starry Heaven** is related the execution or action of the will. To **Saturn**, the receptive, restrictive, and coagulative power of the soul. To **Jupiter**, its natural faculty. To **Mercury**, the fantastic power <note>The faculty of creating mental images or "phantasms."</note> and talent. Finally, to the **Moon**, the property of growing and decreasing, and consequently the property of vegetation.

The harmony, therefore, between the properties of the soul of the supreme heaven and those of the middle is as follows: The **Love of God** has a relation to the **Will**, or the "first mover" of the sensible man; **intelligence** to the **action of the will**; **understanding** to the fixed, stable, and prudent disposition of **Saturn**; **love of neighbor** to the love of **Jupiter**, and his fatherly care concerning life and the vital nature of living things; **reason** to the irascibility of **Mars**, since reason is occupied either with the irascibility proper to Mars or the concupiscence attributed to **Venus**; **hatred of self** is related to the **Sun**, for he who hates himself in respect to this world shall obtain eternal life; **hatred of the world** to **Venus**, since concupiscence and the heat of the love of God makes one despise the world; the **imaginative power** is attributed to the fantastic disposition of **Mercury**; while **Sense** looks toward the **Moon** and the **earth**, for the Moon is like the base and is the "earth" of the middle heaven, and is most aptly related to sense, insofar as it looks toward fluid things with solidity.

There is also a relation of this harmony between the heavenly and elementary properties of the soul, which is as follows: The nine spheres of the lowest region of the world are these: **Fire**, the **upper region of air**, the **middle region of air**, the **lowest region of air**, **fresh water**, **salt water**, the **vegetative sphere of the earth**, the **mineral sphere of the earth**, and finally its **central sphere**, where, as some maintain, the pure element of earth is found. The **Will**, therefore, is related to **fire**; **action** to the **upper region of air**, as the place where the agent acts upon its subject; the **receptive power** of the soul is seen in the **middle region of air**, where hail and snow are generated by the coagulating quality of Saturn; the **natural power** proper to Jupiter is in the **lowest air**, in which the living creatures of every species dwell; the **irascible** in **fresh water**, in which Mars makes his "Diapason" <note>A musical interval of an octave, here used to mean a full range of effects.</note>, bringing forth thunder, other fiery meteors, and whirlwinds; the **solar and vital power** in **salt water**, since salt is the author of life, lying hidden in the center of every living thing; furthermore...

Now at last, before we arrive at the use or practice of the harmony of the simple soul by itself, and then its harmony with the spirit, and finally the symphonic melody of all three <note>The "three" refers to the Soul, Spirit, and Body, which the author treats as a musical triad.</note> among themselves, it is necessary that we recognize the differences by which they are distinguished from one another. Wherefore, as it seems to us, when accepted in such a way, it is not poorly defined by some as *an incorporeal thing adorned with all the beauty of light, made in the likeness of the Holy Trinity, and equated to eternal glory.* Or: *The soul is an incorporeal thing bounded within all the members, colored by no color, made like the most high God, and the most beautiful of all things.* Now truly it must be known what the spirit itself is, which is joined with the soul, the **tincture of life** <note>original: "tinctura vitæ"; an alchemical term referring to the vitalizing essence that "colors" or gives life to the physical body.</note>, the form, and the purest and simplest essence of light. The <term>Spirit</term> <note>From the Latin *spiritus*, meaning "breath" or "wind."</note>, however, is understood as a spiritual nature; namely, that which breathes in the body is called the spirit. Furthermore, the soul and the spirit seem to be the same thing within the body, even though "soul" denotes something different than "spirit." Thus, the soul acts and the spirit is acted upon, and both are so essentially joined to one another according to the laws of nature that no one, except God alone, is able to divide these two from each other.

This is exactly what the Apostle <note>Referring to St. Paul in the book of Hebrews 4:12.</note> seems to suggest with these words: *The word of God is living, and effective, and more piercing than any two-edged sword, reaching even to the division of the soul and the spirit.* By this, he seems to argue that it is impossible for any division to occur between the soul and the spirit except by the word of God alone. Indeed, I can testify to this myself, having been taught by experience in the **anatomy of a certain creature**; there, I saw a virginal and clear spirit, adorned on every side by the rays of the soul, which human ingenuity did not know how to divide from one another.

Therefore, although they differ from each other like matter and form, or the actor and the sufferer, or air and fire, nevertheless—because they were so ordered by nature or created by the Founder—they cannot be otherwise until those indissoluble bonds are dissolved by Him alone who tied the knot. Hence, the spirit is said to be of the same essence as the soul; and it appears that "light" and "spirit" constitute this same thing which we call the <term>Soul</term> <note>Latin: *Anima*.</note>. They are, I say, the same in essence, but they differ in their properties no less than the Father in the Trinity differs from the Holy Spirit, even though both are the same in their "supersubstantial" essence. For one and the same spirit is called "spirit" in relation to itself, but "soul" in relation to the body.

Furthermore, it is called **Spirit** insofar as it is a rational substance endowed with reason, but **Soul** insofar as it pertains to the life of the body. This is why we find in the Scriptures: *He who loses his soul shall save it*, that is, whoever—for the sake of God—willingly despises this life (which currently consists of the temporary, mortal vivification of the body) will receive in the future that same life of the mortal body and soul as eternal and immortal. From this, it is clear that "soul" in its proper naming is sometimes understood as "life" or the "vital faculty."

And yet, sometimes the meaning of "soul" extends more broadly, and is taken for the union of the **mind**, the **rational spirit**, and the **spark of life** with the intermediate spirit, its vehicle; in that case, we call it by the more suitable word <term>Mind</term> <note>Latin: *Animus*. While *Anima* is the life-force, *Animus* is the seat of intellect and will.</note>, which we take to mean the entire "internal man." Thus, *animus* is used in the Holy Scriptures to mean the **heart**. For just as the heart is the center and the interior part of the body, so also the soul—or rather the mind—is the nucleus of the invisible and internal man. For the mind, illuminated by divine wisdom, looks back toward its beginning and knows itself. We read almost everywhere in sacred writings that the "soul," when accepted as the life of a creature, is attributed not only to humans but also to beasts. But sometimes the word "soul"—indeed, most often by Philosophers and even Theologians—is used for the internal man or the *animus*, and we also have sometimes used this word for the internal man. But to return to our subject: the human soul, which exists both in the body and outside the body, can equally be called both soul and spirit. ### CHAPTER II.

### On the Mind and Reason, and once again regarding the Soul and Spirit.

The **Mind** <note>original: *Mens*</note>, according to some, is named after *Mene*. *Mene* <note>original: *Mene*; the Greek word for the Moon, *Mēnē*.</note> in Greek is the name for the Moon or the Light. And truly, just as the Moon waxes and wanes, and changes through various successions, yet restores itself to what it was with a certain perfect novelty; so the mind now raises its head to the highest things, now falls into the lowest; now returning to itself, it refutes the false with the true. At one moment it is turned toward governing bodily things, and at another it clings to eternal reasons or contemplations, according to that saying of **Hermes Trismegistus** <note>original: *Mercur. Trismeg.* An ancient, legendary Egyptian philosopher to whom many mystical and scientific texts were attributed.</note>: *Whoever are supported by this nature of God are, by the comparison of their works, held as immortals among mortals; they embrace all things in their intelligence—those on the earth, those in the sea, and if there is anything beyond these above the heavens—and they raise themselves so high that they may even behold the Good itself.* 

**Reason** itself is the "gaze" of this divine essence, by which it discerns good from evil, chooses virtues, and loves the truth. For by this guidance, the mind is capable of containing the universe and is marked with the likeness of all things; indeed, it is said to be all things by a certain nature, power, and natural dignity. Therefore, it grasps the invisible causes of things through the intelligence, and collects the visible forms of actual things through the passions of the senses. It is either inclined toward sensible things through the senses, or it ascends to the invisible through the intelligence; it draws the likenesses of things to itself, knows the present, understands the absent, inquires into the unknown, and occupies itself with what it has discovered. 

O marvelous operation of divine nature! O ineffable arrangement of the divine ray! Since the mind is said to be "all things," all things are subjected to it and offer it a kind of obedience. What then is this most powerful essence? Is it nature, or is it God himself? It is indeed **Nature** itself, producing all things in the world by the power of the **Word** <note>original: *Verbum*; referring to the Logos or the creative command of God.</note> implanted within it, and providing them with life. It is likewise **God** himself, since it is an uncreated spirit and a ray of the uncreated essence, no less indivisible from the Creator than light or a sunbeam is from the Sun. It is therefore "all in all," from which all things were made, and into which all things must return, as if from a multitude back to unity. This divine mind is that rational and intellectual light by which we reason...

Similarly, the **spirit** itself (which we declared above is a certain power of the soul lower than the mind, where the likenesses of physical things are expressed) has its own proper sight. This spirit is not a body, but is *like* a body. Therefore, the things seen by the spirit are not physical bodies, but are likenesses of bodies. For the spirit is something intermediate between "non-body" (or light) and a body compacted from the elements. Thus, it cannot be seen as a body, but almost as a body, or rather as the image or likeness of a body. For instance, the face of a man is known to us externally, and it holds its own image in our memory—an image that is indeed incorporeal, but similar to a body. Likewise, the wonderful beauty of this world is present to us externally, and it holds its own image in our memory, also incorporeal but similar to a body, to which we return whenever we think of it with our eyes closed. From these things it is gathered that, just as a physical body is perceived in a specific place by the physical eyes through the bodily senses, so too is the likeness of a body perceived in the memory by the "eyes" of the spirit through the sharpness of the soul. For there is a certain intensity of pleasure involved in joining the body that is seen with the act of vision; and this same intensity of pleasure exists in joining the image of a body (which is in the memory) with the vision of thought. I could uncover many hidden things in this place regarding this subject, were it not that necessity calls me away to other more common matters. For it seems to me that we have deviated too far from our goal of the **harmony of the soul**. Therefore, I shall now turn the thread of my discourse back to that subject.

Yet there can be a difference between spirit and soul, because every soul is spirit, but not every spirit is soul. For as was said in the preceding parts, spirit is not "soul" unless it is prepared for this office by a proper portion of the light of each thing. Furthermore, regarding the difference between soul and spirit, we see that the property of the lower spirit is one thing, that of the middle another, and that of the higher another. And yet it is one and the same spirit, but named in different ways according to the greater or lesser portion of light predominating in it. In this same way, all light is only one, and yet one is fire, another the Sun, another the Moon, another Saturn, another Jupiter, etc., while nevertheless all these are the same light, contracted within different bodies, some denser and some thinner. 

From these things, therefore, we see what kind of harmony the soul produces from the number five <note>original: *quinario*; the "quinary" number, representing the five faculties or senses</note>, by which the soul, existing in the human body by the way of a concordant symphony, raises itself from the deepest abyss of the multitude to the summit of unity. the substance in these three consists full and perfect, namely, in **rationality**, **concupiscibility** <term>the faculty of desire or longing</term>, and **irascibility** <term>the faculty of spirit, courage, or anger</term>, as if in its own kind of trinity: And this entire trinity is a certain unity of the soul, and the soul itself. In this, however, it differs from God, because God is all His own attributes, whereas the soul is only some of its own; for these are natural things and all are the soul itself. Therefore, the entire essence of the mind is contained in these powers, yet it is not divided into parts, since it is simple and indivisible; if indeed it is sometimes said to have "parts," this should be understood by way of a likeness <note>original: *ratione similitudinis*; meaning a metaphor or analogy</note> rather than the truth of its composition. For the soul is a simple substance; and reason is neither something else nor something less in the substance than the soul; but one and the same substance receives different names according to its different powers.

Through the first power, namely, **rationality**, the soul is capable of being illuminated to know something: specifically below itself, above itself, and beside itself, as was said before. Indeed, it knows God above itself, the Angel beside itself, and whatever is contained within the circuit of the heavens below itself. Through **concupiscibility**, it is capable of desiring and loving something; and through **irascibility**, it is capable of fleeing something and pursuing it with hatred. From this it is gathered that every sense arises from rationality, and every "affect" <note>an "affect" refers to an emotion or a movement of the soul's will</note> arises from the other two. We call **Reason** the gaze of the soul by which it contemplates the truth through itself; but we call **Reasoning** the inquiry or searching of the reason. Therefore, the former (reason) is needed for seeing, while the latter (reasoning) is needed for inquiring.

Moreover, the **affect** which arises from the other two powers of the soul is known to be fourfold: namely, from concupiscibility come **joy** and **hope**, for we either already rejoice in that which we love, or we hope to rejoice; and from irascibility arise **grief** and **fear**; for we already grieve over that which we hate, or we fear we must grieve. These four affects of the soul are, as it were, certain principles and the common material of all vices and virtues. And, since virtue is a "habit of a well-composed mind," therefore the affects of the mind must be composed, established, and ordered toward that which they ought, and in the manner they ought, so that they can produce virtues; otherwise, they will easily slide into vices. 

Therefore, when love and hatred are established prudently, modestly, strongly, and justly, they rise up into virtues: specifically into **prudence, temperance, fortitude, and justice**, which are as the origin and hinges of all virtues, and all these are established effectively and virtuously in the soul. Through hatred of the world and of the self, the soul profits in the love of God and neighbor; through contempt for temporal and inferior things, it grows in the desire for eternal and superior things. 

From this, therefore, it is evidently clear that reason does not become immune from error unless it is illuminated through the mind. Whence it happens that its good affects, produced by the illumination of the mind, are called **virtues**, but the evil ones, proceeding from a defect of illumination, are called **vices**. For the mind is always illuminated by God, yet it does not always illuminate <note>The author suggests God's light is constant, but the human mind may fail to pass that light down to the lower faculties</note>. For the "First Light" in God surpasses all understanding: wherefore it cannot be called an "intelligible light" <term>light that can be grasped by the intellect</term>; but that light, when it is poured in by an immediate radiation from God, is called **intelligible**, because it can be understood. 

Then, when it joins with reason by distilling through the mind, it becomes **rational**, and can not only be understood but also thought about. Afterward, when it is poured through the reason into the "idol" of the soul—where the phantasy or imagination operates—it is made not only thinkable and rational, but also **imaginable**, though not yet corporeal. When, however, it migrates from there into the "ethereal vehicle" of the soul, then for the first time it is made **corporeal**, though not yet manifestly sensible, until it passes into the elementary body (whether the simple airy body or the composite one), in which it becomes light manifestly visible to the eye.

## CHAPTER V.
### Concerning the mutual harmony of the body and the soul.

Wonderful is the love and partnership of the flesh and the soul—that is, the spirit of life and the mud of the earth <note>original: *limi terræ*; a reference to the biblical creation of man from dust</note>—since the whole human being is said to be forged from these joined together. For thus it is written: *God made man from the mud of the earth, and breathed into his face the breath of life,* giving him sense and intellect; so that through **sense** he might bring life to the clay associated with him, and through **intellect** he might rule it. Similarly, through the intellect he might enter within to contemplate the wisdom of God, while through the senses he might observe the works of His wisdom without. God illuminated the intellect within, but decorated the senses without, so that the whole human being might find restoration in both: within for happiness, and without for delight.

But because external goods cannot long endure, man was commanded to return from exterior things to the interior, and to ascend from interior things to the superior; namely, from **sense** to **imagination**, from imagination to **reason**, from reason to **intellect**, and from that to the **mind** or **intelligence**, and so to God. It was a marvelous and unspeakable thing—indeed, full of miracle—that things so diverse, divided, and contrary in nature as the body and the soul could be joined to one another. No less admirable was it that God contracted Himself into our mud, so that God and mud might be coupled to each other; such great sublimity and such great vileness; for nothing is more sublime than God, and nothing viler than mud. 

The first union was wonderful <note>The creation of man</note>, the second was wonderful <note>The Incarnation, or the indwelling of God in man</note>, and no less wonderful will be the third, when the same man, Angel, and God shall be one spirit. For a man is good by the same "Good" by which an Angel is good, and by that same Good both are blessed—provided they both desire that same thing with the same will and the same spirit. And if God was able to join the disparate natures of the flesh and the soul into one federation and friendship, it will by no means be impossible for Him to exalt the rational spirit (which was humbled even to the partnership of an earthly body) to the company of the blessed spirits who persist in their purity, and to raise it to a participation in His glory with that same body now glorified. For the Most High created man for this purpose out of **charity** <term>divine, selfless love</term> alone, and by no necessity, so that He might make him a partaker of His own beatitude. 

Therefore, if there is such great joy and gladness in this temporal life, which consists of the presence of the spirit in that corruptible body, how much gladness and how much joy will there be in the eternal life, which consists of the immediate existence of the Deity within the rational spirit? Let the body therefore be subject to the soul, and the soul to God, and it shall be "one spirit" with Him, provided the spirit remains in humility and acknowledges the grace of its Creator, through which it is to be glorified and exalted. 

Man, then, consists of flesh and soul, and each has its own "good" in which it rejoices and exults. The Good of the soul is God, with the flowing sweetness of His presence. The Good of the flesh is the world, with its abundance of delights. But the world is exterior, while God is interior—than whom nothing is more inward, and nothing more present. He is more interior than every thing, because all things are in Him; and He is more exterior than every thing, because He Himself is above all things. Therefore, ascending from this world to God, and striving upward as if from the bottom, we must pass beyond our very selves. For to ascend to God is to enter into oneself, and not only to enter oneself, but in an unspeakable way to pass through one's own center. 

Hence **Mercurius Trismegistus** <note>The legendary Hellenistic figure Hermes Trismegistus, associated with ancient wisdom</note> says: *He who, passing inward and penetrating within, transcends himself, he truly ascends to God.* Indeed, so that this may happen, [one must be] distracted from this world...

...let us gather our heart from distractions and recall it to internal joys. And if we cannot always keep our heart fixed upon these, let us at least restrain it from illicit and vain thoughts, so that we may at last be able to fix it upon the light of divine contemplation. For this is the rest of our heart: when it is fixed through desire in the love of God. This is the life of our heart: when it contemplates its God and is sweetly refreshed in that very contemplation. It is always sweet for the purpose of considering, loving, and praising; for nothing seems more excellent for a blessed life than—as if the carnal senses were closed and one were outside the flesh and the world—to turn one’s entire affection inward, and, having estranged one’s affection from mortal desires, to speak only to oneself and to God. 

Since, therefore, the soul is incorporeal, it governs the body through a subtler nature of body—that is, through fire and air (which are the more excellent bodies in this world, and therefore more familiar to the spirit). These former elements [fire and air] receive the commands of the vivifying soul because they are closer in nature to the incorporeal than are moisture and earth; thus, the entire mass [of the body] is governed through their immediate service. For neither of these two [earth and water] has sense within the body, nor is there any spontaneous movement of the body within the soul. Fire and air, because they are light, move the earth and water, which are heavy. 

Wherefore we see that bodies move not at all after the departure of the soul, because the fire and air—which are held within the earthy and moist body through the presence of the soul so that a tempering of all things may occur—escape to the higher realms and free themselves after that same soul departs. 

Regarding the composition of the body, it must be understood that the body consists of functional <term>original: *officialibus*; members that perform a specific office or duty</term> members; these functional members consist of similar parts <note>likely referring to tissues like muscle or bone</term>, and those similar parts likewise consist of humors, the humors from food, and the food from the elements. Whence we see that the soul is none of these things, but rather it acts within them as if in instruments <note>original: *organis*; implies both biological organs and musical instruments</note> naturally destined for its use. Through these, it provides for the body and for this life, by which man was made into a living soul. 

If, therefore, those parts are tempered and ordered, they are fit for vivification, and the soul never departs; but if they become distempered and confused, the soul departs against its will, drawing all things with it: namely, sense, imagination, reason, intellect and intelligence, the capacity for desire, and the capacity for anger. According to its merits, the soul is then affected by these toward either delight or pain. 

And so, the body—which was previously whole, like a tempered and disposed instrument <note>original: *organum*</note> intended to sound a melody and harmonize at a touch—now lies, on the contrary, broken and mutilated. The soul, however, while the parts of the elements return to their own homeland, has nowhere to exercise its powers; it rests only from those movements by which it moved the body through time and space. For although the instrument <note>original: *organum*</note> may perish, the melody <note>original: *melos*</note> does not perish, nor does that which moved the instrument. 

From these things, then, as if with open eyes, we can behold that admirable harmony by which those two extremes—namely the most precious [soul] and the most base [body]—are chained together and harmonize with one another. We see that the intermediate spirit of the world, the vehicle of the soul, is the bond holding them in concordant peace and symphony. We see that God is the blower <note>original: *sufflator*; like one who pumps bellows for an organ</note> of human music, or the plucker of the monochord's string <note>original: *chordæ monochordii pulsator*</note>, or the internal principle, producing from the center (as if of the whole) the movements of harmony and the effects of life in the Microcosm <note>The "Little World," i.e., the human being as a reflection of the universe</note>. 

The string, through its vibration, disperses the bright effects of the breather—like accents and sounds of love—through the Macrocosm <note>The "Great World," the universe</note> and the Microcosm. This string is the clear spirit which, by its nature, position, and placement, participates in both extremes and connects both extremes to one another. Similarly, it marks out the steps or keys <note>original: *claves*</note> of the human system, by which the descent of the soul from the heights into the body occurs, and conversely, its ascent to the higher realms or place...

276 TREATISE I. SECTION I. BOOK XIII.

Here we see the whole man drawn extended in his own image; in the middle of which, according to his continuous length, we have drawn a straight line representing the whole diameter of the Microcosm <note>The "Microcosm" is the human being viewed as a miniature reflection of the entire universe (the Macrocosm).</note>. Furthermore, the semi-diameter A. C. of this string measures out the tones and semitones of the monochord <note>A monochord is a single-stringed instrument used by ancient and Renaissance scientists to demonstrate the mathematical laws of music.</note>, and yields musical proportions similar to those found in the harmony of the world. Therefore, on his left side, we have explained a music very similar to that of the world; while on his right, we have quite properly depicted the symphonic aspect of the soul descending from heaven to earth, and its ascent again from the earth or body into heaven or spirit.

On the left, then, we have shown that the proportion between the intellect and life is found to be double on the monochord, which contains the spiritual **Octave** <note>original: "Diapason spirituale"</note>. Similarly, we showed that in the same proportion of the monochord, the interval extending from the sphere of the heart (or the Sun) to the earth (or the genitals) sounds the corporal **Octave** <note>original: "Diapason corporale"</note>, uniting life and sense, or the carnal nature that inhabits the lowest belly. Therefore, just as on the string of a musical monochord, if its half-part is pressed, one Octave sounds downward and another upward, so also the heart—situated in the middle of the human semi-diameter, just like the Sun in the middle of the world—regards the lower parts through one Octave harmony, namely the nature of the lowest region, and through the other, the highest heaven of the Microcosm, where the mind, intellect, and reason hold dominion.

On the right side of the Microcosm, we have also established an **Octave** <note>original: "Diapason"</note> harmony between the intellect and the imagination; specifically, a **Fourth** <note>original: "Diatessaron"</note> between the intellect and reason, and a **Fifth** <note>original: "Diapente"</note> between reason and the imagination; which, when joined together, create the spiritual and invisible Octave. Similarly, by extending downward from the sphere of the heart, we find the same proportion between the imagination and the body or center of the earth. For the space of movement from the imagination to the sense corresponds to a **Fourth** <note>original: "Diatessaron"</note>, while that between the sense and the flesh or body corresponds to a **Fifth** <note>original: "Diapente"</note>; these joined together form the corporal and, as it were, visible Octave.

The first breath of life, breathed directly by God into the face of man, administers motion to all these things; according to its movement—as the first mover <note>A reference to the *Primum Mobile*, the outermost sphere of the universe that sets all others in motion.</note> of the Microcosm—the voluntary faculties of the lower regions are carried along by involuntary movements. For thus we see that the animal action contained in the highest region is voluntary; but the others common to the lower regions, namely the vital and natural actions, are called involuntary.

We have also explained the Day and Night of the Microcosm in the aforementioned demonstration, insofar as the sources of rational, vital, and natural light always ascend and rise above the "earth" of man—or his center—while the man is living; whereas beneath his earth, nothing is found except his two supports or columns <note>The legs.</note>, sustaining and steadying the whole mass upon shoulders like those of Atlas. In the upper hemisphere of the Microcosm, therefore, the light of the first heaven—namely, the mind, illuminated by divine splendor—always shines; in the middle is the heart, filled with solar light; and in the lowest is the liver, overflowing with the heat of the fiery and airy elements.

And in this way, I have presented the whole nature of man, both internal and external—though perhaps not as elegantly as desired, yet as diligently as possible—for the one looking clearly upon it as a son of light and not of darkness. I believe I have done so quite clearly, and not without offering great and most grateful thanks to God my Creator, while scorning, neglecting, and disregarding the bitter curses of Momus <note>Momus was the Greek god of mockery and criticism; here Fludd refers to his intellectual critics.</note>, the wicked slanders of the malevolent, and the impious derision of the envious. I treat the virulent bites of such viperous tongues with the balsam of patience and the antidote of an unblemished conscience...

### CHAPTER I.

*On the Author's diligence in acquiring and refining*
*the art of memory in foreign*
*lands.*

[Decorative initial C] WHEN I, in my travels, especially wandered through the kingdom of France here and there, I finally reached the city of Nîmes <note>original: "Nemofiensem"</note>, drawn by the fame of the antiquities remaining there. There, with a certain man quite famous for his skill in the art of memory, I first began to taste the sweetness of that art. Soon thereafter, in the city of Avignon, situated on the river Rhône, I cultivated this art, having approached it with laborious effort, with no teacher at all leading the way. As I emerged more experienced in its practice, I was summoned to many places in Provence by several Princes of France, both for the sake of this art and by reason of other mathematical sciences—namely, by the Marquis of Orizontis, the Viscount of Cadineta, and the Bishop of Riez <note>original: "Rhtenfi," likely referring to the Bishop of Riez</note>, whom they declared to be a great prince of that place. 

But I at last, having refused the rest—and indeed those were great promises—arrived at Marseille. There I began to teach the mathematical arts to the Duke of Guise and his brother, the Prince of Lorraine, and to this Knight of Malta <note>original: "Mitilenæ militem," referring to a member of the Order of St. John/Malta</note>, a youth of remarkable character and graceful body; and among the other arts, I also proposed that art [of memory] to the youth. He, being certainly capable of the sciences in a wonderful way, in a very short interval of time so excelled in knowledge that he surpassed the other nobles who were present there in science in a brief space of time. Therefore, first at Nîmes, then at Avignon, then at Aix-en-Provence <note>original: "Aquasextiis"</note>, and finally at Marseille, investigating the inner secrets <note>original: "penetralia"</note> of this science to the best of my ability, I saw and learned something in it. Whatever this may be, I most gladly offer it to you (reader) for free, though it cost me no small price and labor.

CHAPTER <note>original catchword: "CAP."</note>

### CHAPTER II.

*What is memory and how many types are there? Also, the method for retaining the mental forms of both types of memory.*

**B**efore we enter the field of this art, we judge it especially necessary to know what that thing is which this art concerns, so that we may proceed methodically in this treatise of ours. *Memory, therefore, is the most faithful guardian and preserver of things received and of images—or rather, of things whose species <term>species: mental forms or representations of things perceived by the mind</term> have been perceived by the intellect. Or, it is a certain habit that recalls these species after some time has passed, the object of which is always in the past.* And since we are dealing here with memory, which is common to both humans and brute animals <note>original: "brutis," referring to non-human animals</note>, I would have the reader understand that human memory differs from the memory of brutes in this: that the latter is merely sensitive, receiving only sensible things and the phantasms <term>phantasms: internal sensory images or "mental pictures" of physical objects</term> of things, while the former is both intellectual and sensitive at the same time. These things having been carefully observed, we believe we should proceed to the types of intellectual memory in this way:

### CHAPTER IV.
### On the twofold action of the phantasy concerning the artificial memory.

**P**hantasy <term>phantasy: the mental faculty that creates and manipulates internal images</term> works in two ways toward the complete perfection of the art of memory: namely, either by **ideas**, which are properly forms separated from corporeal things—such as spirits, shadows, souls, etc., and likewise Angels, which we shall treat especially in our **"round art"** <term>round art: Fludd’s system of memory based on celestial, spiritual, and universal principles</term>. For we do not use the word "idea" here in the way Plato did, who used it to mean the Mind of God; rather, we use it for any thing not composed of the four elements—that is, for some other simple thing conceived through the imagination in the ethereal or spiritual part of the world. For example: for Angels, Demons, the effigies of stars, and the images of Gods or Goddesses to whom celestial things are attributed, and which participate more in a spiritual nature than a corporeal one; likewise for the shadows of virtues and vices conceived and fashioned in the imagination, which are also to be regarded as "demons."

But if the student’s talent is unable to imprint the figures of these kinds of ideas onto his conception, he can make his choices among **beasts, men, and inanimate things** that meet and occur to the senses, and conceive their images in the regions of the heavens in place of shadows and ideas.

Or, the phantasy works by **images of corporeal things** which, although they are perceived in a "phantastic" manner, are nonetheless not considered as incorporeal things, but are depicted from corporeal action and fashioned by the imagination alone. For example: if we imagine a **wolf killing a lamb**, or **Peter the knight swallowing a sharp-pointed sword**, or a **venomous serpent clinging to the leg** of some man well-known to you with its slippery coils, etc. For the practitioner must consider sensible things through the imagination and in a phantastic manner alone—that is, he must figure those things in his phantasy just as a skilled painter is accustomed to depict and adorn visible things with living colors.

From these points, therefore, we see that memory can only be corrected artificially either by **medicines**, or by the **operation of the phantasy**—dealing either with "ideas" (which properly belong to the round art) or with "images" of corporeal things (which are more suited to the **"square art"** <term>square art: Fludd’s memory system based on mundane, terrestrial, and physical structures like buildings</term>). Therefore, we think those people are hardly consistent with themselves who want there to be some art of memory without the operation of medicines or the phantasy, and who confidently believe so. This indeed arises either because they are entirely ignorant of natural philosophy, or they are deceived by wordy scoundrels and impostors who seduced them into that opinion, thinking there is an art of memory in the nature of things that can be learned while abandoning all ideas and images. A certain lawyer of **Aix-en-Provence** was of this same stripe, who boldly claimed that he had seen a certain man in the city of **Toulouse** who—

<summary>This page explains that memory is aided by balancing humors through medicine or by using the "phantasy" to visualize either spiritual "ideas" (the Round Art) or physical "images" (the Square Art). The author dismisses any memory system that claims to work without these mental visualizations as the work of impostors.</summary>

### CHAPTER V.
### Whether the memory is more conveniently expressed in a round or square art.

Our **Spherical Art** is without doubt much more convenient, both by reason of the capacity of the shape (which is round and consequently more useful for the work), and because every place on the sphere possesses its own natural partition in every sphere of the world. Furthermore, every sphere has its own natural site and position without any alteration of its placement. From this, the practitioner is certain that he is always contemplating his own **invariable places**. Similarly, no **Planet** is known to move or deviate outside its own orbit, but always enjoys its own operation, act, and dominion in its own proper sphere. Therefore, this spherical art of ours is able to wonderfully assist the natural memory of the **Microcosm** <note>The "Microcosm" refers to the human being, viewed as a miniature reflection of the entire "Macrocosm" or universe.</note>, and can certainly provide much more in many respects because of the relationship it has to the parts and actions of the Microcosm.

In the **square art**, however, nothing natural is found: neither place, nor partitions, nor images. And yet common squares (which are called the "common places" of this art) are more beneficial to those unskilled in **Astronomy** than the other, insofar as the shapes of a square hall, chamber, or bedroom are more easily impressed upon the conception of unlearned men than ideas considered by contemplation alone. And thus it happens that this square art is preferred by the greater part of men over the round art; although the latter is by far worthier and more in harmony with nature, while the former is more familiar to art and more subject to the senses.

### CHAPTER VI.
### On the notable error of some engaged in this art, and the refutation especially of those who use imaginary palaces.

Some involved in this art have wished to locate their square art in **palaces** newly fabricated or constructed by the invention of the imagination. We shall briefly explain how inconvenient this opinion of theirs is. For if we compare the operations of the imagination or phantasy primarily to the **science of optics**, we shall see that the matter stands quite differently. For if we arrange many mirrors in such a way that the image of an object seen in the first mirror is reflected into the second, and that image seen in the second mirror is reflected into the third, and that image of the third mirror into the fourth, and so on for the rest, we will perceive that the image in the first mirror is clearer, more transparent, and more complete than the image in the second mirror, and this second one clearer than the third, and

He also begins a critique of those who invent entirely fictional "memory palaces," using an optical analogy of mirrors to show how mental images degrade the further they are removed from reality.</summary>

So also we say, that the more a practitioner of this art penetrates into the **inner recesses of the phantasy** <term>phantasmatis penetralia: the deepest parts of the imaginative faculty where sensory data is processed</term>, the weaker the likenesses of his **imaginary icons** become. Consequently, the operative power of the imagination will be more crippled and deficient. From this it follows that the more closely and more immediately the likeness in the imagination proceeds from the **reality of sense**, the more certain, powerful, durable, and effective it is in this art.

Yet men of the **aforementioned sort** <note>original: "praedictae farinae homines"—literally "men of the aforementioned flour," an idiom meaning people of that specific type or kidney.</note> attempt to seek the foundation of their operation not from reality, but from a **chimera**, as it were, and a figment of a thing which never existed in the nature of things. ## CHAPTER VII.
### Against those who place only brute beasts, and those firmly, in the common places of both arts.

Indeed, we cannot consider as experts in this art those who are accustomed to imprint brutes—that is, irrational animals—upon the places <term>locis: the specific spots or "stations" in a memory palace</term> of a palace or a house and its chambers, even though they do so according to the order of the alphabet, for instance by assigning a donkey to the first place, an ox to the second, and so on. For these very things, insofar as they are brutes, cannot represent a rational matter or an act proper to man alone. Therefore, the irrationality of the image will perhaps be the cause for the practitioner to forget the rational subject, due to the impossibility of the action attributed to the beast. 

For example: if I wish to imprint an orator in the first place by using a donkey, we must imagine a donkey dressed in the manner of an orator with a book in his hand and a cap on his head. This will indeed seem entirely absurd to reason, by which man is governed; for a donkey possesses neither clothes, nor a book, nor hands. Because of this, we think it better and more correct to assign rational images <note>In this context, "rational images" refers to human figures capable of complex, human actions.</note> to the said places, since there is no action—whether beastly or human—which a man cannot clearly express through his own action, whether by imitating it or by performing his own roles. If, therefore, we wish to represent a donkey, we can imagine that the image of a man, fixed in that place, leaps upon the back of a donkey, or teaches the donkey the art of reading, and so forth.

## CHAPTER VIII.
### Against those who use empty places to retain imaginable species.

There are also some practitioners of this art who fall into even greater error; indeed, they seem to rise up against the laws of nature, since they follow a path even more difficult than those mentioned previously and use a worse method. For these men recede so far from the error of those described above that, by employing empty places <term>loca vacua: memory locations without a specific "agent" or "image" residing in them</term>, they imprint nothing at all upon them. Instead, they store the things to be committed to memory in these spots naked and uncovered, insisting upon that frequent axiom of the Philosophers: *It is done in vain through more which can be done through fewer.* <note>original: "Frustrà fit per plura, quod fieri potest per pauciora." This is the principle of parsimony, commonly known as Occam's Razor.</note> 

But I could also argue in this way: that the invention of the Tetrachord, Pentachord, and Hexachord <note>ancient and medieval musical scales of four, five, and six notes respectively</note> in music is pointless and useless, since the entire dimension of music is found in the Monochord <note>a single-stringed instrument used to demonstrate mathematical proportions of intervals</note>. And yet those who are skilled in music find it more easily and fully in the polychord than in the monochord. In a similar way, we do not deny that the art of memory can be achieved using empty places; nevertheless, we say this is further from the perfection and ease of the art and more difficult for the student to grasp. 

Furthermore, it is certain that there is no distinction between places unless some figure or image, distinguished by a phantastic shape <term>figura phantasticâ: a shape created within the "phantasy" or imagination</term>, is imprinted on each of them. Hence, this error of theirs will produce no small amount of confusion in this art. And therefore it will be necessary, if we wish to avoid that, to assign distinct images to each place, lest confusion and absurdity arise in this art, since by their presence each place is best distinguished from another.

## CHAPTER IX.
### *On the common place of the circular art, and on its division into specific places for the recollection of words.*

The common place <term>locus communis: a general setting or "palace" used in memory systems</term> of the circular art is the ethereal part of the world, namely the celestial orbs, counting from the eighth sphere <note>The "eighth sphere" refers to the Firmament or the sphere of the fixed stars, including the Zodiac.</note> and ending in the sphere of the Moon. We have made a twofold division of it: one indeed by reason of place and order, by which we naturally distribute it first according to the division of the Zodiac into twelve equal parts, which astrologers have called the celestial signs. 

The other division is by reason of time, in which a subdivision occurs. For, because the *primum mobile* <term>the "first moved" sphere, which in pre-Copernican astronomy was believed to drive the daily rotation of all other spheres</term> completes its rapid course in one natural day—namely from the east to the west—therefore any hour of the day corresponds to five degrees of the Zodiac, which space is half of a sign <note>Each of the 12 Zodiac signs occupies 30 degrees; Fludd is here mapping temporal units (hours) onto these spatial divisions for mnemonic purposes.</note>. Moreover, the length of a sign outlines the movement of the Sun in the quantity of one hour of the day. Having completed the Zodiac or the eighth sphere, one must begin with the heaven of Saturn, and so on through the rest of the periphery of the middle heaven, descending toward the sphere of fire <note>The "sphere of fire" was considered the highest of the four elemental layers, located just below the sphere of the Moon.</note>, as is explained in the following figure.

## CHAPTER X.
### *On the description of the eastern and western theater.*

I call a "theater" that place in which all actions—whether of words, sentences, parts of speech, or subjects—are shown, just as in a public theater where comedies and tragedies are performed. You will imagine one form of these theaters to be situated at the point of the East; it should not be considered as something real or corporeal, but as if made of an **ethereal vapor** <note>Fludd suggests the memory palace should be visualized as a shimmering, ghost-like structure in the mind rather than a solid, physical building.</note>. Let that shadow of a theater be filled with the likenesses of **acting spirits** <note>original: "spirituum agentium." These are the "memory images"—vivid figures or actors that the practitioner "places" in the theater to represent specific ideas.</note>. 

Therefore, the first theater will have a **white color**, lucid and splendid, representing the day and daytime actions. For this reason, it will be placed in the East, because the Sun, rising from the East, begins the day and promises brightness to the world. The second, however, will be imagined as imbued with a **black**, dusky, and dark color; you will imagine it placed in the West, because the Sun, being in the West, announces that night and darkness will shortly arrive. Each of these theaters will have **five doors** distinct from one another and nearly equidistant, the uses of which we will demonstrate later.

### CHAPTER XI.
#### *On the general location of the square art, and on its division into suitable places; likewise on the selection and arrangement of rooms for the work of this art.*

The general <term>locus: "place" or "location," the fundamental unit of a memory palace</term> for this art will be a chamber or room whose sides are equally square or parallel. This type of room should not be fictional or conceived by the imagination alone—unlike the method of those who used to conceive of palaces only in the mind—because confusion and obscurity would follow in the operations of the fantasy, overwhelming the power of the action. Therefore, we think it necessary that **real rooms** be chosen, and specifically those which are pleasing to the eye in their decoration, beauty, view, or some other quality, so that they may be best distinguished from one another. Furthermore, a **notable story** should be painted above the door of each room, such as (for example) Hercules killing the hydra, or Hercules throwing down Cerberus <note>Cerberus was the three-headed hound of the underworld; Hercules capturing him was his final Labor.</note>, or Medea murdering her brother <note>A reference to the myth of Medea and Jason, where she kills her brother Absyrtus to delay her father's pursuit.</note>, or Actaeon transformed into a stag, or others of this kind. All such images of stories should be depicted on the outside, above the doors of the chambers. As for the internal locations, which are called "less general," we have organized their orders, their partitions, and the subdivisions of those parts into the following classification for the sake of a better method.

->The Place is twofold, namely:<-

**External**, in which images are depicted above the door on the outside for a more complete distinction of one room from another, expressed as if by their own proper name.

**Internal**, which is subdivided into places:

**General**, which are six, namely:
*   The four square sides of the room.
*   The base or ground.
*   The roof or the "heaven" of the room.

**Non-general**, which are either:
*   **Less proper**, such as the two outer parallelograms, specifically 1 and 3.
*   **More proper**, such as the four square parts of the extreme parallels subdivided into 1, 2, 3, 4, and the parallelogram in the middle.

First, therefore, we are accustomed to begin from the **right side** at the entrance of the door, because the movement of the practitioner ought to be the same as the daily motion of the Sun, which begins its course from the right part of the heavens and runs down into the left part of the world—that is, from the East to the West. Thus, those who begin from the left side do not work well or methodically, claiming that we are accustomed to observe such a motion in writing. But truly, it is fitting for art in all its actions to always **imitate nature**.
