### CHAPTER III.
*How many types of ideas there are in this art, and which actions are to be assigned in any given place of the sphere.*

<margin>The idea or imaginary form of this art is:</margin>

Either **principal**, which acts in every principal word or part of a member of a speech or sentence: This will be the image of the Ram <note>Aries</note> in the first place of the first circle. But if the action of the predominant word is not sufficient to express the thing to be signified, then it can be assisted by the actions of the lord of that same sign, namely **Mars**; but this happens rarely.

Or **less principal**; when, for the sake of more distinguished detail, a story is impressed upon the nature of the sign in the "Oriental Theater" <note>The Eastern or rising part of the memory map.</note> of the sign. Let **Jason** then be placed in the first spot, holding the Golden Fleece in his hand; **Medea** in the second; **Paris** the shepherd in the third; **Daphne** in the fourth; and **Phoebus** <note>Apollo/The Sun</note> in the fifth, signifying that the constellation is diurnal <note>Active during the day</note> and masculine: and likewise in the other Oriental theaters.

In the **Western theaters**, however, we ought only to imagine the shadows of the forms of the first theater appearing in a dark manner; because the color of this theater, insofar as it is the beginning of night, is accustomed to appear dark to the eyes of the imagination.

***

### CHAPTER IV.
*On the principal order of ideas through the spheres of the Planets.*

Throughout the entire sphere of **Saturn**, the principal order will be as follows: The first ascending place of this sphere will be **Capricorn**, and so following according to the succession of the signs, insofar as Capricorn is the day house of Saturn. Thus Saturn in Capricorn is a most wealthy king; in **Aquarius**, a most prudent old man and leader; in **Pisces**, a fisherman; in **Aries**, angry and envious; in **Taurus**, slippery and lustful; in **Gemini**, stammering but nevertheless most learned and prudent; in **Cancer**, a merchant melancholic from loss; in **Leo**, a fortunate and noble old man; in **Virgo**, shrewd, but fleeing the society of men, like <term>Diogenes</term> <note>A reference to Diogenes the Cynic, who lived in a tub and rejected social norms.</note>; in **Libra**, a pleasant man and a good companion; in **Scorpio**, a man who is vital but squalid, poor, and of a poisonous disposition; in **Sagittarius**, rich and powerful but contentious. Let Saturn, therefore, put on garments and have actions suited and convenient to the aforesaid things, according to the nature of the place and sign in which he is found.

Next, let the sign of **Sagittarius** arise, where **Jupiter** will appear as a heavenly king with the highest honor; in **Sagittarius** [again], faint-hearted; in **Capricorn**, a most poor priest; in **Aquarius**, powerful and of great honor and riches; in **Pisces**, a most fortunate leader in war; in **Aries**, captured by love; in **Taurus**, a merchant of good faith; in **Gemini**, a friend of princes and held in value among the great; in **Cancer**, wise and amiable; in **Leo**, endowed with knowledge; in **Virgo**, a Bishop, or wealthy in the affairs of the Church; in **Libra**, a friend of some prince.

### CHAPTER V.
*Concerning the less principal images.*

Perhaps the sheer multitude of "less principal" shadows <note>The author uses "shadows" (umbrarum) to refer to the mnemonic images or ideas used to store information.</note> will be unpleasing to some. Therefore, so that this art might be more agreeable to them once these images are excluded, it should be known that those memory places can be distinguished from one another by colors in this manner:

The first place shall be **white**, like a meadow covered in snow.
The second shall be **reddish**, having the appearance of a meadow existing before a theater gate where a battle was fought, so that its surface, stained with blood, displays a red color.
The third place shall be **green**, a certain area before a gate conspicuous for its grass and flourishing trees.
The fourth shall be **blue**, and on every side like a valley before a gate, watered by springs.
The fifth and last shall be a **subterranean cave** or very dark cavern, showing a black color.

Opposite these meadows, let five columns be imagined, which must likewise be distinguished by shape and color. For the shape of the two at the ends <note>the 1st and 5th columns</note> shall be circular and round; the middle column <note>the 3rd</note> shall have a hexagonal shape; and those that are in between these <note>the 2nd and 4th</note> shall possess a square shape. They will also differ from one another in color in this way: their colors should have a relationship with the colors of the theater gates opposite them, but in an opposite or inverse ratio. That is to say, whiteness is set against blackness, and so on.

By a feat of the imagination, you can also attach rings and chains to these columns. Animals tied to these will signify **Adverbs, Conjunctions, Prepositions, and Interjections**, as will be explained in the section on sentences. The order among them will be this: a silver ring is imagined fixed to the white column with a silver chain; to the red column, a copper ring with a chain made from a branch; to the livid <note>bluish-grey or lead-colored</note> column, a leaden ring and chain; and finally, to the black column, an iron ring and chain is considered fixed. However, where the words themselves carry the primary meaning, it is necessary that they be denoted by a "principal image" or idea, and not otherwise, as will appear in the recording of sentences.

CHAPTER VI.
*On the various ways in which the principal images can be depicted in empty locations, both in the circular art and the square art.* <note>original: "arte rotunda, quàm quadrata"; Fludd refers to the two primary mnemonic systems: the "round" art based on the circular Zodiac and the "square" art based on man-made buildings.</note>

The actions by which images are represented in their locations are usually either:

**Cruel**, namely when someone sees a monstrous thing or a deed committed cruelly and against the laws of nature. Of this kind are: a Tyrant killing someone, or Lucretia taking her own life. <note>Lucretia was a legendary Roman figure whose suicide after being dishonored was a common dramatic image used to trigger a strong emotional—and thus more permanent—memory.</note>

**Obscene and shameful**: such as if anyone is engaged in an indecent matter and is shamefully affected by it.

CHAPTER I.
How many types of words there are: And on the manner of explaining significant words within places.

I call a **significant word** that which can be explained through some living action of an image or idea within a specific place <note>original: "loco". In the "Art of Memory," a "place" (locus) is a mental architectural space—like a room or theater—where a memory image is stored.</note>. But I call a **non-significant word** that which cannot be signified by itself within those places due to a lack of action.

All words are either:
{
  **Significant**,
  such as
  {
    **Verbs**, such as to kill, to dance, to sing, etc.
    **Substantives** <note>In 17th-century grammar, "substantives" refers to nouns that represent concrete objects.</note>, such as book, sword, bull, etc.
    **Adjectives**, such as brave, violent, sad, cheerful, etc.
    **Participles**, such as striking, burning, sickening, etc.
  }
  **Non-significant**
  {
    **Heard words** <note>original: "Audita". These are words that exist in the language and are recognized by the ear, but do not immediately conjure a "living action" for the memory.</note>
    {
      **Less significant**, such as
      {
        **Adverbs**, such as no, now.
        **Conjunctions**, such as and, nor, and also.
        **Prepositions**, such as through, in.
        **Interjections**, such as oh!, alas!
      }
      **More significant**, such as
      {
        **Substantive names** <note>Nouns that represent abstract concepts or specific individuals rather than general objects.</note>
        {
          **Proper**, such as Peter, John, Sara, Mary, etc.
          **Not proper**, such as labor, intellect, spirit, etc.
        }
        **Pronouns**: such as who, that, this, mine, etc.
      }
    }
    **Unheard words** <note>original: "Inaudita". These are nonsense words or foreign terms that have no meaning to the practitioner and thus provide no inherent image.</note>, such as Gorocoga, Abricalac, Arbroc, etc.
  }
}

->### CHAPTER II.<-
->*On the remembrance of significant words in the spherical art.*<-

As was said above, once the places have been distinguished and the history of Medea has been described in the first theater across five meadows, it is necessary to work according to the aforementioned rule for the expression of **significant words** <note>In this context, words that easily conjure a visual image.</note> in this manner: for example, if I wish to denote the word (*Book* <note>original: "Liber"</note>) in the first place, I will imagine Medea in the white meadow, like a subtle spirit hanging in the ether or sitting in a fiery chariot, looking into a magic book. And this kind of imagination must be noted by a real expression in its own proper place. Furthermore, let the second word be (*He was exalting* <note>original: "exaltabat"</note>); we can therefore imagine that the spirit of Medea is looking out from the top of a tower and anxiously observing whether her father is pursuing her or not. Let the third word be (*Broad* <note>original: "Latus." This serves as a mnemonic pun for "laetari," meaning to rejoice or be glad.</note>), and to explain this we will imagine that Medea’s spirit rejoices for two reasons: first, because of the beauty of the place, and second, because she finds herbs suitable for her purpose. Let the fourth word be (*Small knife* <note>original: "cultellus"</note>); let us then persuade ourselves that Medea throws her knife, with which she slaughtered her brother, into the sea. Let the fifth word be (*Light* <note>original: "Lux"</note>). To signify this, we will imagine that in the conflict of Jason with the watchful serpent and the bulls breathing out flames, an extraordinary light and a huge multitude of sparks leap forth from the cave. And in this way, one must proceed to the fifth Western theater, in whose darkness we ought to observe the essential actions of Medea like reflecting shadows.

->### CHAPTER III.<-
->*On the remembrance and placement of significant words in the square art.*<-

If the words are significant, they will be expressed either by **relation**, or **similarity**, or by **real presence**. Thus, I shall express the meaning of the word (*Lion* <note>original: "Leo"</note>) in the first gate of the first place through relation, namely by Samson clothed in a lion’s skin, or by a real action through Samson fighting with a lion. If the second word is (*Sword* <note>original: "Ensis"</note>), we will imagine through relation that Delilah, moved by a heat of anger, breaks the scabbard she found belonging to her husband; or we might imagine by a real action that, in her despair, she brings death upon herself with a sword. If the third word is (*Fly* <note>original: "musca"</note>), we will imagine, either by real presence, that one of the Philistines, seeking to avoid the violence and fervor of Samson, sits upon a fly and flies away into the air; or by relation, that he has putrid flesh corrupted on all sides by flies; or by similarity, that he flees from one place to another with wings very similar to those of a fly.

->### CHAPTER V.<-
->*On the remembrance of known proper names.*<-

When you wish to remember proper names, both known and common, it is necessary to place others of the same name—whom you know either personally or from reading histories—into the memory places, and indeed simply with such an action as they were commonly accustomed to use. For example: if I want to remember someone named **Charles** <note>original: "Caroli"</note>, I will place there a certain Charles well known to me; who, if he were a Notary, Secretary, or blacksmith, etc., shall also perform this office in that place where he happens to be placed, with the evident help of the image and his notable action. Or I might even choose someone famous in history, such as **Charlemagne** <note>original: "Carolum Magnum"</note> warring against the infidels. So if I want to remember **Clement**, I will place in my common place Pope Clement with a horn in his hand for better distinction, and so for the rest.

### CHAPTER VI.
*On the remembering of proper names that you have never heard before.*

In this rule, alphabetical sequences are most required: for a **beast** shall signify the first letter, a **man** the second, a **dead object** the third, and a **bird** the fourth. This is done through an extraordinary action of the image, which will perform some unseemly act involving the brute, the human, and the bird. For example, according to the Sibyl <note>The Sibylline Oracles were a collection of oracular utterances; Fludd often cites them as ancient authorities on the divine.</note>, the Angels who are guardians are numbered as Heromiel, Saniel, Uriel, and so on.

In the first memory location, therefore, I place a **Hydra**, which kills the principal image of that location with its poison. Upon the back of the Hydra, I will imagine **Eteocles** <note>In Greek mythology, Eteocles was a King of Thebes. Fludd uses him here simply as a representative "man" for the letter E.</note> burning and holding a **basin** <note>original: "labrum"</note> in his hand, so that its water might extinguish the fire; but a **swan** <note>original: "olor"</note>, standing near his head and seized by a great thirst, drinks up all the water. 

In this scene, nothing remains but the sound "miel" <note>This creates a phonetic code: **H**ydra, **E**teocles, **R**eservoir/Basin, **O**lor (Swan), spelling H-E-R-O. The student only has to remember the suffix "miel" to complete the name Heromiel.</note>, which is very easy to remember once "Hero" is retained. For the Hydra signifies H, Eteocles signifies E, the Basin signifies R, and the Swan signifies O. The action, moreover, will be that whoever touches the hydra falls down dead. 

In the second location, I will place an **Ape** <note>original: "Simiam"</note>, which **Adam**, leading it out of Paradise, strikes repeatedly with a pitchfork. I will then imagine the blood flowing from the ape nourishes an **Ibis** bird. The essential action of the image will be the wounding of Adam, because he very often entered his house with his Ape and his Ibis. 

In the third location, I will place a **She-Bear** <note>original: "Ursam"</note> upon whose back **Raymond Lull** <note>original: "Raimundus Lullius." Lull (c. 1232–1316) was a philosopher and pioneer of memory arts; here he represents the letter R.</note> shall be raised up with vials and glass alembics <note>Alembic: a tool used in alchemy for distillation.</note>. The furious bear, however, will break or shatter the vials, and for that reason, she will be struck by Raymond with a pestle.

But this same thing can also be done in another, easier way: for if you wish to retain in your memory a word previously unheard of, you may place in the designated locations certain other words—either proper names or other meaningful terms—that express almost all or some of the syllables of that unheard-of word you wish to remember. 

For example: if you wish to remember **Uriel**, you will place in the first location **Uriah** <note>The biblical Uriah the Hittite.</note>, who by the order of David was killed in war; and because this word expresses two syllables of your unheard or unusual name ("Uri-"), you will imagine him to have been killed by a **pitchfork** <note>original: "furca"</note>, which signifies the number **two**. You will place him in the right-hand part of your memory location to remind you that he denotes the first syllables. In the left-hand part, you will place **Elijah** <note>original: "Eliam"</note> ascending into heaven and holding a **spear** in his hand, which shall signify **one** syllable ("-el"). This can be done for the others as well. In this way, you can also operate within the **round art** <term>round art: Fludd’s memory system based on circular diagrams and the zodiac, rather than rooms and buildings.</term>

### CHAPTER VII.
*On the remembering of sentences in both the round art and the square art.*

After you have learned the perfect method for meaningful words, you will be able—if you wish to work with precision—to place all words in a fitting order in some single location, so that they are held distinct from one another. But because that would be tedious and infinite in a great multitude of sentences, we shall instead proceed by another way. 

Therefore, in this work, let the following rules be observed:
1. First, you should express the perfect sense of any part of a sentence through some true and proper **action**. For example, in this sentence: *The first division of bodies is into simple ones*, you will imagine an image that divides bodies, or makes a division into the elements, which are simple things. 
2. Second, if the starting word or initial is "non-significant" <note>An abstract word like "if," "the," or "nevertheless" that does not easily create a mental picture.</note>, or can only be signified with difficulty, then you shall express it through an image as described in the second book; in this way, it will perform an action with the word immediately following it...

...resolved, every simple motion is either straight or circular. In this case, Orpheus <note>The mythical musician; Fludd uses him as a "moving" image to represent specific concepts.</note> will be moved straight and circularly; or the Sun will be formed in the hand, signifying motion through relation. ### CHAPTER VIII.
### *On orations and poems.*

In orations and poems, there is a need for the aforementioned proposition and in precisely the same manner; but in poems, this is most easily accomplished because of the necessity of the meter.

### CHAPTER IX.
### *On subjects, and in how many ways "subject" is understood here.*

A "Subject," as it is understood in this place, is the perfect action of some intention, which is expressed either by some relation, or likeness, or at least in reality, in a single location. I call the "perfect action of an intention" that by which the sense of some history, or the saying of a wise man, or a law, or an aphorism or similar things is expressed, and is perfectly explained in a single place. But because the mode of operation is varied in all of these, we shall proceed in a certain methodical order. 

In the subjects of histories, therefore, it must be known that a history is expressed in memory locations in two ways: namely, either **generally** or **specifically**. A history is expressed **generally** when its entire sequence and sense is explained in only a single location. For example, if I wished to express the entire history of the second book of Virgil’s *Aeneid* <note>Book II of the Aeneid describes the fall of Troy.</note> generally in one place, I would imagine that the image of the location sees from afar, on the summit of a mountain, the means by which a huge wooden horse is led into the city by night, and also how thereafter, while the night is still dark, the city itself is set ablaze in a lamentable manner on every side. However, a history is expressed **specifically** when each of its parts is explained separately.

### CHAPTER X.
### *On the method of expressing arithmetical figures in the aforementioned locations.*

We made mention of this matter in our book on *Universal Arithmetic*, where we also proposed one or two chapters specifically regarding "Memorative Arithmetic." By that method, we taught the way of counting, adding, subtracting, multiplying, and dividing through the apt positioning of memorative figures in convenient locations. Therefore, we refer you from here to that treatise of ours, so that we may briefly bring an end to this second portion of the section.

->### BOOK I<-

->### On the Science of the Vital Soul joined with the Intellectual Soul, that is, on Genethlialogy <note>original: "Genethlialogia." This term is derived from the Greek word for "birth" or "origin," referring to the practice of casting nativities or birth charts to predict a person's life.</note>.<-

->### CHAPTER I<-
->#### On Astrology and its parts.<-

[Large decorative initial 'V' set in a square frame with floral patterns]
The ancients categorized four distinct parts of Astrology. They intended the first to deal with changes in the air, storms, and other matters of this kind; through this branch, they were accustomed to predict health, diseases, and the abundance or scarcity of the harvest. The second part deals with the beginnings, changes, and destructions of empires, principalities, commonwealths, or cities, as well as war and other similar alterations of that nature. The third part is divided into three branches or species: the first is occupied with the election of times <note>The practice of "Electional Astrology," or choosing the most auspicious moment to begin a task, like starting a journey or a war.</note>, concerning which we have written an entire book in our general *Treatise on Astrology*; the second deals with questions and interrogations <note>Also known as "Horary Astrology," where a chart is cast for the specific moment a question is asked.</note>; and the third, which is deservedly considered the prince of all other parts of Astrology, is called **Genethlialogy**, which is what we chiefly intend to discuss in this place. The fourth and final species is called **Elemental Magic** <note>original: "στοιχειωματική" (stoicheiomatike). This refers to the creation of animated statues or talismans, often associated with the Hermetic tradition.</note>, which consists of the making of characters, seals, and statues, the miraculous effects of which are celebrated in many kinds of histories. However, because the diabolical art often mingles itself with this branch (just as we very frequently see a good thing stained and defiled by the abuses of the wicked), we shall reject it, and briefly prepare ourselves for the investigation and explanation of Genethlialogy.

->### CHAPTER II<-
->#### What is Genethlialogy, and upon what does its judgment depend?<-

We define **Genethlialogy** as that part of Astrology which teaches what goods of the soul, what goods of the body, and what goods of fortune ought to happen to one who is born, and from where those things flow, and by what signs the future events concerning him are denoted. Therefore, the judgment of this astrological part...

...judgment or practice is divided into the inquiry of the goods of the body, the soul, or of fortune: all of which a skilled Astrologer will not hesitate to predict from a diligent observation of the celestial houses, the Planets occupying them, and the consideration of their natures and their mutual aspects and relations.

### CHAPTER III.
### *On the uncertainty of common Astrologers in finding the Lord of the Birth.*

When we must act concerning the practice or judgment of this science, after first erecting a chart <note>original: "schemate seu figura cœlesti." This refers to the drawing of a horoscope or birth chart.</note> in the manner we previously declared in our *Treatise on Astrology*, we believe one must first proceed to the knowledge of the true Lord of the Birth <note>original: "Domini genituræ." This is the planet considered to be the primary ruler or "governor" of an individual's life and character.</note>. But truly, in this labor, the great uncertainty of common Astrology occurs, insofar as there is no small diversity of opinion among Astrologers in choosing the Lord of the Birth. For Firmicus <note>Julius Firmicus Maternus, a 4th-century Roman lawyer and astrologer whose work "Matheseos libri octo" was a primary source for Renaissance astrologers.</note>, a man indeed skilled in this art, chooses for the Lord of the Birth that planet which is observed to rule the sign that the Moon enters immediately after the birth, with the exception of Leo and Cancer, which the two luminaries [the Sun and Moon] rule. For example, if at the time of birth the Moon is traveling through Taurus, since it will next migrate into Gemini, which is the house of Mercury, therefore Mercury will be the Lord of the birth.

However, some others establish that planet as the Lord of the Birth which is stronger in the hemisphere at the point of birth—that is, the one which at that time possesses more essential dignities <term>essential dignities: the strength a planet gains by being in a specific sign or degree where it has traditional influence, such as its "exaltation" or "home."</term> in the heavens. Yet others want the Lord of the birth to be the one who obtains the most and primary dignities in the five hylegial places <note>original: "quinque locis hylegialibus." The "Hyleg" is the planet or point in a chart responsible for determining the life force and longevity of the newborn.</note>: namely, in the locations of the Sun, the Moon, the Horoscope <note>In this period, the "Horoscope" refers specifically to the Ascendant, or the degree of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon at the moment of birth.</note>, the Part of Fortune, and the conjunction or opposition of the luminaries immediately preceding the birth; and so on with others. Indeed, these diverse opinions have, through the ignorance of practitioners, given birth to such great uncertainty in this most certain art that this most noble art—simple and pure in and of itself, and etched into the heavens by the finger of Almighty God—is falsely held and reputed by common men to be sophistical, spurious, and deceptive. Therefore, what our own opinion is regarding the choosing of the Lord of the Birth, we shall declare below.

### CHAPTER IV.
### *On finding the place of Fortune in the Birth.*

Almost all those practiced in Astrology are accustomed to diligently seek the finding of the place of fortune in the art of casting nativities <term>Genethlialogica: the branch of astrology dealing with the prediction of an individual's destiny based on their birth.</term>; since this place is held by them in the highest regard. Truly, I was instructed to investigate the place of fortune in this manner by my Master in this art, a man certainly most excellent in Astrological and Mathematical science, Mr. Allen of Oxford <note>Thomas Allen (1542–1632) was a famous English mathematician and scientist, often associated with occult studies and rumored to be a sorcerer by the uneducated public. He was Fludd's mentor.</note>: The place of the Sun is to be subtracted from the place of the Moon in this way: If it happens that the Sun (☉) is at 7 degrees and 18 minutes of Libra (♎), one must count all the signs from the first sign, namely from Aries (♈), and six signs will be found—namely ♈, ♉, ♊, ♋, ♌, ♍—and 7 degrees with 18 minutes of Libra (♎). These are to be subtracted from the place of the Moon. Let the Moon (☽) therefore be at 14 degrees and 9 minutes of Sagittarius (♐). Therefore, the Moon (☽) is distant from the beginning by nine signs—namely ♈, ♉, ♊, ♋, ♌, ♍, ♎, ♏, ♐—and 14 degrees with 9 minutes of Sagittarius (♐). Let them be arranged, therefore, in this way:

Moon: 9 signs, 14 degrees, 9 minutes.

**Remainder:** 3 signs, 6 degrees, 51 minutes.

Therefore, after the subtraction is made, the signs interposed between Aries <note>The first sign of the zodiac, used as the starting point for calculations.</note> and the sign of the Ascendant must be added to the remainder, along with the degrees and minutes of that same sign. And it is called the "Place of Fortune" because in that location or degree, the greatest fortune of the person born is situated. Furthermore, if the signs of the Moon are fewer than those of the Sun, then 12 signs must be added to the signs of the Moon, and then the place of the Sun is to be subtracted from the place of the Moon, as above. And if, after the addition is made, more than 12 signs are produced, the Zodiac [12 signs] should be cast away, and the remainder in degrees and minutes should be observed. For example: let the Horoscope <note>In this context, "Horoscope" refers specifically to the Ascendant, or the degree of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon at birth.</note> be Cancer at 10 degrees and 20 minutes. | 4 | ————— | 20 | ————— | 30 |
| 9 | ————— | 29 | ————— | 40 |

This being done, the signs with degrees and minutes interposed between Aries and the sign of the Ascendant must be added. But because after the addition 12 signs must be cast away, and the remainder with degrees and minutes selected, we will find that 1 sign, 12 degrees, and 0 minutes was the Place of Fortune.

| 3 | ————— | 10 | ————— | 20 |
| **1** | ————— | **10** | ————— | **0** |

That is to say, the Place of Fortune will be Taurus at 12 degrees and zero minutes.

### CHAPTER V.

->ON THE VITAL SOUL WITH INTELLECTUAL SCIENCE 75<-

...indeed, only a subtle intellect could—or certainly only with great difficulty and effort—lay bare their hidden and abstruse intention, or in any way elicit their meaning and the truth of their science from their own writings. Thus have the Alchemists written concerning their physical stone <note>The Philosopher's Stone, the legendary substance capable of turning base metals into gold and granting long life.</note>, and so have the truly natural Mages written of their magic; either hiding their secrets under an enigmatic sense, as if in nature's sanctuary, or covering the marrow of their mystery under the names of Demons and Angels, or revealing the truth of the matter to the scientifically minded through fables and fictitious narratives, so that by this path they might deceive the foolish and the fatuous (to use their own words) and cause them to go astray. Nevertheless, there exists a certain, infallible secret of this and other aforementioned sciences, sent by divine providence to men from the holy heavens along with Wisdom itself, but revealed to very few. Since we have received the Cabalistic <term>Cabalistic: Fludd refers to an oral tradition of secret, mystical knowledge handed down through generations.</term> tradition of this secret from no one as yet by living voice and open words, we shall be content to follow a simpler and easier path alongside others well-versed in this common science. We shall use this path, having abandoned all the complex and fabricated names and operations of the [other] Astrologers.

Thus, in the first place, we shall look to the Lord of the Ascendant—that is, the Planet predominating in the sign occupying the first house—whether it be weak or strong. According to its disposition, we shall judge the habit of the body, stature, complexion, health, and other such matters, as well as the character and inclinations of the soul. Next, for the wealth and resources of the person born, we shall consider in the second place the second house, and the nature of its sign and its Lord, and the Lord’s position in which he is found at the time of birth. In the third place, having considered the third house, its sign, and the Lord of the sign, we shall observe the number of brothers and sisters and their nature and disposition toward the person born; and similarly, we shall learn something of the prosperity or misfortune of the born person’s short journeys, and also concerning religion. 

The fourth house, with its sign and the sign’s Lord, will indicate things coming to the person born from secret sources, hidden treasures, his happiness or unhappiness in agriculture, and likewise the houses, buildings, and possessions coming to him from his parents' side. The fifth house, its sign, and the sign’s Lord will demonstrate the fertility or sterility of the person born, and the multitude or fewness of children; it will similarly indicate the comforts, gifts, and rewards promised to him in life. The sixth, with the aforementioned elements appropriate to it, will denote the sicknesses and diseases the person born will face in life, as well as the faithfulness or unfaithfulness of servants, and the prosperous or adverse fortune or success of the person born regarding small animals or livestock. 

The seventh, with its sign and its Lord, will declare the wife of the person born, marriage, and lawsuits and contentions. The eighth will explain the character, nature, labor, and sadness in the life of the person born, and the inheritances from the dying. The ninth will foreshadow the religion, faith, visions, and wisdom of the person born, and the success of long journeys. The tenth will open to us the dignities, offices, and favor with the Prince <note>Referring to social standing, honors, or political influence.</note> of the person born. The eleventh will indicate the hope of the person born, his confidence, and the multitude of friends, and their faithfulness or unfaithfulness. And finally, the twelfth will detect the hidden enemies, deceivers, and envious people of the person born, as well as the evil thoughts and whisperings of men; it will similarly teach of his fortune or misfortune regarding larger animals.

From which we clearly see that by this path, we can judge and pronounce upon any uncertainty in the future life of the person born in a simple and plain astrological manner, thus freeing ourselves from the infinite trifles and fabrications of the ancient astrologers. Nor, however, do we wish to entirely neglect the more powerful Lord of the whole heaven <note>Likely referring to the Sun as the primary celestial power.</note>, but by mixing his nature with the other Lords of the signs for good or ill, we shall temper our predictions. Indeed, we shall say that the predicted matter will be all the more confirmed the more strongly the rays of the Emperor <note>original: "Imperatoris" - Fludd uses this term to denote the Sun as the ruler of the planetary system.</note> are mingled with the Lord or the sign of the house in which that matter is contained according to the natural disposition of the signs. We, therefore, have been accustomed in this simple way...

### TREATISE ONE.
### SECTION II.
### PORTION IV.
### BOOK II.
#### On the Astrology of the Microcosm <note>original: *Microcosmi Genethlialogia*. "Genethlialogy" is the branch of astrology dealing with the prediction of a person's life based on their birth chart.</note>.

#### CHAPTER I.
#### On the nature of the first house of the celestial scheme in explaining the disposition of the native.

The natural property of the first house, along with its sign and the Lord of that sign, is primarily to explain a twofold disposition of the native <note>original: *nati*, referring to the subject whose birth chart is being cast.</note>: one is the proper constitution of his body, and the other is the natural inclination and aptitude of his mind in his character.

#### CHAPTER I. PART I.
#### On the habit and constitution of the native's body.

In the precise investigation of the native’s physical likeness—whether their build be thick or thin, and their stature short, medium, or tall—we are accustomed first to consider the degree of the ascending sign at the time of birth. Next, we look to the nature and disposition of the Lord of the Ascendant and the sign in which it is found. Finally, we blend the power of the stronger planet of the entire sky with the others, just as a painter, in the mixing of various colors, is accustomed to produce one that differs from the rest. Nor should the two luminaries <term>Luminaries: The Sun and the Moon, regarded in traditional astrology as the primary influences on vitality and the physical body.</term> be neglected. #### CHAPTER I. PART III.
#### Whether the native will be thin or fat.

The first half of *Sagittarius, Gemini*, and *Scorpio* disposes the native toward weakness of body, thinness or slenderness, and leanness.
*Virgo, Libra*, and *Sagittarius* attribute a good complexion, proportion, and physical habit to the body.
The first half of *Leo, Aries*, and *Taurus* promises fatness to the native, while the latter half promises leanness.

#### CHAPTER I. PART IV.
#### Concerning the qualities and impediments of the soul.

Although we can perceive the qualities of the soul quite clearly from what has been written above, nevertheless, if anyone still desires a more exact inquiry into that matter, I would wish him to follow the doctrine of *Schöner* <note>Johannes Schöner (1477–1547) was a famous German astronomer and astrologer whose works were standard texts for students of the stars during the Renaissance.</note>, who wrote copiously and excellently in his seventh chapter on the qualities of the native's soul, and also fully expressed the impediments of that soul in his eighth chapter.

### CHAPTER II.
### Concerning the Second House.

#### CHAPTER II. PART I.
#### Concerning the fortune, or substance of the native.

To make this judgment, one must look to the second house, its sign, and the Lord of that sign; nor should the Part of Fortune and its Lord be neglected <term>Part of Fortune: A specific point in an astrological chart calculated from the positions of the Sun, Moon, and Ascendant, used to determine where a person might find material success.</term>.
As for the sign itself: if it is good, it portends good; if bad, the opposite of good. Therefore, a good sign promises possessions, riches, and substance—and even more so if a star of the first or second magnitude is found on the cusp of the second house, provided it has the property and simple nature of either Jupiter or Venus. This is especially true of Jupiter, as he is the primary promiser of riches.
The Lord of the second house, when fortunately placed and receiving benevolent rays from other planets, also promises substance and treasures. We call the position of the Lord "fortunate" when the Lord of the second house is established in some angle or favorable house, in which a favorable sign is also found—either belonging to his own *Triplicity* <term>Triplicity: A group of three zodiac signs belonging to the same element (Fire, Earth, Air, or Water).</term> or in another way suited to him.
The Part of Fortune (the calculation of which we discussed above) is also highly considered among those most skilled in astrology; if its Lord is found in a good place,

If the Part is found in a good and fortunate place, it foretells that the person born will be wealthy. Similarly, if the Part itself <note>original: *pars ipsa*. This refers to the "Part of Fortune," a specific mathematical point in an astrological chart calculated from the positions of the Sun, Moon, and Ascendant to determine prosperity.</note> is discovered in a good and fortunate place, it promises much good; if in a bad place, much evil; but if in a mediocre place, their fortune will likewise be mediocre. Furthermore, even a malefic planet <note>original: *Planeta malus*. Usually Saturn or Mars, considered to bring challenges or "bad" luck.</note> in a good place usually stains and infects the area with a kind of poison and hatred toward the native, and thus it depraves the goodness of the location. If, however, the Part of Fortune falls in the degree of the Ascendant <note>The degree of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon at the moment of birth.</note>, it denotes that the native will become rich for a slight reason. But if the Lord of the Part of Fortune <term>Lord of the Part: The planet that rules the zodiac sign where the Part of Fortune is located.</term> is found in some misfortune, it predicts that the native will fall from being wealthy to being poor by some sudden accident.

Note that if Jupiter is the Lord of the place of fortune, or is found within it, or if it is the Lord of the second house and found in a good place, it promises immense riches to the person born.

### CHAPTER II. PART II.
#### On the manner of acquiring possessions or riches.

The celestial scheme must be examined for the place or sign in which the Lord of the second house <note>In astrology, the "Second House" governs personal wealth, possessions, and income.</note> is found. By mixing its own specific nature with the nature of the sign in which it is discovered—that is, by investigating the manner of both their influences—we will know how the native is to acquire his wealth. Thus, if the Lord is found in the third house, he will acquire his riches from brothers, sisters, friendship, or travels. If in the fourth house, he will receive them from his parent. If in the fifth, he will acquire them through the benefit of children, or through gifts or legacies; and so on, proceeding through the rest of the houses of the celestial figure.

Similarly, it should be known that among the planets, Mars, Venus, and Mercury are said to have the chief power over skills or bodily exercises. For Mars makes the native skilled in military service; he also makes fighters and coppersmiths, smelters, those who use cautery and surgeons, etc. Similarly, in ♈ [Aries], ♌ [Leo], and ♍ [Virgo], he will make hunters. Venus makes musicians, also courtiers, those promoted by the favor of women, painters, dealers in gems or precious clothes, pharmacists, spice merchants, etc. Mercury makes scholars, mathematicians, arithmeticians, scribes, poets, businessmen, those devoted to trade, mint-masters, money-changers, sculptors, etc. And yet these effects of the signified skills are increased or diminished according to the proportion of their configuration with Saturn, Jupiter, and the Sun, and also according to the nature of the houses and signs in which they are placed.

### CHAPTER III.
#### On the third house, namely concerning siblings.

For the number of siblings, you should see whether the fortunate planets occupy these following places: namely the angle of the Midheaven <term>Midheaven: The highest point in the chart, representing career and public life.</term>, the place of Venus in a daytime birth, and the place of the Moon in a nighttime birth. For then a multitude of them is indicated. But if unfortunate planets are found there, the opposite is shown.

But if two planets occupy bicorporeal signs <term>Bicorporeal signs: "Double-bodied" signs like Gemini, Pisces, and Sagittarius, which often indicate plurality.</term>—namely ♊ [Gemini], ♓ [Pisces], ♐ [Sagittarius]—and another possesses a single-bodied sign, they will denote that five siblings are to be born.

Note that masculine planets denote brothers, while feminine ones denote sisters. Furthermore, the Oriental planets <note>original: *Orientales*. Planets that rise before the Sun.</note> will signify the earlier-born, while the Occidental planets signify the later-born, and so on in other matters. Here I would also have it observed that the more learned and profound practitioners in common astrology take the *almuten* <term>Almuten: The planet with the most combined strength or "dignity" at a specific point in the zodiac.</term> for the significance of siblings from the cusp of the third house and its lord, etc.

### CHAPTER IV.
### *In what manner Astrologers are accustomed to gather other hidden and future matters of the person born from the observation of the remaining celestial houses.*

A similar method must also be employed regarding other questions and predictions pertaining to the life and course of the person born <note>original: *nati*. Often translated as "the native" in astrological contexts.</note>; namely, if we wish to know their nature, friendships, prosperity, poverty, and other such things. Regarding the parents of the native, and whether the father or mother loves the child more, or which of them will die first—the father or the mother—and other matters of this sort, we must consult the significator of the father, which by day is the **Sun**, and by night is **Saturn**. Likewise, we must look to the **fourth house** and its Lord. At the same time, the locations of the aforementioned points in the figure <note>The "figure" refers to the drawn astrological chart or square.</note> must be diligently inspected: one must begin from the cusp <note>The starting point or "boundary" of an astrological house.</note> of the fourth house, and proceed in the same way with the rest.

If we wish to know the father's fertility or sterility, or the future number of children, their quality, stature, and obedience, we shall first look at the **fifth house**, and consider its Lord. Nor should knowledge of the **tenth** and **eleventh houses** be rejected; and it should be noted that **Venus** is always the natural significator of children. We believe one should proceed in this way with the remaining matters. To repeat all these things here would perhaps be tedious for both us and you, and no less useless and superfluous, since all Astrologers practiced in the art of Genethlialogy have dealt with the significations of the particular houses at great length and in abundance. Among these authors, however, I would especially recommend to you the method and science of **Johannes Schöner** <note>Johannes Schöner (1477–1547) was a celebrated German polymath, globe-maker, and astrologer whose works were standard textbooks in the 16th and 17th centuries.</note>, who discussed these matters most excellently according to the common method and in a way most suited to simplicity in his volume *On Nativities*.

### CHAPTER V.

When the predominating Planet at the time of a man’s birth is in a **masculine degree**, this degree will be favorable to him in strength; a similar reasoning applies to the birth of a woman, namely, if the Lord or Lady <note>The ruling planet of the sign or house.</note> is found in a **feminine sign**.

Therefore, when the **Moon** is in any of these signs at the moment of birth, it announces some such defect in the person born.

When the signifying Planet is in **lucid** <note>bright or clear</note> **degrees**, this will be the native's strength in the significance of good things; it will also denote beauty, light, and form.

When it is in **tenebrous** <note>dark or shadowy</note> **degrees**, it signifies hardship, slowness, and a horrible, dark, and evil matter.

When the significator is in **smoky and empty signs**, it will announce a vain and horrible thing.

If it is found in **pitted signs** <note>original: *signis puteis*. These are specific degrees, sometimes called "the pits" or "abysses," where a planet was thought to lose its power or "fall into a well," losing its ability to help the native.</note>, it will denote that the beauty and appearance of the person born will be diminished and weakened.

->**CHAPTER VI.**<-
->*How one must judge a birth by the observation of an Eclipse.*<-

If the **Moon** suffers an eclipse or a defect in an angle <note>The "angles" are the four most powerful houses in a chart: the 1st (Ascendant), 10th (Midheaven), 7th (Descendant), and 4th (Imum Coeli).</note> of a person’s birth, it will bring some impediment to the native, and indeed in that limb which corresponds to the sign in which the eclipse occurs, or in the promise of the house: For example: if the eclipse occurs in the **tenth house** <note>The house of career, social standing, and authority.</note>, it will hinder the native in business with the king: But if it is in the **Oriental angle** <note>The 1st house or Ascendant, representing the self and the physical body.</note>, it will hinder the entire body of the native, and especially that limb to which the rising sign is assigned: for instance, the head, if the sign is **Aries** (♈), and so on. Furthermore, if it is in the angles of the revolution <note>The 'revolution' refers to the solar return chart—a chart cast for the person's birthday each year.</note>, that impediment will be less than in an angle of the birth: Likewise, it will not be difficult to know the hour of the announced impediment if we observe how many hours the eclipse lasted: For if it was an eclipse of the **Sun**, the hours will signify years; if indeed of the **Moon**, months. If there were [square with a cross symbol] <note>A symbol indicating fractions or minutes of an hour.</note> fractions of an hour, a day is given to each of them. 

Then one must see how great a part out of **180** was that which is between the degree of the ascendant and the degree of the eclipse (but we shall designate those 180 degrees between the degree of the east and the west). Afterwards, one must take from that total time which the eclipse signifies a part as large as the aforementioned part of 180, because that will be the time from the beginning of the eclipse until the hour in which the evil begins. 

For example: An eclipse of the **Moon** (☾) was in the first [part] of **Saturn** (♄) <note>Likely referring to a planetary term or face.</note> because it was the angle of the Midheaven, and it lasted for three hours: it will signify, therefore, that the kingdom and dignity of the native will suffer detriment for three months: but if we wish to know when this detriment will begin, one must see how great the space is between the degree of the ascendant and the degree of the eclipse, and we find that it is half of that which is between the degree of the ascendant and the degree of the descendant: Let us therefore take half of that which the eclipse signifies, namely a month and a half, and accordingly we shall say that within a month and a half after such a revolution, that impediment will happen to the native. This same thing must also be done with an eclipse of the **Sun**.

Furthermore, those more skilled in Astrology teach that the angle nearest to any eclipse must be looked upon, along with the figure of that angle at the point or time of birth or revolution; and they say that if it was an evil sign, and the eclipse was total <note>original: *universalis*.</note>, it denotes much more evil than if it were partial; moreover, the aspects of the planets, whether good or evil, increase or diminish the future evil; and that especially if they were **stationary** <note>When a planet appears to stop in the sky before changing direction; this was believed to concentrate its power.</note>. Similarly, observe diligently what kind of degree ascended at the time of the **Moon's** (☾) eclipse: For when the **Sun** comes into that sign and degree, then the effect of the future matter will appear in full. Thus also, as was said in the preceding sections, see how many hours the **Sun** remained in eclipse: For the effect of the matter or impediment considered in the eclipse will last for that many years. And likewise also, however many hours the eclipse of the **Moon** has, that many months will be signified.

->**CHAPTER VIII.**<-
->*On the direction and the place of promise from the Ascendant to the place of death or the danger thereof.*<-

When the chart <note>Original: "figura," referring to the horoscope or birth chart.</note> is erected in the usual manner, you must seek the opposition through the **direction** <term>Direction: A predictive technique where a planet or point in the chart is "moved" forward at a rate of roughly one degree per year to see when it meets another point.</term> of the **killing planet** <note>Original: "Planetae interficientis," the planet designated as the significator of death in a birth chart.</note> or the ruler of the **eighth house** <note>The eighth house is traditionally the house of death and inheritance.</note>, or a **square aspect** <note>Original: "□ aspectum." A square is a 90-degree angle, considered a "hard" or challenging aspect.</note>.

For example: if **Saturn** ♄ were at 18 degrees and 22 minutes of **Sagittarius** ♐ in the eighth house, you would seek its opposition, which is 18 degrees and 22 minutes of **Gemini** ♊. Let the **Ascendant** <note>The degree of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon at the moment of birth.</note> then be at 24 degrees and 14 minutes of Gemini ♊. 

You should then seek that degree of Gemini in the tables of **oblique ascension** <term>Oblique Ascension: The arc of the celestial equator that rises with a star or point in the zodiac for a specific latitude.</term>, and you will find that the value <note>Original: "aequatio."</note> is 51 degrees and 13 minutes. Next, I find the 18th degree of Gemini ♊, whose value will be 79 degrees and 8 minutes. And because 79 degrees and 8 minutes is the larger number, I therefore subtract 51 degrees and 13 minutes from 79 degrees and 8 minutes in this manner:

| Degrees | Minutes |
| :--- | :--- |
| 79 | 8 |
| 51 | 13 |
| [Horizontal line] | |
| 27 | 55 |

Wherefore, I judge that a dangerous illness or death will occur for the person born in the 27th year and the 55/60ths part of a whole year (which is divided into 60 parts). And from the nature of the sign and of **Saturn**, I say that the illness will be **melancholic** <note>In traditional medicine, "melancholy" was the humor associated with the Earth element and Saturn, manifesting as cold, dry diseases or depression.</note>. 

Note that according to **Ptolemy** <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century author of the *Tetrabiblos*, the foundational text for Western astrology.</note>, each individual degree signifies one year.

Also, observe diligently that for any direction to be calculated, one must always take the **Part of Misfortune** <note>Original: "pars infortunii." A calculated point in a chart (similar to the Part of Fortune) used to identify areas of hardship.</note> which possesses some malignant aspect. Therefore, the **trine and sextile** <note>The trine (120°) and sextile (60°) are considered "soft" or beneficial aspects and are excluded from calculations involving death or danger.</note> aspects are excluded.

In the natural philosophy of this period, the "vital soul" was associated with the heart and life-force, while the "animal soul" related to the brain, senses, and movement. # BOOK I.
## On Physiognomy in general.

### CHAPTER I.
#### On the etymology of Physiognomy, its definition, praise, and utility.

[Large decorative woodcut initial N]
**N**onetheless, some among the ancients wish for Physiognomy to be named from *gnome* <note>original Greek: γνώμη</note>, that is, a sign, and *physis* <note>original Greek: φύσις</note>, that is, nature: Whence Physiognomy is called, as it were, a "sign of nature," and is defined as a certain observation by which we denote the qualities of the soul from those signs which are naturally present in the body. For it is customary, as the proverb goes, for the instruments to show the craftsman, and the house to show what sort of master dwells within. And although the ignorant and the common crowd may spurn this science and are accustomed to deride it, it is nonetheless most holily guarded among the wise within the secrets of Socratic and Pythagorean Philosophy.

And truly, if this art is well considered by a discerning and sagacious man, it will bring him a great harvest of utility; for it will teach him to safely trust his property to one person, to rely on another, to enter into marriage, to entrust children to teachers, to converse with the honorable, to flee the shameful and obscene, to not rashly choose societies and friendships, and to avoid the wickedness of criminals without any loss or danger. Finally, this Science makes those who master and cultivate it both prudent and fortunate: for as soon as we behold a person, we are able through it to judge the disposition of their soul for good or evil. 

Furthermore, even **Hippocrates** <note>The famous Greek physician often called the "Father of Medicine."</note> seems to assert, as **Galen** <note>An influential Roman physician and philosopher whose work dominated Western medical science for centuries.</note> testifies, that whoever practices medicine and is ignorant of that philosophy which teaches how to make judgments about things based on their nature (which they call **Physiognomy**), the minds of such people, wandering in darkness, grow weary and old. He says that such men not only fail to act rightly, but are also frequently deceived: for he says that the mind of those who are ignorant of Physiognomy is consumed and exhausted by error. From this, therefore, the praises of Physiognomy clearly shine forth, as well as its utility both in health and in every...

...[from every] unnatural imbalance <note>original: "intemperie." In Galenic medicine, this refers to a disruption of the four bodily humors.</note>, there is a necessity and notable utility. As for the inventor of this science, I find that authors vary: however, I perceive the most common rumor to be that *Phylomon* <note>Likely referring to Philemon or Polemon of Laodicea, a 2nd-century sophist and author of a major treatise on physiognomy.</note>, the supreme Doctor and Master of Physiognomy, truly discovered his qualities and nature from the very composition of man. *However we read it, Physiognomy is a noble science, which the ancients used through the length of days in the investigation of the beauty of nature in this science; the perfection of which is attributed, among the number of the ancients, to Phylomon, as has been said. This science was also cultivated by Aristotle, Avicenna, Constantinus, Polemon, Trogus, etc.*

# CHAPTER II.
## That the Science of Physiognomy declares the disposition of the middle soul, which is subject to fatal disposition.

**J**ust as air enclosed in a bladder <note>original: "vesicæ." In early science, animal bladders were used as containers to study the properties of air and vapors.</note> is accustomed to alter the bladder itself according to its own state—so that if the air is vaporous and moist, it makes the bladder wetter, softer, and whiter; if it is ignited by heat, it makes it drier, rougher, and of a more yellow disposition; but if it is greatly inflamed, it dries it out and contracts it in a wrinkled fashion, as appears in a bladder or parchment near air inflamed by fire—so much so, that we are even accustomed to recognize the nature of the internal or contained air through the external appearance and state of the bladder or containing vessel. So also does the matter stand in finding the internal disposition of the human soul through its exterior, and in knowing the Master of the house through the observation of the house itself. 

For when the middle soul <note>original: "anima media." In the Hermetic tradition, this is the part of the soul that bridges the gap between the eternal Mind and the physical body.</note> is nurtured by a Martial genius <note>An astrological reference to the influence of the planet Mars.</note>, and draws to itself a hot disposition from it, it is observed to mostly render the body yellow in color, the hair black and curly, with a dry and thin disposition tending toward roughness. Whence from such a disposition of the body, as if from the effect to the cause, we can most easily judge its interior and indicate the nature of the soul. And therefore we shall say that such a man is by nature bold, irascible, impetuous, rapacious, and warlike, given to drunkenness and lechery. 

Yet nevertheless, the practitioner is sometimes deceived in this conjecture of his—namely, when the middle soul adheres to the Mind (*Mens*). For this science, insofar as it is an index of human nature, is powerful in those in whom the Fatal Genius (which we mentioned in the preceding part of this section) holds supreme dominion; that is, in those in whom the middle soul, by neglecting the Mind and its Archangel <note>The "Archangel" or "Daemon" was thought to be a divine guardian or higher rational guide for the soul.</note>, adheres to the animal or sensitive soul. For in these people, Fate performs its parts and renders the man prone to all the influences of the heavens, so that those things which the celestial bodies naturally and fatally threaten usually happen to human souls by necessity; for the Mind in such men either works very little, or is observed for the most part to be vacant. 

Otherwise, if the soul is obedient to the Mind and adheres firmly to it, the Artist will be deceived in his judgment; insofar as this soul, by the power of the Mind and the direction of the Archangel or sacred Spirit, will emerge from the tracks of fate and will even rule over the stars. This will indeed become known from the following account concerning Hippocrates: When his disciples had brought his likeness, painted on parchment, to a certain Philosopher named *Phylomon*—who was indeed most skilled in this art and surpassed all of his age in it—and had questioned him about the nature and disposition of the image, they are said to have received such an answer from him, after his most diligent inspection and examination of the figure, its qualities, and its parts: *Him whom you say is represented by this image, we pronounce to be a person devoted to lust...*

It begins a famous anecdote about a physiognomist misidentifying the character of Hippocrates based on his physical features.</summary>

Nevertheless, because I observed and considered that these shameful traits were to be rejected, I established my soul as a king over itself, and I withdrew it from those things, and I triumphed by restraining and curbing my lusts." From this it is clearly evident that only he should be called wise who has dominion over his own soul; that is, who has so devoted himself to the mind and to super-celestial things that he is accustomed to direct and govern celestial and natural matters—and thus even the **middle soul** <note>In this context, the "middle soul" is the vital link between the physical body and the divine intellect.</note> itself, which is fused from them—against the necessity of fate or the inclination and laws of nature.

# CHAPTER III.
## On the method of judging in this Science.

**B**efore we approach the method of judging, it must be understood exactly how many kinds of signs of judgment there are; then, once these are known, how one should approach judgment through them. It must be known first of all that the signs of judging, according to **Aristotle**, are twofold: namely, either **common** or **proper** <note>In the logic of this era, "common" signs are general traits shared by many, while "proper" signs are specific to an individual or a particular part of the body.</note>. **Common** signs are again subdivided into three parts: namely, those which are judged by **color**, **form**, and **motion**. The **proper** signs, however, are manifested chiefly in certain peculiar and specific parts of the body. These things having been considered beforehand, it must be noted diligently that you ought not to rush your knowledge, opinion, or judgment, but rather understand the testimonies of all signs as a whole. And when diverse and adverse signs are offered to you, one must always prudently lean toward the better and more probable part.

# BOOK II.
## On Physiognomic signs
### PART I.
### On common Physiognomic signs.

# CHAPTER I.
## On universal color.

**D**he experts in this science have said that a woman's womb is like a pot for cooking a dish. From this they say that whiteness combined with a leaden <term>livido: a bluish-gray or lead-like hue</term> color, and likewise a yellow color, is a sign of diminished "cooking" <note>This refers to the ancient medical theory of "coction," where the body's internal heat "cooks" or processes humors to create a healthy, well-formed person.</note>. If, therefore, a deficiency in this process occurs within the developing creature, its nature will be likewise diminished. Hence they warn us to flee every leaden-colored and yellow person, for such people are prone to vice and lust.

Whiteness mixed with redness, and a balanced dark <term>fuscus: dusky or brown</term> color in a person who possesses a sound body, an upright stature, a medium-sized head, and a rarity of words—speaking only what is necessary—and a moderate voice, indicates a good disposition.

They also hold that a pale white color indicates a lazy, phlegmatic <note>Phlegm was one of the four "humors"; a phlegmatic person was thought to be cold, moist, and slow.</note>, intemperate, effeminate, incontinent, and weak person.

A tawny color <term>fulvus: reddish-yellow or brownish-orange</term> denotes a deceitful and multifaceted, or changeable and inconstant person; yet it promises a goodness of intellect.

A saffron <term>croceus: bright yellow</term> color in healthy people signifies heat of the liver and a choleric temperament. Hence it happens that such people are untamed, irritable, lustful, and devoted to love—or "amorous"—because of the heat of the liver, according to the saying: "The liver compels one to love" <note>original: "Cogit amare jecur." In ancient and medieval medicine, the liver was considered the seat of physical passion and desire.</note>.

A muddy yellow color <term>luteus: the color of mud or clay</term> suggests a greedy and envious person.

A honey-colored complexion denotes an angry person, a glutton, a babbler, and a timid person.

A flaming color in a slightly reddish body, if it persists, suggests goodness of nature, aptitude, readiness in grasping disciplines, and nobility of mind.

A red color suggests a complete birth <note>Likely referring to a successful "coction" or a full-term, healthy development in the womb.</note>.

A moderate color between white and red signifies a balanced temperament, a perfect intellect, and a devotion to virtues.

# CHAPTER II.
## On signs taken from the movement of the body.

Common signs according to a person’s movement are taken from its variation in speed or slowness.

A slow movement signifies a soft and sluggish person who suffers easily from illness, or is easily overcome by passions. The reason for this is that slowness of movement denotes a weakness of the <term>vital spirits: the subtle substances believed to travel through the arteries to animate the body</term>.

A sharp or swift movement suggests a person who thinks much about worldly status and perfection; likewise, it indicates those who are "hot" and sharp-witted, and those who abound in these life-giving spirits. These are the ones who, in their disposition, are compared to foxes: they are shrewd, clever, cautious, and deceptive.

Broad and slow steps denote laziness, yet such a person will have prosperous success in their endeavors; just as, conversely, short steps indicate impetuous, suspicious, and troublesome people of ill will.

***

# CHAPTER III.
## On the shape and stature of the body.

Common signs taken from physical shape are manifold; some are considered in the defects or excesses of nature, others in perfect and complete bodies.

*Thus, we are warned to beware of a person who is deformed, or diminished, or enlarged beyond the balanced laws of nature, as if they were an enemy.*

*A long face signifies a merciful person, while a round face indicates a deceitful and perverse person.*

Men of prodigious height possess little or no wisdom at all; they are also impetuous, and this is further confirmed if they are lean and long-bodied with a stork-like neck <note>original: "collo ciconiano"</note>.

*Those who walk stooped do not possess much wisdom.*

A small or lowly stature suggests a proud person. From this arose the proverb: *I have rarely seen a tall man wise, or a small man humble.*

A medium stature, decently plump <note>original: "decenter obesa"</note>, denotes a clever, prudent person, ready in all things. For a creature is more balanced and temperate when a medium stature is joined with dark eyes and hair, and a roundness of the face.
